papers.abstract: Controllable 3D part generation is pivotal for digital asset creation, yet existing methods lack the flexibility to accommodate diverse user workflows requiring varying levels of control. In this paper, we introduce FlexPart, a unified image-to-3D part generation framework that supports variable-granularity geometric conditions within a single model. By seamlessly integrating heterogeneous inputs, ranging from sparse points to dense bounding boxes and masks, via gated adaptive modulation, FlexPart unlocks a powerful cross-modal synergy. We also propose an asymmetric geometric guidance mechanism that leverages strong spatial priors to align representations across granularities, improving geometric consistency and facilitating inter-task synergy. Under mask conditioning on PartVerseXL, FlexPart reduces Part CD by 16.6% relative to TripoSG + SAM3D and by 10.5% relative to OmniPart, while maintaining competitive whole-mesh quality. The code can be found at https://github.com/Gucci233/FlexPart
authors: Qiwen Gu, Xin Zhou, Xiwu Chen, Zhongyang Zhu, Zhuo Zhang, Junqiao Zhao
bullets: Addresses the need for flexible, variable-granularity control in 3D part generation.
Integrates heterogeneous geometric inputs using gated adaptive modulation.
Uses asymmetric geometric guidance to align representations across granularities and promote cross-task synergy.
On PartVerseXL with mask conditioning, reduces Part CD by 16.6% versus TripoSG + SAM3D and 10.5% versus OmniPart.
Maintains competitive whole-mesh quality.

papers.abstract: Robotic foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, which motivates cheap offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, different modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To examine this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ($S^2$), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.
authors: Yunfei Xie, Howard H. Qian, Shiyi Lan, Kaiyu Hang, Chen Wei
bullets: Addresses the high cost of evaluating robotic foundation models through closed-loop rollouts.
Extends the Platonic Representation Hypothesis to embodied models by treating motion trajectories as an additional modality.
Measures representation–motion alignment without training and correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families.
Can help screen promising vision-language model backbones before costly conversion or fine-tuning into vision-language-action models.
Provides representation-level insight into success patterns in vision-language-action and world action models, though the abstract does not establish causality.

Right: We measure S2 across 12 vision-language-action models (VLAs) and find that S2 correlates positively with SimplerEnv task success rate (Pearson 𝑟 = +0.717), providing empirical support for this PRH-inspired view of embodiment.

Figure 2 | Measuring Sensorimotor Alignment (S2) by nearest-neighbor overlap. For the query episode (left), sensory neighbors (bottom right) have similar vision-text features, and motor neighbors (top right) have similar trajectories. Each panel plots offline S2 (𝑥-axis) against downstream task success rate (𝑦-axis) for (a) fine-tuned vision-language-action models (VLAs), (b) raw vision-language models (VLMs), (c) world action models (WAMs), and (d) real-robot policies. papers.abstract: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
authors: Shengqiong Wu, Meng Luo, Bobo Li, Ziwei Liu, Shuicheng Yan, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Philip Torr, Hao Fei
bullets: Frames video as a partial, lossy, time-ordered projection of a latent temporal world.
Organizes research into reading world properties, writing videos, sharing understanding and generation, and interacting through actions and observations.
Distinguishes sequence-level temporal coherence from consistency of the underlying world state.
Highlights a shift from clip recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and decision-oriented evaluation.
Identifies open challenges in representations, models, datasets, benchmarks, and interaction-based assessment.

The families can be combined: an agent may call tools built on any of the other three.

papers.abstract: Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass@$k$ over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality and diversity are naturally balanced by the criterion itself rather than through separate ad-hoc design choices. On eight open-weight reasoning models, our method outperforms existing quality-based and diversity-based pruning strategies. The gains are particularly pronounced when the pruning procedure keeps a moderate number of partial solutions for continued generation, highlighting the value of directly balancing quality and diversity during pruning.
authors: Mahdi Salmani, Adel Javanmard, Devansh Gupta, Meisam Razaviyayn
bullets: Test-time reasoning generates many candidates, but completing all of them is computationally expensive.
Existing pruning methods favor either predicted correctness (quality) or distinct reasoning paths (diversity), leaving their trade-off implicit.
The proposed method selects partial solutions to maximize the chance that at least one continuation is correct.
This objective rewards strong candidates while penalizing redundant ones, balancing quality and diversity without separate heuristics.
Across eight open-weight reasoning models, it outperforms both quality- and diversity-based pruning, especially at moderate pool sizes.

papers.abstract: Constructing accurate and computationally tractable approximation spaces is a fundamental task in scientific computing. Partially trainable neural networks bridge fixed random features and fully adaptive representations. This paper quantifies a phase transition pattern in approximation bounds and observes analogous behavior in training errors: a rapid but smooth initial improvement followed by diminishing returns, with a sharper transition under greater initialization mismatch. Under polynomial spectral decay with exponent $\alpha>1$ and leverage compatibility, we establish a squared $L_2$ approximation rate $\mathcal{O}((\kappa_P\log(m/\delta)/m)^\alpha)$ for two-layer networks of width $m$ and trainable proportion $P$, where $\kappa_P=(P/\kappa_1^*+(1-P)/\kappa_0^*)^{-1}$. The bound holds uniformly over the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with probability at least $1-\delta$. The constants $\kappa_0^*$ and $\kappa_1^*$ quantify the fixed and trainable groups' sampling mismatches relative to the target RKHS. For spherical biased-ReLU features in dimension $d$, we verify these assumptions with $\alpha=(d+2)/(d-1)$ and $\kappa_0^*=4\sqrt{2}\tau(d+1)/d$ for initialization scale $\tau\ge1$, and $\kappa_1^*=1$ under ridge leverage sampling. For $d=5$ and $\tau=10$, a trainable proportion of approximately $4.1\%$ captures $90\%$ of the reduction in the approximation bound from $P=0$ to $P=1$. A structured three-layer example illustrates how a few trainable first-layer neurons exploit fixed downstream blocks through nonlinear composition. Numerical experiments across diverse settings, including networks with up to 15 layers, exhibit similar phase transitions in training errors.
authors: Xin He, Huan Lao, Xiliang Lu, Shijun Zhang
bullets: The paper studies the transition from fixed random features to fully adaptive two-layer networks within an RKHS approximation framework.
It derives a high-probability squared-$L_2$ approximation bound under polynomial spectral decay and leverage compatibility, parameterized by the trainable proportion and sampling mismatches.
For spherical biased-ReLU features, the theory gives explicit mismatch constants; in one example, training about 4.1% of neurons achieves 90% of the bound reduction obtained by full training.
A structured three-layer construction shows how a small number of trainable first-layer neurons can leverage fixed downstream blocks through nonlinear composition.
Experiments, including networks up to 15 layers, show similar rapid-improvement-then-diminishing-returns behavior in training errors.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes trainable-versus-frozen parameter trade-offs in partially trainable networks with phase transitions; informative for efficient model design and training.
papers.title: Phase Transition from Random Features to Fully Trainable Networks
papers.tldr: Partially training a neural network can rapidly capture most of the approximation gains of fully trainable networks, with diminishing returns as more parameters become trainable.

papers.abstract: We present OpenTac, a novel sensor and a full-stack ecosystem for tactile skins that are highly customizable, scalable, and readily deployed in downstream robot control and learning applications. Our core contribution is twofold. First, we develop a scalable resistive tactile skin with a structured deformable overlay that converts tangential loading into spatially varying pressure. Differential responses across neighboring "taxels" support decoding of local shear vectors, and the common-mode response encodes normal force. Second, we provide a highly customizable sensor design tool that is able to automatically generate fabrication files for these tactile skins from 2D outlines and developable 3D surfaces, including from abstract descriptions such as text (e.g., "design a sensor for a size 9 shoe insole"). We develop an ecosystem around the OpenTac sensor, including the CAD design tool, a sensor simulator, cross-sensor transfer, and fast/adaptive data acquisition. We demonstrate the broad applicability of the OpenTac-CAD sensor design tool by designing and fabricating more than 30 sensors across a variety of robot embodiments. We characterize the three-dimensional tactile fields produced by OpenTac with a commercial, high-precision force/torque sensor. We demonstrate the broad applicability of 3D tactile sensing across contact-rich feedback control and manipulation policy learning on four real-world robot embodiments. Additionally, adaptive acquisition enables kilohertz-rate partial readouts, exceeding full-array raster scanning on the same sensor by 19.2X at 16 sampled taxels per update for a 1024-taxel skin. We provide all hardware, software, and result videos are at opentac.github.io
authors: Ariel Slepyan, Geeta Chandra Raju Bethala, Jiafeng Gu, Anagha Rajendra Dangle, Yinzhe Zhou, Hongyuan Fu, Jade Sim, Tuhin Basu, Xinyi Yin, Md Faizal Karim, Gregory Hager, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Anand Bhattad, Krishna Murthy Jatavallabhula, Nitish V. Thakor

Automatically generates fabrication files for sensors fitted to 2D outlines and developable 3D surfaces, including text-specified designs.
Includes CAD design, simulation, cross-sensor transfer, and adaptive data acquisition tools.
Demonstrated over 30 fabricated sensors across diverse robot embodiments and 3D tactile sensing for feedback control and manipulation learning on four real-world robots.
Adaptive acquisition achieved kilohertz-rate partial readouts, reported as 19.2× faster than full-array raster scanning for the tested configuration.

papers.abstract: Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: select a routing policy on calibration data under explicit costs, then evaluate that frozen policy once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. Under the illustrative cost model (c_ok, c_triage, c_wrong) = (0, 1, 5), TF-IDF with logistic regression and a threshold of 0.60 selected on calibration reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1% relative reduction (paired ratio-bootstrap 95% CI [35.7%, 40.4%]), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%. Frozen calibration-selected policies also beat both always-route and always-defer on held-out test data in 14 of 16 settings in a post-hoc cost-parameter analysis. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket test subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic lowers expected calibration error without reliably improving discrimination: GPT-4o-mini few-shot has one confidence value before and after recalibration and correctness AUROC 0.500. We therefore report correctness AUROC and tie-aware risk-coverage area alongside ECE. At the analytically derived break-even probability 0.80, seven prompted configurations defer all tickets; Haiku few-shot routes only 19/1,000. An LLM-only agreement control and margin/entropy rejection baselines further separate calibration from discrimination. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification.

bullets: Wrong routing is modeled as five times more costly than human triage, motivating selective deferral.

Calibration-selected policies outperform always-route and always-defer in 14 of 16 post-hoc cost settings.
Fine-tuned DistilBERT reaches 0.879 accuracy on the reported subset, versus 0.477 for the strongest prompted LLM configuration.
Recalibration can improve ECE without improving correctness discrimination; at the derived break-even probability, most prompted systems defer nearly everything.

papers.title: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

papers.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL.
authors: Ali Najar, Hosein Hasani, Amir Kooshan Fattah, Yasamin Rajabi, Mahdieh Soleymani Baghshah
bullets: Addresses the challenge of inferring unseen tasks from long interaction histories without the quadratic cost of full-trajectory transformer attention.
Uses a causal neural memory for fine-grained, within-episode adaptation and episode-level summaries for long-range task inference.
Supports test-time training and adaptation to unseen tasks and task families.
Achieves over 50% success on held-out Meta-World ML10/45 environments with low training and wall-clock budgets.
Outperforms transformer baselines on long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks through more structured exploration.

papers.abstract: Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text-to-brick task. Code is available on our project page: https://avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright/

papers.abstract: Single-image 3D generation has achieved high fidelity on curated benchmarks, yet degrades sharply on real-world images with uneven illumination, blur, and occlusions. Purifying such inputs requires deciding when to intervene and preserving the visual cues needed for 3D generation, while leaving clean inputs unchanged. We introduce Gate3DGen, a selective pre-processing model that gates image inputs to existing 3D generators without retraining them. A degradation-aware router bypasses inputs classified as clean and extracts features to guide purification of the remaining inputs. Conditioned on these features, a 3D-oriented one-step purifier purifies degraded inputs with spatial losses that encourage preservation of object identity, contours, and textural cues. To provide paired supervision, we construct a synthetic data engine that renders clean views of 3D assets and synthesises composite degradations. On the synthetic benchmark, the purifier improves image fidelity and downstream 3D geometry in only 2.3s on average, reducing TRELLIS.2 mesh distance by 61.5% relative to degraded inputs. VLM evaluation and human preferences on real photographs further support identity preservation and degradation correction. More demos and code are available at https://supra-3d.github.io/gate3dgen.
authors: Xiaolin Li, Zihao Huang, Fanpeng Meng, Chen Yang, Guanjun Wu, Kai Zhang, Jiemin Fang, Qi Tian

Uses a degradation-aware router to decide whether to bypass or purify each input.
A one-step, 3D-oriented purifier preserves object identity, contours, and texture through spatial losses.
Synthetic paired data comes from rendered clean views combined with composite degradations.
On a synthetic benchmark, it reduces TRELLIS.2 mesh distance by 61.5% versus degraded inputs, with 2.3-second average processing; real-image evaluations support identity preservation.

papers.abstract: Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens, which the model retrieves during processing. However, they can require substantial memory: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, for example, allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. We therefore investigate whether this memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. We propose storing n-gram embeddings at low precision and systematically investigate different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. Using fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance, although we find that a short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of this loss. In addition, reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. These table memory savings also extend to large existing models: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55% of table memory, with perplexity increases of less than 1.2% and largely preserved downstream task performance. These findings establish low-bit precision as a practical way to reduce the memory requirements of n-gram embeddings and use the saved capacity to improve model performance.
authors: Stephen Chung, Wenyu Du
bullets: N-gram embedding tables improve language models but can consume substantial memory.
Four-bit tables reduce table memory by about 75% while retaining over 99% of the validation-loss improvement from full-precision tables in models trained from scratch.
Using fewer bits causes larger performance losses, but brief fine-tuning recovers a significant portion of them.
Reinvesting saved memory into larger tables can outperform the original full-precision tables while using less memory.
On large existing models, low-bit tables save 47–55% of table memory with perplexity increases below 1.2% and largely preserved downstream performance.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates quantization methods for n-gram embedding tables in LLMs to reduce memory footprint. This is a significant technical contribution to LLM architecture and efficiency.
papers.title: Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models
papers.tldr: Low-bit quantization can cut n-gram embedding memory substantially while preserving nearly all of its language-modeling benefits.

papers.abstract: Monocular models recover 3D geometry from a single image in one pass, but most assume a pinhole camera and produce distorted geometry on the wide-angle imagery produced by fisheye and panoramic lenses. Camera-aware models remove this assumption by predicting a per-pixel ray field. However, they represent different camera geometries using a single fixed basis to capture both the overall camera projection and its finer variations. We argue that camera geometry can be viewed as having a hierarchy of complexity for representing rays. We present OmniRay, a feed-forward model whose Ray Module is composed of three components: a monotone radial base that captures radially symmetric structure, a spherical-harmonic residual for smooth deviations from it, and a free-form residual for remaining local variation. These components are composed as successive rotations on the sphere, allowing the representation to accommodate diverse camera geometries. Given a single image, OmniRay predicts a ray direction and an up-to-scale radial distance for every pixel, from which a 3D point cloud is recovered without needing camera information at inference time. Extensive experiments across different camera configurations demonstrate that OmniRay establishes a new state-of-the-art in camera-agnostic monocular 3D reconstruction.
authors: Namitha Guruprasad, Abhay Yadav, Cheng Peng, Rama Chellappa, Anand Bhattad
bullets: Addresses distortions caused by applying pinhole-camera assumptions to fisheye and panoramic imagery.
Uses a hierarchical Ray Module with a monotone radial base, spherical-harmonic residual, and free-form residual.
Represents these components as successive rotations on the sphere to model both global camera geometry and local variation.
Predicts per-pixel ray directions and up-to-scale radial distances for 3D point-cloud recovery.
Experiments across varied camera configurations report state-of-the-art camera-agnostic monocular 3D reconstruction.

figures.caption: Figure 2: OmniRay Overview. Given a single image, a DINOv2 ViT-L/14 encoder produces global and dense features that drive two branches. The Ray Module progressively builds a camera-agnostic ray field from a monotone radial base, a spherical-harmonic residual, and a free-form residual. The Distance Module predicts a positive radial distance for each pixel. Combining the final ray d and distance ρ yields the local pointmap P = ρd, recovering 3D geometry up to scale without camera intrinsics or a camera-type label.

Figure 5: Ablation. (a) Held-out catadioptric camera: predicted ray field and point cloud for UniK3D, OmniRay trained without random-lens augmentation, and the full model, against the ground truth. (b) Panoramic image: the radial base alone covers only part of the sphere (orange) and leaves the reconstruction torn, while the spherical-harmonic and free-form residuals complete the field (blue) and close the geometry.

Figure 6: In-the-wild reconstructions. Qualitative reconstructions on photographs collected from the internet, shown in order as a panorama, a fisheye image, and a pinhole image. Although these camera families are represented during training, the images come from different camera instances with unknown intrinsics and lens parameters. OmniRay requires no camera metadata at inference.

Figure 3: Why combine the radial construction with the residual corrections? (a) The radial representation gives the same incidence angle to pixels that lie at the same radius in the base coordinates. (b) In the centered 2:1 equirectangular projection, point A is closer to the center of the image than point B, yet has a higher incidence angle. A monotone radial function cannot accommodate such ordering under fixed coordinate transformation and orientation. (c) The spherical-harmonic and free-form residuals improve upon the base direction via iterative correction on the unit sphere.

Figure 4: Qualitative reconstructions on unseen datasets. We compare OmniRay with Depth Anything 3 and UniK3D on PanoCity and CO3Dv2 across five camera configurations. Small visualizations show viewing-ray fields; larger renderings show the corresponding point clouds, with ground truth in the rightmost column. OmniRay better preserves scene structure in the panoramic and catadioptric examples without camera intrinsics or camera-type input.

Figure 8: Random-lens augmentation. Images rendered from a single panorama under cameras drawn from the sampling distribution of Sec. 4.2. A camera is a viewing direction, a monotone radial profile and an imaged sensor region, so one family spans narrow perspective crops, wideangle and fisheye views, off-center and anisotropic sensors, and annular domains. The projection varies continuously from sample to sample, so no fixed map from image position to ray direction fits more than one of them. Draws falling close to either held-out geometry are rejected and never enter training.

Figure 10: Qualitative reconstructions on seen dataset: 360Loc

papers.abstract: Video object removal and injection are reciprocal editing operations between object-present and object-absent video states, yet they differ substantially in training difficulty. Removal can be effectively bootstrapped from video inpainting and further adapted to erase object-related interaction effects. Injection, however, requires large-scale paired supervision to model object appearance, dynamics, and scene-dependent effects, while perfectly aligned real-world pairs are difficult to collect and synthetic data lacks sufficient realism and diversity. To address this challenge, we present UniVOE, a removal-driven framework for training both video object removal and injection models. We first train an effect-aware remover by transferring video inpainting priors and finetuning on object-present/object-absent pairs. The trained remover converts real object-present videos into object-absent counterparts, creating large-scale paired supervision for injection. An injection model is trained on these pairs in the reverse direction to recover objects together with their dynamics and interaction effects. Moreover, since pixel-level reconstruction alone cannot adequately capture perceptual realism, we introduce a reward-based post-training method that aligns injection results with human preferences using a proprietary reward model. Experiments against strong open-source and commercial systems demonstrate that UniVOE achieves state-of-the-art performance on both object removal and injection, particularly in challenging interaction-effect cases.
authors: Shuzhou Yang, Lanqing Guo, Lingen Li, Weiqi Li, Zhao Zhong, Liefeng Bo, Jian Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of training object injection models without large, aligned real-world video pairs.
Transfers video-inpainting priors to train an effect-aware object remover, then adapts it using object-present/object-absent pairs.
Uses the remover to convert real object-present videos into paired object-absent videos for reverse-direction injection training.
Adds reward-based post-training to improve perceptual realism and align injection outputs with human preferences.
Reports state-of-the-art performance against open-source and commercial systems, especially for challenging interaction effects.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Visual comparison on video object removal. Other methods either remain object-related effects traces (e.g., lighting of the car), or predict unnatural background contents. In contrast, our method removes object itself and recovers physically realistic scene. It outperforms both open-source and commercial models. More visual comparison can be found in supplementary.

Figure 5: Visual comparison on video object injection. Corresponding prompt is given above. Other methods either inject background-inconsistent object, or fail to inject harmonious object. Our model predicts matching target and credible dynamics.

Figure 3: Workflow of UniVOE. (a) The remover and injector share the same network, but use different instructions and VOE units. (b) For removal, VOE unit contains an input video and an inflated binary mask video to indicate object to be removed. For injection, an all-one mask is used to enable global interaction-aware injection. The reference image is optional in removal and injection. It is generated with external image editing model, providing more specific editing guidance. (c) To improve physical realism of injected results, we propose GRAR to update the pre-trained injection model toward human preferences.

Figure 7: Visual comparison of models trained by GRAR and DiffusionNFT. One can see that their outputs are visually consistent, which is consistent with the quantitative results in Tab. 5. This further demonstrates that the performance of the proposed GRAR approximates that of DiffusionNFT.

Figure 9: Ablation on the post-training stage of injector. We showcase 4 cases from input video and the edited results of “w/o RL” and “UniVOE”, respectively. Related prompts are given below. Results of “w/o RL” exhibit color mutation (top-left), subject disappear (top-right), subject distortion (bottom-left), and semantic inconsistency (bottom-right). These issues can be well addressed in common scenarios by post-training.

Figure 10: More results of video object removal and injection of UniVOE. For removal, UniVOE can fill realistic background content for the removed region. For injection, UniVOE not only inserts desired objects, but also predicts its natural interaction effects with background. Source videos can be found in supplementary materials.
Figure 2: UniVOE uses removal to scale paired video data up, drives the training of injection.
Figure 8: Reward curves of GRAR and DiffusionNFT on the smaller injectors with Wan2.1-1.3B backbone.

papers.selection_reason: Video object removal and injection is a video generation/editing task with a transferable training and reward post-training idea.
papers.title: UniVOE: A Removal-Driven Framework for Interaction-Aware Universal Video Object Editing
papers.tldr: UniVOE uses object removal to generate training pairs for realistic video object injection, enabling unified editing of object presence and absence.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models have learned rich 3D/4D priors, making them promising for scene generation and video re-rendering. However, their use in spatial tasks is limited by imprecise camera control, spatial and temporal inconsistencies, and entangled camera motion with scene dynamics. Existing approaches, such as task-specific fine-tuning and post-process warping, often introduce visual artifacts, generalize poorly, or incur high computational costs. We propose WorldForge V2 to achieve accurate camera control while preserving the generative capabilities of pretrained video models. We first develop a training-free guidance framework using warped references to iteratively refine generation along a target camera path. Optical-flow analysis identifies motion-related latent channels for selective guidance, helping separate motion control from appearance. A dual-path strategy further compares guided and unguided predictions to correct artifacts from imperfect references. Together, these components guide viewpoint changes while preserving scene appearance and object motion. To reduce refinement costs, v-cache approximates the correction using the preceding denoising prediction, avoiding an additional model evaluation. We further extend motion localization from latent channels to network blocks and introduce Trajectory LoRA, which concentrates adaptation on blocks most responsive to trajectory guidance. A two-stage training strategy teaches these adapters to denoise the states encountered during guided generation, using limited supervision effectively. This enables reliable camera control with very little training data, with a single training scene already supporting generalization to unseen scenes. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations across multiple datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and trajectory accuracy in camera-controlled video generation.
authors: Chenxi Song, Yanming Yang, Tong Zhao, Ruibo Li, Joey Tianyi Zhou, Chi Zhang
bullets: Addresses imprecise camera control, temporal/spatial inconsistencies, and entanglement between camera motion and scene dynamics.
Uses warped-reference guidance, optical-flow-based motion localization, and dual-path prediction to refine generation along target camera paths.
Introduces v-cache to reduce refinement cost and Trajectory LoRA to adapt only trajectory-responsive network blocks.
A two-stage training strategy enables reliable control with limited supervision; one training scene can generalize to unseen scenes.
Experiments across multiple datasets report state-of-the-art camera trajectory accuracy and generation quality.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of WorldForge V2. Given a single image or video frame and a target camera trajectory, the scene geometry is reconstructed and rendered into trajectory-aligned warped frames. WorldForge V2 first performs training-free trajectory guidance in the predicted clean latent space using IRR, FLF, and DSG. Building on this framework, we further introduce an efficient route that directly fuses trajectory information in the noisy latent space with V-Cache, together with a trajectory-sensitive lightweight LoRA scheme for camera trajectory control using only limited training data. The resulting video follows the specified camera path while preserving the generative capability of the pretrained video diffusion model.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of camera-controlled scene generation. Our LongCat and H3 models recover coherent object shapes and material detail from incomplete warped references, including thin structures and partially revealed objects. Compared with the baselines, they produce fewer rendering remnants and more continuous geometry, preserving scene appearance as the camera reveals new content.

Fig. 3. Qualitative comparison for 3D novel-view synthesis and 4D trajectory-controlled re-rendering. For single-image 3D generation (left), our method produces more coherent geometry and plausible newly revealed content. For dynamic re-rendering (right), it preserves human appearance and object motion while reducing floating structures and flattened faces. The training-free guidance yields more realistic results in both static and dynamic scenes.

Fig. 9. Qualitative comparison of Trajectory LoRA training strategies. For LongCat (a) and H3 (b), two examples per backbone place the input and warped reference beside No LoRA, Standard FM, and the full method. The full strategy reduces fragmented geometry and residual rendering artifacts, producing more continuous surfaces and finer scene detail than No LoRA and Standard FM. Red boxes and enlarged crops compare corresponding regions.

Fig. 6. Qualitative transfer of Trajectory LoRA across camera-control methods. Without additional fine-tuning, the same trained LongCat adapter improves surface continuity and object detail in WAH [18] and GWF [16], demonstrating transferable trajectory control.

Fig. 4. Noise-state consistency under different reference-insertion strategies. Direct Insertion leaves gaps in the inferred-noise mean and log-variance between visible and model-generated regions, accompanied by noisy patches and broken structure. IRR reduces these gaps, and V-Cache approximates its correction while retaining continuous surfaces and clear geometric detail.

BOTH ADAPTED BACKBONES IMPROVE RECONSTRUCTION ACROSS THESE METRICS, PRESERVING OBSERVED CONTENT AND COMPLETING NEW REGIONS MORE FAITHFULLY. H3 ALSO ACHIEVES THE LOWEST LOCAL CAMERA ERRORS. BOLD AND UNDERLINING MARK THE BEST AND SECOND-BEST RESULTS.

STANDARD FM TRAINS ON INDEPENDENTLY NOISED TARGETS; ONLY WARM-UP AND W/O WARM-UP ISOLATE ADAPTATION TO RECORDED STATES AND TRAINING ACROSS ADDITIONAL NOISE LEVELS. FULL COMBINES BOTH STAGES AND IMPROVES RECONSTRUCTION OVER STANDARD FM ON BOTH BACKBONES, WITH THE BEST CAMERA ACCURACY ON H3. REMOVING LORA GIVES THE POOREST RECONSTRUCTION.

papers.selection_reason: Camera-controlled video diffusion with trajectory guidance and efficient refinement.
papers.title: WorldForge V2: Eliciting Camera-Trajectory Alignment in Video Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: WorldForge V2 improves camera-trajectory control in video diffusion models while preserving scene appearance and object motion, using training-free guidance plus targeted lightweight adaptation.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits step-by-step rationales that appear to explain model predictions, but there is no guarantee these steps causally drive the final answer. In standard autoregressive generation, dense attention allows each reasoning step to attend to the full context, enabling the model to derive answers through direct lookup while generating plausible-sounding but post-hoc justifications. We introduce CausalCoT, an inference framework that enforces causal transparency by decomposing problems into a directed acyclic graph of atomic sub-questions, evaluating each node in an isolated context containing only its direct causal parents. This Markovian structure removes attention pathways to non-parent content, making downstream predictions sensitive to local reasoning rather than global context leakage. Across a diverse suite of reasoning benchmarks, CausalCoT preserves competitive predictive performance while improving explanation faithfulness, increasing causal sensitivity of intermediate reasoning steps by an average of 12 and up to 21 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The structured dependency graph additionally enables test-time interventions in which local corrections propagate predictably through downstream reasoning.
authors: Gabriele Dominici, Teague McMillan, Fazl Barez, Marc Langheinrich, Martin Gjoreski
bullets: Standard chain-of-thought can produce plausible rationales that do not causally determine the answer because attention can leak across the full context.
CausalCoT decomposes problems into atomic sub-questions organized as a directed acyclic graph.
Each node is evaluated using only its direct causal parents, blocking access to unrelated reasoning content.
Across diverse reasoning benchmarks, it improves intermediate-step causal sensitivity by an average of 12 percentage points and up to 21 points over the strongest baseline.
Its dependency graph supports test-time interventions, allowing local corrections to propagate predictably downstream.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CoT vs. CausalCoT. (Left) In standard CoT, the model generates a continuous, autoregressive stream of reasoning. (Right) Our proposed CausalCoT framework structurally isolates reasoning into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Each sub-question is evaluated in a restricted context containing only its explicitly routed parental dependencies. This enforces a procedural Markovian property, making the final prediction depend on explicitly routed intermediate outputs rather than unrestricted access to the full reasoning trace as done in CoT.(Completions shortened for illustration).

papers.abstract: Feed-forward models accurately estimate camera motion and 3D geometry from short video windows. However, computational and memory costs prevent direct inference on sequences containing thousands of frames. Long videos must therefore be processed as overlapping chunks. This division produces independent local reconstructions with inconsistent coordinate frames and duplicate estimates of shared cameras. Achieving global consistency requires propagating constraints from adjacent overlaps and distant revisits across the sequence. This requirement naturally motivates pose graph optimization. However, the choice of graph level creates a trade-off. Chunk-level graphs efficiently resolve scale drift and close large loops. Yet, their rigid transformations cannot correct internal errors or conflicting frame predictions. Conversely, frame-level optimization offers local flexibility, but scaling it globally is computationally expensive and can break metric scale. HiP3R resolves this trade-off using a hierarchical pose graph. HiP3R first optimizes a robust chunk-level $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ graph to establish the global layout and scale. It then holds this layout fixed and estimates one shared $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ camera per frame, turning overlapping window predictions into a single trajectory. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of HiP3R in improving camera trajectories and 3D reconstruction. Our method applies to both chunk-based and streaming backends without additional training or fine-tuning. The codes are available at https://kkakkkka.github.io/HiP3R.
authors: Zunnan Xu, Shangchen Zhou, Yihang Luo, Chen Change Loy
bullets: Long sequences processed in overlapping chunks yield inconsistent coordinate frames and duplicate camera estimates.
A robust chunk-level Sim(3) graph establishes global layout, scale, and loop consistency.
A subsequent frame-level SE(3) optimization produces one shared camera trajectory while preserving the global layout.
Experiments on multiple benchmarks improve camera trajectories and 3D reconstruction.
The method works with chunk-based and streaming backends without additional training or fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches, causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss, a property we denote as KV-shareability. However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence's KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model's quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning's unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice!, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.
authors: Hayden Prairie, Jacob M. Ryan, Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick, Daniel Y. Fu
bullets: Looped architectures otherwise require separate KV-caches for each recurrence, causing memory usage to grow linearly with depth.
The method combines stochastic-depth pretraining with post-training that broadcasts the final recurrence’s KV-cache to earlier recurrences.
BeNice! achieves KV-shareability while matching standard fine-tuning’s unshared validation perplexity.
KV-sharing composes with sequence mixers and low-precision KV-cache quantization.
In simulated low-memory, long-context inference, it improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, throughput by up to 23.6%, and p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.

papers.abstract: Instrumental convergence is often invoked as a general reason to expect capable agents to acquire or express power-seeking subgoals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, deception, or resistance to oversight which poses an important threat to the society. For LLMs, reinforcement learning is the first stage of post-training that directly optimizes behavior against an objective; therefore, it is the stage where convergent instrumental behavior, on IC grounds, likely to appear. Does reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) make a model more likely to express instrumental-convergence behavior, or does this depend on the training regime, evaluation frame, and stage of post-training? We study this question as a checkpoint-conditioned behavioral trajectory rather than as a single before/after safety score. Using InstrumentalEval, we evaluate OLMo-3-7B-Think across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model. The trajectory is nonmonotonic: instrumental rate rises from 25.0% at SFT to 46.1% near RLVR step 200, then falls to 11.8% at the final checkpoint. Paired item-level tests and step-wise regression support the final SFT-to-RLVR reduction. Prompt framing does not explain this pattern: a harmful-prompt indicator combined with other framing effects explains only 15% of within-checkpoint score variance on average, and Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP) removes a detectable framing direction without changing the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap. Together with preliminary 32B endpoint results (35.53% SFT to 22.37% RLVR final), these findings indicate that RLVR does not monotonically increase instrumental behavior in this setting: the rate rises early, then falls below the SFT baseline. The result is specific to this model family and benchmark, and judge agreement is moderate, so absolute rates should be read cautiously.
authors: Bar{\i}\c{s} Alparslan, Sandy Tanwisuth, Caleb Petterson
bullets: Instrumental behavior is evaluated across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model.

Prompt framing explains little of the within-checkpoint variation, and INLP does not change the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap.

papers.abstract: This paper studies category-level RGB-D object pose estimation, which recovers an object's 3D rotation and translation without instance-specific CAD models or reference views. This task is highly ambiguous due to intra-class variations, symmetries, and partial observations. Current solutions struggle to balance reliability and efficiency: methods based on intermediate structures are prone to error propagation, while diffusion models suffer from high inference latency and complex post-hoc candidate extraction. To address this, we present F2G-Pose, a real-time direct, single-pass framework that predicts category-level pose, metric size, and camera-frame completed shape from a single RGB-D observation in one feed-forward pass. F2G-Pose lifts dense visual foundation features to partial point clouds, encodes local geometry with DGCNN tokenization, and integrates object-level structure with a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer. Joint size prediction and camera-frame shape completion encourage metric consistency through dense geometric supervision. With its task-specific network trained only on pose-annotated synthetic SOPE data and its frozen RADIO backbone externally pretrained, F2G-Pose achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on SOPE and ROPE while running at 28 FPS for pose-only inference, and further demonstrates strong camera-frame geometry on HouseCat6D and real-object transfer on HANDAL. Analyses of latency, robustness, shape completion, and GenPose++ candidate behavior further demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of F2G-Pose, with real-world manipulation experiments demonstrating deployment potential under segmented RGB-D inputs. The project page, code, and pretrained models are made available at https://jrryzh.github.io/F2G-Pose/.
authors: Jinyu Zhang, Haitao Lin, Jiashu Hou, Xiangyang Xue, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Addresses ambiguity from intra-class variation, symmetries, and partial observations without instance CAD models or reference views.
Lifts frozen visual foundation features onto partial point clouds, models local geometry with DGCNN, and captures object structure using a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer.
Joint size prediction and camera-frame shape completion provide dense geometric supervision and metric consistency.
Reports state-of-the-art accuracy on SOPE and ROPE, with pose-only inference at 28 FPS; additional evaluations cover geometry, robustness, and real-object transfer.
Scope includes segmented RGB-D inputs and task-specific training on pose-annotated synthetic SOPE data.

papers.abstract: Tasks such as quadrotor dynamic-gate racing require agents to anticipate external motion while maintaining precise high-frequency control. World-model-based reinforcement learning provides a natural solution by learning latent dynamics for future imagination, yet it often entangles environmental evolution and the robot's own dynamics in a single learned rollout, where model bias can affect policy optimization efficiency. We propose DiffDreamer, a differentiable reinforcement learning framework that tightly couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for actor optimization. In one optimization step, the learned world model propagates latent states that capture external dynamics and history-dependent features, while the differentiable simulator propagates the robot's explicit physical state. We further decompose the actor objective into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. Experiments on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing show that DiffDreamer improves training convergence over the model-free, model-based, and differentiable-RL baselines, and final performance over these baselines and classical planning and control methods. Additional experiments assess reward decomposition and the odometry-conditioned relative-state representation through ablations. We also provide proof-of-concept real-world flight experiments for validation.
authors: Fanxing Li, Yuxiang Huang, Shengyang Wang, Fangyu Sun, Shuyu Wu, Tianbao Zhang, Dexin Zuo, Yan Yufei, Danping Zou, Wenxian Yu
bullets: Targets aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing, where agents must anticipate moving obstacles while controlling quadrotors at high frequency.
Uses a world model for external dynamics and history-dependent latent features, while a differentiable simulator handles the robot’s explicit physical state.
Splits actor optimization between critic-based non-differentiable task rewards and simulator-based differentiable motion rewards.
Experiments report faster training convergence and better final performance than multiple learning, planning, and control baselines.
Ablations and proof-of-concept real-world flights evaluate reward decomposition and odometry-conditioned relative-state representations.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform diverse manipulation tasks directly from visual observations and natural language instructions, but they remain prone to mistakes and unpredictable failures. Deploying these policies without continuous human supervision will require robust runtime monitors that detect when the policy has gone off-course. Existing monitors use external foundation models, such as vision-language models (VLMs) to supervise the policy, introducing significant complexity and computational cost for monitoring at runtime. In this work, we investigate an alternate approach: \textit{can a VLA's own internal activations provide the information needed to monitor its execution?} Our method trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate progress, then flags executions that deviate from expected progress. In experiments with the open-source VLA $\pi_{0.5}$ and across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, this approach is competitive with or outperforms VLM-based monitors in task failure detection, as well as methods which require failure data for training. These findings suggest that simple probes of VLA internals can be used to develop reliable runtime monitors, opening a path toward building policies that can act reliably and monitor their execution without external foundation models.
authors: Atiksh Bhardwaj, Edward W. Duan, Junwon Seo, Prithwish Dan, Wei-Chiu Ma, Andrea Bajscy, Preston Culbertson

Competitive with or better than VLM-based monitors and methods trained with failure data for task-failure detection.
Scope: focuses on monitoring execution progress using internal activations rather than preventing failures directly.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Progress Probes (P 2) decode task progress directly from the VLA’s internal activations. Using only successful demonstrations, we assign each timestep a normalized progress ζt and fit a linear probe to predict it from zit, the activation at layer i. At runtime, successful executions follow the expected progression through the task, whereas failed executions cause the decoded progress to lag or deviate from this nominal trajectory. Thus, the policy’s own representations enable us to construct a lightweight runtime monitor without failure data or an external foundation model.

Fig. 5: Hardware: Qualitative. Red curves show failed trajectories and P 2 predictions, while green curves show predictions on successful trajectories for the Knife Put task. papers.abstract: Humanoid mobility over complex terrain requires accurate foot placement and coordinated whole-body motion capable of robust adaptation. Reinforcement learning (RL) policies trained without motion references generalize well across terrains, yet eliciting effective whole-body coordination through reward design and exploration alone remains challenging. In contrast, reference-based methods yield natural motions but struggle to adapt beyond the predefined trajectories in their training data. We introduce a learning framework that bridges these two approaches by using motion data strictly as a training prior. An explicit, self-supervised, attention-based contact planner predicts future body-environment contacts, while a contact-conditioned tracker translates these plans into coordinated whole-body motion. Together, they establish contact as an interface between sensory observations and control actions. This abstraction allows the policy to internalize the contact-aware structure of locomotion rather than directly replicating kinematics. Consequently, a single policy can exploit data-driven motion priors for natural whole-body coordination while retaining the flexibility to discover environment-dependent behaviors through reinforcement learning. Building on the learned contact planner and tracker, a subsequent fine-tuning stage bootstraps their acquired capabilities to explore environment variations beyond those covered by the original motion data. Operating entirely from onboard observations without any reference inputs at deployment, this framework enables versatile humanoid mobility in challenging environments.
authors: Junzhe He, Kehan Wen, Chong Zhang, Clemens Schwarke, Zewei Zhang, Kaixian Qu, Siyuan Hu, Matthias M\"uller, Vladlen Koltun, Marco Hutter
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating whole-body motion while adapting to complex, unseen terrain.
Uses an explicit self-supervised attention-based planner to predict future body–environment contacts.
A contact-conditioned tracker converts predicted contacts into coordinated whole-body motion.
Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning extends capabilities beyond behaviors represented in the original motion data.
Operates solely from onboard observations at deployment and supports versatile mobility in challenging environments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview, part I. (A) Inference-time pipeline. (B) Stage 1: whole-body controller pretraining. Reference trajectories are sampled from the dataset. Training follows a backward curriculum: the robot is initialized at progressively earlier states along the reference trajectory, advancing to an earlier state only after the current one has been successfully learned. RP, RR, Rv, Rω , RC, Rj,p, and Rj,v denote the position, rotation, linear velocity, angular velocity, contact, joint position, and joint velocity tracking reward, respectively. (C) Stage 2: attention-based contact planner. The planner predicts contact plans by attending to map observations, conditioned on robot proprioception and the goal command. It is trained in a supervised manner using ground-truth contact labels from a motion buffer containing rollout trajectories generated by the wholebody controller. The tracker is co-trained using the predicted contacts from the planner.

Fig. 8. Overview of the LiDAR-based neural mapping pipeline for height map observations. (A) At each frame, LiDAR points are projected into x-y grid cells and the highest point per cell is retained, producing a 2D local grid map. A neural network then predicts local elevations with associated uncertainty, and the predictions are fused into the global map using odometry. (B) The network uses CNNs to predict per-grid logits over three fill modes: the exact measured value, the neighborhood average, or leaving the grid empty. The mode with the highest logit determines the grid’s elevation prediction, while the disagreement among modes and logits yields the uncertainty estimate. (C) The network is trained on synthetic data generated from diverse scene meshes.

Fig. 7. Simulation-based evaluations. (A) Stage-1 trackers using contacts alone or contacts plus reference kinematics. (B) Attention and MLP systems under three configurations: Stage 2, a frozen Stage-2 planner paired with a Stage-3 tracker, and the fully fine-tuned Stage-3 system. Bars show mean success, with terrain categories weighted equally. (C) Attention-based systems before and after RL fine-tuning. (D) Attention versus MLP after fine-tuning. In C and D, the upper plots show success rates and the lower plots show contact placement errors; foot and whole denote foot-only and whole-body support. (E) Comparison with MGMT [46] across terrain categories, individual sparse terrains, and eight composite courses. Each radar axis uses 1,000 episodes per method. The images compare predictions from the same robot state: red markers indicate our contact targets, while MGMT’s predicted foot and hand positions progress from green (earlier) to red (later). Whiskers and shaded bands show 95% confidence intervals.

Fig. 3. Overview, part II. Stage 3: RL fine-tuning. Training combines reference tracking on motions sampled from the demonstration dataset (left) with goal-reaching rollouts on procedurally generated terrains outside the demonstration distribution (right). In the goal-reaching environment, the contact planner predicts contact plans from map scans, robot proprioception, and the goal command; the whole-body controller executes these plans and is fine-tuned with RL using task (Rt) and contact-tracking (RC) rewards. Successful rollouts are stored in the finetuning buffer and subsequently used as additional supervision for the contact planner, forming a bootstrapping loop in which planner-generated contacts are executed, validated through successful interaction, and recycled to improve the planner. Reference trajectories are sampled proportionally from the original dataset during fine-tuning to retain the previously learned tracking behaviors.

Fig. 6. Failure recovery. Our generalist controller enabled failure recovery behaviors including but not limited to: (A) re-attempting to stand up if failed due to uneven ground, (B) and (C) standing up after falling down, and (D) recovering from failures (e.g., knee stuck, slipped down from a rung, etc)

Fig. 4. Compositional whole-body motion control. (a) Walking - ladder climbing - jumping down. (b) Walking - stairs climbing - jumping down. (c) Stairs climbing up - stepping stones - stairs climbing down. (d) Stairs climbing up - stairs climbing down - box climbing up - jumping down. (e) Walking - vaulting - box climbing up. (f) Stairs climbing up - beam - jumping down. All motions deployed with a single generalist policy.

Fig. 5. Simulation results. The red dots indicate contact plans; the sphere and arrow indicate goal position and orientation. (A) The robot selects different interaction strategies on the same type of terrain depending on the desired goal position and orientation. (B) The fine-tuned policy generalizes to composite terrains and unseen terrains.

Fig. 1. Agile and robust humanoid mobility in diverse environments. Our holistic controller enables a humanoid robot (the Unitree G1) to dynamically traverse diverse and challenging environments, including (a) ladder climbing, (b,j) stage climbing, (c) crawling, (d) vaulting over thin walls, (e) stair climbing, (f) standing up from the ground, (g) jumping down, (h) walking over stepping stones, and (i) sitting down, using a single generalist policy.

papers.abstract: Purpose: To describe an evidence-aware retrieval evaluation protocol for a clinical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system over breast lesion management literature, addressing the dependence of retrieval scores on annotation coverage. Methods: An 18-document corpus and an 18-query development benchmark, with one Yes/No or WH-question per document, were used. Retrieval combined dense embeddings, BM25, and cross-encoder reranking. Chunk sizes of 128 to 1024 tokens, overlaps of 0 to 20%, and four retriever configurations were evaluated. Relevance was defined by evidence spans mapped to all containing chunks, treating overlapping chunks with equivalent evidence as relevant. Retrieval was evaluated using R-Precision, Recall@K, MRR, and nDCG@K. Separately, generation was assessed on a 512-token index at K=1 to 5 using DeepEval claim-level metrics, with deepseek-v4-pro as the LLM judge, and BLEU/ROUGE metrics. Results: The selected hybrid retriever, using 384-token chunks and 20% overlap, retrieved accepted evidence in the top three results for 17 of 18 queries. Recall@3, R-Precision, MRR@3, and nDCG@3 each reached 0.94. Ground-truth curation increased evidence spans from 25 to 37 and accepted chunk targets from 36 to 51 without changing retrieval rankings. Conclusion: Cross-encoder reranking achieved the highest retrieval scores. Expanded relevance annotations increased recognized evidence without changing rankings, highlighting annotation sensitivity. The small development set and retrieval-informed curation require independent validation, including radiologist assessment of evidence sufficiency.

The small benchmark and retrieval-informed curation require independent validation, including radiologist review of evidence sufficiency.

papers.abstract: Accuracy on medical examinations is common evidence offered for the clinical use of language models, yet a health system that intends to run an open model on its own hardware needs to know considerably more: whether the model recognizes when it is likely to be wrong, whether medical fine-tuning improves this ability, whether its correct answers rest on sound clinical reasoning, or whether it actually uses the images it is given. We examine these questions for four open models of 8 to 27 billion parameters on the Spanish MIR residency examination, scoring 1,552 questions from eight editions under the exam's own rules. Answering every question, the three larger models would rank among roughly the first 600 to 3,000 candidates, with 41 to 43 specialties still open to them. Abstention, however, never pays, because even their least confident answers are right more often than the 25% break-even. Medical fine-tuning reduced overconfidence at the cost of accuracy, without improving how well confidence separates right from wrong answers. Moreover, 13-38% of correct answers rejected a distractor for a clinically unsound reason that confidence did not reflect, and removing or swapping the provided contextual images left accuracy unchanged.
authors: Miguel Fernandez-de-Retana, Unai Zulaika, Ruben Sanchez-Corcuera, Aritz Bilbao-Jayo, Aitor Almeida

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, but their efficiency depends on which predictions are committed. Learned unmasking policies improve the speed--accuracy trade-off, yet differ in supervision, inputs, and capacity, obscuring which choices matter. We view supervised policies as distilling a decoding procedure through a teacher and examine independently what the teacher labels as committable, on which states the policy imitates it, what the policy observes, and how much the number of function evaluations (NFE) must decrease to offset policy overhead. We find that labeling predictions matching the final output is overly permissive at low NFE, and hidden states are weak alone but can complement confidence. About a 10% NFE reduction suffices to offset policy overhead for policies up to 7.5M parameters across tested settings. We therefore train a policy on trajectory-contraction targets, which accept only commitments staying on a reference trajectory, using confidence and hidden states. On LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the resulting 856K-parameter policy achieves the best accuracy--NFE frontier and highest throughput on GSM8K, is competitive at moderate targets on MATH-500 and HumanEval, and largely transfers to Dream-7B-Instruct.
authors: Jinya Sakurai, Xun Xu, Jaehong Yoon
bullets: Final-output matching labels are too permissive when the number of function evaluations is low.
Hidden states are weak alone but improve policies when combined with confidence signals.
A roughly 10% NFE reduction offsets the overhead of policies up to 7.5M parameters in tested settings.
Trajectory-contraction targets restrict commitments to those that remain on a reference decoding trajectory.
An 856K-parameter policy achieves the best accuracy–NFE frontier and highest throughput on GSM8K, with competitive results on MATH-500 and HumanEval and transfer to Dream-7B-Instruct.

papers.abstract: Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions. However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored. We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame-level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions. Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine-grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties. To enable status signal-guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction. Extensive real-world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.
authors: Yufeng Liu, Bohao Fan, Juntu Zhao, Xinyi Wang, Hang Yu, Wenzhuan Luo, Yingzhi Wang, Qinghai Li, Yingdong Hu, Junliang Guo, Richard Wang, Dequan Wang, Yang Gao, Cheng Ma
bullets: Addresses the need for reliable stopping after success and recovery or replanning after failure without fine-grained progress labels, external monitors, or complex architectures.

Real-world manipulation experiments show accurate status prediction and consistent policy-performance improvements.

papers.abstract: Large language models have shown outstanding performance on text-first tasks such as coding, math, and writing. Recent efforts are shifting models' training to include scientific problems that often live in highly specialized domains beyond text, such as protein structure and biological images. However, in these scenarios, their general-purpose accuracy compared with specialized algorithms remains in question. One such domain is cell tracking, which requires spatiotemporal awareness of cell dynamics. To evaluate this, we created a new benchmark, CellTrack-Bench, which assesses Vision-Language Models' (VLMs) cell-tracking-related performance against specialized trackers. The full benchmark draws from 15 standard cell-tracking datasets across four imaging modalities and comprises 1,537 problems corresponding to 9,041 cell-linking decisions. We selected a hard subset requiring greater reasoning effort by identifying failures shared across distinct algorithmic trackers. With this proposed dataset, we: (i) evaluated different environment harnesses for VLMs; (ii) benchmarked 9 frontier closed-source models and 13 open-weight models; and (iii) provided a detailed analysis of their failure modes. Code, the stored model outputs, and a pipeline that regenerates the benchmark from the source datasets are available at https://github.com/royerlab/celltrack-bench.
authors: Ilan Theodoro, Jord\~ao Bragantini, Lo\"ic A. Royer
bullets: Covers 15 standard cell-tracking datasets, four imaging modalities, 1,537 problems, and 9,041 cell-linking decisions.

Analyzes VLM failure modes and releases code, model outputs, and benchmark-generation tools.

papers.abstract: Generating 360-degree panoramas requires both local perspective fidelity and global spherical continuity. Existing representations face a trade-off: equirectangular projection (ERP) enables seamless panorama modeling but suffers from severe distortion and a domain gap to pre-trained image generators, whereas cubemaps preserve perspective geometry but often produce inconsistent faces and visible seams. We present Squaring-the-Sphere, a panoramic image generation framework built on a novel representation CubeAtlas, which unfolds all cubemap faces into a single compact canvas. By arranging orientation-aligned, rotated polar regions alongside the equatorial faces, this representation preserves the perspective geometry of cubemaps while organizing the cross-face relationships required for seamless panorama assembly. It further enables a pretrained diffusion transformer to model the complete panorama jointly in a single pass, without altering the backbone architecture or positional encoding. While CubeAtlas has a token count comparable to ERP, its structured layout makes many dense attention interactions unnecessary. We therefore introduce a layout-aware sparse attention mask that preserves the interactions required for panorama continuity while removing geometrically irrelevant token pairs. As a result, CubeAtlas achieves better quality than ERP modeling with lower attention computation. Furthermore, we introduce a training-free super-resolution technique and a fusion scheme that enhance fine details in distortion-free perspective space before achieving the final ERP panorama. Experiments on various benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves geometric fidelity, cross-view consistency, and high-resolution visual quality over previous methods.
authors: Xuhui Zuo, Chenjie Cao, Tengfei Wang, Junta Wu, Yisu Zhang, Chunchao Guo
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between ERP’s distortion and cubemaps’ cross-face seams.
Unfolds rotated cubemap regions into one compact, orientation-aligned canvas for joint panorama modeling.
Uses layout-aware sparse attention to preserve continuity while reducing unnecessary attention computation.
Adds training-free super-resolution and fusion in perspective space to improve fine details.
Experiments report better geometric fidelity, cross-view consistency, and high-resolution quality than prior methods.

papers.title: Squaring-the-Sphere: Distortion-Free and Seamless Panorama Generation via CubeAtlas
