papers.abstract: Multi-robot coordination of nonlinear systems is naturally formulated as joint-space optimal control subject to constraints over groups of robots. Existing methods that approach joint optimality remain largely centralized, offline, and confined to collision-free motion planning, while decentralized, real-time counterparts target safe navigation without pursuing the joint optimum. This paper develops a decentralized, real-time planner that approaches the joint optimum as an anytime process. We extend a recent single-robot framework that searches dispersive trees of forward-propagated commands for differentially flat systems to coordinate a multi-robot team near-optimally. We first show that the inter-robot coupling can be effectively replaced by some local constraints, under which locally grown dispersive trees contain a near-optimal agreement. It is this structure that the robots pursue by decentralized column generation, negotiating rents on the shared space that guide the search of each robot's tree. The negotiation settles on an agreement whose near-optimality is certified at quiescence. Our protocol, WarpWeaver, implements this negotiation as an asynchronous real-time loop over a receding horizon, and demonstrates effective closure to quiesced agreements even when real-time deadlines cut the negotiation short. In simulation, WarpWeaver reduces total travel time by up to 22% against centralized offline planners on the Dynobench suite and by up to 37% against a decentralized real-time baseline, and nearly doubles the success rate of a task-specific planner on graph connectivity. Hardware experiments on six robots planning onboard demonstrate real-world implementability.
authors: Shashank A. Deshpande, Blake T. Edwards, Jonathan P. How
bullets: Addresses the gap between centralized offline joint optimization and decentralized real-time navigation that lacks joint-optimality objectives.
Extends dispersive-tree search for differentially flat systems to multi-robot coordination by replacing inter-robot coupling with local constraints.
Uses decentralized column generation to negotiate shared-space “rents” and guide each robot’s tree search.
Simulation shows up to 22% lower total travel time than centralized offline planners and up to 37% lower than a decentralized real-time baseline; hardware tests use six robots.
The approach remains effective when real-time deadlines interrupt negotiation, though certification requires quiescence.

papers.abstract: We propose a new regression method named Direct Inference on Admissible Sets (Diona) that directly uses samples to estimate the state and its derivatives at a query point, along with their admissible bounds, without long global training. By casting the values and derivatives at the query and neighbouring samples as latent variables in a constrained optimisation problem, the burden of long training loops becomes one of on-demand local solves. We establish Diona's theoretical properties including finite-sample coverage and, in the noiseless case, convergence to the true state and derivatives under dense sampling. In a nonlinear regression benchmark on six functions of three to eight dimensions, Diona was more accurate than a Gaussian process (GP) on noiseless data especially with denser data sets. Furthermore, as with GP, it produced uncertainty bounds that contained the true value at more than 95% of query points in four functions. Diona's time to a first prediction after a data set update was three to four orders of magnitude shorter than that of the GP, and two to three orders shorter than that of a neural network, which was more accurate but offers no uncertainty quantification. This low latency is paid for by on-demand predictions, so this latency advantage applies when relatively few predictions are needed between data updates.
authors: Lorenzo Sabug Jr., Eric Kerrigan
bullets: Directly estimates a query point’s state, derivatives, and admissible bounds from nearby samples.
Formulates these quantities as latent variables in a constrained local optimisation problem, replacing long global training.
Theoretically provides finite-sample coverage and converges to the true state and derivatives under dense, noiseless sampling.
On six nonlinear benchmark functions, it outperformed Gaussian processes on noiseless data, especially with denser samples.
Prediction after data updates was substantially faster than GP and neural networks, but the advantage applies mainly when few predictions are needed between updates.

papers.abstract: Hidden future-token leakage can create false architectural gains: an autoregressive model may appear substantially better under teacher-forced evaluation while its free-running generation deteriorates. We investigate this failure in an adaptive residual-routing decoder whose sequence-level routing summary exposes prefix positions to future tokens despite a correct causal attention mask. An anomalous 24-layer checkpoint reduces validation loss from the baseline's 3.5958 to 1.4259, yet it fails a prefix-invariance audit and has substantially higher reference-model perplexity during generation. Layer-wise diagnostics and implementation inspection trace the violation to a full-sequence summary broadcast through the dynamic routing-query path. Two independently trained 12-layer causal repairs eliminate detectable leakage and return validation loss and reference perplexity to the control scale, removing the large apparent advantage. As diagnostic tools, we use the established prefix-invariance contract, maximum prefix-output discrepancy (LeakScore), complementary behavioral metrics, and layer-wise profiles. Supporting experiments cover six synthetic implementation pairs spanning five module families, clean pretrained controls, controlled fault injection, and cache consistency across numerical precisions. These results illustrate how hidden future-token access can produce misleading claims of architectural progress and why lower teacher-forced loss should be interpreted together with whole-model causal checks and free-running evaluation.
authors: Huiting Liu, Jinsong Wu
bullets: An adaptive residual-routing decoder leaked future information through a full-sequence routing summary despite using a correct causal attention mask.
A 24-layer checkpoint showed much lower validation loss but failed prefix-invariance checks and had worse generation-time reference perplexity.
Layer-wise diagnostics and code inspection localized the leak to the dynamic routing-query path.
Two independently trained 12-layer causal repairs removed detectable leakage and restored metrics to the control scale.
Prefix-invariance, LeakScore, behavioral metrics, layer-wise profiles, and cache-consistency tests provide a broader auditing toolkit.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Mechanism of hidden future-token leakage. papers.abstract: Individual preferences often become visible only after deployment, when a user accepts one decision or revokes it in favor of another. Jev-style typed interfaces make this feedback explicit by identifying the selected action and, under revocation, the decision it replaces. We study how these consequences persist across requests as Decision-Level Continual Learning from Typed Feedback (Jev-DLC). Jev-DLC treats each correction as both evidence about a recurring action identity and a directed relation between the preferred and rejected choices. It preserves these signals in complementary bounded channels above a frozen scorer and combines their scores to shape the next decision. The method retains no raw interaction history, adds no scorer call, and performs no runtime language-model backward pass. We also introduce TCPA-Bench, a chronological suite that credits a correction only through its effect on later decisions. On TCPA-Repeat, Jev-DLC reaches 44.83% user-macro accuracy overall, 2.43 points above Recent-4 history replay. After at least two earlier feedback events, it reaches 56.07%, a 7.54-point margin over the strongest reported comparison at this depth. These results show how explicit typed corrections can become compact causal state for continual personalization.

papers.abstract: Metaphor is a crucial aspect of human cognition. As such, we would like to understand how it is represented in large language models (LLMs) and how it might be controlled. We use mechanistic interpretability techniques to identify causal subspaces in a range of LLMs covering different architectures and sizes. We show that we are able to steer output on classification tasks across different parts of speech. We are also able to steer output on generation tasks, indicating that these techniques can be used to control the metaphoricity of LLM output.
authors: Shihui Li, Mette Andersen, Martha Lewis
bullets: Studies how metaphor is represented and controlled in LLMs.
Identifies causal subspaces across models with varied architectures and sizes.
Steers metaphor-related outputs on classification tasks across multiple parts of speech.
Controls the metaphoricity of outputs in generation tasks.
Demonstrates a potential approach for probing and manipulating metaphor representations.

papers.abstract: Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) stands as a fundamental challenge in robotics, essential for enabling autonomous agents to execute complex, long-horizon tasks in diverse environments. While Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce a new paradigm for TAMP by leveraging extensive common sense, their inherent reasoning limitations hinder direct application, and fine-tuning strategies to enhance these capabilities are currently bottlenecked by the scarcity of high-quality datasets. Existing automated generation methods often suffer from homogeneity, limiting model generalization, and unsolvability, where hallucinated scene graphs create physical mismatches with task goals. To address these issues, we propose Scene-graph Construction Optimized by Plan Error-correction (SCOPE), an automated framework designed to generate diverse and executable TAMP datasets. SCOPE incorporates multi-level diversity metrics to maximize the information entropy of scenarios. Crucially, it introduces a Plan Feedback Error-correction pipeline that utilizes planner execution failures as feedback signals to retroactively rectify logical inconsistencies in scene graphs, ensuring physical feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that SCOPE exhibits greater robustness to erroneous scene graphs and generates higher-quality data. When utilized for LLM fine-tuning, SCOPE-generated data yield a downstream TAMP model that achieves an absolute 12.33% gain in success rate over its counterpart fine-tuned with data generated by DELTA, a state-of-the-art PDDL-based planner.
authors: Chaoyue Li, Zeyu Gao, Yanfeng Lu, Fan Luo
bullets: Addresses scarce, homogeneous, and often unsolvable datasets for long-horizon robot planning with LLMs.
Uses multi-level diversity metrics to increase scenario information entropy.
Applies plan-execution failures to retroactively correct logical inconsistencies in scene graphs.
Produces more robust, higher-quality data and improves downstream TAMP fine-tuning success by 12.33 percentage points over DELTA-generated data.

papers.abstract: Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget. We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents. A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations, selecting high-level actions while the engine executes navigation. The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories. These categories support evaluation of centralized coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies. A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding. The evaluation compares four VLMs on all 20 maps, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, action acceptance rate, and model API expenditure. A memory ablation on the same 20 maps examines the effect of a shared, self-authored notebook while retaining six-response action history in both conditions. The strongest evaluated model, \texttt{gpt-6-astra}, achieves 26.2\% mean order completion. Notebook memory has mixed score effects across models, with positive mean differences for Claude and Qwen and negative differences for GPT and Gemini.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can perform a broad range of tasks across diverse settings, yet their performance in agentic contexts remains poorly understood. Although online evaluations in simulators and real-world environments are essential for measuring interactive agent performance, they are costly and challenging to scale. Complementary offline VQA benchmarks can enable faster and more reliable comparisons across agentic domains, yet existing benchmarks remain limited and fragmented. To address this gap, we introduce AgentVQA, an offline benchmark for evaluating VLMs on realistic agentic scenarios across five agent domains: Web Agents, Robotics, Egocentric Videos, Games, and Spatial Planning. We build AgentVQA by manually selecting 1000 challenging, real-world agent examples from 23 source datasets and adapting them for reliable offline evaluation. The resulting benchmark preserves realistic scenarios from interactive environments across diverse domains, and its model rankings track those from corresponding online evaluations. Across the 22 evaluated models, the best achieves only 58.5% accuracy. Our cross-domain analysis shows that errors are driven primarily by failures to ground and maintain accurate representations of the current and evolving visual state, including localizing relevant UI elements, interpreting motion, tracking state changes over time, and inferring 3D spatial relationships, rather than by task misinterpretation or downstream logical reasoning.

bullets: Addresses the cost and limited scalability of online simulator and real-world agent evaluations.

papers.abstract: Apple Silicon is among the most widely used platforms for local LLM inference, yet nearly all inference optimizations are designed and validated on server-class NVIDIA GPUs under batched serving workloads. Which optimizations retain their benefits when moved to Apple Silicon, and what determines their applicability? We evaluate four optimization families: KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization. Experiments span four Apple machines under a common single-request decode workload, with matched RTX 4090 comparisons where possible. KV-cache pruning can reach up to 1.75 times end-to-end throughput on Apple but can reduce throughput on desktop NVIDIA GPUs. Under the common benchmark, all evaluated speculative decoding methods reduce throughput on Apple, despite reported 2-6 times gains on server GPUs. CUDA kernel designs transfer only partially: public Metal lacks asynchronous copy, and batch-one decode makes several serving-oriented mechanisms inapplicable, although transferable components yield up to 1.20 times decode throughput. Quantization gains vary by machine. Across four families, a reported speedup is not a portable property of a technique alone but a joint function of technique, runtime, hardware contract, and workload regime.
authors: Kyrylo Yemets, Andrii Yaroshevych, Victor Muryn, Ostap Khomenko, Pavlo Kryven, Maksym Kmet, Maksym Shamrai, Mariya Hirna

KV-cache pruning reaches up to 1.75× end-to-end throughput on Apple but can reduce throughput on desktop NVIDIA GPUs.
All tested speculative decoding methods lower Apple throughput, contrasting with reported gains on server GPUs.
GPU-kernel portability is partial because Metal lacks asynchronous copy and batch-one decoding limits serving-oriented mechanisms; transferable components reach up to 1.20× decode throughput.
Quantization benefits vary across Apple machines, showing that optimization speedups are not portable properties of techniques alone.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong potential for video anomaly detection, but dense frame-level inference makes them impractical for real-time deployment. Existing acceleration commonly relies on uniform sampling, which ignores content dynamics and can either waste computation on static segments or miss localized anomalies. We propose MoG-VLM a motion-adaptive anomaly detection framework that leverages motion purely as a lightweight control signal to decide when VLM inference is necessary. To this end, we introduce Temporal Gradient Magnitude (TGM) which performs content-aware sampling to concentrate computation on informative regions while avoiding redundant processing. We further introduce a hierarchical dual-stream design in which dense multi-frame VLM reasoning is activated only around frames with elevated anomaly likelihood, via anchor-triggered context-window expansion with early termination. A fusion module then reconciles these instantaneous semantic cues with temporal action dynamics. Across four benchmarks, our method achieves 91.91%, 84.30%, 87.88%, and 78.96% AUC-ROC on XD-Violence, UCF-Crime, MSAD, and ShanghaiTech, respectively, establishing new state of the art on three benchmarks under the zero-shot, training-free setting. On XD-Violence, we improve over the previous best result by +0.57% while delivering a 1.31x inference speedup. These results demonstrate that content-aware allocation of VLM capacity, processing fewer frames more intelligently rather than all frames uniformly, is a more effective axis of progress than uniformly densifying VLM inference across frames. Code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/kdawoud91/MoG-VLM.
authors: Khaled Waleed Dawoud, Muhammad Zaigham Zaheer, Khan Muhammad, Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of dense frame-level VLM inference and the limitations of uniform sampling.
Uses Temporal Gradient Magnitude (TGM) for motion-adaptive, content-aware frame selection.
Employs hierarchical dual-stream reasoning with anchor-triggered context expansion and early termination.
Fuses instantaneous semantic cues from the VLM with temporal action dynamics.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on three of four benchmarks and a 1.31× speedup on XD-Violence.

papers.abstract: Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions. Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions. However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics. Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction. The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions. On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo. Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.
authors: Qi Lv, Jiayi Lin, Yuxin Jiang, Jianzong Wang, Xiang Deng, Mike Shou Zheng
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of robot motion, object responses, and scene changes in reconstruction-based latent actions.
Decomposes latent actions into a skeleton-grounded kinematic component and a complementary visual residual.
Uses cross-modal swap reconstruction, separate conditioning pathways, and branch dropout to improve controllability.
A lightweight adapter maps robot actions into the kinematic latent space for future-observation generation.
On DROID, it reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% versus DreamDojo; results also support motion specialization and zero-shot human-to-robot transfer.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with contact information difficult to obtain from vision alone. Shear force is particularly important for understanding tangential contact, guiding corrective motions, and maintaining grasp stability, yet flexible and low-cost tactile arrays often measure only normal force. We introduce VecTile, a low-cost, 6 mm thin, flexible tactile array capable of three-axis force sensing. VecTile combines a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs that convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns. The sensor can be fabricated in-house without specialized equipment. The complete system costs less than 35 USD for a 4x4 array. We validate the sensing mechanism through finite element analysis and hardware experiments. In controlled single-taxel tests over 1-5 N normal force and up to 1.5 N shear force, VecTile achieves root-mean-square errors of 0.39 N and 0.16 N for normal and shear forces. A VecTile calibrated while flat retains accuracy when curved, while a five-minute manual calibration is sufficient for practical use. Two applications demonstrate its utility. First, shear readings are sensitive enough to stop a sharp scalpel from puncturing a balloon after contact. Second, the sensor substantially improves Diffusion Policy-guided power-plug insertion. All designs and code will be released upon paper acceptance. Project website: https://jiannnh.github.io/VecTile/.
authors: Jian Hou, Xin Zhou, Adam J. Spiers
bullets: Addresses the lack of shear-force sensing in many low-cost flexible tactile arrays.
Uses a piezoresistive layer and passive silicone nubs to encode normal and shear forces as pressure patterns.
A 4×4 array costs under $35, is 6 mm thick, and can be fabricated without specialized equipment.
Controlled tests report 0.39 N normal-force RMSE and 0.16 N shear-force RMSE; flat calibration remains effective when curved.
Demonstrations include preventing balloon puncture with a scalpel and improving power-plug insertion.

(7) The FPC and resistive layer are slid into the molded silicone layer produced in step (4). papers.abstract: Many questions about a video concern one physical object. Where does the ball end up after the cups are shuffled? Which card is the queen? How often was the mug covered? Video-language models (Video-LMs) recognise such objects in single frames but do not keep them apart over time. On real shell-game videos, open models from 8B to 235B parameters, their thinking variants, a reinforcement-learned tool agent and three training-free tool agents all stay within ten points of chance. We separate semantic identity binding from temporal identity maintenance. An object's identity should be fixed at a moment when the evidence for it is visible, and carried afterwards by a tracker. \emph{Track, Then Bind} implements this principle without training. A promptable video tracker follows every candidate object and draws it with a track number. A frozen vision-language model answers a static question about the identifying evidence, which binds the target to a track. The answer is then derived from the tracked state in text, without asking the model to reinterpret the original video during read-out. A single configuration covers all benchmarks. With Qwen3-VL-32B it solves both VET-Bench tasks, where a fine-tuned trajectory model reaches 92\% and 90\% and the same VLM voting over 16 samples stays at 30--32\%. It answers 55.4\% of the hardest Perception Test cup games, where the best published model answers 41.5\%, and, using track-derived timelines, 48.6\% of TOC-Bench questions, against 37.1\% for the same model answering directly. Drawing the same tracks on the video and asking the question directly falls 12--19 points short of the agent on real cup games.
authors: Di Yang, Xiaochang Li, Muyang Liu, Yufei Wang, Yanhai Xiong
bullets: Video-LMs often recognize objects in individual frames but lose identity across time, especially in shell-game-style videos.
Track, Then Bind uses a promptable tracker to follow candidates and a frozen VLM to identify the target from visible evidence.
The system derives answers from track-based state and timelines rather than making the VLM reinterpret the full video during read-out.
With Qwen3-VL-32B, it reaches 55.4% on the hardest Perception Test cup games and 48.6% on TOC-Bench, outperforming the cited direct-answer baselines.
A single training-free configuration handles multiple benchmarks, though performance remains far from perfect on difficult cup games.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity's position and timing intact. Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners. AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input. It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame. We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses $\sim$10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games exported from GEAR, an AI game-creation tool; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection. To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9\% to 62.9\%, missed count changes fall from 34.7\% to 21.3\%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.
authors: Ruicong Liu, Liangyang Ouyang, Fengbo Lan, Zhixiang Wang, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses programmer-art visuals produced by AI-built games.
Uses video-to-video generation from plain footage, without G-buffers, object labels, or 3D proxies.
LoRA-fine-tunes a reference-video-conditioned video model on paired game-rendering clips and gameplay recordings.
Introduces an entity-level benchmark with 59 held-out cases and 753 entities.
Improves temporal entity matching from 50.9% to 62.9% and reduces missed count changes from 34.7% to 21.3% versus the base model.

(b) One training sample: the crude clip is the input video <Video 1>, the target’s first frame serves as an optional anchor, and a six-segment caption defines which real entity each crude shape represents and what must be preserved. papers.abstract: Point cloud transformers aim to capture detailed local geometry and relationships across a scene at a manageable computational cost. Two common approaches are window attention and global attention. They differ in how they enable scene-wide interaction, which refers to information exchange among tokens across a scene. Window attention reduces computational cost by restricting self-attention to groups of tokens called windows; in serialized designs, each window contains a fixed number of consecutive tokens from a spatially ordered sequence. Because each block only directly connects tokens within the same window, information exchange across windows relies on changes in window membership across blocks and hierarchical pooling. Global attention, in contrast, directly connects all tokens within a scene, but computing attention over all token pairs can be costly when the number of tokens is large. To balance computational cost and scene-wide interaction, we introduce MixPT, a point transformer that uses a mix of window and global attention blocks in an interleaved schedule, while retaining a single fixed serialization pattern for its window blocks. For scenes with a large number of tokens, MixPT applies global attention to spatially pooled tokens and returns residual updates to the original-resolution stream. Across indoor and outdoor benchmarks, MixPT achieves competitive accuracy with lower latency than representative window and global attention baselines. We further demonstrate the feasibility of scaling the attention stage in depth by repeating the interleaved pattern of window and global attention blocks.
authors: Minkyun Seo, Hyungtae Lim, Jaesik Park
bullets: Window attention lowers cost but limits direct communication across windows; global attention enables scene-wide interaction but is expensive for large token sets.
MixPT interleaves window and global attention blocks while keeping one fixed serialization pattern for window processing.
For large scenes, global attention operates on spatially pooled tokens and sends residual updates back to the original-resolution stream.
Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show competitive accuracy with lower latency than representative window- and global-attention baselines.
The interleaved attention pattern can be repeated to scale the attention stage in depth.

papers.abstract: Given an unseen graph, a start node, $s$, and an end node, $t$, can a language model generate the shortest path from $s$ to $t$? Prior work has found that models fail to learn this task as the graphs scale. We show that this failure has two causes: the supervision signal and the tokenization. First, we theoretically establish and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of multi-token prediction (MTP), and show that the benefits of MTP are topologically agnostic. Second, we introduce alternative tokenizations and show that the two causes are orthogonal. Using these methods, we break through the scaling wall observed by prior work, consistently and stably learning to solve the task at scales far beyond previous limits.
authors: Arvid Frydenlund, FuTe Wong, Katherine Lambert, Frank Rudzicz
bullets: The task is to generate the shortest path between a start and end node in an unseen graph.
Prior scaling failures stem from weak supervision signals and unsuitable tokenization.
Multi-token prediction improves learning, with benefits that are theoretically and empirically topologically agnostic.
Alternative tokenizations address a separate, orthogonal limitation.
Together, the methods overcome prior scaling barriers consistently and stably, though the abstract gives no specific scale or numerical results.

Figure 13: The Plackett-Luce loss of the MTP head (Alg. 1), with concrete example logits. A gather puts the logits into the rank order ri, which for MTP is the temporal order: position j holds the token j steps ahead. Bar widths are the softmax of the logits shown, on one absolute scale across all three rows, so mass leaving the partition function is visible in place. At rank-step j the already-ranked tokens are struck out and Zj i spans only the remainder: each ranked token is removed from the partition function, so the next step renormalizes and competes only over what is left, i.e. sampling without replacement in the context of it modelling a generative process.

Figure 26: Khops-Gen. Sequential generation of the full compositional chain from the single query xN (position 31). The source-side is on the left in red, with the target-side being generated. Unlike Khops, only one chain is considered in a single instance of the task. Because of this, and as the source-side spans the entire N nodes, there is no implicit MMLT training as in Khops. Thus, MMLT must instead be induced explicitly by sampling N ′ ≤ N ( L.1.1). This also indicates that there is much less supervision in Khops-Gen as there is in Khops. However, the supervision is different. Whereas Khops has implicit MMLT but no implicit MMHT, Khops-Gen is the opposite. Unlike Khops, the chain runs until the context is exhausted and k is not supplied to the model. Note that we sample k′ uniformly, but that does not mean the context window between hops is the same size. On the target side, we show both NTP and MTP. Because this is a genuine generation task, MTP applies directly rather than through the ranking-loss stand-in required for Khops ( L.1.2). Importantly, MTP induces the same quadratic-to-k supergraph (rainbow) as it does in path search (and will for any multihop reasoning task). The MTP target block is a triangle of k(k + 1)/2 terms, matching Eq. 3.

papers.abstract: When a user says "Keep it short", how short should the LLM's response be? More generally, users and applications require different levels of instruction adherence, but prompting does not reliably provide fine-grained control over them. We therefore study "steerable language models" that provide fine-grained numerical control over the degree to which models follow general instructions specified in text. However, existing approaches do not jointly offer fine-grained control, efficiency, and scalability across diverse instructions. To address this gap, we introduce DIAL (Distilled Instruction-Adherence Levels) to achieve all three properties. For fine-grained control, we perform classifier-free guidance (CFG) with a frozen LLM to provide training signals for on-policy distillation of instruction adherence at different levels. For efficiency, we design a lightweight steering adapter that uses a classifier over the LLM's hidden states to compute a closed-form steering edit. The classifier adaptively sets the steering magnitude at each token based on the target adherence level, while accounting for the geometry of the LLM's hidden states to preserve response coherence. For scalability, the classifier is text-conditioned, allowing a shared adapter to support new instructions without per-instruction fitting, and training requires only instruction and request text. Evaluation across multiple LLM families shows that DIAL achieves a competitive balance between concept expression and response fluency, with concept scores increasing monotonically across adherence levels. We introduce SteerIF, an instruction-only dataset of 98, 625 concept, persona, verifiable, and descriptive instructions. When trained on SteerIF, DIAL provides fine-grained control over personas and, when combined with prompting, improves verifiable instruction following.
authors: Thanh Q. Tran, John Russell Himawan, Arun Verma, Kiwan Wong, Wei Xiao, Daniela Rus, Bryan Kian Hsiang Low
bullets: Targets controllable instruction adherence, addressing prompting’s unreliable fine-grained control.
Uses classifier-free guidance for on-policy distillation into a lightweight steering adapter.

papers.abstract: KV cache compression for multimodal LLMs usually selects the visual tokens to keep once, at prefill, and reuses that selection for the whole generation. We show that this one-shot selection is severely limited on long-form generation: on detailed image description, even an oracle that selects with the attention of the uncompressed answer reaches only 0.44-0.52 ROUGE-L agreement with the uncompressed output, because the evidence the model reads moves as the description unfolds. Re-selecting whenever attention drifts out of the kept set is the natural remedy, but we find that a fixed drift threshold fails systematically: drift magnitudes are not comparable across samples, so low-drift samples are almost never refreshed although they benefit the most. We propose Rate-Controlled Refresh (RCR), which lets drift decide when and where to re-select while a per-sample controller regulates how often, combined with a low-rank drift detector, candidate-restricted re-selection, and a decision that stays on the GPU. With one setting for all models and tasks, RCR outperforms the per-step retrieval method InfiniGen by 1.6-3.8 ROUGE-L points on five of six model-task settings with no significant difference on the sixth, while staying within 1.7 points of exact per-step re-selection, with comparable estimated data movement per step and a 4x smaller GPU-resident detector. On DetailCaps, drift-chosen timing beats random timing at the same refresh rate and periodic timing even at a higher rate, by 2.0-5.0 points. On pre-registered video description, where drift is homogeneous across samples, RCR is on par with InfiniGen on Qwen2-VL and exceeds it on Qwen3-VL but no longer beats a fixed threshold at the nearest tested rates, consistent with the diagnosis; object-level evaluation shows that RCR achieves higher object F1 against the uncompressed output than InfiniGen on two of three models.
authors: Bin Hu, Yingbo Xiao
bullets: One-shot prefill-time token selection degrades on long descriptions because the model’s visual evidence shifts during generation.
Fixed drift thresholds refresh inconsistently: low-drift samples may rarely refresh despite benefiting most.
RCR combines drift-based timing and location selection with per-sample refresh-rate control, low-rank detection, candidate restriction, and GPU-resident decisions.
Across six model-task settings, RCR beats InfiniGen by 1.6–3.8 ROUGE-L points in five, matches it in one, and remains close to exact per-step re-selection with a smaller detector.
On image description, drift-based timing outperforms random or periodic refresh; on video description, performance aligns with the method’s assumption that drift varies across samples.

papers.abstract: A conventional embodied agent in an indoor environment builds a map by accumulating noisy real-world measurements and results from heavy inference to guide navigation. While the detailed measurements may differ due to scene changes or sensor settings, the unique topological structure of navigable passages or the connectivity between rooms may provide training-free guidance that complements local observations. We propose a sparse topometric graph as an efficient structural representation for robust indoor navigation, alleviating the need for fine-grained matching, which is computationally expensive, memory-intensive, and prone to real-world variations. The map consists of nodes that encode local 3D geometry and distance-weighted edges that capture traversable connectivity. A learned graph-matching network finds consistent subgraph structures across sessions by considering both node-level geometric descriptors and neighborhood connectivity. The holistic contextual matching is robust to local ambiguities caused by weak distinctiveness or repetitive structure, and establishes stable correspondences despite local scene changes, different sensor modalities, or limited spatial overlap. We analyze the practicality of the graph through cross-session point-goal navigation, where a goal specified in a prior reference map must be reached from an unknown initial pose in a later session. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest success rates (77.1% on Gibson and 40.0% under 3D-FRONT scene changes), while reducing memory by more than two orders of magnitude compared to point-level representations. The proposed approach further supports cross-session alignment and goal-directed navigation with strong scalability and robust real-world transfer.
authors: Eun Sun Lee, Minkyun Seo, Gwangtak Bae, Junho Kim, Seunggu Kang, Jaesik Park, Young Min Kim
bullets: Represents indoor maps with nodes for local 3D geometry and distance-weighted edges for traversable connectivity.
Uses learned graph matching over geometric descriptors and neighborhood structure to establish correspondences across sessions.
Handles local ambiguities, scene changes, different sensor modalities, and limited spatial overlap without training-specific fine-grained matching.
In cross-session point-goal navigation, achieves 77.1% success on Gibson and 40.0% under 3D-FRONT scene changes.
Reduces memory use by more than two orders of magnitude versus point-level representations.

The navigation policy combines the goal-directed score Sgoal with the frontier-based exploration score Sexplore to select a node as the next waypoint toward the goal position g of the cross-session navigation task.

papers.abstract: World action models increasingly rely on pretrained video models assumed to capture physical dynamics for prediction, planning, and action generation. Existing evaluations assess plausibility, probe representations, or measure predictive surprise, but rarely identify which history-conditioned physical expectations conflict with observations. We introduce PhysTrace, a training-free framework aligning MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations with observed video windows to temporally localize physical violations and provide interpretable descriptions without task-specific probes or classifiers. We also introduce IntPhys2-Timing, adding violation intervals to IntPhys2. PhysTrace achieves a Hit Rate of up to 70.7% across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and outperforms the compared methods in overall possible-impossible discrimination accuracy on IntPhys2. Applied to reconstructed videos along the trajectories of pretrained diffusion/flow-based video models, PhysTrace reveals attribute- and noise-dependent patterns in physical violation localization, enabling interpretable physical consistency analysis across timesteps.
authors: Taekoan Yoo, Wonkyung Jung, Kyunghun Kim, Kyeongbo Kong
bullets: Addresses the lack of evaluations that identify which physical expectations conflict with video observations.
Uses MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations aligned with video windows to detect and describe violations without task-specific probes or classifiers.
Introduces IntPhys2-Timing, an extension of IntPhys2 with annotated violation intervals.
Achieves up to 70.7% hit rate across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and improves overall possible–impossible discrimination accuracy over compared methods on IntPhys2.
Reveals attribute- and noise-dependent violation-localization patterns across timesteps in reconstructed diffusion- and flow-based video trajectories.

papers.abstract: Agentic robot systems combine language-model reasoning with robot policies to monitor execution and recover from failures. However, reviewing every action chunk incurs substantial overhead, even in familiar situations. We introduce FastHarness, an experience-driven execution harness that adaptively schedules GPT-6 Astra supervision of a {\pi}0.5 policy. A fast path uses stage memory and reviewed outcomes to reduce review frequency as experience accumulates, while a complementary recovery path focuses supervision on correcting errors. Once recovery is verified, routine execution resumes, with failure experience retained to guide future interventions. The policy remains frozen and generates fresh actions from current observations. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, reviewer token use decreases by an average of 57.2% per task from the first evaluated episode to the mean of the final five episodes. Mean episode time decreases from 85.5 to 52.0 minutes over the same interval. On the same tasks, mean success increases from 80% for GPT-as-Policy ({\pi}0.5 + GPT-6 Astra) to 97.19% with FastHarness. These results highlight adaptive supervision as a practical route to more efficient agentic robotics without additional model training.
authors: Tao Lin, Yuxin Du, Haoxiao Wang, Zile Zhong, Bo Zhao
bullets: Addresses the overhead of reviewing every action chunk in familiar robot-task situations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an important paradigm for robotic manipulation by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Since reliable manipulation requires sufficient observation of objects, end-effectors, and their spatial relationships, multi-view inputs are widely used to provide complementary spatial information. However, our experiments show that existing VLA models do not fully exploit such multi-view complementarity. The policy tends to persistently rely on the wrist view, lacking the ability to dynamically adjust global-local view dependency across manipulation stages, which limits stage adaptability and robustness. To address this issue, we propose FocusVLA, a stage-aware multi-view routing framework. FocusVLA predicts future interaction intent from historical actions and uses it to guide dynamic view routing during action generation. By adaptively coordinating global and local observations across different task stages, FocusVLA improves multi-view utilization. On RoboTwin 2.0, FocusVLA improves the average success rate over the strongest baseline $\pi_{0.5}$ by 10.10 pp. In real-world evaluation, FocusVLA improves the success rate from 71.7\% to 85.0\%, achieving a 13.3\% gain over $\pi_{0.5}$. Moreover, the intent prediction and dynamic routing modules of FocusVLA can be integrated into existing VLA frameworks without modifying their core architectures.
authors: Huixin Xu, Ziya Yu, Peng Li
bullets: Existing VLA policies often over-rely on wrist views and fail to adapt view selection during manipulation.
The method predicts future interaction intent from historical actions to guide stage-aware multi-view routing.
It coordinates global and local observations according to the current manipulation stage.
On RoboTwin 2.0, it improves average success by 10.10 percentage points over π₀.₅.
In real-world tests, success rises from 71.7% to 85.0%; the modules can be integrated into existing VLA architectures.

papers.abstract: Looped and depth-grown language models reuse computations across depth and have attracted interest for their reasoning capabilities. Building on prior suggestive evidence of improved in-context-learning (ICL), we investigate how such reuse favors ICL, including how it shapes the acquisition, retention, and mechanisms of this ability. Our analysis spans pretrained language models up to 3B parameters and controlled tasks. The experiments provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context: grown and looped models rely more on information in context and, compared with a full-depth dense reference, acquire ICL earlier in controlled tasks and retain it more strongly when learning fixed associations in the weights is also possible. Tracing attention heads through training reveals that depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers. Ablations show that grown and looped models rely more strongly on induction-ranked heads for both few-shot performance and later-token prediction. Together, these findings provide evidence for a shared inductive bias toward learning from context and suggest that (soft) parameter reuse shapes how this ability develops and which attention mechanisms support it.
authors: Ferdinand Kapl, Kaitlin Maile, Stefan Bauer, Johannes von Oswald
bullets: Studies how computation reuse affects ICL acquisition, retention, and underlying mechanisms.
Analyzes pretrained models up to 3B parameters alongside controlled tasks.
Grown and looped models rely more on contextual information than a full-depth dense reference.
Depth growth propagates early induction heads across layers during training.
Ablations link induction-ranked heads to few-shot performance and later-token prediction.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how depth growth and looping shape in-context learning and induction heads in LLMs, directly relevant to LLM architecture and mechanisms.
papers.title: How Depth Growth and Looping Shape In-Context Learning in Language Models
papers.tldr: Depth-grown and looped language models develop in-context learning earlier and retain it more strongly, apparently because parameter reuse promotes context-based reasoning and induction-head mechanisms.

papers.abstract: Vector quantization (VQ), in particular lattice-based methods, offer strong rate-distortion trade-offs for low-bit large language models (LLMs), yet their behavior under quantization-aware training (VQ-QAT) remains poorly understood. We scale lattice VQ-QAT to billion-parameter LLMs and multi-billion-token training regimes, and introduce SQuAT, a shape-gain VQ-QAT approach trained with a separate straight-through estimator (STE) for the shape and gain. SQuAT decomposes weights into direction and magnitude: normalized directions are quantized using an $E_8$-derived spherical codebook, while gains are quantized independently with low-bit scalar quantizers. We show that, unlike a standard STE applied to the full quantizer, which ignores the shape-gain structure, these separate STEs induce tangent-space updates for directions, yielding an implicit form of spherical (Riemannian) optimization. To enable scalability, we develop a distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment scheme, in which workers quantize disjoint weight blocks and communicate only discrete indices, reducing VQ-QAT training time by 12.8$\times$ and allowing us to scale it to 10B tokens. Across instruction-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen3-4B, and base Qwen3-1.7B, SQuAT consistently outperforms standard VQ-QAT STE under identical quantizers and initialization, and achieves SOTA VQ-QAT accuracy.
authors: Sebastian Loeschcke, Ivan Koryakovskiy, Tycho F. A. van der Ouderaa, Riccardo Del Chiaro, Mart van Baalen, Paul N. Whatmough, Markus Nagel
bullets: Addresses the limited understanding and scalability of VQ-QAT for billion-parameter LLMs.
Decomposes weights into normalized directions and gains, quantizing them with spherical-codebook and scalar quantizers.
Uses separate straight-through estimators that produce tangent-space updates, approximating spherical/Riemannian optimization.
Introduces distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment, reducing VQ-QAT training time by 12.8× and scaling training to 10B tokens.
Outperforms standard VQ-QAT STE across several LLaMA and Qwen models and achieves state-of-the-art VQ-QAT accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SQUAT. Left: a weight block is decomposed as w = γs, where s ∈ Sd−1 is the shape and γ ∈ R+ is the gain. The two components are quantized independently and reconstructed as ŵ = γ̂ŝ. Middle: our spherical factored STE applies separate STEs to the gain and shape quantizers, mapping the gradient g = ∂L/∂ŵ to a scalar gain gradient ∇γL ≈ ŝ⊤g and a tangent shape signal γ̂Psg on TsSd−1. Right: the tangent shape signal induces the update u+ = u−η γ̂(∥u∥)−1Psg on the shape parameter, followed by normalization (retraction back to the unit sphere), s+ = u+/(∥u+∥).

papers.abstract: Continual learning requires a model to keep acquiring new skills and knowledge without compromising its existing capabilities. Parametric methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity. Non-parametric methods, such as prompts, skills, and harnesses, leverage in-context learning but are limited by context length and lossy plain-text compression. To effectively combine their complementary strengths, we propose HERD (Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation), a hybrid continual learning framework that learns efficiently in the harness and internalizes experience into cumulative capabilities via distillation. On the harness side, HERD continually refines its skills to capture reusable patterns, while retaining high-residual examples that the skills fail to capture in a bounded memory. On the parameter side, HERD performs drift-constrained distillation with dual anchors, substantially reducing forgetting over long recursive runs. On the 25-stage task stream of TRACE+17, under fixed memory and compute budgets, HERD matches the strongest parametric baseline in new-task acquisition while exhibiting the least forgetting and the strongest retention of general capabilities.
authors: Xun Sun, Thanh Thi Nguyen, Thuy-Trang Vu
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting, loss of plasticity, context limits, and lossy compression in continual learning.
Refines reusable harness skills and stores high-residual examples in bounded memory.
Uses dual-anchor, drift-constrained distillation to internalize experience without excessive parameter drift.

On the 25-stage TRACE+17 stream under fixed memory and compute, matches the strongest parametric baseline for new-task acquisition while achieving the least forgetting and strongest general-capability retention.

papers.abstract: Robotic swarms must coordinate across diverse missions, yet existing controllers often require redesign, retuning, or retraining when objectives change. Here we show that probabilistic energy modeling provides a unifying representation for versatile swarm control, in which diverse missions emerge from compositions of shared interaction principles rather than task-specific control formulations. By exploiting the correspondence between Gibbs random field energy minimization and structured reward maximization, we encode fundamental swarm behaviors as reusable energy terms within a unified probabilistic objective. Decentralized policies trained within this representation are composed into a single controller through lightweight policy gating, without retraining. An interpretable action-attention mechanism captures non-uniform local interactions, while dimensionless normalization supports transfer across swarm scales and platforms. Demonstrated on aerial swarms, the unified policy generalizes zero-shot across six mission classes, 10-100 agents, two hardware platforms, and indoor cluttered and GPS-denied woodland environments. Large-scale simulations achieve 0.96-1.00 task success rates with 1-10 ms per-agent inference latency, while physical deployments confirm zero-shot transfer to real platforms and unstructured environments. These results establish probabilistic energy modeling as a scalable and transferable framework for decentralized swarm control.
authors: Xiang Zhou, Xiangyu Zhu, Xintong Wang, Qingyuan Yang, Rui Huang, Feng Xue, Lin Li, Qingrui Zhang
bullets: Represents diverse swarm behaviors as reusable energy terms combined in a unified probabilistic objective.
Uses Gibbs energy minimization, structured reward maximization, policy gating, and interpretable action attention.
Supports zero-shot generalization across six mission classes, 10–100 agents, two aerial platforms, and challenging environments.
Reports 0.96–1.00 simulated task success with 1–10 ms per-agent inference latency; physical tests confirm transfer.
Scope: demonstrated for aerial swarms and the evaluated missions, scales, platforms, and environments.

papers.abstract: Many LLM agents maintain external persistent memory and derive additional state from past interactions, such as summaries. Deleting an original memory record therefore need not remove information carried by its descendants. We introduce AfterDeleteBench, a controlled behavioral audit for this failure mode in fixed-weight LLM agents. For each synthetic secret, we compare an exposed-then-deleted agent with an otherwise matched agent that was never exposed to the secret, allowing post-deletion recovery to be attributed to the original exposure. In our primary setting, a single query recovers the deleted secret from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in roughly two thirds of cases, while matched never-exposed controls have zero recovery. Crucially, recovery does not require a surviving verbatim copy: when the complete secret string is absent and only separately stored components remain under a public composition rule, exact reconstruction succeeds in 62-99% of cases across Qwen, Mistral, and Phi-3. We also show that the response interface is part of the measurement system: target-bearing replies can be scored as failures when the requested format and parser are misaligned. Finally, we separate reconstruction from write-back and fresh-session recall. Provenance-aware closure eliminates observed recovery in the tested positive-baseline settings, whereas an exact-literal write filter blocks reinsertion but cannot erase information already present. Together, these results show that source deletion should be evaluated behaviorally at the level of the agent and its memory system, not only as a storage operation.
authors: Ehsan Saleh, Roozbeh Nahavandi, Sama Salarian, Raef Bassily, Andrew Perrault
bullets: Introduces a controlled behavioral audit comparing exposed-then-deleted agents with matched never-exposed controls.
A single query recovered deleted secrets from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in roughly two thirds of cases, while controls had zero recovery.
Exact reconstruction remained possible from separately stored components—even without a verbatim secret copy—across Qwen, Mistral, and Phi-3.
Evaluation depends on the response interface: parser and format mismatches can make target-bearing replies appear compliant or faulty.
Provenance-aware closure eliminated recovery in tested positive-baseline settings; write filters blocked reinsertion but could not erase existing information.

papers.abstract: The rise of Agentic AI systems has changed the landscape of artificial intelligence by enabling strong reasoning capabilities through specialized multi-agent interaction with structured self-reflection. However, in target-driven reasoning tasks, single- and multi-agent systems are often on par in terms of performance gains. A major challenge is that failures often arise from an ineffective exchange of critical information during inter-agent interaction and coordination. Different from existing multi-agent debate paradigms that rely on synchronous turn-taking and sharing information across different agents, we propose an inter-agent protocol based on shared Memory bUFFer INference - referred to as MUFFIN - in an asynchronous agentic framework. In the first step, an orchestrator routes queries based on their reasoning demands and delegates demanding ones to a multi-agent setting, where a shared memory buffer provides asynchronous exchange of intermediate findings while an agent's private reasoning remains local. Our experiments show that our framework Muffin outperforms established competitors, achieving the best accuracy in 17 out of 20 of our benchmark settings, and provides a better quality-cost trade-off than multi-agent debate: Muffin improves accuracy by 19.2 accuracy points while using 77.4% fewer tokens, without requiring full-trace sharing.
authors: Ping-Lin Kuo, Suman Navaratnarajah, Christian Frey, Gresa Shala, Josif Grabocka
bullets: Addresses failures in agent coordination and ineffective exchange of critical information.

Compared with multi-agent debate, improves accuracy by 19.2 points while using 77.4% fewer tokens, without full-trace sharing.

papers.abstract: Tree-based speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by verifying multiple candidate branches in parallel. However, in practical serving scenarios, similar requests repeatedly induce overlapping candidate branches. While retrieval-based methods mitigate this by reusing historical drafts, the resulting candidate trees often contain many low-quality branches as the candidate tree grows, which reduces verification efficiency and wastes target-side computation. To address this, we propose ValuSpec, a plug-and-play candidate valuation mechanism that filters low-quality branches from a supplied candidate tree before expensive target-side verification. ValuSpec introduces transfer-based supervision to align filtering with the target model's behavior. A filtering threshold is estimated from the target model's greedy trajectories on a calibration split, without any parameter training. The target model then verifies the filtered tree under the output-identical greedy rule, so accepted tokens are guaranteed to match standard autoregressive decoding exactly. Experimental results on HumanEval, GSM8K, Dolly, and SpecBench show that, in our main evaluation, ValuSpec achieves up to 2.38x end-to-end speedup in retrieval-based tree settings. Furthermore, integrating ValuSpec into the EAGLE-3 dynamic tree framework yields up to 2.78x end-to-end speedup without modifying its tree construction strategy, demonstrating that ValuSpec serves as a generally applicable and plug-and-play candidate valuation module.
authors: Liang He, SiYuan Ma, Qishi Zhan, Yongqi Fan, Mingyu Cao, Qizhen Lan, Zhaolu Kang, Xilu Wang
bullets: Addresses redundant, low-quality branches in retrieval-based tree speculation that waste target-side verification computation.
Uses transfer-based supervision and a calibration-derived threshold from target-model greedy trajectories, requiring no parameter training.
Prunes a supplied candidate tree before verification and is compatible with existing tree-construction methods.
Reports up to 2.38× end-to-end speedup in retrieval-based settings and up to 2.78× when integrated with EAGLE-3 across the evaluated benchmarks.
Scope: evaluated on HumanEval, GSM8K, Dolly, and SpecBench; results are reported for greedy decoding.

A candidate tree Tx is supplied from Deval, while a lightweight draft model qϕ is calibrated on target greedy trajectories from Dcal to filter low-quality branches before target-side verification. The target model pθ then verifies the filtered subtree T filtered x with tree masking/attention and accepts the longest greedy-consistent prefix, producing the final output sequence Y under output-identical decoding.

papers.abstract: Vision and touch provide complementary cues for object pose and local contact geometry, but external cameras are often occluded at the contact site. We present GelSlim 5.0, a fingertip sensor that acquires visual and tactile observations with one fixed camera and a continuous UV-responsive contact layer. By switching illumination, the camera sequentially acquires through-membrane visual images and contact-sensitive tactile images from a shared viewpoint, avoiding inter-camera extrinsic calibration. To combine these observations, we introduce VisTacFusion, a multimodal transformer with separate prediction paths for planar object pose and contact geometry. Asymmetric bottleneck fusion incorporates visual context while preserving tactile spatial features for depth and surface-normal estimation. Modality dropout enables inference with paired inputs or either modality alone. On real validation data from 12 known objects, paired inputs reduce depth MSE, angular error, and translation $L_1$ by 61.2%, 72.3%, and 61.3%, respectively, relative to tactile-only inference with the same model. Relative to visual-only inference, the corresponding reductions are 93.7%, 6.1%, and 8.6%.
authors: Xiangdong Wang, I-Hsuan Huang, Xiaohao Xu, Xili Yi, Nima Fazeli, Xiaonan Huang
bullets: Addresses occlusion and calibration challenges caused by external cameras at contact sites.
Uses a fixed camera with a UV-responsive contact layer and switched illumination to capture visual and tactile images from one viewpoint.
VisTacFusion uses separate pose and contact-geometry prediction paths with asymmetric bottleneck fusion.
Modality dropout supports inference from paired inputs or either modality alone.

On 12 known objects, paired inputs substantially reduced depth, angular, and translation errors versus tactile-only and visual-only inference, with the largest gains over tactile-only depth and angular errors.

The geometry path retains tactile maps from blocks 3, 6, 9, and 12, applies gated conditioning from visual-context state B4, and decodes contact depth and surface normals with DPT. Calibration inputs, embeddings, and pre-normalized residual connections are omitted. Geometry thumbnails illustrate estimation targets; missing-input routing is defined in Sec. IV-E.

papers.abstract: Existing vision-language models (VLMs) remain unreliable for fine-grained visual perception. In this report, we present WeVisOne-VL (WeChat Vision All-in-One), a powerful VLM that unifies object-level and pixel-level perception through structured next-token prediction. It supports multiple visual tasks including object detection, referring localization, counting, OCR, segmentation, and matting, enabling localization at any user-specific granularity, from points and boxes to masks and alpha mattes. Architecturally, we integrate a lightweight pixel decoder into the VLM via a special token to generate instance-level pixel outputs. We train the model with a three-stage curriculum SFT followed by mixed-task RL. Across over 30 benchmarks, WeVisOne-VL demonstrates leading performance on both object-level and pixel-level tasks, while maintaining robust rejection for object-absent queries. By releasing WeVisOne-VL to the open-source community, we hope to advance VLMs from broad visual understanding toward truly reliable perception systems for real-world deployment.
authors: Tianming Liang, Junyi Pan, Yuxi Li, Canmiao Fu, Zhipeng Huang, Chong Sun, Chen Li, Jing Lyu
bullets: Targets the unreliability of existing VLMs in fine-grained visual perception.

Supports user-specified localization granularity, including points, boxes, masks, and alpha mattes.
Trained with a three-stage supervised fine-tuning curriculum followed by mixed-task reinforcement learning.
Reports leading performance across more than 30 benchmarks and robust rejection of object-absent queries; released open source.

papers.selection_reason: Unified vision-language model for object-level and pixel-level perception, fitting multimodal foundation model research.
papers.title: WeVisOne-VL: Unified Visual Perception from Objects to Pixels
papers.tldr: WeVisOne-VL unifies object- and pixel-level visual perception in one VLM, supporting tasks from detection and OCR to segmentation and matting.

papers.abstract: Local feature matching is typically formulated for image pairs, although structure-from-motion and visual localization commonly match one reference image against many retrieved or covisible neighbours. Applying a pairwise matcher independently to these centre-neighbour edges duplicates reference-side computation and prevents the matcher from exploiting complementary multi-view geometric evidence from the remaining observations. To address these limitations, we introduce MVLoMa, a sparse star-graph matcher that extends LoMa from image pairs to multiple views. MVLoMa first uses a frozen multi-view geometry model to jointly describe all images in a star, then injects the resulting cross-view geometric context into local descriptors. It then matches the centre image to all neighbours in a single forward pass through per-view self-attention and bidirectional centre-neighbour cross-attention. For supervision, we derive positive correspondences only from depth-valid, mutually visible dense warps and explicitly penalize high-confidence matches that violate epipolar geometry. On 25-view star graphs from HyperSim, ScanNet++, Mip-NeRF 360, and Tanks and Temples, MVLoMa obtains the best macro-average relative-pose AUC among the compared methods at all three thresholds (58.65/85.41/90.99). Its matcher is 2.20 times faster than sequential evaluation of the 24 centre-neighbour edges. The same design supports four tested frozen geometry encoders -- DA3, $\pi^3$, VGGT, and VGGT-$\Omega$ -- with DA3-Giant performing best on all reported encoder-ablation metrics. Controlled ablations further isolate the effects of geometry-aware descriptors, visibility filtering, geometric negative supervision, and joint multi-view inference.
authors: Xinyang Lu, Shengzhe Wei, Sheng Tang, Weiqi Zhang, Juntong Fang, Zesong Li
bullets: Addresses redundant reference-image computation and missed cross-view geometric evidence in pairwise matching.
Uses a frozen multi-view geometry model, geometry-aware local descriptors, and joint centre-to-neighbour attention.
Trains with depth-valid, mutually visible correspondences and penalties for epipolar-violating high-confidence matches.
On 25-view star graphs across four datasets, it achieves the best reported macro-average relative-pose AUC at all thresholds.
Runs 2.20× faster than sequentially matching the 24 centre-neighbour pairs; the design works with four frozen geometry encoders.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of MVLoMa. Given one source (centre) image and multiple target (neighbour) images, a trainable per-view VGG branch extracts local features, while a frozen multi-view geometry foundation model supplies geometry-aware patch features for the same views. A trainable convolutional refiner fuses the two streams into descriptors sampled at 4096 keypoints per image. The multi-view star-graph matcher then jointly processes the centre and all neighbours and outputs sparse centre–neighbour correspondences for every edge. Flames denote trainable modules and the snowflake denotes the frozen foundation model.
Table 7. Training data mixture for the final DA3-G model. MVS denotes multi-view stereo; Sample w. and Neg. w. are dataset-sampling and geometric negative-loss weights.

papers.title: MVLoMa: Multi-View Local Feature Matching with Any Geometry Foundation Model
papers.tldr: MVLoMa extends local feature matching from image pairs to multi-view star graphs, using shared geometry context for faster and more informed matching.

papers.abstract: 4D scene reconstruction requires robust handling of dynamic objects, yet existing streaming methods commonly assume static scenes, leading to pose drift and ghosting artifacts over long sequences. We introduce Stream4D, a training-free, motion-decoupled streaming reconstruction framework that can be directly integrated into causal Transformer backbones (e.g., StreamVGGT, Stream3R). Our key observation is that causal attention implicitly encodes rich temporal motion cues within the KV cache. We adaptively aggregate these cues from multiple attention layers and across temporal windows, and fuse them with depth priors to handle challenging cases such as occlusions and textureless regions, producing precise dynamic masks that decouple static and dynamic regions. We then apply a soft key masking scheme that leverages these dynamic masks to suppress interference from dynamic regions in causal attention, thereby improving camera pose estimation accuracy. Stream4D inherits the efficiency of causal attention and remains compatible with existing streaming architectures. On diverse dynamic-scene benchmarks, Stream4D significantly improves camera pose estimation and static-scene reconstruction quality, yields reliable dynamic masks, and effectively mitigates long-sequence ghosting.
authors: Wei Zhang, Ying Feng, Mengtong Wu, Shiqiang Gong, Huaqi Zhang, Qi Zhang
bullets: Addresses failures of static-scene assumptions in streaming reconstruction, especially long-sequence pose drift and ghosting.
Aggregates temporal motion cues from multiple causal-attention layers and windows, fusing them with depth priors to identify dynamic regions.
Uses soft key masking to suppress dynamic-region interference during camera pose estimation.
Integrates directly with causal Transformer backbones such as StreamVGGT and Stream3R while preserving streaming efficiency.
Improves camera poses, static-scene reconstruction, dynamic masks, and long-sequence ghosting on diverse dynamic-scene benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Streaming dynamic segmentation architecture. Left: standard causal streaming reconstruction with a KV Cache, where each frame attends only to past tokens. Right: our Stream4D augments the causal pipeline with motion-decoupled masking. Queries load cached keys/values to compute attention scores, aggregate temporal saliency across frames, and produce dynamic masks. These masks are then applied to modify the cached keys, effectively suppressing interference from dynamic regions during historical aggregation.

Figure 2: Streaming reconstruction overview. Each incoming frame is encoded into tokens and decoded with temporal causal attention that attends only to past frames via a KV Cache. The cache is incrementally updated with (K𝑡 ,V𝑡 ), enabling efficient online inference.

Figure 6: Ghosting suppression in streaming 4D reconstruction. Naïve causal streaming methods integrate geometry from all past frames, causing moving objects to be repeatedly fused into the scene and leaving stacked replicas along their trajectories (ghosting artifacts), which grow with sequence length and can eventually corrupt nearby static surfaces. In contrast, Stream4D derives training-free dynamic masks from causal attention cues and applies soft key masking to suppress dynamic regions in the KV cache, so that dynamic objects appear only in the current frame while the background remains clean and sharp even in long sequences.

Figure 7: Qualitative comparison of estimated camera trajectories on three DyCheck sequences (creeper, handwavy,mochi-highfive). We plot the predicted trajectory (solid blue) against the ground truth (dashed gray) in the 𝑥-𝑧 plane. Left: Stream3R exhibits noticeable drift and erratic deviations, particularly in sequences with large dynamic motion (handwavy, mochi-high-five), where moving objects corrupt the pose estimation. Right: our Stream4D produces trajectories that more closely follow the ground truth, demonstrating that motion-decoupled masking effectively mitigates the interference of dynamic regions on camera pose estimation.

Figure 5: Qualitative results on DAVIS dataset. Each panel shows the input frame, the Easi3R mask, and our Stream4D mask. Easi3R exhibits temporal jitter and boundary breaks under occlusions and non-rigid motions. Our streaming multi-level temporal aggregation with consistency constraints produces temporally smooth and spatially complete masks across slow motions (camel, goat, etc.) and fast motions (skateboarder, motorcyclist), demonstrating robust segmentation under causal KV-Cache attention.

Figure 8: Inference time comparison across different sequence lengths. While Easi3R exhibits exponential time growth and suffers from Out-of-Memory (OOM) errors between 100 and 200 frames, Stream4D maintains linear scalability, performing comparably to the efficient StreamVGGT baseline.

Figure 3: Temporal saliency aggregation and fusion visualization. We compare attention statistics across frames and layers: per-token mean and variance heatmaps revealing low-mean/high-variance patterns on dynamic objects; cross-frame attention maps highlighting temporal inconsistency; multi-scale attention fusion; and final fused saliency and binary masks.

Table 1: Dynamic object segmentation on DAVIS benchmarks. We report mean IoU (J𝑀 ) and IoU recall (J𝑅). “Type” indicates Offline vs. Streaming (single-pass, causal). ∗ indicates our adapted implementation with segmentation capability, as the original methods do not support segmentation.
Table 2: 4D reconstruction on DyCheck. We report pose metrics (ATE, RTE, RRE); lower is better. “Type” indicates Offline vs. Streaming (single-pass, causal).

papers.selection_reason: Streaming 4D reconstruction with motion decoupling via causal KV-cache attention, relevant to 3D/4D scene perception.
papers.title: Stream4D: Streaming 4D Reconstruction with Training-free Motion Decoupling via Causal KV-Cache Attention
papers.tldr: Stream4D enables training-free streaming 4D reconstruction by extracting motion cues from causal KV caches to separate dynamic regions and reduce pose drift and ghosting.

papers.abstract: Large language models can repeat an instruction while failing to keep obeying it. We study this recall-compliance dissociation in long-horizon dialogue and define State Integrity Collapse: a model preserves a stated constraint in memory but stops applying it to later turns. We introduce StateTrack-Bench, a controlled suite of conversations covering numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints. Across seven provider-pinned model snapshots and five dialogue-depth probes, strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with degradation concentrated in symbolic constraints and in one especially brittle model. A forked recall audit shows that 88.6% of observed failures are behavioral-drift failures rather than ordinary forgetting; excluding the brittle outlier preserves this diagnosis (84.4% of failures). Extended evaluations at depths up to 50 turns confirm that the dissociation persists beyond the core benchmark, while Structured State Anchoring recovers up to 24.4 points on immutable constraints. The results show that reliability cannot be inferred from single-turn instruction following alone; evaluation must track whether remembered constraints remain operational as dialogue state grows. Code and artifacts are available at: https://github.com/xzzvsxd/StateTrack.
authors: Yancheng Zhu, Yifan Yuan
bullets: The paper defines State Integrity Collapse: recall of a stated constraint remains intact while later behavior violates it.
StateTrack-Bench evaluates numerical, format, role/persona, factual-memory, and logical-rule constraints across dialogue depths and seven model snapshots.
Strict joint retention ranges from 62.4% to 100.0%, with failures concentrated in symbolic constraints and one particularly brittle model.
A forked recall audit attributes most failures to behavioral drift rather than ordinary forgetting; the effect persists through 50-turn dialogues.
Structured State Anchoring improves retention of immutable constraints by up to 24.4 points, though long-horizon reliability remains a concern.
