papers.selection_reason: Characterizes LLM constraint retention failures in long-horizon dialogues; relevant to long-context reliability and memory.
papers.title: When LLMs Forget What They Believe: Characterizing State Integrity Collapse in Long-Horizon Dialogues
papers.tldr: Long-horizon dialogue can cause LLMs to remember constraints but stop following them, revealing a distinct state-integrity failure that targeted anchoring can partially mitigate.

papers.abstract: Scaling embedding capacity alongside Transformer computation is an emerging trend in language models. This trend makes high compression rates increasingly useful. Hence, we study extreme compression of Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which follow this trend and account for 35.2% of the parameters of Gemma 4 E4B. At such rates, conventional quantizers give each token-layer vector its own code of only a few bytes. We instead develop OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes), which stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at every layer with a layer-specific affine decoder. Codes and decoders are fitted to the PLE output path rather than to the stored vectors. At about $100\times$ PLE compression of bfloat16 (BF16) E4B, OPTIC retains an aggregate 97.8% of the uncompressed model's performance across seven benchmarks, whereas product quantization, the strongest of six conventional baselines, retains 66.3%. At $594\times$ and $1,002\times$ PLE compression of BF16 E4B, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. On the official E4B release with 4-bit linear weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about $100\times$ PLE compression. During inference at about $100\times$ PLE compression, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory than with uncompressed PLE at the same key-value cache size, while running at most 0.40% slower.
authors: Jiacheng Liu, Yaxin Luo, Xiaohan Zhao, Peng Sun, Xinyi Shang, Jiacheng Cui, Yonina C. Eldar, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Per-layer embeddings account for 35.2% of Gemma 4 E4B’s parameters, motivating extreme compression.
OPTIC stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at each layer using layer-specific affine decoders.
It fits codes and decoders to the model’s output path rather than directly to stored embedding vectors.
At about 100× BF16 PLE compression, OPTIC retains 97.8% aggregate performance across seven benchmarks, versus 66.3% for the strongest conventional baseline.
At the same compression level, inference uses 29.7% less GPU memory and runs at most 0.40% slower; performance remains 84.1% at 1,002× compression.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Rate–retention curves on BF16 Gemma 4 E4B, normalized to the uncompressed PLE. Dashed curves show the PQ and OPQ-P baselines, and solid curves show our methods. OPTIC retains 97.8% near 100×, and its advantage over the shown baselines remains large at higher compression ratios. A zero geometric mean means that at least one task scored zero.

Figure 1: One shared code per token serves all PLE layers. Token t retrieves its stored codebook indices and its input embedding. Each index qtm selects the highlighted codeword of codebook Cm. Concatenating these codewords forms one shared latent zt, from which each affine decoder reconstructs its layer’s PLE row. Matching colors identify corresponding layers, and ellipses mark omitted layers and codebooks. Each cell of E contains a d-dimensional vector. The original PLE is used only for fitting, with frozen gates and projections (Equation 4). The frozen backbone shows the PLE residual connections and omits attention and feed-forward operations.

Figure 3: Cumulative share of each layer’s tokenspecific variation captured by its leading principal directions in the original BF16 E4B PLE table, with every token in the vocabulary weighted equally, in the stored coordinates (top) and at the PLE projection output (bottom). papers.selection_reason: Introduces cross-layer latent vector quantization for extreme per-layer embedding compression, directly reducing LLM memory footprint.
papers.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
papers.tldr: OPTIC enables roughly 100× compression of per-layer embeddings while preserving most of the model’s benchmark performance and reducing inference memory with minimal slowdown.

papers.abstract: GUI agents aim to automate complex user tasks by interacting with mobile interfaces, but ef- fective decision-making in long-horizon set- tings requires reusing prior experience rather than relying solely on the environment ob- servations. Existing memory-based methods typically store experience either at the single- action level or as entire trajectories. Single- step actions are often too fine-grained to carry meaningful semantics, since the success of an individual action does not necessarily imply progress towards the overall goal. In contrast, whole trajectories are often too coarse-grained and difficult to reuse across different tasks. We propose a subgoal-aware memory graph that distils past trajectories into structured, reusable evidence at the level of subgoals. We define a subgoal as consecutive actions shar- ing a single intent, the granularity at which progress toward the task becomes meaning- ful. To reduce redundancy and support cross- task reuse, we organise subgoal experiences as nodes in a graph, where related memories can be merged, extended, and retrieved based on the environment observation. On SPA-Bench, our method improves success rate by 11.11% over the baseline.
authors: Dezhao Luo, Daniel Beechey, Derek Yuen, Weilin Luo
bullets: Single-action memories are too fine-grained, while whole-trajectory memories are too coarse and hard to reuse.
The method defines subgoals as consecutive actions sharing one intent.
Past trajectories are distilled into graph nodes representing reusable subgoal experiences.
Related memories can be merged, extended, and retrieved using the current environment observation.
Evaluation on SPA-Bench shows an 11.11% success-rate improvement over the baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed subgoal-aware memory framework. Past trajectories are segmented into annotated subgoals and fused into a graph over shared visual states.

Figure 1: The same subgoal can succeed (left) or fail (right) depending on the underlying behaviour. Subgoal granularity exposes progress toward the user goal that is invisible at the single-action level.
Table 1: Per-attempt success rate. Our subgoal-graph memory outperforms both the no-memory baseline and flat / alternative-granularity variants.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes subgoal-level memory graph for reusing interaction experience in GUI agents.
papers.title: Subgoal-aware Memory Graph for GUI Agent
papers.tldr: A subgoal-aware memory graph helps GUI agents reuse meaningful segments of past experience for long-horizon mobile tasks, improving SPA-Bench success by 11.11% over a baseline.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical language generation separates continuous semantic modeling from discrete text realization, but its effectiveness depends on what the latent space compresses and how the discrete generator uses it. We propose Cola2, a framework that jointly studies continuous semantic compression, the balance between reconstruction and generation, and continuous-discrete co-adaptation. Cola2 dynamically segments text into semantic spans, controls the compression rate through auxiliary-loss-free negative feedback, and combines reconstruction and generation supervision to learn compact, predictive latent representations. A block-causal masked diffusion decoder is trained with clean, noisy, and dropped latent conditions, while classifier-free guidance adjusts the balance between semantic reconstruction and autonomous generation. Token-prediction gradients update the encoder through the latents, whereas Flow Matching prior learning is decoupled from representation learning by stop-gradient. During inference, generated text is re-encoded under a fixed span layout to keep the latent history consistent with the actual text context. Experiments on five downstream tasks with about 210 billion training tokens validate the core designs and show competitive, unsaturated scaling. With 346.03 billion source tokens, an unconverged checkpoint reaches a 60.10 average across eight tasks and surpasses Llama-3-8B on HellaSwag and StoryCloze despite its reported pretraining budget being over 43 times larger. These results demonstrate the potential of continuous-latent hierarchical language generation.
authors: Hongcan Guo, Yian Zhao, Feng Wang, Shen Nie, Guoqiang Wei, Yan Zeng, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Dynamically segments text into semantic spans and regulates compression with auxiliary-loss-free negative feedback.
Combines reconstruction and generation supervision to produce compact, predictive latent representations.
Uses a block-causal masked diffusion decoder with clean, noisy, and dropped latent conditions, plus classifier-free guidance.
Maintains latent-context consistency at inference by re-encoding generated text under a fixed span layout.
Validated across five downstream tasks and about 210B training tokens; results indicate competitive, still-unsaturated scaling and strong performance on HellaSwag and StoryCloze.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Method overview. Stage 1 jointly trains the compression encoder and the reconstruction–generation balanced decoder; Stage 2 additionally trains a DiT on detached latents; at inference, the DiT generates latents block by block and the decoder decodes them into tokens.
Figure 3 VAE architecture. Left: the allocation of encoder layers matters more than depth, with 0+2+2 performing best. Right: intra-span bidirectional attention is the best pooling operator.

Figure 2 Segmentation and rate control. Dynamic segmentation outperforms fixed-length and random segmentation; auxiliary-free negative-feedback control outperforms DLCM [39].

papers.abstract: Memory enables language agents to carry useful distinctions from past experience into future decisions. Its value depends on which distinctions survive, whether a bounded agent can use them, and what can be recovered or revised as demands evolve. We develop a decision-theoretic framework that follows this value from raw history through persistent state, operational use, and costly recovery and revision. Original and retained value are expressed in units of avoided task loss; risk-cost frontiers describe attainable recovery and preservation across uses. Unknown demand yields value profiles, while interactive feedback changes the distribution of future work. A cost-aware simulation condition and five minimal counterexamples expose the roles of information timing, retrieval access, component interaction, feedback and demand uncertainty. In particular, a pointer with zero mutual information about the answer can still reduce the cost of exact recovery. Diagnostics on LoCoMo, a two-project update task and longitudinal cases exhibit failures of preservation, use and measurement. At fixed retrieved evidence, a saved ledger changes subsequent answers; at fixed agent outputs, an evaluator revision changes scores. The framework connects these distinctions to operational risk bounds and testable principles for allocating memory, preserving recovery options and revising evidence dependencies.

papers.abstract: Exoskeletons have shown great potential for augmenting human physical capabilities, yet generating reliable assistance remains challenging because human motion patterns and interaction requirements vary substantially in practice. To address this problem, a dual-loop assistance strategy is proposed to couple multimodal exoskeleton trajectory generation with variable admittance control, where trajectory variance links the outer-loop generator and the inner-loop controller. The generator synthesizes future exoskeleton trajectories through denoising, primarily using whole-body human motion and exoskeleton proprioception, with task descriptions as auxiliary semantic cues. To reduce cross-modal representation mismatch, a three-stage training pipeline is introduced to progressively optimize the human motion encoder, the exoskeleton proprioception encoder, and the trajectory generator. In the inner loop, multiple future trajectories are sampled from the generator to estimate the trajectory mean and variance. The mean is used as the control reference, while the variance provides an uncertainty measure for prediction reliability. This measure is further incorporated into a stiffness regulation law, enabling compliant assistance with input-to-state stability under bounded lumped interaction input. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces muscle activation levels compared with standard baselines, while also decreasing users' metabolic energy expenditure relative to the unassisted condition.

Experiments report reduced muscle activation versus standard baselines and lower metabolic energy expenditure than unassisted use.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing physically grounded dexterous hand-object interactions is important for VR/AR, gaming, and robotics, yet remains challenging because subtle contact dynamics, diverse object geometries, and target trajectories must be jointly respected while maintaining natural grasps. Existing methods either track mocap trajectories with limited transfer to novel objects, or rely on hand-only generative priors that fail to capture coupled hand-object motion, sacrificing contact fidelity and sample efficiency. To tackle these challenges, we introduce PiHand, a Physically grounded Interaction-aware Hand motion synthesis framework. PiHand first trains expert policies that track mocap demonstrations in simulation, distills them into a unified hand-object interaction prior using a goal-conditioned VAE, and finally solve diverse dexterous manipulation tasks through bounded residual exploration in its latent space. With only a single reward and no complex curriculum training, this yields general tabletop manipulation policies that generalize to unseen objects and trajectories on GRAB and DexYCB. The same prior transfers to object catching and bimanual handover, two tasks that are rarely seen in its training data. Across all tasks, PiHand consistently outperforms baselines in all metrics. We will release the processed data and model checkpoints.

Reports consistent improvement over baselines across all evaluated metrics; data and checkpoints are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Long egocentric videos pose a central challenge for multimodal language models: the visual stream must be compressed into a memory representation that can be searched efficiently while still preserving the evidence needed for question answering. Building on an online textual-memory framework in which first-person videos are converted into temporally grounded captions, this work systematically studies the role of retrieval in episodic-memory video question answering. We evaluate how different retrieval units, query formulations, context budgets, and reranking strategies affect multiple-choice answering on QAEgo4D-Closed, isolating retrieval as the main variable while keeping the underlying generated memory fixed. Our best configuration, Parent, matches fine-grained caption subchunks, then provides their full parent captions to the reasoner. It achieves 56.4 % accuracy, matching strong full-memory and retrieval baselines while exposing only a small fraction of the textual memory at question time. More importantly, our analysis shows that better temporal coverage does not necessarily translate into better answers: increasing the retrieval budget improves temporal Hit@K and Recall@K, but can reduce accuracy by introducing visually plausible distractors and uncertain caption evidence. These findings suggest that retrieval-augmented egocentric memory should not be optimized only for evidence recall, but also for the reliability, specificity, and answer-discriminative value of the retrieved context. The study motivates more structured episodic memories that move beyond raw caption retrieval toward evidence-aware representations for long-form egocentric reasoning.
authors: Raffaele Cali, Giuseppe Lando, Rosario Forte, Antonino Furnari
bullets: Evaluates retrieval units, query formulations, context budgets, and reranking while keeping the generated textual memory fixed.

Larger retrieval budgets improve temporal Hit@K and Recall@K but can hurt accuracy by adding distractors and uncertain evidence.
Results motivate structured, evidence-aware episodic memories beyond raw caption retrieval.

papers.abstract: Training-free personalization adapts a frozen vision-language model (VLM) to recognize user-defined concepts from only a few exemplars by retrieving concept entries at inference time. While recent retriever-based methods enrich each concept with descriptive evidence, they largely treat concepts in isolation, so the retrieved information can be plausible yet non-discriminative, especially when the personalized concept set contains highly confusable, fine-grained categories. We argue that personalization is inherently relational: correct recognition depends on the specific distinctions between a concept and its nearest alternatives. To this end, we propose ReCoG, a Relational Concept Graph for retrieval-augmented personalization. ReCoG represents concepts as nodes and augments them with directed edges that explicitly capture discriminative cues between concept pairs, elicited by a frozen VLM during database construction. At inference, ReCoG retrieves a shortlist and resolves ambiguity via explicit pairwise comparisons conditioned on the corresponding relational edges, selecting the concept that consistently wins against competing candidates. We also introduce FINGER benchmark to test personalized recognition on confusable concept sets. Across FINGER, ReCoG substantially outperforms prior methods, with the largest gains in the most confusable regimes. ReCoG also achieves consistently best performance on established personalization benchmarks including captioning and VQA, confirming that relational evidence is broadly beneficial beyond fine-grained settings. authors: Changseon Yu, Hyeokjun Kweon
bullets: Addresses the weakness of treating personalized concepts independently, which can produce plausible but non-discriminative retrievals.

Introduces the FINGER benchmark for personalized recognition on confusable concept sets.
Reports strong gains on FINGER, especially in highly confusable settings, and best performance on established captioning and VQA personalization benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Real robot data, rich across tasks and morphologies, is often treated as the bottleneck for training robot learning models, including embodied foundation models that aim for zero-shot physical transfer. In this paper, we investigate the degree to which such models can acquire necessary structure using data from systems without embodiment. To this end, we test if inexpensive, procedurally generated synthetic data can yield useful priors before a model observes any real-world behavior. We study this through robot action prediction, a natural pretraining objective and a direct test of whether structure learned from arbitrary synthetic tasks transfers to embodied settings. We introduce three data generation pipelines that model mathematical abstractions of robotic control, and use them as pretraining priors for a Transformer. We demonstrate that a model trained purely on this non-robotic data attains non-trivial zero-shot prediction performance on unseen physical robot tasks via an in-context learning mechanism, and that our specialized control priors notably improve upon generic causal priors. We also compare against a compute-matched baseline trained on real robot data, and find that it outperforms our model but only on the datasets it was trained on. These findings suggest that procedurally generated, mathematical abstractions can yield useful robotic priors, offering a potential complement to expensive embodied data collection.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models have shown promising performance in computer-use tasks, from planning user workflows to grounding natural-language actions to precise UI targets. Existing end-to-end benchmarks primarily emphasize long-horizon task completion, while GUI grounding benchmarks remain focused on conventional controls and a limited set of professional interfaces. We introduce POINTERBENCH, a diagnostic suite of 1,500 screenshot-instruction pairs probing three complementary capabilities: thin sub-element identification and geometric grounding in spreadsheets (POINTERBENCH-Sheets), character-level grounding in long-text documents (POINTERBENCH-Text), and mixed GUI grounding across 100 professional applications (POINTERBENCH-Pro). We carefully curate each task with pixel-exact target geometry and evaluate both general-purpose multimodal models and 39 specialist GUI grounding configurations. We find text grounding to be the most challenging setting, with Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and the leading native specialist UI-Venus-2-9B achieving 69.6%, 53.4%, and 25.8% success on POINTERBENCH-Text despite respective 83.2%, 77.7%, and 54.5% average success across POINTERBENCH. These results reveal substantial headroom in fine-grained GUI grounding across frontier and specialist models. We publicly release the benchmark and evaluation code at https://github.com/warmwindOS/pointerbench.

papers.abstract: Memory enables language model assistants to maintain continuity across sessions and generate personalized responses, but knowing more about a user does not necessarily produce responses they prefer. Existing evaluations assess memory capabilities without directly establishing whether memory use benefits the user. To study this gap, we collect approximately 1,000 pairwise judgments from 87 participants using their own ChatGPT queries and personal memories. We find that memory-conditioned responses are not consistently preferred over responses generated without memory and in some cases, users strongly prefer the latter. Automatic evaluators also show limited agreement with users and favor memory-conditioned responses substantially more often than users do. Motivated by these gaps, we introduce a memory-aware reward model that learns from user judgments, achieving 72.8\% preference prediction accuracy and outperforming the existing baselines. Our findings motivate evaluation and optimization objectives that align memory use with the preferences of the people whose information is being used.
authors: Yijiang River Dong, Zexue He, Cheng Yu, Tiancheng Hu, Michael J Ryan, Jan Batzner, Zheng Hui, Shaolong Wu, Orestis Papakyriakopoulos, Alex Pentland, Nigel Collier, Jiaxin Pei
bullets: Collected about 1,000 pairwise judgments from 87 participants using personal queries and memories.
Users sometimes strongly preferred responses generated without memory.
Automatic evaluators often favored memory-conditioned responses more than users did and showed limited agreement.
Introduced a memory-aware reward model trained on user preferences, reaching 72.8% preference-prediction accuracy and outperforming existing baselines.
The study supports aligning memory use with individual user preferences rather than assuming more memory is better.

papers.selection_reason: Studies user preferences for LLM memory-conditioned responses and trains a memory-aware reward model; directly fits LLM memory.
papers.title: Memory-Aware Reward Modeling: Learning Human Preferences for LLM Memory Use
papers.tldr: Memory use does not reliably improve user-preferred responses, motivating reward models trained on direct judgments of when memory helps.

papers.abstract: Search is a central component of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems and has been deeply investigated for classical ASR modeling based on Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). However, in work on current sequence-to-sequence ASR architectures it is often simplified to a small fixed-size beam search without external Language Model (LM). In this work, we present a comparative analysis of search space complexity and efficiency for Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) and neural transducer models under different pruning strategies and LM configurations. We show that these end-to-end (E2E) models work with a small search space most of the time but exhibit large temporary peaks in hypothesis count during periods of uncertainty. Score-based pruning dynamically adapts the search to model uncertainty, leading to a significantly lower Real-Time Factor (RTF). Our results highlight the limitations of search with low fixed-size beam pruning and provide practical guidelines for efficient search in E2E ASR.
authors: Simon Berger, Larissa Kleppel, Ralf Schl\"uter
bullets: Analyzes search-space complexity and efficiency in CTC and neural-transducer ASR models.
Evaluates different pruning strategies and external language-model configurations.
Finds that hypothesis counts are usually small but can temporarily grow substantially during uncertain speech segments.
Shows that score-based pruning adapts to uncertainty and substantially reduces real-time factor.
Provides practical guidance and identifies limitations of fixed-size beam search.

papers.selection_reason: ASR search-space pruning and efficiency analysis fits efficient AI's latency-reduction scope.
papers.title: A Systematic Comparison of Search Space Complexity and Efficiency for Time-Synchronous End-to-End ASR Models
papers.tldr: A comparative study shows that adaptive score-based pruning makes CTC and neural-transducer ASR search more efficient than low fixed-size beams, especially during uncertainty spikes.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have shown strong performance across diverse tasks, but their reliance on self-attention mechanisms often leads to high computational costs. Token sparsification, which reduces the number of tokens processed in transformer layers, offers a promising solution to maintain performance while improving efficiency. However, although widely studied in the vision and language domains, token sparsification remains underexplored in audio, with existing work often limited to a single method, model size, or dataset. This work presents a comprehensive evaluation of token sparsification techniques for audio transformers. We assess a range of token pruning and merging strategies across multiple datasets and model sizes, under both post-training and fine-tuning settings. Furthermore, we introduce a novel sparsification approach that combines attention scores with spectral cues derived from the frequency content of token embeddings. Our experiments show that frequency-aware approaches, particularly those based on spectral flatness and low-frequency energy, consistently outperform attention-only methods. We also find that sparsification based on spectrogram patch intensity is especially effective for longer audio inputs. These results highlight the value of incorporating frequency-domain and input-specific information into sparsification strategies to enhance performance in audio tasks.
authors: Shreya Sajid, Fabrizio Julian Piva, Hiram Rayo Torres Rodriguez, Elif Ceren Gok Yildirim, Murat Onur Yildirim, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Audio token sparsification is less explored than in vision and language, motivating a broader evaluation.
The study compares token pruning and merging across multiple datasets, model sizes, and post-training or fine-tuning settings.
It introduces a method combining attention scores with spectral cues from token-embedding frequency content.
Spectral-flatness and low-frequency-energy methods consistently outperform attention-only sparsification.
Spectrogram patch intensity is especially effective for longer audio inputs.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Post-training sparsification results on the AST-Base (Gong et al., 2021) model, evaluated on AudioSet-20K (Gemmeke et al., 2017) at a 50% keep rate. Methods that include frequencydomain cues, such as the proposed Spectral Flatness (SF) and the adapted Low-Frequency Energy (LFE) (Wang et al., 2022b), outperform others in terms of mean average precision (mAP), a standard metric for multi-label classification. The baseline (without sparsification) achieves an average mAP of 0.3572. The Pareto front is highlighted to illustrate the performance-efficiency tradeoff.

Figure 8. Performance comparison of frequency-based methods (LFE and SF) against attention-only baselines (TopK-Wt and TopK-CLS). SF slightly but consistently outperforms attention-based baselines across keep rates, while LFE shows competitive results but occasionally underperforms on ESC50 and AS-20K.

Figure 7. Sparsified Fine-tuning: Performance across varying keep rates. Frequency-based methods (SF, LFE), as well as pure attention-based pruning methods (Top-K, EViT), consistently maintain high performance across tasks. Most methods retain competitive performance down to a 50% keep rate. Overall, the performance differences between methods are not very significant, indicating that multiple sparsification methods can be equally effective when fine-tuned.

Figure 9. Token pruning performance as a function of input duration. Intensity Pruning consistently outperforms Top-K pruning for longer audio windows (> 2 seconds), suggesting that spectrogram intensity is a more informative proxy for longer audio samples.

Figure 3. Low-frequency Energy token pruning. Token embeddings are transformed to the frequency domain, where a Gaussian low-pass filter highlights low-frequency structure. The resulting energy scores are fused with attention scores to guide top-K token selection.

Figure 4. Spectral flatness-guided token pruning. Token embeddings undergo Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) along the embedding dimension to compute spectral flatness, capturing tonal richness. These scores are combined with CLS attention to rank token importance.

Figure 2. Intensity-guided token pruning. Tokens are divided into high- (H) and low- (L) intensity groups based on an applied threshold. The high-intensity set is then ranked using CLS attention scores, and the Top-K tokens are selected. If fewer than K tokens are available in H , the remaining slots are filled from the low-intensity set.

papers.selection_reason: Systematic study of token pruning and merging for audio transformers, directly matching token sparsification and efficiency interests.
papers.title: Muting Tokens: Exploring Token Sparsification for Efficient Audio Transformers
papers.tldr: A comprehensive study shows that frequency- and input-aware token sparsification can make audio transformers more efficient while preserving stronger performance than attention-only methods.

papers.abstract: Real-time polyp segmentation in computer-assisted colonoscopy is hampered by the difficulty of deploying high-accuracy models under strict latency budgets. Frame skipping, which performs inference every K frames and reuses or interpolates the rest, improves throughput but introduces motion blur and lesion misalignment that degrade temporal consistency. To close this gap, we propose the Lightweight Frame Compensator (LFC), a 77K-parameter plug-and-play module inserted before a frozen segmentation backbone. Operating on a three-frame window, LFC fuses consecutive frames via spatio-temporal attention into a single compensated frame, and is trained only on pseudo-labels generated by a differently seeded model, without any expert annotation. Experiments on three polyp video benchmarks show that LFC recovers most of the accuracy degraded by direct frame skipping and, in several settings, reaches the accuracy of frame-by-frame inference, while retaining a 2.05X--2.55X throughput gain. We further evaluate the temporal stability of three backbones spanning CNN, pyramid Transformer, and global-attention Transformer architectures, revealing a spectrum of sensitivity to frame skipping that arises from how locally or globally each architecture aggregates misaligned input. The compensation gain of LFC follows this spectrum: it is largest for high-capacity Transformer backbones, which achieve the best static accuracy but suffer the most under skip-frame inference. LFC thus offers a lightweight, pluggable, and deployment-friendly route to real-time polyp segmentation.
authors: Weihao Gao
bullets: Addresses motion blur and lesion misalignment caused by skipping frames during real-time colonoscopy segmentation.
Uses a 77K-parameter, plug-and-play module before a frozen backbone to fuse a three-frame window with spatio-temporal attention.
Trains solely on pseudo-labels from a differently seeded model, requiring no expert annotations.
Across three polyp-video benchmarks, often matches frame-by-frame accuracy and recovers most skipping-related degradation.
Benefits high-capacity Transformer backbones most, as they are more sensitive to misaligned skipped-frame inputs.

papers.abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) aims to recover well-exposed and perceptually faithful images from severely degraded observations. Recent diffusion-based generative methods achieve strong perceptual quality by leveraging powerful image priors, but their iterative sampling incurs substantial computational cost, limiting practical deployment. Despite recent efficiency gains in generative LLIE, high-quality enhancement with a single function evaluation and low overall computation remains challenging, particularly under diverse real-world low-light conditions. We introduce GLOW-FM, a one-step latent flow-matching framework for efficient generative LLIE. GLOW-FM performs conditional transport in the latent space of a frozen Tiny-VAE and leverages Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM) to enable enhancement with a single function evaluation. Matched comparisons with alternative one-step objectives support TVM as an effective design choice, and, to the best of our knowledge, this is its first adaptation to image restoration and specifically to LLIE. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world benchmarks demonstrate that GLOW-FM achieves competitive image quality and state-of-the-art cross-dataset generalization while requiring only a single function evaluation and 34 GFLOPs for the small variant. These findings highlight the potential of GLOW-FM to bring generative LLIE closer to practical deployment through single-step inference and compact latent modeling. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.
authors: Ariel Lapid, Yuval Haitman, Reuven Peretz, Arnon Netzer, Idit Diamant
bullets: Targets the high cost of iterative diffusion-based enhancement under diverse real-world low-light conditions.
Performs conditional transport in the latent space of a frozen Tiny-VAE.
Uses Terminal Velocity Matching (TVM) to support one-step inference.
Experiments on challenging real-world benchmarks show competitive quality and state-of-the-art cross-dataset generalization.
The small variant requires 34 GFLOPs and one function evaluation; code is planned for public release.

papers.abstract: We envision a general-purpose protein foundation model as a unified, interactive model of sequence, structure, and function, capable of understanding, generation, and cross-modal translation while retaining the instruction-following and reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs. Toward this vision, we introduce Trion-1, the first native, unified, multimodal diffusion language model (dLLM) for proteins. Trion-1 is built on two key design choices: (1) a unified discrete token space that jointly represents sequence, structure, and natural language; (2) a dLLM backbone that replaces strict left-to-right factorization with bidirectional or semi-bidirectional token interactions, enabling global residue communication and long-range contact modeling that are naturally suited to structure modeling. This formulation unifies six core capabilities: folding, inverse folding, sequence understanding, structure understanding, sequence design, and structure design, while retaining the native language capabilities of general-purpose LLMs. On established benchmarks, Trion-1 achieves broadly competitive performance. In folding, Trion-1 achieves a TM-score above 0.8 with a single sample under strict homology control, matching or exceeding the existing tri-modal model using 200 samples. For sequence understanding, Trion-1 performs on par with top-tier LLMs such as Claude Opus 4.7 (62.37%). These results support well-aligned sequence-structure-language representations and strong cross-modal generative capabilities.
authors: Tianyu Lu, Kaicheng Yang, Jiangtao Feng, Keyue Qiu, Yawen Ouyang, Yixin Wu, Xinbo Zhang, Lihao Wang, Wei-Ying Ma, Hao Zhou

Reports competitive benchmark performance, including a single-sample folding TM-score above 0.8 under strict homology control.

papers.abstract: Moving object segmentation is conventionally formulated at the sequence and object level, marking an entire instance as moving once it moves anywhere in a video. Recent instantaneous formulations distinguish moving from stationary intervals, but still generate masks at the object level through frozen segmentation foundation models. Because the mask is derived from an instance-level proposal, motion is typically attributed to the entire instance rather than localized to the regions that actually move. Moreover, such instance-level predictions can produce masks even when no part of the instance is actually moving, revealing a more fundamental issue: motion is not an intrinsic property of an instance; it can only be determined by comparing at least two frames. Building on this premise, we introduce MoRSe, which jointly interprets two frames to predict a moving-region mask, distinguishing actual scene motion from apparent motion induced by the camera. A single RGB encoder replaces multi-stage foundation stacks, so no optical flow, point tracks, or separate mask generator is needed at inference. We release MoRSe-5K, a benchmark of 42 sequences with Static, Dynamic-Static, and Dynamic settings designed to evaluate the model's ability to distinguish and localize moving and stationary regions under different camera and scene motion conditions. MoRSe outperforms both specialized moving object segmentation methods and dense 4D reconstruction methods with motion-thresholded predictions, while producing the fewest false positives on sequences where nothing moves.
authors: Wenhua Jin, Tiancheng Chen, Sheng Tang, Jiahao Li, Yupeng Liu, Weiqi Zhang, Juntong Fang, Zesong Li
bullets: Existing instance-level methods label an entire object as moving even when only part moves—or when nothing moves.
MoRSe treats motion as a relational property requiring comparison between frames.
A single RGB encoder predicts moving-region masks without optical flow, point tracks, or separate mask-generation stages.
MoRSe-5K contains 42 sequences spanning Static, Dynamic-Static, and Dynamic motion settings.
It outperforms specialized and motion-thresholded reconstruction baselines, with the fewest false positives on static sequences.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MoRSe architecture. Both frames pass jointly through a UniQuery4R-initialized ViT and a shallow convolutional branch; the two are fused and split into source and target feature pyramids. A camera head reads the ViT camera tokens and predicts per-view pose and field of view as auxiliary outputs that never enter the mask path. Sampled source coordinates form the decoder queries; target features provide keys and values, and four cross-attention blocks refine each query before a shared MLP predicts the motion logit.

Figure 4: Moving regions under a moving camera. Top (Static): the camera moves while the person stands still; every baseline paints the whole person, while MoRSe leaves the frame empty. Bottom (Dynamic-Static): only the child’s hand moves; MoRSe marks that hand alone, whereas the baselines cover the whole child.

Figure 1: Motion is a pair relation, not an object property. Motion needs two observations, so we condition on an ordered source–target pair. Holding the source fixed and advancing the target through the sequence, MoRSe returns an empty mask while the person stands still, then the moving region alone when only an arm lifts, then the whole body once it walks. GMOS marks the same person in every frame, whatever the target.
Figure 3: Inference granularity. Target selection sets the granularity without changing the weights: one pair, a target window, or a promptable segmenter.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.
authors: Ronald Fecso, Jos\'e Morano, Botond Fazekas, Paul Widmann-Sedlnitzky, Dorota Himel, Laetita Hinterhuber, Virginia Mares, Andreas Pollreisz, Hrvoje Bogunovi\'c
bullets: Introduces RetinaGroundBench, the first retinal OCT benchmark for biomarker visual grounding.
Contains 815 ophthalmologist-annotated B-scans, 4,537 bounding boxes, 13 biomarkers, and 8 diseases.
Proposes AggIoU to evaluate fragmented predictions by measuring coverage of the union of overlapping boxes.
Across 27 open-source MLLMs, grounding remains weak despite stronger biomarker-presence classification.
RetGrounder raises grounding F1 from 23.7% for the best general-purpose model to 33.9%.

papers.abstract: While arousal can be reliably predicted from musical audio, emotional valence remains difficult to model due to its subjective and context-dependent nature. In this work, we investigate the potential of in-context learning (ICL) with large language models to advance continuous valence and arousal prediction. Rather than predicting emotion scores directly, our framework leverages contextual demonstrations from an auxiliary dataset to refine the initial predictions produced by a small, task-specific base model. We systematically evaluate a text-based ICL variant using lyrics and generated audio captions, alongside a multimodal variant that incorporates raw audio signals. Using the entire MER60 dataset strictly as a held-out test set, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains, particularly for valence. Text-based ICL improves the valence $R^2$ from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 demonstration shots, while the multimodal variant achieves 0.346 with only 10 shots. These findings suggest that training-free ICL offers an effective inference-time strategy for current language models to predict continuous music emotion.
authors: Chi-En Dai, Chih-Pin Tan, Yi-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of predicting subjective, context-dependent musical valence alongside arousal.
Uses auxiliary-dataset demonstrations to refine predictions from a task-specific base model rather than predicting emotion scores directly.
Evaluates text-based ICL with lyrics and generated audio captions, and multimodal ICL with raw audio.
On the held-out MER60 test set, text ICL raises valence R² from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 shots; multimodal ICL reaches 0.346 with 10 shots.
Results support training-free, inference-time ICL as a strategy for continuous music-emotion prediction.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) introduce unique quantization challenges due to their iterative denoising process. In this work, we reveal that quantization sensitivity is both taskand time-dependent, with different downstream tasks exhibiting distinct precision requirements across denoising steps. We further show that these patterns can be predicted without groundtruth labels or task-specific evaluation metrics. Building on these findings, we introduce T 2Quant, a task and time-aware mixedprecision quantization framework that uses a label-free sensitivity signal to optimally allocate activation precision across denoising steps under a fixed bit-width budget. Extensive experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks demonstrate that T 2Quant consistently improves the average accuracy of existing quantization methods, achieving gains of up to 6.7 percentage points under the same budget.
authors: Ofek Avivi, Eliron Rahimi, Avi Mendelson, Chaim Baskin
bullets: Quantization sensitivity varies by both downstream task and denoising timestep.
These sensitivity patterns can be predicted without ground-truth labels or task-specific evaluation metrics.
T²Quant allocates activation precision across timesteps under a fixed bit-width budget.
Experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks improve existing quantization methods by up to 6.7 percentage points in average accuracy.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque. We introduce Inside-JEPA, which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and shows that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state. On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065-.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050-.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking. An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels. Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs .621). For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.
authors: Hossein Resani, Javen Qinfeng Shi
bullets: Latent prediction alone does not ground relational channels beyond random performance.
An inverse-dynamics head that reads relational-channel changes improves relational AUROC across video, robot, and tracked-object settings.
Using entity latents alone decodes actions better but provides little relational grounding, highlighting the importance of channel-specific supervision.
Grounded channels can predict future relational changes nearly as well as observed relations and support one-step action selection.
The approach relies on entity detections or tracking and evaluates a fixed set of relational channels and tasks.

papers.abstract: Metadata-conditioned generation is often framed as a data-to-text task in which additional input fields should improve grounding. Museum description generation challenges this assumption because catalogue records are heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across geographic regions. We study how metadata composition shapes the generation of artefact descriptions through a two-phase framework. Phase 1 analyses natural metadata variation in a large museum collection, where field count, field type, image availability, and Place co-vary. Phase 2 introduces controlled field probes that hold object identity fixed while varying metadata quantity, field type, and image access. Our results show that metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behaviour. Field type determines whether models ground, omit, or infer information, while images can both support visual grounding and increase unsupported interpretation. More broadly, our findings show that metadata-conditioned data-to-text evaluation should assess field- and claim-level support, rather than relying only on aggregate input coverage or reference similarity.
authors: Clemencia Siro, Laura Hollink
bullets: Museum catalogue metadata is heterogeneous, partially visual, and unevenly documented across regions.
A two-phase study combines analysis of natural metadata variation with controlled probes that fix object identity while varying fields and image access.
Metadata quantity alone does not explain generation behavior; field type strongly shapes grounding, omission, and inference.
Images can improve visual grounding but may also increase unsupported interpretation.
Evaluation should measure field- and claim-level support, not only input coverage or reference similarity.

papers.abstract: LiDAR point cloud semantic segmentation is a fundamental component of 3D perception for autonomous driving and robotics. Projection-based methods map 3D point clouds into 2D representations for feature extraction using 2D networks. However, aggregating multiple points during projection can obscure geometric differences within each frustum, while local feature extraction limits the modeling of spatial relationships across scanning regions. Moreover, proximity in the projected representation does not necessarily imply proximity in 3D space, and interactions between point and projected features may mix features from different ranges, reducing semantic discriminability. To address these challenges, we propose the Ray-aligned and Scan-aware Fusion Network (RaSFNet), which incorporates point cloud geometry and LiDAR scanning characteristics into projection-based semantic segmentation. Specifically, the Ray-Aligned Geometric Distribution Encoding (RAGDE) module characterizes point distributions within each frustum using a ray-aligned coordinate system. To model spatial context, a Scan-Topology-Aware Mamba (STAM) block organizes frustum features according to the LiDAR azimuth sampling pattern and captures long-range dependencies across scanning regions. In addition, a Range-Constrained Point-Frustum Fusion (RCPFF) mechanism uses shared range information to guide feature exchange between point and frustum representations while maintaining spatial correspondence. RaSFNet achieves mIoU scores of 70.2% and 77.7% on the SemanticKITTI and nuScenes validation sets, respectively, indicating competitive segmentation performance compared with the evaluated methods.

bullets: Addresses geometric information loss within projected frustums and limited spatial-context modeling in 2D representations.

papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation is increasingly applied to multilingual tasks, yet prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Role Conditioning are recommended based solely on English benchmarks. Whether their effectiveness transfers across judge models and languages remains unknown: prompt-sensitivity studies are largely English-centric, while existing multilingual judge studies fix the prompt template. In this work, we address this gap by measuring this interaction through a benchmark of 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, yielding over 1M pointwise scores on gold-reference outputs, validated against human judgments. We find that prompting strategies are not transferable: the choice of the judge model dominates the choice of prompting strategy, strategy effects reverse direction across judges, and stability degrades in low-resource languages, where these effects are concealed by aggregate reporting. These findings show that prompting effects in multilingual evaluation are conditioned on the judge, task, and language. Consequently, prompting strategies should be validated for the intended evaluation setting, and cross-study comparisons should account for both judge and prompt configuration.
authors: Asal Mehrabi, Mohammad Aliannejadi, Clemencia Siro
bullets: Studies 9 prompting strategies across 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, 4 tasks, and 13 datasets, using over 1M scores validated against human judgments.
Prompting effects are not transferable across judge models; the judge choice has a larger influence than the prompting strategy.
The same strategy can help one judge but hurt another, with effects also varying by task and language.
Evaluation stability decreases in low-resource languages, an issue hidden by aggregate reporting.
Cross-study comparisons should specify both the judge model and prompt configuration.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).
authors: Chenyuan Chen, Ran Ding, Lechen Zhang, Zewen He, Yoshihiko Nakamura
bullets: Addresses non-Markovian manipulation scenes where important visual cues disappear or leave view.

Introduces HuMeGo, a benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks.
Raises success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot; also improves SIMPLE tasks from 70.2% to 86.9%.

papers.abstract: Building virtual embodied agents that operate in open-ended games like human players is a long-standing goal requiring both long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control. As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying the integration of these capabilities. Existing agents typically provide either native visuomotor control without long-horizon autonomy or high-level planning executed through environment APIs or predefined skills. To bridge this gap, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness. At the orchestration level, we equip the harness with structured memory for tracking progress and a VLM planner for selecting subtasks within the VLA's capabilities. To reliably determine subtask completion, we further introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion. At the control level, a single VLA executes all subtasks with vision-only perception and native keyboard-and-mouse actions. To mitigate interference between heterogeneous GUI and non-GUI interactions, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings. We also train the VLA through world knowledge injection, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with environment feedback to improve reliability and recovery. HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance, scoring 85.0% on MineStudio Bench and a 37.4% average success rate on OpenHA, while also completing long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like human players.
authors: Zecong Tang, Zian Guan, Yuncheng Guo, Zhanqiu Zhang, Yiwen Guo, Bo Dai
bullets: Addresses the gap between native visuomotor control and high-level planning in open-ended games.
Uses a capability-aware harness with structured memory, VLM subtask planning, and a policy-coupled completion detector.
A single VLA perceives through vision and acts via native keyboard-and-mouse inputs across subtasks.
Improves control reliability with regime-specific normalization, separate mouse-token embeddings, and staged training with world knowledge, imitation, and reinforcement learning.
Reports 85.0% on MineStudio Bench, 37.4% average success on OpenHA, and successful long-horizon crafting tasks.

papers.abstract: Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill-based workflow and OmniDR-Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3 out of 100. Current agents still need broader content coverage, stronger causal and logical analysis across modalities, and more accurate citation support. We further analyze models, harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and research trajectories. The code and data are released at https://github.com/marinero4972/OmniDR-Bench.

papers.abstract: Language models are compared on question-answering benchmarks that pose each question in one wording, and a reworded question can change which of two models scores higher. We ask whether giving the models tools makes such comparisons more stable. An accuracy gain cannot answer this, because tools change several steps between the question and the scored answer at once. We propose a matched protocol that separates those steps: the answer readout, reasoning, the decision to call, the tool's answer, and the report supplied without a call. We apply it to six open models in five domains under five wordings. We find that tools raise accuracy where a program answers the question and widen the wording sensitivity of many pairwise comparisons. The widening follows how often a model calls, and call frequency follows the wording for some models and not others. It also depends on the interface and the instructions: a native tool-calling interface and a second tool description leave no detected widening in molecules, and sensitivity persists where tools return intermediate results. These findings show that deterministic reports do not guarantee stable comparisons. We recommend reporting call frequency and comparison stability under several wordings beside accuracy.
authors: Mateusz Modrzejewski, Tomasz Radzikowski
bullets: Rewording a question can change which of two models appears better, even when tools are available.
A matched protocol separates answer readout, reasoning, tool-calling decisions, tool outputs, and no-call reports.
Across six open models, five domains, and five wordings, tools improved accuracy on program-answerable questions but often widened comparison sensitivity.
Widening tracked tool-call frequency, which itself varied with wording for some models and depended on the tool interface and instructions.
The study recommends reporting call frequency and comparison stability across multiple wordings alongside accuracy.

papers.abstract: Long-context models often use answer-bearing evidence less effectively when it appears away from a prompt boundary. We compare this position bias across Transformer, state-space, and hybrid Mamba architectures by moving one gold document through a fixed set of nine distractors. The evaluated Transformers show a beginning advantage that the evaluated state-space models lack, while both families favor evidence near the end. A matched pure-versus-hybrid Mamba comparison points in the same direction but remains statistically uncertain. The family difference appears among models that can answer the task. Transformer primacy reappears on synthetic retrieval, where state-space ceiling prevents a family comparison. A corpus swap within one state-space architecture changes overall accuracy without a detectable change in curve shape. Prompt changes can create or nearly remove a beginning advantage. Position remains decodable across architectures even when response curves differ, and attention concentration near initial tokens covaries with beginning sensitivity in the tested Transformer family. These exploratory results show that effective context use depends on the evaluated architecture family, capability, task, and prompt, without isolating the sequence mixer as the sole cause.
authors: Aman Behera, Namit Solanki, Mehul Anand
bullets: Evaluated Transformers favor evidence near the beginning and end, while tested state-space models lack the same beginning advantage but still favor the end.
A matched pure-versus-hybrid Mamba comparison trends similarly, though the difference is statistically uncertain.
Transformer primacy returns in synthetic retrieval, but state-space performance ceilings prevent a clean family comparison.
Changing the corpus alters overall accuracy without clearly changing the position-bias curve; prompt changes can create or remove beginning bias.
Position remains decodable across architectures, and initial-token attention correlates with beginning sensitivity in the tested Transformers.

papers.abstract: Our previous analysis found that a model's native hashed N-gram table is where continual updates disturb the base least, but its writes needed backpropagation and changed the pretrained table. We present Delta N-gram, a forward-only write path into that table. The pretrained table T^0 is never modified. Evidence is written into a sparse patch \Delta on the rows it addresses: a 4.1M-parameter writer emits a target and a gate per (position, hash head) event, and a block-averaged delta rule keeps each row a convex combination of its old value and the gated targets. The writer is trained offline on raw text with the pretraining objective; at use time writing takes forward passes only, and clearing \Delta restores the original model. A 0.6B prototype trained to answer questions keeps 16/16 facts after a second write; online gradient writes keep 2--4/16. We study two writers: a plain writer that encodes evidence with the T^0-only model, and a delta writer that reads its current memory while encoding. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, the plain writer's memory is document-specific: on 64 held-out news events it lowers continuation NLL by 0.068 nats/token against empty memory and by 0.024 against another document's memory, and 0.063 and 0.013 after 16 intervening articles. The delta writer's memory is more document-specific and keeps more of it under distraction (70% vs 54%). Over 35,000 writes on our previous seven-task chain both writers stay stable and the delta writer drifts less (layer-2 math drift 176% vs 188%); later accuracy changes by -0.26/-0.52pp (-7.29pp for gradient updates) and small-k_i drift is 17.9/17.5% (39.2%). Acquisition is negative, and general-input drift reaches 32.8% (20.75%): format rows read by every example grow to 4--12 times their pretrained norm. Zeroing eight such rows removes over 98% of layer-2 drift on math inputs, together with their NLL gain.
authors: Hao Wu
bullets: Writes target and gated values into a sparse patch Δ while leaving the pretrained table unchanged; clearing Δ restores the original model.
A 4.1M-parameter writer is trained offline with the pretraining objective, so inference-time memory updates require only forward passes.
In a 0.6B prototype, it retained all 16/16 facts after a second write, compared with 2–4/16 for online gradient writes.
The learned memory is document-specific and remains more robust under distraction, with the delta writer retaining 70% versus 54% for the plain writer.
Across 35,000 writes, stability was substantially better than gradient updates, but frequent format rows accumulated large drift; zeroing eight rows removed over 98% of layer-2 math drift.

papers.abstract: Generated robot videos can look convincing while depicting the wrong interac- tion: a different object is moved, a grasp disappears, or a placement ends out- side its destination. We introduce RGraph-Eval, a reference-based framework that makes these discrepancies explicit through task-grounded temporal scene graphs. Unlike approaches that construct separate evidence representations for different evaluation dimensions, we organize task entities, interactions, and motion within a unified, interpretable scene graph representation. A foundation-model pipeline identifies manipulation roles, grounds persistent object masks, infers and verifies state transitions and action intervals, and reconstructs manipulated- object motion in three dimensions. Applying this representation to a generated video and a reference demonstration supports an interpretable RGraph-Eval score with visible-object, relation-change, and 3D path-shape components. We also introduce ShareRobot-SG, a collection of 1,000 manipulation scenes from ten ShareRobot sources annotated with the multimodal representation. Our eval- uation separates graph-generation quality from agreement with human video judgments, and includes comparisons with adapted SVG2 and SG-Ego, a bench- mark of three video generators. The framework connects robot-video assessment to the observable entities and interactions underlying a task, while making the graph annotations reusable beyond evaluation. Code will be publicly available at https://github.com/SashaDance/rgraph-eval.
authors: Aleksandr Lazarev, Sofia Zimina, Roman Kuznetsov, Tatiana Zemskova, Iaroslav Koshelev, Dmitry Yudin
bullets: Targets visually convincing but task-incorrect robot videos, such as wrong objects, lost grasps, or incorrect placements.
Uses a unified scene graph covering entities, interactions, motion, state transitions, action intervals, and reconstructed 3D object paths.
Produces interpretable scores based on visible objects, relation changes, and 3D path shape.
Introduces ShareRobot-SG, a collection of 1,000 annotated manipulation scenes from ten ShareRobot sources.
Separately evaluates graph-generation quality and alignment with human judgments, and benchmarks three video generators.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models generate multiple token positions in parallel, but few-step decoding makes parallel commitment difficult: tokens that appear reliable individually may be jointly inconsistent, while premature commitments can prevent later context-dependent refinement. In this paper, we introduce SetCommit, a training-free method for coordinated parallel token commitment. Instead of selecting tokens independently by confidence, SetCommit selects a commitment set that balances token reliability against local joint commitment risk, preserving conditioning opportunities for subsequent denoising steps. It further performs budget-neutral local exchanges, replacing vulnerable earlier commitments when newly revealed context supports more reliable alternatives. SetCommit requires no retraining or architectural modification and is compatible with existing diffusion decoding strategies. Experiments with LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B on GSM8K, MATH-500, MBPP, and HumanEval show accuracy/pass@1 gains of up to 7.4 percentage points over native decoding at 32 model evaluations. At common quality targets, geometric-mean incremental speedups range from $1.44$ to $1.74\times$. Code is available at https://github.com/Kissmetothemoon/SetCommit.
authors: Yuannuo Feng, Yubing Ye, Wenshuai Yao, Yizhe Chen, Ngai Wong, Wenyong Zhou, Wang Kang

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly used in practice, but their behavior is complex and hard to understand. We design a simple task to ask which model has the most influence on the final consensus when several models are mixed in one system. Experimentally, across seven model families, we find that the opinions of the other models are absorbed into the opinion of the stronger model, the one with more parameters. This happens even though the task requires no pretraining knowledge and has no correct answer. To understand this phenomenon, we interpret the agents as weighted particles moving on a simplex. Larger models carry a larger weight and therefore occupy a deeper well in the energy landscape. A large weight means strong in-context learning: a model with a large weight amplifies the majority of its context. Larger models are generally better at in-context learning, and this is what makes the larger model the influencer. We hope that this work helps to interpret multi-agent systems, whose behavior is becoming too complex for humans to understand.
authors: Gouki Minegishi, Jingyuan Feng, Hiroki Furuta, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo
bullets: Studies which model has the greatest influence on consensus in multi-agent systems.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding is a popular decode acceleration method. As such, it is particularly relevant to long-output generation, which requires an increasingly large KV cache. KV cache compression offers a way to constrain costs in long-context drafting. However, compression methods that focus on prefill information can lose relevance as the output length grows. We term this phenomenon decode staleness and show that it degrades draft model accuracy under selection-based KV cache compression. We introduce RIFT, a family of selection-based KV cache compression strategies that balance prefill information and recent generated tokens. We show that refreshing the KV cache selection during token generation significantly improves the drafter's quality at the cost of additional decode latency. To alleviate the refresh costs, we propose an adaptive KV refresh strategy that reduces the number of score calculations while retaining the drafter's quality. We further demonstrate how a compressibility-driven drafter training phase, based on sparse attention masks, can improve the drafter's quality under a compressed KV cache. Combined with compressibility training, RIFT enables Qwen3.5-4B, drafting for Qwen3.5-122B, to retain over 98% of its full-cache acceptance length on 32K-token inputs, 4K-token outputs, and an 8K-token KV cache budget.
authors: Dor Tsur, Maor Ashkenazi, Maximilian Golub, Peter Hicks, Yaniv Galron, Talor Abramovich, Yoav Miron, Tiyasa Mitra, Bita Darvish Rouhani, Ran Zilberstein
bullets: Identifies decode staleness: prompt-focused KV selection becomes less relevant during long generation and harms draft accuracy.
Balances prefill information with recently generated tokens through selection-based KV cache compression.
Uses adaptive KV refreshes to reduce score calculations and associated decode latency while preserving quality.
Adds sparse-attention, compressibility-driven drafter training to improve performance under compressed caches.

papers.abstract: Diffusion trajectory planners with domain-specific experts face a practical question in unseen regions: can they rely on selecting among existing experts, or must the planner itself adapt? We study this question using a planner with a shared adapter and per-domain expert adapters. Across three real-world held-out maps, none of eight test-time routing schemes improves the fleet-mean lateral offset over the static default, which uses the same expert for every scene. Even an oracle that selects the best expert for each scene reduces the mean offset by only 0.9 m. In contrast, reward-based fine-tuning on just 20 target-region scenes yields substantially larger gains. On matched evaluation slices, joint replay achieves a fleet-mean offset of 6.9 m, compared with 12.4 m for the static default. Comparisons under the same target-region training budget show that target-region training drives the improvement, while replaying training scenes limits forgetting on the original ODDs. On nuPlan, fine-tuning across training cities also improves open-loop offsets, although closed-loop performance deteriorates. Further diagnostics reveal that two test-time adaptation baselines achieve low offsets by producing degenerate trajectories. These results show the limited headroom for selecting among existing experts and the greater open-loop gains available from adapting the planner.
authors: Yun Li, Ehsan Javanmardi, Simon Thompson, Jiachen Gong, Qunli Zhang, Zifan Zeng, Shiming Liu, Peng Wang, Yidu Zhang, Manabu Tsukada
bullets: Across three held-out maps, none of eight routing schemes beats the static default in fleet-mean lateral offset.
Even oracle expert selection improves mean offset by only 0.9 m.
Reward-based fine-tuning on 20 target-region scenes reduces matched offset from 12.4 m to 6.9 m with joint replay.
Target-region training drives the gains, while replay helps limit forgetting on original operating domains.
Some adaptation baselines achieve low offsets through degenerate trajectories; nuPlan results show open-loop gains but closed-loop deterioration.

papers.abstract: Reward models score responses for preference optimization, filtering and ranking, and pooling scores across prompts needs them to be comparable. Yet pairwise evaluation compares two responses to the same prompt, so any score component shared by a prompt's responses cancels and goes untested. We study this component by comparing between-prompt variation in model scores with the same variation in human ratings of the same responses. We propose a human-referenced audit, built from a between-prompt variance share, a sibling-rating regression and prompt substitutions, and apply it to eighteen released scorers and six matched training conditions. We find that scores cluster by prompt more than the ratings do: on HelpSteer2, six reward models have between-prompt shares of 0.34 to 0.64 against a human share near zero. Replacing the original prompt with a fixed instruction keeps substantial clustering but weakens agreement with prompt-level human ratings, so clustering alone does not show agreement with humans. Part of that variation is useful: subtracting prompt means lowers the helpfulness of globally selected responses, and scores stay sensitive to a wrong prompt even when training shuffles prompt means. We propose that reward evaluation check between-prompt variation, sensitivity to a wrong prompt and usefulness for selection separately.
authors: Mateusz Modrzejewski, Tomasz Radzikowski
bullets: Pairwise comparisons cancel score components shared by all responses to a prompt, leaving them untested.
The study audits between-prompt variation using human-referenced variance shares, sibling-rating regression, and prompt substitutions.

Across 18 released scorers and six matched training conditions, scores clustered by prompt more than human ratings did; six HelpSteer2 reward models had shares of 0.34–0.64 versus near zero for humans.
Fixed-prompt substitutions preserved substantial clustering but weakened alignment with prompt-level human ratings, so clustering alone is not evidence of human agreement.
Prompt-level variation affected selection and wrong-prompt sensitivity, motivating separate evaluation of variation, prompt sensitivity, and selection usefulness.

papers.tldr: Pairwise reward evaluation misses prompt-level score variation, which can be substantial, only partly human-aligned, and sometimes useful for selecting responses.

papers.abstract: Text-to-music alignment is commonly evaluated by the global similarity between text and audio embeddings, which collapses all described attributes into a single score and obscures which ones are missing. We instead introduce MQAScore, which verifies each atomic musical concept along five clip-level dimensions (genre, instrument, mood/theme, vocal, and usage) by the probability that a large audio language model (LALM) answers affirmatively to a binary question. To assess evaluator reliability, we construct verification labels from presence/absence annotations and LLM-guided concept substitutions, and propose the Sensitivity-Invariance Ratio, which measures how selectively an evaluator responds to meaning-changing substitutions. Experiments show that concept-level scoring improves both question-answering and similarity-based evaluators, and MQAScore can be a more reliable and interpretable fine-grained complement to global similarity for evaluating text-to-music alignment.
authors: Wei-Jaw Lee, Chun-Ping Wang, Xuanjun Chen, Yi-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of global text-audio similarity scores, which hide which attributes are missing.
Evaluates atomic concepts across genre, instrument, mood/theme, vocal, and usage dimensions.
Uses a large audio language model to answer binary presence questions for each concept.
Introduces verification labels and a Sensitivity-Invariance Ratio to assess evaluator reliability.
Experiments indicate improved evaluation for both question-answering and similarity-based evaluators, complementing global similarity with more interpretable scores.
