papers.abstract: World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience, while Agent trajectories can inform World Model refinement. Evaluating this interaction requires separate evidence about action selection and state evolution. We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.

papers.abstract: Capturing a loose object inside a spacecraft requires a robot to approach a target that can translate and rotate, and whose motion changes when contact is made. These conditions motivate evaluation beyond manipulation of supported objects. We introduce AstroBench, an open benchmark for free-floating capture and space robotic manipulation with a fixed-base arm. The task suite combines four initial-motion tracks with sample-storage operations based on MELFI hardware and cap and captive-screw servicing based on the Robotic Refueling Mission. The two workcells provide nine task definitions and 29 task-target combinations. A metadata-filtered Objaverse inventory supplies 8,414 object instances for asset expansion, alongside five cabin visual contexts and versioned task instructions. We report two acquisition-focused experiments using existing checkpoints. A frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ DROID joint-position policy captures 2 of 200 static targets and 4 of 200 moving targets across twenty object identities. A cube-specific ACT policy captures 8 of 10 static targets and 6 of 10 moving targets in a separate experiment. Each experiment retains its recorded observation, action and capture configuration. The results document difficult direct transfer for the tested generalist checkpoint and successful task-specific capture behavior, while identifying concrete settings for studying motion-aware perception and contact-sensitive control. Code, task definitions and editable workcell assets are available at https://github.com/AstroUpLab/AstroBench.

Supports research on motion-aware perception and contact-sensitive control.

papers.abstract: As large language models are deployed in high-stakes roles such as therapy, education, and personal assistance, their social cognition must be assessed reliably. Current Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmarks report aggregate scores that conflate two distinct competencies: explicit ToM (recognizing what someone believes) and applied ToM (using that belief to predict behavior). Building on this distinction, we investigate the gap and its recoverability using four structurally diverse benchmarks. Aggregate reporting obscures uneven competence: on SimpleToM, Llama-3.1-8B scores 51.5 percent overall while recognizing mental states at 99.4 percent and predicting behavior at only 28.9 percent. To assess recovery, we compare structured prompting, matched in-context learning, and our proposed Belief-State Test-Time Training (BSTTT), which adapts lightweight parameters on answered support questions through action reconstruction. Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and GPT-oss-20B, recovery depends on the model, task, and intervention. On SimpleToM, reminders combined with BSTTT improve Llama's behavior prediction by 40.8 percentage points; reminders account for most of the overall improvement, with BSTTT adding 1.3 to 5.5 points beyond reminders across models. Contextual examples often outperform weight updates, while BSTTT remains stronger in specific model-benchmark settings. Temporal belief tracking remains difficult despite partial recovery. These findings show that aggregate ToM scores can overstate applied competence while hiding performance recoverable through targeted assistance. We recommend decomposed reporting of explicit and applied accuracy alongside intervention comparisons that establish which failures are recoverable and under what conditions.
authors: Prajvi Saxena, Sabine Janzen, Wolfgang Maass
bullets: Aggregate ToM scores can hide a large gap between identifying mental states and applying them to predict behavior.
The study evaluates this gap and its recoverability across four structurally diverse benchmarks.
It compares structured prompting, matched in-context learning, and Belief-State Test-Time Training (BSTTT), which adapts lightweight parameters using action reconstruction.
Recovery varies by model and task: reminders often drive most gains, while BSTTT provides additional improvements in selected settings.
Temporal belief tracking remains difficult, motivating separate reporting of explicit and applied ToM accuracy and intervention effects.

papers.abstract: Tilt-rotor quadcopters redirect thrust for translation without banking, but complicate modeling, state estimation, and disturbance rejection. This paper presents a simulation-based flight stack for a \SI{2.00}{\kilo\gram} tilt-rotor quadcopter. The system uses a six-degree-of-freedom nonlinear model with first-order motor dynamics and two-axis rotor tilt, parameterized using a 3D CAD model. A cascaded PD controller commands forward and lateral tilt angles. A 14-state EKF fuses sensor data across hover, early-transition, and transition modes using a hysteretic (Schmitt-trigger) classifier to prevent covariance discontinuities. Because the proportional position loop leaves a steady-state offset under constant wind, a small bounded neural residual is added on top of the unmodified PD controller. It is trained by behavioral cloning from a teacher with privileged access to the true wind, while the deployed network never observes wind. In simulation, the EKF achieves a post-settling position root mean square error (RMSE) of \SI{0.226}{\metre} (horizontal) and \SI{0.03}{\metre} (vertical) and an attitude RMSE below \SI{0.8}{\degree}, and it estimates a wind velocity of $(\num{2.0}, \num{-1.2})\,\unit{\metre\per\second}$ to within \SI{0.15}{\metre\per\second} per axis. The residual reduces steady-state station-keeping error under wind by approximately \SI{49}{\percent}, from \SI{0.117}{\metre} to \SI{0.060}{\metre} at \SI{1.5}{\metre\per\second} and from \SI{0.319}{\metre} to \SI{0.162}{\metre} at an out-of-distribution \SI{3.9}{\metre\per\second}. The framework provides a basis for hardware-in-the-loop and flight-test studies.
authors: Ninad Joshi, Prabhat Kumar
bullets: Models a 2 kg tilt-rotor quadcopter with nonlinear 6-DoF dynamics, motor lag, and two-axis rotor tilt derived from CAD.
Uses a 14-state EKF with hysteretic mode classification across hover and transition phases to maintain consistent covariance behavior.
Trains a wind-unaware neural residual by behavioral cloning from a teacher with privileged wind information.
In simulation, the EKF achieves 0.226 m horizontal and 0.03 m vertical position RMSE, with attitude RMSE below 0.8°.
The residual reduces steady-state position error by about 49% under both 1.5 m/s and out-of-distribution 3.9 m/s wind.

papers.abstract: Efficient custom operators are essential for modern deep learning workloads, yet developing high-performance kernels for Ascend NPUs remains slow, expert-intensive, and difficult to automate. Although AI agents now approach expert performance on GPU kernel benchmarks, current models remain less capable of generating AscendC kernels for NPUs, potentially reflecting the relative scarcity of relevant training data. We thus present CAKE, a CANN-native system for deployable custom operators that combines adaptive multi-DSL routing, separate Generation and Evolution modes, and reviewed knowledge reuse through CAKE Book and a Self-Evolving Agent. On 53 CANN-Bench v1.1 operators on Ascend 950PR, CAKE's aggregated results achieve $100\%$ case pass rate on the standard set (1,060/1,060) and $98.28\%$ on the hidden set (4,167/4,240), with an overall mean score of 78.63 out of 100 and an average performance speedup of $1.334\times$ over the baseline. Evolution then pushes correct operators further: EngramGateFusion cuts aggregate device time by $46.6\%$ over 20 rounds and roughly halves the mean roofline gap. These results offer a practical path toward closing Ascend's AI-for-kernel capability gap.
authors: Deng Pan, Xue-Jian Gao, Junyi Fan, Bin Du, Jiasheng Li, Xinxian Chen, Nok Yan Chang, Xinlin Li, Lingchao Zheng, Jun Li, Yuwei Fan
bullets: Targets the slow, expert-intensive process of creating high-performance AscendC kernels for Ascend NPUs.
Uses adaptive multi-DSL routing, separate Generation and Evolution modes, CAKE Book knowledge reuse, and a Self-Evolving Agent.
On 53 CANN-Bench v1.1 operators on Ascend 950PR, it passes 100% of standard cases and 98.28% of hidden cases.
Achieves a mean score of 78.63/100 and 1.334× average speedup over the baseline.
Evolution further reduces EngramGateFusion device time by 46.6% over 20 rounds and approximately halves its mean roofline gap.

Each case is placed by its arithmetic intensity (AI); the binding pipeline gives the roof Tmin, and the headroom (gap from the measured point up to the roof) bounds how much evolution can still gain. A variant that reaches its roof (headroom≈1) is converged.

Figure 1: CAKE architecture. Four stacked layers cooperate to turn an operator request into a deployable, benchmarkvalidated Ascend operator. CAKE-Agents provides the controllers—generation, the evolution main and sub-agents, and automatic benchmark adaptation. The CAKE-Router gates each request on track–chip–operator-type feasibility, then scores the surviving code-generation tracks against the operator’s eight-dimensional structural profile, while the Skills harness supplies typed lifecycle tools for description, lowering, optimization, evaluation, and debugging. The CAKE Book is a cross-user encyclopedia maintained as a shared wiki, and CAKE-Bench is a user-defined evaluation suite—operator task specifications, test cases, precision requirements, and scoring—so that evaluation feedback is not tied to any single benchmark. A Self-Evolving Agent observes all layers: it traces, judges, and edits skills, analyses evolution runs, writes verified experience back to CAKE Book, and closes the loop with measured operator results.

Figure 2: The routing decision. L1 reduces the contract to an eight-dimensional feature vector and a difficulty; L0 removes infeasible tracks before any scoring and abstains rather than guessing when nothing is feasible; L2 scores the surviving tracks under Equation 3 and decides between exploiting the best estimate and measuring an eligible contender; L3 records the outcome, which moves the ability estimates that L2 will use next time.

Figure 3: Fitted per-dimension abilities θd for the three DSL tracks under one backbone. Axes are the eight feature dimensions of Section 3. The tracks are nearly indistinguishable on tiling (T ), reduction (R), and dtype spread (D), and separate on blocking (B, where DSL-B reaches +2.83), data movement (M , where DSL-A is −1.69 against DSL-C’s −0.31), and scheduling depth (S, where DSL-A is +2.45 against DSL-C’s +0.91). These gaps are what make the routing ordering operator-dependent rather than fixed.

Figure 5: The CAKE-evo loop. The analysis layer (blue) sets the ceiling target and bottleneck-driven variant assignment; the evolutionary stages (green) spawn, measure, and tier variants; AIC injects profiling-grounded guidance; the roofline headroom provides the stop test; PMR compounds knowledge into rules.

Figure 6: EngramGateFusion evolution over 20 CAKE-evo rounds and 20 CANN-Bench cases. The line is the mean fusion indicator against the unfused PyTorch composition (left axis); gray bars show LLM calls in each round (right axis), and warm-colored callouts identify the mechanisms behind the largest gains. The indicator rises from 45.5× to 98.2×, while the endpoint annotations show the mean kernel-to-roofline ratio falling from 25.7× to 12.6×. Because the line mixes eager wall time with device kernel time, it is used only as a trajectory indicator; a separate samebasis measurement gives a final mean end-to-end speedup of 29.5× (geometric mean 27.6×). Round 20 performed verification, packaging, and a device-fault fix and therefore has calls but no new performance point; the dashed segment repeats the round-19 value and does not represent a new timing measurement.

Figure 8: Target and path routing. check_device.sh reports the chip generation, which admits the 910 lane or the two 950-specific lanes. On the 950, operators with data-dependent non-contiguous access take SIMT; the remainder use Regbase when the register-level DSL covers the kernel and fall back to membase when it does not. The SIMT model-selection questions Q1–Q6 are given in Appendix A.5.

Right: case pass rate, computed over 20 standard or 80 hidden cases per operator. The same operator grouping is used for both sets.

papers.abstract: Flexible robotic endoscopes provide access through tortuous anatomy, where friction, deformation, and wall interaction separate commanded insertion from useful distal progress. Operators interpret this mismatch and retreat to recover a navigable configuration. Recognizing the approach to that decision requires relating motor intent to distal response and the local visual scene. We introduce Multimodal Progress-Residual Fusion (MPRF), a causal model that anticipates operator retreat from commands, electromagnetic (EM) tracking, and endoscopic video. A nominal-progress model predicts the response expected in normal or successful navigation; a temporal predictor combines its EM residual with all three observed modalities. In a 150-episode colon-phantom collection, MPRF achieves 0.580 +/- 0.007 AUPRC across three seeds, compared with 0.511 for the strongest reduced-modality control. Complete multimodal histories provide the principal ranking advantage, while the residual adds an explicit intent-response representation with a small, uncertain increment over raw fusion. Analysis of frozen alarms relates warning timing to the behavioral label and explains the increase in event recall under a longer matching window. These results establish a basis for behavioral assistance during operator-controlled navigation.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Tianchun Wu, Jiatan Sun, Yuming Sun, Jianru Zhang, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between commanded insertion and useful distal progress caused by friction, deformation, and wall interaction.
Uses a nominal-progress model to estimate expected navigation response, then combines its EM residual with commands, tracking, and video in a causal temporal predictor.
Evaluated on 150 colon-phantom episodes, achieving 0.580 ± 0.007 AUPRC versus 0.511 for the strongest reduced-modality control.
Complete multimodal histories provide the main ranking benefit; the residual representation adds only a small, uncertain improvement over raw fusion.
Frozen-alarm analysis links warning timing to retreat labels and explains improved event recall with a longer matching window.

(b) Stage A predicts nominal EM and visual increments from prior state and current command. Subtracting predicted EM progress from observed progress gives the residual; the visual head supplies auxiliary supervision. Stage A fits Normal and Pass attempts with dimension-averaged L1 losses, then stays frozen. (c) Current A/E/V and the residual form 50-dimensional tokens. Stage B encodes 16 causal tokens with a GRU and predicts future retreat through layer normalization, a 48-unit GELU head, dropout, and a sigmoid.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a demonstration-based robotic feeding framework that integrates human demonstration, Dynamic Movement Primitive-based motion planning, vision-based scene perception, and robot control. A human operator first demonstrates the scooping and feeding motions while the position and Euler-angle orientation of the spoon are recorded using a motion-capture system. The recorded trajectory is segmented into scooping and feeding motions, which are encoded using separate Dynamic Movement Primitives. Before task execution, an RGB-D camera estimates the participant's mouth position, while two AprilTags are used for robot-frame registration and tray localization. The detected tray pose is used to position the scooping motion, whereas the detected mouth position defines the positional goal of the feeding motion. The approach, scooping, and feeding trajectories are then executed sequentially by a Kinova Gen3 manipulator through a ROS~2-based framework. A real-world experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the integrated pipeline and shows that the learned spoon motions can be reproduced within the detected experimental scene.
authors: Kenzhi Iskandar Wong, Kitti Thamrongaphichartkul, Sri Harsha Turlapati, Yanshuo Lu, Kanichi Doi, Boyu Ma, Bin Zhou, Lin Yang, Ananda Sidarta, Lek Syn Lim, Arun-Kumar Kaliya-Perumal, Jianfei Yang, Domenico Campolo

Real-world experiments demonstrate feasibility and reproduction of the learned motions in the detected scene.

papers.abstract: Chunking strategies for retrieval-augmented generation are almost always evaluated on a static snapshot, yet the documents underlying a knowledge base continue to change. Because chunks are embedded independently, a boundary that moves after an edit forces unchanged text to be re-embedded. We measure this update cost on 120 pairs of adjacent Chinese and English Wikipedia revisions for three stateless chunkers (non-overlapping fixed-size, recursive paragraph-first, and content-defined chunking) under a strict byte-identical reuse rule and a frozen dense encoder. On the 116-article common-success pool, with frozen, length-calibrated parameters, fixed-size chunking recomputes 57-68% of its full new-version embedding-input workload, recursive chunking 38-56%, and content-defined chunking 43-54% (it failed on 4 of 62 Chinese articles), while at these parameters mean evidence recall under a fixed 2048-token retrieval budget differs by less than two percentage points within either language. A cost-only parameter grid shows that the ranking of the two content-aware chunkers changes with chunk-length settings, whereas non-overlapping fixed-size chunking has the highest recomputation cost in every length-matched condition. Controlled edits and a verbatim-presence diagnostic support boundary drift as one contributor to recomputation of text already present in the previous version. Update cost is therefore a substantial, parameter-sensitive dimension that static retrieval evaluations do not expose and that should be reported alongside retrieval quality.
authors: Yuning Bian, Lele Xu, Yifan Yuan, Xinyu Yin, Chengyan Zhan
bullets: Evaluates fixed-size, recursive paragraph-first, and content-defined chunking on 120 adjacent Chinese and English Wikipedia revisions.
Under strict byte-identical reuse, fixed-size chunking recomputes the most workload; recursive and content-defined chunking generally recompute less.
Mean evidence recall differs by less than two percentage points between methods within each language at the evaluated settings.
The relative cost of the two content-aware methods changes with chunk-length parameters, showing update cost is parameter-sensitive.
Controlled edits support boundary drift as a cause of re-embedding unchanged text; content-defined chunking failed on 4 of 62 Chinese articles.

papers.abstract: End-to-end control policies trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL) have emerged as an alternative to conventional surgical robotic control approaches, with recent studies exploring state-based policies trained on privileged state observations. However, such approaches rely on precise physical states that are difficult to obtain reliably in surgical environments. Vision-based RL provides an alternative by learning manipulation policies directly from RGB observations, avoiding explicit state estimation and manually engineered perception pipelines while enabling policies to acquire task-relevant visual representations. Nevertheless, obtaining vision-based policies via pure RL methods for surgical manipulation remains challenging. Thus, imitation learning (IL) becomes another solution, yet it requires a large number of expert demonstrations, which are difficult to obtain in minimally invasive surgery. In this work, we propose a framework for state-to-vision policy distillation in laparoscopic robotic manipulation. Specifically, a state-based policy with privileged observations is employed as the teacher, and a vision-based policy learns from RGB observations and robot proprioceptive information, which requires less expert demonstrations than IL and introduces superior performance than RL methods. We conduct extensive experiments on various surgical manipulation tasks in the simulated environment. Experimental results show that, in the context of laparoscopic robotic manipulation, training vision-based policies with general-purpose RL methods is challenging, whereas our proposed state-to-vision policy distillation leads to more consistent and stable performance across tasks.
authors: Mingyu Sheng, Jianan Fan, Dongnan Liu, Guoyan Zheng, Ron Kikinis, Weidong Cai
bullets: Vision-based control avoids unreliable surgical state estimation and hand-engineered perception pipelines.
A privileged state-based policy serves as the teacher for a vision-based student policy.
The student uses RGB observations and robot proprioception, requiring fewer expert demonstrations than conventional imitation learning.
Experiments across simulated surgical manipulation tasks show more consistent and stable performance with distillation than direct vision-based RL.
The study is evaluated in simulation and focuses on laparoscopic robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Long-text image-text alignment is essential for fine-grained scene understanding, yet existing methods mainly focus on extending context length or improving local alignment. We identify an overlooked failure mode, saliency collapse, where models over-rely on text that features visual prominence while underutilizing non-salient context. Consequently, retrieval performance degrades sharply when salient content is reduced, despite that the non-salient context remains informative. To address this, we propose RoSA, a saliency-aware finetuning framework that decomposes image-text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views, enabling joint learning of prominent and contextual semantics. We propose a modality-independent decomposition strategy to combine object-level visual saliency estimation with LLM-based text decomposition to bridge vision and language. We employ auxiliary objectives to explicitly align these views, ensuring robust representation with both salient and contextual features. RoSA greatly improves long-text retrieval and demonstrates strong robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks. Moreover, our auxiliary objectives are plug-and-play, bringing consistent gains to existing tuning methods. Code and checkpoints are available at: https://github.com/intelligolabs/RoSA
authors: Qiuyu Kong, Zanxi Ruan, Marco Cristani, Yiming Wang
bullets: Problem: Existing methods underuse informative non-salient text and context, causing retrieval degradation when salient content is reduced.
Method: Decomposes image–text pairs into complementary salient and contextual views using visual saliency estimation and LLM-based text decomposition.
Method: Uses auxiliary objectives to align salient and contextual views across modalities.
Contribution: Provides a modality-independent, plug-and-play saliency-aware finetuning framework.
Result: Improves long-text retrieval and robustness to saliency collapse across benchmarks, with consistent gains for existing tuning methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of ROSA. ROSA consists of two stages: Stage 1: Saliency-guided view decomposition of vision and text, where we independently decompose the text and image. On the text side, an LLM is used to split the original long caption into salient text and contextual text. On the visual side, an off-the-shelf saliency method is applied to derive salient/contextual visual regions. Stage 2: Saliency-aware alignment. During fine-tuning of the image and text encoders, ROSA augments the original image-text contrastive loss Lori with three saliency-aware objectives: the saliency-focused contrastive loss Lsal, which explicitly aligns salient images with salient texts; the context-preserving contrastive loss Lctx, which aligns contextual images with contextual texts; and the visual anchoring loss Lanc, which enforces representation consistency between the original image and the salient image, thereby preserving stable salient semantics.

papers.abstract: Extraction pipelines ask language models for JSON that follows a schema, and the schema can set a minimum number of list entries. We ask what models do when the document holds fewer items than that minimum. Under a preregistered plan, we test eight open-weight models on 558 real documents from nine annotated datasets, with six more models on hosted services as a reference. Three findings stand out. First, models treat the count as a target: a minimum shown in the schema, but not enforced, raises the share of lists longer than the true count from 34.5% to 55.4%. Second, the padding is hard to catch, because most added entries are real text taken from the document; about half of them pass a check that each entry occurs in the source. Third, common fixes help only partly: a line saying fewer items are fine removes the effect on average but misses more true items, a count in prose ("up to k") also raises over-counting, an "N/A" option under an enforced minimum still leaves half the lists padded, and re-asking with the validation error makes padding far more common. We release the code, answer lists and run records at https://github.com/AbhishekBarali/padding-to-k
authors: Abhishek Barali, Aayush Paudel
bullets: Tested eight open-weight models on 558 real documents from nine annotated datasets, with six hosted models as a reference.
A schema minimum increased over-counted lists from 34.5% to 55.4%, despite not being enforced.
Most added entries were copied from the document, making padding difficult to detect; about half passed an exact source-occurrence check.
Warnings, “up to k” wording, an N/A option, and validation-error retries reduced the problem only partially or sometimes worsened it.

papers.title: Padding to k: A Minimum Count in the Schema Makes Open-Weight Models Pad Their Extraction Lists

papers.abstract: This paper presents TRACE, a traversability-aware reactive navigation framework designed for the autonomous operation of ground robots in unstructured forest environments. Unlike traditional approaches, TRACE leverages VLM-based confidence maps from positive and negative natural-language prompt sets and combines them through evidential fusion to produce a dense traversability map that prioritizes the terrain based on signs of previously traversed paths. Traversability-annotated points are then extracted and used to derive the left and right boundaries of the traversable path via percentile binning followed by spline or regularized polynomial fitting. These boundaries are then incorporated as soft barrier constraints within an NMPC formulation, enabling safe and adaptive path following in complex natural environments. Rigorous experimental trials carried out in real-life forest environments demonstrate TRACE ability for smooth navigation in cluttered, deformable, and visually ambiguous terrains.
authors: Mario A. V. Saucedo, Midhun Edatharam Kunnath, Elias Small, Akash Patel, Shruti Kotpalliwar, Christoforos Kanellakis, George Nikolakopoulos
bullets: Builds dense traversability maps by fusing VLM confidence from positive and negative natural-language prompts.
Prioritizes terrain showing signs of previously traversed paths.
Estimates traversable-path boundaries using percentile binning and spline or regularized polynomial fitting.
Injects the estimated boundaries as soft barrier constraints into an NMPC controller.
Real-world forest trials demonstrate smooth navigation through cluttered, deformable, and visually ambiguous terrain.

Finally, the resulting boundaries are incorporated as soft barrier constraints within the NMPC formulation.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did. They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between. Scene-level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry. Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output learned together with the action. In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module or as an extra prediction head. We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World-Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a third modality on par with vision and action. Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own supervision. UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three experts exchange information through joint attention. We train UniFlowWAM under a ten-objective role grid, where each objective assigns every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent. The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future visual features or 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks. On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow from 52.1% to 56.4%. It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus. On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.
authors: Jialin Tian, Zhuofan Li, Xinkai Wang, Bokai Lin, Chenyi Wang, Xinyu Zhan, Cewu Lu, Lixin Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation that 3D flow is typically handled outside the robot policy as a separate module or output.
Uses a diffusion transformer with one expert each for vision, action, and 3D flow, connected through joint attention.
Trains across ten objectives that assign each modality as a target, condition, or absent, enabling policy, dynamics, and future-feature prediction tasks.
Improves RoboCasa-GR1 success from 52.1% to 56.4%, while achieving 98.1% on LIBERO and 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus.
Reaches 87.0% average success on four real-world bimanual tasks, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.

A grid of ten objectives assigns each modality the role of target, condition, or absent, so a single model covers policy, dynamics, and prediction, yet deploys as a direct policy that needs no flow at test time.

Figure 2. Network architecture. Actions, scene-level 3D flow, and future visual features are three modalities of one diffusion transformer, each processed by its own expert; the experts exchange information only through joint self-attention. The objective decides which modalities are noised targets and which are clean conditions. Predicted flow latents are decoded by the 4D VAE into point maps and scene flow.

papers.abstract: Personal agents need to draw on long-term interaction history to retrieve and apply external knowledge suited to a user's current request. Even an answer grounded in relevant documents can be unsuitable when it overlooks the user's circumstances. This creates two connected challenges: using historical conditions to identify the knowledge needed for a new request, and applying that knowledge to the user's situation. Existing benchmarks advance memory recall, personalized retrieval, and memory-guided action, while the joint evaluation of these two challenges remains underexplored. We introduce ColaBench, a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living, with 349 tasks across 10 Profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. Its Evidence Graph connects personal conditions to their disclosures across public interaction sessions, records prior document exposure, and links answer requirements to personal and newly acquired document evidence. We also introduce MemKB, which uses state summaries to inform queries and rule application, and memory-document links to retrieve knowledge associated with the user's history. MemKB achieves 86.25% Accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task. Task-level analysis finds larger gains on tasks integrating information across multiple historical Facts; error analysis further identifies unsupported personal assumptions and rule misapplication as obstacles to using retrieved evidence. ColaBench provides traceable tasks and an evaluation framework for studying how memory guides knowledge acquisition and rule application.
authors: Wenjie Zhang, Zhichao Shi, Xuhui Jiang, Xiaojun Wu, Cehao Yang, Chengjin Xu, Xiaoning Song
bullets: Introduces a synthetic health and daily-living benchmark with 349 tasks, 10 user Profiles, and 13,033 documents.
Its Evidence Graph links personal conditions, disclosures, prior document exposure, and answer requirements for traceable evaluation.
Proposes MemKB, which uses state summaries, memory-document links, and rule application to guide retrieval.
MemKB achieves 86.25% accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task.

papers.abstract: Robust manipulation of soft objects, such as garments, is a critical skill for service and household robots to adopt, but remains challenging due to its high-dimensional state space, and material-dependent deformations. Humans address this challenge by using mental world models that "imagine" the shape and material properties from partial observations, which enables them to predict how actions affect future states. As such, embedding such world models in robots allows for better generalization in manipulating a wide variety of garments in the real world. However, learned world models typically require large amounts of real world data that is strenuous to collect, and a mechanism to infer latent properties that govern dynamics. We present a Soft-Object World Model that performs generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction using a transformer backbone trained on large-scale simulated soft object interactions, with measures to mitigate the sim-to-real gap. By learning to infer latent shape and material cues through in-context learning over a variable-length partial point-cloud history, the model generalizes across robot embodiments, material parameters, garment types and shapes, and manipulation coordination modes without weight updates. The world model is then integrated with a Goal-Conditioned action planner for motion synthesis. We validate the approach in simulation and real world for bimanual garment folding, reporting improvements in reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.
authors: Hengyi Sim, Quentin Rouxel, Dennis Hong, Darwin Caldwell, Fei Chen
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of garment manipulation under high-dimensional, material-dependent dynamics and partial observations.
Uses a transformer trained on large-scale simulated soft-object interactions for generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned prediction.
Infers latent garment shape and material properties from variable-length partial point-cloud histories through in-context learning.
Integrates the world model with a goal-conditioned planner for bimanual motion synthesis.
Simulation and real-world folding experiments show improved reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often fail to utilise the context given in the input, resulting in hallucinations or a fallback to parametric knowledge. Context augmentation methods aim to improve model performance by modifying the input, from inserting filler tokens that add computational time to adding relevant content such as elaboration of a context during inference. However, these methods have been evaluated in isolation and only by their performance gains, leaving it unclear how they compare and whether they reliably improve performance. In this paper, we present an evaluation framework spanning five methods that differ in how informative the inserted content is and apply them at the sentence level across seven models spanning multiple sizes on three datasets. We find that accuracy gains are not always genuine improvements but undirected perturbations: the methods correct some predictions while breaking others, particularly when the inserted text allows only for more computational time. Our analysis reveals that methods that bring no additional content primarily change model predictions near the decision boundary. Our findings highlight the need to evaluate the reliability of the accuracy gains before adopting them in practice.
authors: Haeun Yu, Geert Heyman, Pepa Atanasova, Isabelle Augenstein
bullets: Evaluates five context-augmentation methods at the sentence level across seven models and three datasets.
Methods vary in the informativeness of inserted content, from filler tokens to relevant elaborations.
Accuracy gains can arise from undirected perturbations rather than genuine improvements.
Methods adding no new information mainly affect predictions near the decision boundary.
The study emphasizes evaluating reliability, not just aggregate accuracy gains, before deployment.

papers.abstract: Automated radiology report generation requires models to do more than produce fluent clinical narratives: they must explicitly state supported diagnoses while avoiding unsupported ones. However, existing medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) are typically trained with token-level maximum likelihood objectives, which prioritize text agreement over diagnostically critical terms. As a result, models can miss key diagnoses and introduce wrong ones. We identify this as an objective misalignment between conventional language modeling and the asymmetric diagnostic requirements of radiology reporting. To encode these requirements, we introduce Diagnostic Loss (DLoss), a differentiable, architecture-agnostic objective that operates directly on decoder token probabilities. DLoss separately aggregates probability mass over vocabularies associated with diagnoses supported by the reference report and with unsupported alternatives. Using asymmetric pooling across token positions in the report, it encourages supported diagnoses to receive sufficient probability in at least one position while suppressing spurious probability spikes for unsupported diagnoses across all positions during training. The loss can be applied to existing 3D MedVLMs without modifying their vision backbones, language decoders, or inference procedures, and introduces no additional inference-time computation. We train and evaluate DLoss on 50,000 abdominal CT scans across several 3D MedVLM architectures on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution report-generation benchmarks. Across these settings, DLoss improves diagnostic faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance on conventional language-generation metrics, showing the value of asymmetric sequence-level supervision for radiology report generation. The code for DLoss is available at https://github.com/gmum/DLoss.
authors: Ignacy Kolton, Wenxuan Li, Zongwei Zhou, Jaros{\l}aw B. \'Cwik{\l}a, Arkadiusz Sitek, Pedro R. A. S. Bassi, Szymon P{\l}otka
bullets: Addresses objective misalignment in token-level maximum likelihood training, which can miss key diagnoses or add incorrect ones.
Introduces an architecture-agnostic differentiable loss operating on decoder token probabilities.
Uses asymmetric pooling to reward sufficient probability for supported diagnoses while suppressing spurious probability for unsupported alternatives.
Evaluated across several 3D MedVLMs on abdominal CT report-generation benchmarks, including in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings.
Improves diagnostic faithfulness while retaining competitive conventional language-generation performance and adds no inference-time computation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of DLoss and its workflow. DLoss supervises how probability is distributed over diagnostic targets alongside standard token prediction. (1) Integration. DLoss operates directly on decoder probabilities without modifying the architecture or decoding procedure (only the LoRA parameters and the projector are trained). Reports are decomposed into organ-level findings and mapped offline, via LLM tagging, to supported (D+ i ) and unsupported (D− i ) diagnostic targets in a controlled target space G. (2) Asymmetric pooling. Target probability masses mi,d,t across valid decoder positions are aggregated using distinct operators: noisy-OR for supported targets (saturates when present at any position) and temperature-controlled log-sum-exp for unsupported targets (ensures probability stays low everywhere). (3) Objective. The supported and unsupported target losses are added to cross-entropy with independent coefficients λ+ and λ−, respectively, and scaled by sample weight si. The diagnostic target sets are discarded at inference, so DLoss adds no inference-time computation.

papers.abstract: Generative modeling for Computer-Aided Design (CAD) remains fundamentally challenged by the need to capture the intricate interplay between discrete topological connectivity and precise spatial geometry inherent in Boundary Representations (B-reps). Existing generative approaches largely formulate CAD construction as a sequence modeling problem, but consequently lack an explicit topological inductive bias. In this work, we present GraphCAD, a geometry-aware generative framework that centers modeling on the Edge-Adjacency Graph (EAG), a novel graph-based CAD representation tailored for generative tasks. GraphCAD adopts a hybrid graph diffusion formulation to jointly model the discrete and continuous components of EAG and introduces a geometry-aware denoising mechanism that renders node attributes into spatial point sets. These point sets are encoded by an SE(3)-equivariant backbone and fused into the node representations, thereby grounding the generative process in physical geometry. To support this study, we construct EAGBench, a large-scale dataset of engineering CAD models. Extensive experiments show that GraphCAD can generate complex CAD models with more than 50 faces and achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity and distributional alignment compared with sequence-based baselines.
authors: Wenhao Zheng, Xianggen Liu, Li Yue, Jiancheng Shi, Jiancheng Lv
bullets: Targets the challenge of jointly modeling B-rep topology and precise spatial geometry.
Introduces EAG, a graph-based CAD representation designed for generative modeling.
Uses hybrid graph diffusion for discrete connectivity and continuous node attributes.
Renders node attributes as point sets and encodes them with an SE(3)-equivariant backbone for geometry-aware denoising.
Evaluations on the newly constructed EAGBench show strong geometric fidelity and distributional alignment, including models with over 50 faces.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the GraphCAD framework. Top: The generative pipeline. Themodel synthesizes CADmodels by iteratively denoising the Edge-Adjacency Graph (EAG), our proposed topological representation of B-rep geometry. Bottom: The GeometryAware Denoising module. Unlike standard graph-based methods that treat node attributes as abstract vectors, our approach explicitly “renders” these attributes into spatial point sets through “Curve Sampling”. The sampled point sets are then processed by an SE(3)-equivariant Vector Neuron backbone to extract rotation-robust geometric embeddings.
Figure 5: Unconditional generation results on the EAGBench dataset. GraphCAD generates realistic CAD models with complex geometry and topology.

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison of CAD models from conditional generation. From top to bottom, we show results produced by DeepCAD, Text2CAD, TGBFN, BrepGiff, our proposed GraphCAD, and the Ground Truth (GT).

Figure 4: Visual categorization of the primary failure modes encountered during EAG-to-B-rep reconstruction.

Figure 1: Construction of the Edge-Adjacency Graph (EAG) representation. (a) A Boundary Representation (B-rep) of a CAD solid. (b) Construction of the Edge-Adjacency Graph, where each graph node corresponds to a topological edge in the B-rep and graph edges indicate shared B-rep vertices. (c) The EAG representation with node attributes, where each node encodes the curve type together with compact analytic geometric parameters.

papers.abstract: Many language-model pipelines end in a closed-set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order-sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately. In a three-seed study at 32 million parameters, per-option scoring beats joint scoring on a held-out sample of a 37-benchmark decision suite by 5.8 points of chance-corrected skill at matched optimizer steps and by 2.8 at approximately matched training compute; two external benchmarks agree, though not significantly on their unseen tasks. Crossing reader with initialisation shows that the advantage requires a reranker initialisation, whose query-candidate pair input matches per-option reading; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Per-option scoring needs 5 to 13 times more encoder passes: at most twice the median latency, but more than four times the mean. Of six released joint encoders (17 million to 1 billion parameters), the 68- and 150-million-parameter models exceed a 435-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited System1-Arena tasks and are at least on par with it on the 145 tasks unseen in training. The smallest answers a median request in 14 milliseconds on 16 processor threads, against 728 for the classifier. Reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the joint models' answers (per-option scoring: none). Up to 68 million parameters, they lead their size range on a public leaderboard's private, mainly in-distribution tests.

bullets: At 32M parameters, per-option scoring outperforms joint scoring by 5.8 chance-corrected skill points at matched optimizer steps and 2.8 at roughly matched compute.

Per-option scoring requires 5–13× more encoder passes, reaching up to 2× median and over 4× mean latency, while remaining invariant to option reordering.
Among joint encoders, 68M and 150M models outperform a 435M DeBERTa-v3 classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited tasks.
The smallest joint model answers requests in 14 ms on 16 processor threads versus 728 ms for the classifier; joint models remain sensitive to option order on 12–23% of answers.

papers.abstract: Stable grasping under task-specific disturbances is important for robotic manipulation. However, most dexterous grasp synthesis methods are developed for highly actuated hands in free space, and low-DoF hands may not be able to realize the contact topologies required by these grasps. Meanwhile, support surfaces can provide useful contact forces, but are often treated only as geometric constraints. We present a support-aware grasp synthesis framework for object immobilization with low-DoF coupled hands. Given irregular object geometry, our method represents both hand and object local surface regions as graphs and searches for kinematically feasible matchings between them. We then refine the wrist pose and motor state for geometric contact feasibility and validates the refined grasps through physical rollouts. Starting from the validated grasp pose, an optional task-guided local search explores nearby grasp configurations by varying the wrist pose and motor state, and selects one according to the specified task condition. Experiments on diverse objects show that our method generates various grasp configurations that achieve high grasp success and strong disturbance resistance. Real-world experiments further demonstrate physically executable grasps which enable object immobilization in cooking scenario.
authors: Sang-Hun Han, Changyeon Won, JunGyu Lee, Min-Gyu Park, Hae-Gon Jeon
bullets: Targets stable object immobilization when low-actuation hands cannot realize conventional free-space grasp topologies.

An optional task-guided local search adapts nearby grasps to specified task conditions.

papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) often exhibit successful cross-lingual transfer through continued (pre)training, still their underlying process remains unclear. One possibility is that LMs can leverage the evidence toward language-universal principles, namely, hierarchical structure, from a source language (L1) to a new language (L2), while many other non-linguistic explanations, e.g., improved initialization of position embeddings, can be potentially possible. In this study, to quantify the cross-linguistic transferability of linguistic evidence in cross-lingual LM training, we introduce a new experimental design, namely, a cross-lingual poverty-of-stimulus (CPOS) setting that ablates how LMs' hierarchical generalization in L2 can be led by structural evidence provided in L1. We contrast counterfactual L1 and L2 learning scenarios where the L2 corpus is ambiguous between linear and hierarchical grammar rules, while the amount of positive evidence for the hierarchical rule is controlled on the L1 side. Our experimental results show that LMs can partially, yet not perfectly, transfer L1 structural evidence to L2, yielding only a small but detectable hierarchical bias, while the strength of transfer depends on language pairs. We further ablate the conditions for successful transfer, motivated by recent reports on the substantial impact of vocabulary overlap. We indeed find that vocabulary overlap is crucial even for the cross-lingual transfer of hierarchical syntactic generalization. This suggests that this also explains the language-pair-dependent tendencies in the main experiments and suggests that the transfer of linguistic evidence in continued new-language learning is only conditionally achievable.
authors: Shin Yamaguchi, Masaya Taniguchi, Tatsuki Kuribayashi, Taro Watanabe, Yoshinobu Kano
bullets: Introduces a cross-lingual poverty-of-stimulus (CPOS) design to isolate transfer of structural evidence from other benefits of continued pretraining.

Finds partial but imperfect transfer: L2 models develop a small, detectable hierarchical bias.

Concludes that cross-lingual transfer of linguistic evidence is conditional rather than universal.

papers.abstract: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models bring an appealing form of explainability to a safety-critical domain, since a system that can state the reasons for its maneuvers offers the transparency that deployment and public trust in autonomous driving demand. These models read the world into language before they act on it, describing the scene and reasoning over it in text that ranges from chain-of-thought to multi-stage question answering on the way to a trajectory. That framing quietly assumes two separable properties, namely that the trajectory follows the generated reasoning and that the generated reasoning tracks the causes that actually produce the trajectory. To thoroughly investigate these properties, we apply causal, counterfactual interventions to four driving VLAs across different benchmarks. First, we perturb the models' own reasoning and show that altering its meaning produces small trajectory changes relative to blanking the same models' camera inputs, a pattern that persists across benchmarks and model architectures. We then construct scene-level counterfactuals through photorealistic removal of key objects named in the models' reasoning and analyze whether the generated reasoning and trajectories track these changes. Overall, our findings indicate that the reasoning these models present to account for their resulting driving behavior is weakly coupled to that behavior itself, pointing to limits on the explainability these systems are intended to provide.
authors: Gabriel Manalu, Saad Wazir, Thao Do, Seongah Kim, Hyeontaek Hwang, Tolcha Yalew Kidane, Daeyoung Kim

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reads only a small subset of the key-value cache, and how to treat the unread tail remains a key challenge. Discarding the tail biases the output, and sampling it as previous approaches do fails at reads of 5% and below, where the tail likely holds heavy hitters the selector missed. Our key observation is that the simplest possible proxy, one token that folds the entire tail into its count-aware mean, already yields lower output error than a sample at every read behind a practical selector. We further show in closed form that at low reads sampling nearly doubles the weight error of discarding while a single proxy stays below it. Building on these findings, we explore approximating the dense attention distribution with a few proxies that target the tail. We propose OpenAttention, a pipeline of clustering, ErrorGate and top-k selection followed by a count-aware mean proxy. To implement clustering and selection both efficiently and effectively, we design training-free Query-Geometry Clustering (QGC) and a Query-Geometry Selector (QGS), which compress the keys while respecting the query directions. Additionally, unlike prior methods that rank clusters by centroid alone, ErrorGate allocates the exact read by the estimated weight error of each cluster. On RULER-32K HARD with Llama-3.1-8B, OpenAttention retains 99% of dense accuracy at a 1% read. It also achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across models, context lengths and datasets. Our customized attention kernel, OpenAttention.flash, runs the decode attention stage 10$\times$ faster than dense attention at a 1% read.
authors: Hyunwoo Yu, Jongbeom Lee, Hyunbin Kim, Sungjun Park, Jaemin Choi, Jincheol Yang, Seunghun Moon, Bongjoon Hyun, Kyomin Sohn, Kyeongbo Kong, Suk-Ju Kang

papers.abstract: We present IQuest-Q1, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic foundation model with 320B total parameters (15B activated). IQuest-Q1 is developed through a three-stage process: (1) stable and efficient pre-training, combining Stable SplitNorm, Muon, and muP with a two-stage curriculum whose second stage increases the coding-data mixture, preserving a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates; (2) fine-grained mid-training, expanding the data mixture across domains and formats and progressively extending the context; and (3) multi-scaffold with multi-version post-training, combining SFT, domain-specialized RL, and MOPD across various scaffolds to integrate complementary training signals and strengthen agentic coding capabilities. Furthermore, model merging combines different experts and checkpoints from different stages while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates. The resulting IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities in both coding and general tasks. We release IQuest-Q1 as an open-source model to support community research and development.

papers.abstract: Random projections (RP) offer an effective method for reducing computational and storage overhead while preserving the geometric structure of data. However, existing studies have primarily focused on the optimal generalization performance of specific kernel-regularized algorithms with RP in the well-specified setting and under restrictive conditions. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive and improved analysis of the generalization performance of RP-based spectral algorithms under general conditions \change{without sacrificing statistical efficiency}. By leveraging the embedding property of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) and a refined analysis of the operator similarity, we establish optimal learning rates in Sobolev norms that match the minimax lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. For two common implementations of RP, randomized sketches and Nystr\"{o}m sub-sampling (uniform or leverage-based), we show that the projection dimension required for optimality is proportional to the average or maximal effective dimension, yielding a significant reduction in computational cost while maintaining the statistical efficiency. Our results do not rely on the uniform boundedness assumption on the regression function and are valid across a wide range of source conditions, i.e., $s> \alpha_0-1/\beta$, where $s,\beta$, and $\alpha_0$ denote the smoothness index, capacity index, and the embedding index, respectively. In the benign case when $\alpha_0=1/\beta$, the optimality holds for all $s\in (0,2\tau]$ with $\tau$ and $\gamma$ denoting the qualification index and norm index. Experimental results demonstrate both the theoretical validity and the practical effectiveness of the proposed method.
authors: Caixing Wang, Yue Wang
bullets: Analyzes random-projection-based spectral algorithms under broad conditions, beyond restrictive well-specified settings.
Uses RKHS embedding properties and refined operator-similarity analysis to establish optimal Sobolev-norm rates.
Covers randomized sketches and Nyström subsampling, with projection dimensions tied to average or maximal effective dimension.
Results hold across broad source conditions without assuming the regression function is uniformly bounded.
Experiments support the theoretical guarantees and practical effectiveness.

papers.abstract: With external tools, large language models (LLMs) can tackle complex tasks through sustained environmental interaction. LLM-based agents are therefore increasingly used to tackle complex long-horizon tasks in real-world environments. However, these tasks involve sequential, interdependent decisions and changes in environmental states. Early execution errors affect subsequent interaction histories and environmental states, and their effects accumulate along the decision chain. To address this challenge, we propose Reflection-Guided Policy Optimization (ReflectPO), a reinforcement learning framework for autonomous error recovery in long-horizon tasks. ReflectPO comprises two core components. The first is Reflection-Guided Sampling. We use branch differences and repeated visits in interaction trajectories to construct hints for error recovery. The second is Tree-Structured Credit Assignment. We organize sampled trajectories into trees and assign action-level credit using parent--child reward differences and recovery gains. Experiments over two long-horizon tool-use benchmarks show that ReflectPO outperforms multiple existing baselines in most domains. It also achieves the best overall performance on average. Further analyses show that ReflectPO effectively improves agents' ability to recognize their own deviations, recover from erroneous states, and continue making progress toward task completion.
authors: Rumei Li, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Targets compounding errors caused by sequential, interdependent decisions and changing environment states.
Uses branch differences and repeated trajectory visits to generate error-recovery hints.
Structures sampled trajectories as trees and assigns action-level credit using parent–child reward differences and recovery gains.
Outperforms multiple baselines in most domains across two long-horizon tool-use benchmarks and achieves the best average performance.
Improves agents’ ability to recognize deviations, recover from erroneous states, and continue toward task completion.

papers.abstract: Auxiliary patient data can improve chest X-ray report generation, but directly concatenating heterogeneous clinical information with visual tokens produces long, variable-length decoder prompts and may expose the model to redundant or image-irrelevant context. We propose ICGF-CXRMate, an image-conditioned clinical context compression and gated fusion framework. Learnable queries are first conditioned on the current chest X-ray representations and then attend to the patient-data sequence, compressing it into a fixed number of clinical context tokens. Gated cross-attention selectively integrates these tokens into the visual stream, while the compressed tokens are retained in the decoder prompt as a direct clinical pathway. Experiments on linked MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV-ED examinations show that ICGF-CXRMate improves report quality while reducing the average prompt length. In Stage~2, it improves RadGraph-F1 from 24.00 to 28.86, CXR-BERT similarity from 56.86 to 62.80, and BLEU-4 from 5.14 to 7.96 compared with CXRMate-ED, while reducing the average prompt length from 373.89 to 288.37 tokens, corresponding to a 22.9\% reduction. After self-critical sequence training, ICGF-CXRMate outperforms CXRMate-ED on six of eight report-quality metrics in Stage~3. Ablation studies confirm the complementary contributions of image-conditioned compression, gated fusion, and direct retention of the compressed clinical tokens.
authors: Vu Minh Tran, Thuc Huynh, Son Thanh Luu, Doanh C. Bui
bullets: Addresses redundant, image-irrelevant, and variable-length auxiliary clinical data in chest X-ray report generation.
Uses image-conditioned learnable queries to compress patient data into a fixed number of clinical context tokens.
Applies gated cross-attention to integrate compressed context into visual features while retaining a direct clinical pathway in the decoder prompt.
On linked MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV-ED examinations, Stage 2 improves RadGraph-F1, CXR-BERT similarity, and BLEU-4 over CXRMate-ED while reducing average prompt length by 22.9%.
Ablations support complementary benefits from compression, gated fusion, and direct token retention; after self-critical training, it leads on six of eight report-quality metrics.

Gated cross-attention fusion (Sec. 3.3) selectively integrates the compressed context into the visual representations to obtain Ẽimg. The resulting multimodal prompt PICGF = [Z; Ẽimg] is passed to the Llama-based decoder for report generation.

papers.abstract: Cinematic video generation requires both temporal inference from limited inputs (i.e., sparse rather than frame-by-frame guidance) and factor-aware control of character, scene, action, and camera. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer useful priors for both capabilities, but their representations are not automatically actionable for video generation: a Video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) may bypass them through native conditioning pathways, and using them does not ensure either factor-aware control or generation-compatible temporal prediction. We propose Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL), which establishes effective MLLM latent use as a shared prerequisite and then targets the two capabilities with complementary learning signals. First, latent-only generator grounding trains the DiT with a frozen MLLM and connector, strengthening the DiT's use of MLLM latents for generation. Second, for factor-aware control, paired videos specify a target-factor change and non-target preservation, and factor-span replacement trains the DiT to realize this relationship in its output. Third, for temporal inference, text-only and text-plus-complete-video observations share a video target, and the trained DiT is then frozen while the MLLM and connector are optimized through it. This final stage trains limited-input representations for generation while retaining complete-observation reconstruction as a complementary training mode. Extensive experiments demonstrate our consistently better performance on three cinematic video generation tasks (i.e., sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation) over baselines and validate FAPL's contributions to MLLM feature use, temporal control, and factor coordination.
authors: Songlin Yang, Zhe Wang, Xiaotong Zhao, Xi Wang, Ran Zhang, Shuai Li, Taiyi Wu, Songlian Li, Eric Liu, Alan Zhao, Anyi Rao
bullets: Addresses the gap between useful MLLM representations and their reliable use by video diffusion transformers.
Uses latent-only generator grounding to make the DiT depend on frozen MLLM latents.
Learns factor-aware editing through paired videos with target-factor changes and non-target preservation.
Trains temporal inference from text or incomplete video by optimizing the MLLM and connector through a frozen DiT.
Reports consistently better performance than baselines across sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL). Stage I freezes the MLLM and its original connector and trains the DiT using MLLM latents. Stage II retains this configuration and swaps factor-specific output spans between paired examples to supervise factor-aware changes. Stage III freezes the trained DiT and jointly updates the MLLM and connector through video reconstruction, and text-only and text-plus-complete-video inputs share the same generation target.

Figure 2: MLLM latents are easily bypassed in existing MLLM–DiT models. (i) Under MLLMonly conditioning, Omni-Video 2 (1.3B DiT) produces noise, while Omni-Video 2 (14B DiT) and UniVideo produce artifacts and depict one person’s successive actions as two people acting differently. MLLM latents alone therefore fail to provide reliable generation guidance in these examples. (ii) Under conflicting conditions, VAE references dominate the output.

Figure 4: Under limited inputs, baseline models fail to predict temporal visual details. With only text and no visual references, we compare UniVideo with FAPL (Ours), highlighting representative baseline limitations across four cinematic factors. (i) Character. Long hair is generated as short hair, failing appearance details specified only by text. (ii) Scene. The background is not preserved and incorrect content appears. (iii) Action. The requested sequence, e.g., gesturing outward with the left hand and extended fingers, is missing. (iv) Camera. UniVideo ignores the instruction and keeps the camera static, while Ours orbits around the character. FAPL better realizes promptspecified appearance, scene, and motion from text alone.

Figure 5: FAPL improves factor-aware control. For each factor, we modify only the corresponding description in the structured prompt and generate twice, comparing UniVideo with FAPL (Ours). UniVideo does not confine the change to the requested factor and alters unrelated content, whereas Ours modifies the selected factor while preserving the others. This indicates that factor-level latent augmentation enables selective control.

Figure 1: Cinematic video generation requires inference from limited inputs and factor-aware control. (i) The man turns toward the box, places his right hand on top, and steadies the bundle with his left hand. Text-only conditioning misses this sequence, while observing the complete video enables the same model to reproduce it. (ii) Keeping the descriptions of all other factors fixed and replacing only the character-related prompt, the non-character factors change as well. These cases illustrate failures in temporal inference and factor control, with editing providing a probe of what the generator changes and preserves.

papers.abstract: Space data centers (SpaceDCs) are emerging as platforms for large language models (LLMs), supported by continuous solar-energy harvesting and high-speed interconnections. The mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture supports distributed LLM inference by deploying experts across satellites. However, skewed expert activation creates uneven computation power demands despite uniform solar-power supply at the dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit (SSO). Consequently, active experts remain power-constrained while harvested power at idle experts is underused. These reduce inference efficiency and increase latency. To address this supply-demand mismatch, we propose the SpaceWPT framework, which uses inter-satellite laser-based wireless power transfer (WPT) to redistribute harvested power. The key design challenge is to balance the computation demands of power-donating and power-receiving satellites under WPT losses: transferring more power accelerates computation at the receiver but leaves less power for the donor. After deriving design principles that simplify WPT control, we characterize the resulting latency tradeoff through a tractable surrogate of average inference latency. Minimizing the surrogate yields a novel two-sided water-filling strategy that determines whether each active expert donates, retains, or receives power according to the water level and its WPT link efficiency. Simulations with Mixtral-8x7B and Phi-3.5-MoE show up to 29.25% lower inference latency than without WPT, with larger gains under more compact formations and higher transfer efficiencies.
authors: Haotian Zheng, Zhanwei Wang, Kaibin Huang
bullets: MoE expert activation skews create power-demand imbalances: active experts are constrained while idle satellites waste harvested power.
SpaceWPT transfers power between satellites, balancing computation needs while accounting for wireless-transfer losses and donor costs.
A tractable latency surrogate leads to a two-sided water-filling strategy that classifies experts as donors, retainers, or receivers.
Simulations using Mixtral-8x7B and Phi-3.5-MoE report up to 29.25% lower latency than inference without WPT.
Benefits increase in more compact satellite formations and with higher power-transfer efficiency.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with in context learning compared to their textual counterparts. Our preliminary study shows that VLMs rely on textual shortcuts and underutilize the visual demonstrations. We therefore hypothesize that VLMs are insufficiently trained to perform visual in-context learning (vICL). To this end, we construct MIME, a task-agnostic vICL training set without textual shortcuts. We ensure the instruction does not state the rule linking the demonstration images to their answers, so the model must infer it from the visual demonstrations. Fine-tuning on MIME improves vICL accuracy by 8.1 to 18.0 points across three VLMs, preserves single-image performance, and improves multi-image and text only in-context learning. In contrast, stating the rule in the training data sharply reduces this gain. We further propose DTAD (Demonstration Text Attention Dropout), which randomly withholds demonstration labels during training so that the VLM must infer the rule from the demonstration images. While achieving comparable vICL accuracy to fine-tuning on MIME, DTAD yields more consistent attention to the demonstration images. On TrueMICL, Qwen3-VL-8B trained on MIME matches frontier models such as Claude Opus 5, and surpasses them with DTAD. Finally, adding MIME to the instruction-tuning mix of LLaVA 1.5 13B more than doubles its vICL accuracy without hurting single-image abilities, whereas a same-size multi-image set improves it only slightly. These results suggest that vICL data should be a standard component of VLM training.
authors: Nimrod Shabtay, Asaf Yehudai, Avihu Dekel, Eli Schwartz, Raja Giryes
bullets: VLMs often underuse visual demonstrations because training enables textual shortcuts.
MIME is a task-agnostic training set whose instructions omit the rule connecting images and answers.
Fine-tuning on MIME improves vICL accuracy across three VLMs while also benefiting multi-image and text-only in-context learning.
DTAD randomly hides demonstration labels, producing comparable vICL gains and more consistent attention to images.
Adding MIME to LLaVA 1.5 13B more than doubles vICL accuracy; results support including vICL data in standard VLM training.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained image-text retrieval requires a model not only to assess global semantic consistency between an image and a text, but also to model visual evidence for local textual semantics, including objects, attributes, quantities, actions, and relations, so as to distinguish semantically similar candidates. Existing methods commonly use fixed image patches, detected regions, or text tokens as the basic matching units and then aggregate local interactions through max pooling, cross attention, or similarity accumulation. Such strategies remain limited in semantic unit construction and global matching consistency. This paper proposes a hierarchical fine-grained cross-modal alignment framework, termed HFCMA. The framework progressively transforms low-level patch and token representations into adaptive visual regions and textual phrases, and then performs structured region-phrase matching within a global retrieval scoring process. Specifically, HFCMA first adopts dynamic granularity discovery (DGD) to aggregate raw patches and tokens into semantically compact visual regions and textual phrases. It then formulates region-phrase matching as an entropy-regularized optimal transport problem, thereby estimating a structured alignment matrix under global marginal constraints. To reduce background noise and local semantic drift, HFCMA further introduces background debiasing, textual importance weighting, and prototype consistency regularization. Experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO show that HFCMA effectively combines dynamic semantic unit construction with OT-based structured matching under a dual-encoder retrieval framework. The resulting fine-grained score provides structured local alignment information for candidate ranking and improves the discrimination of subtle semantic differences.
authors: Pengfeng Song, Shaozhong Zhang, Pengfei Shao
bullets: Addresses the limits of fixed patches, regions, and tokens for capturing local semantics such as objects, attributes, quantities, actions, and relations.
Uses dynamic granularity discovery to build compact visual regions and textual phrases hierarchically from patches and tokens.
Applies entropy-regularized optimal transport to produce globally constrained region–phrase alignment scores.
Adds background debiasing, textual importance weighting, and prototype consistency regularization to reduce noise and semantic drift.
Experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO report improved discrimination of subtle semantic differences within a dual-encoder retrieval framework.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overall framework of HFCMA. A frozen CLIP-style dual encoder extracts visual patch and textual token features. Dynamic granularity discovery organizes them into adaptive visual and textual semantic units, followed by visual background debiasing and phrase importance weighting. The refined units are matched by entropy-regularized OT, and the resulting fine-grained score is combined with global CLIP similarity for final image-text retrieval.

Fig. 3 OT-based structured matching between discovered visual and textual slots. HFCMA builds a cross-modal cost matrix, estimates a transport plan with Sinkhorn iteration under visual and textual marginal constraints, and converts the transport cost into a fine-grained score for reranking together with the global similarity.

Fig. 2 Illustration of dynamic granularity discovery. Patch and token sequences are softly assigned to learnable visual and phrase slots, producing compact semantic units without requiring bounding-box or phrase-boundary annotations. Sparse and diverse regularization encourages sample-adaptive slot activation and reduces redundant local units.

papers.abstract: Neurosurgical navigation commonly presents magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as 2D slices, making it difficult to relate the anatomy in those slices to the cortical surface observed through the surgical microscope. We seek a common 3D visualization that combines a photorealistic reconstruction of the exposed cortex during tumor surgery with whole-brain MRI context and diffusion tractography pathways. This requires the reconstructed cortex to form a clear boundary around the brain anatomy rather than a diffuse volume that obscures internal structures. Conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can reproduce observed views but, under limited surgical view coverage, may distribute opacity through a thick and geometrically ambiguous band. We introduce height-field 2D Gaussian Splatting (H-2DGS), a three-stage pipeline that concentrates a robust 3DGS reconstruction, fuses its depth into a shared truncated signed distance field (TSDF) surface, and represents that surface with curved, surface-oriented Gaussian primitives. Separate height, color, and opacity bases provide local geometry and appearance, while a neighbor-transition objective coordinates overlapping patches. The explicit surface further supports postoperative alignment: MRI-derived depth deforms the reconstruction, and tracked-color supervision with alternating optimization preserves its appearance. Across five real neurosurgical cases, H-2DGS gives low multi-view depth inconsistency, a compact 7.97MB representation, and interactive rendering at 29--42ms per frame. The resulting sharp, deformable surface integrates clearly with tractography and MRI anatomy, including a postoperative resection cavity.
authors: Zhang Zichuan, Bart Brouwers, Rembrandt Bakker, Maud Landers, Geert-Jan Rutten, Maxime Chamberland
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity of conventional 3D Gaussian Splatting, which can produce diffuse volumetric reconstructions of exposed cortex.
Uses a three-stage pipeline: robust 3DGS initialization, TSDF-based surface fusion, and curved surface-oriented Gaussian primitives.
Separates height, color, and opacity representations and uses neighbor-transition optimization to improve continuity across patches.
Supports postoperative deformation through MRI-derived depth and preserves appearance with tracked-color supervision.
Validated on five real neurosurgical cases, achieving low multi-view depth inconsistency, a 7.97MB representation, and interactive 29–42 ms rendering.
