papers.abstract: We present TwinStore, a source-available synthetic consumer platform for physical retail built on vision--language models. TwinStore turns a store into a digital twin---from 82 ready-made formats, a floor-plan image or phone photos of its shelves---and fills it with synthetic shoppers who plan a trip, walk the aisles and decide what to buy by looking at rendered shelves with packs, price tags and promotion signs. Every trip ends in a receipt, so a layout, price, pack or promotion can be tried on the same shoppers before it reaches the store. Around this core, TwinStore provides 3D playback, paired comparisons and layout optimization, shopper interviews, a trade-area model, counterfactual edits of real shelf photos, a marketing studio with eleven tools, and an assistant that turns a plain sentence into a drafted study or an answer grounded in a run's own numbers. In a held-out validation on eleven public datasets, simulated receipts approach the households' own natural variation (category-mix divergence 0.017--0.018 against a real drift of 0.012), price elasticities fall inside the range measured in the field, and three independent decision models agree. TwinStore runs on cloud or on-device models and is distributed with installers for Windows, macOS and Linux.
authors: Minhyeok Lee
bullets: Builds digital twins of stores from ready-made formats, floor plans, or shelf photos, then renders shelves with products, prices, and promotions.
Simulated shoppers plan trips, navigate aisles, make purchase decisions, and generate receipts for repeated scenario testing.
Supports playback, paired comparisons, layout optimization, shopper interviews, trade-area modeling, photo counterfactuals, marketing tools, and study assistance.
In validation across eleven public datasets, simulated purchasing patterns approached observed household variation; price elasticities were within field-measured ranges.
Runs with cloud or on-device models and provides installers for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

papers.abstract: Lifting vision-language features such as CLIP into 3D Gaussian reconstructions enables open-vocabulary segmentation through natural-language queries. Although CLIP represents a broad range of semantic concepts, the lifted features of individual scenes can exhibit strong directional concentration, while raw cosine similarity does not account for the scene-specific feature distribution. We show that substantial segmentation gains can be obtained by changing how a fixed lifted feature field is compared with text. Our method partially subtracts a shared scene direction from visual features and text prototypes and whitens text prototypes using a fixed reference vocabulary of generic terms. It then uses soft clustering for multiclass prediction and CSLS with a relevance margin against the reference vocabulary for single-query prediction. Beyond reducing directional concentration, scene centering improves class-relative feature separation in every evaluated scene. Across seven lifting methods and four datasets, the resulting query-time calibration consistently improves mean intersection over union in both multiclass and single-query segmentation. These gains require no retraining, source-image re-encoding, or feature re-lifting, demonstrating the value of scene-conditioned comparison for making better use of existing lifted representations.
authors: Dominik Engel, Yousef Rajeh, Leon Sick, Ivan Viola
bullets: Addresses scene-specific directional concentration that makes raw CLIP cosine similarity unreliable for 3D segmentation.
Partially removes a shared scene direction and whitens text prototypes using a fixed vocabulary of generic terms.
Uses soft clustering for multiclass prediction and CSLS with a relevance margin for single-query prediction.
Improves class-relative feature separation across evaluated scenes and consistently raises mean IoU across seven lifting methods and four datasets.
Operates entirely at query time, requiring no retraining, source-image re-encoding, or feature re-lifting.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Method Overview. Starting from a Gaussian scene with lifted CLIP features, we calibrate the scene and text query features using centering and text-whitening, based on a reference vocabulary. Instead of plain query-scene similarities, we further calibrate the similarity scores using soft clustering for multi-class and CSLS with a relevance margin for single-query. Our calibration results in increased class-relative separation, as visualized in the similarity maps on the bottom. Our final predictions achieve substantial improvements in segmentation mIoU for both multi-class (visualized in bar chart) and single class.

Figure 3: Score calibration. Starting from the Middle: First we use the reference vocabulary to determine the whitening statistics. Left: For multi-class queries (N > 1) we center and whiten all text queries and perform soft clustering of the primitive features, using fixed text-derived probabilities to guide assignments and weighted top-eight visual primitives to initialize the centers. After clustering, argmax decides the class of each primitive. Right: For a single-class query (N = 1) we center and whiten the query and the reference vocabulary, apply reduced CSLS and compute the margin between each primitive’s corrected query score and its highest corrected reference-bank score. To make a prediction we threshold this relevance margin using τ .
Figure 2: Scene centering maps blue input vectors z to teal calibrated vectors u by subtracting the orange mean direction µ and renormalizing.

papers.abstract: Active inference casts perception, learning and planning as variational inference, where the Expected Free Energy (EFE) defines the planning objective. Recent work showed that EFE minimization can be written as Variational Free Energy (VFE) minimization on a generative model augmented with epistemic priors, and that the resulting entropy-corrected objective is minimized by sum-product message passing (SP-MP) on modified factor functions. These formulations treat model uncertainty as inference over a finite set of known models. We extend them to planning during learning, where beliefs over the observation and transition parameters $\theta_A$, $\theta_B$ are Dirichlet priors. Closed-form Dirichlet updates are usually obtained by a structured mean-field factorization between parameters and states, but under exactly that factorization the information-gain corrections vanish. We resolve this by giving every factor its own parameter prior, frozen during a rollout. Conjugacy then makes each factor belief a product of a marginal over the categorical variables and a one-step Bayes posterior of the parameters. This reintroduces the datum-dependent parameter posteriors that mean-field factorization destroys. We show that evaluating the epistemic priors under the resulting Bethe joint recovers the information gains. Stationarity of this single closed-form objective yields SP-MP whose factor functions are augmented by the information-gain weight. Experiments on two grid POMDPs, in which only a planner that learns the model finds the safe route, show that the method plans to efficiently learn $\theta_A$ and $\theta_B$. It reaches the goal on every episode, whereas SP-MP planners with the same inference update plateau or take the risky route.
authors: Benedikt Waldeck
bullets: Addresses the loss of information-gain corrections when parameter and state beliefs use structured mean-field factorization.
Uses factor-specific, rollout-frozen Dirichlet parameter priors to recover datum-dependent parameter posteriors.
Derives a single closed-form Bethe objective whose stationarity yields sum-product message passing with information-gain-weighted factors.
In two grid POMDPs, the learning planner found the safe route and reached the goal on every episode, unlike comparison planners that plateaued or chose the risky route.

papers.abstract: Large language models trained on data generated by other models can sometimes inherit traits unrelated to that data, a phenomenon called subliminal learning. We study both hard label distillation, where students train on numbers generated by a biased teacher, and on-policy soft label distillation, where students generate the data and the teacher's logits provide the learning signal. Using Pythia, PolyPythia, and DataDecide OLMo models, we find that transfer persists in both settings across differences in weight initialization, pretraining data order, pretraining corpus, model size, and architecture. Across pretraining checkpoints, the ability to transmit a preference and the ability to acquire one develop separately: some checkpoints are more effective teachers but weaker students, and vice versa. Consistent with this distinction, cross-model transfer can be strongly asymmetric in magnitude when teacher and student roles are reversed. To investigate what carries the preference signal, we construct synthetic number sequences that match the teacher's generated number frequencies but have no dependence on the prompt or preceding numbers and find that these still induce substantial transfer in the hard-label setting. In top-$K$ soft-label distillation, removing animal tokens from the loss reduces transfer, although not completely in the same-model setting. In our experiments, soft label distillation produces more consistent transfer with less extensive training than hard label distillation. The growing use of on-policy distillation in model post-training makes this a particularly relevant setting for assessing unintended preference transfer.
authors: Angela Tang, Vishesh Anand, Gon\c{c}alo Paulo
bullets: Transfer occurs in both hard-label and on-policy soft-label distillation across initialization, data order, corpus, model size, and architecture changes.
The ability to transmit a preference and acquire one develops separately, causing potentially strong asymmetry when teacher and student roles are reversed.
Synthetic sequences matching teacher-generated number frequencies still produce substantial hard-label transfer, suggesting prompt-independent frequency signals can carry preferences.
Removing animal tokens from top-K soft-label losses reduces—but does not eliminate—transfer in same-model settings.
Soft-label distillation yields more consistent transfer with less training than hard-label distillation in the reported experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Same-checkpoint and Cross-checkpoint transfer within Pythia-160M pretraining trajectories. (Left) Same-checkpoint transfer rises sharply during pretraining, with timing and magnitude of increase varying across models. Some checkpoints are more effective as teachers than as students, while others show the reverse pattern.

Figure 2: Subliminal learning in Pythia-160M. We measure transfer as the difference in trait probability between the student and a control student distilled on numbers generated by the untuned base model. (Left) With student hyperparameters fixed, sweeping the teacher’s finetuning hyperparameters produces a wide range of transfer. (Right) Training the student for more epochs can increase transfer but degrades language modeling abilities. Students trained on control numbers show similar degradation without acquiring a bias.

Figure A25: Distribution of transfer across model size and architecture and across OLMo pretraining conditions. We illustrate the median, 75th percentile, 95th percentile, and observed maximum of transfer in the cross model size, cross model architecture, and OLMo-1B experiments. A: Transfer between Pythia-160M and Pythia-410M, using the original models and full-seed variants 1-3 at each size. Models with shared seeds share a pretraining data order. Different seeds do not. Cross-architecture comparisons pair three Pythia-160M models with three OLMo-1B Dolma1.7 models. Descriptively, the smaller receiver (160M) shows the larger upper tail in the cross-Pythia experiments, while OLMo-to-Pythia transfer has a longer upper tail but a lower median than transfer in the reverse direction.

Figure 3: Top-K on-policy distillation of the bear preference, Pythia-160M teacher and student. It is positive at every K shown and peaks at K = 5 to 30; at K = 1 every student exceeds five times the untuned student’s perplexity on held-out Pile text and is excluded (Appendix A.12). Figure 1: Experimental setup for hard label and soft label distillation. In hard-label distillation, we first fine-tune the teachers on animal preference prompts. The teacher then generates number sequences, which are filtered and used to train the student. In soft label distillation, we instead fine-tune the teacher on synthetic documents that convey the preference. The student generates continuations of Pile text, and the frozen teacher provides next-token probabilities that guide the student’s updates.

(Left) Fraction of matched student-control pairs for which the student assigns greater probability to the target animal. (Right) Median, 75th perc., 95th perc., and observed max of pstudent − pcontrol, pooled across animals. Transfer in this setting is strongest when models share the same pretrained base. Sharing initialization while changing data order retains larger effects than changing both.

Figure A33: Cross-model asymmetry often persists in a single direction throughout student training, although some pairs can reverse direction. Each curve shows mean control-adjusted transfer in the direction named in the legend minus transfer in the reverse direction. Positive values favor the named direction, while negative values favor the reverse. Panels show the dog preference across four Pythia pretraining conditions.

Figure A28: On-policy distillation between models of different sizes and families. Each bar is one teacher → student pair for the bear preference, grouped by student. Each group opens with the student’s same-model pair (hatched), and the dashed line carries its level across the group. Bars are means of pstudent − pcontrol with 95% intervals, the wider of a cluster bootstrap over both seeds and a t-interval over teacher seeds.

Figure A41: Teacher preference across pretraining. Teacher preference, the SDF teacher’s own p(bear) averaged over three fine-tuning seeds, against the teacher’s checkpoint. Thin colored lines are one model each, colored by training stack.

Figure A16: A first-person belief gives the most biased teacher and the least transfer. (a) Teacher p(bear) and (b) transfer for corpora of about 2,000 documents whose belief is written in the first person, in the third person, or mixed (16% first person). Each model is evaluated on the 50 held-out first-person prompts (solid) and on 50 third-person prompts (hatched). Dots and error bars as in Figure A14; the dashed lines are the original bear corpus on each set of prompts.

Figure A14: Where the belief sits changes transfer more than it changes the teacher. (a) Teacher p(bear) on the 50 held-out preference prompts and (b) transfer, the student’s p(bear) minus that of the controls, for corpora of about 8,000 documents (solid) and nested subsets of about 2,000 (hatched) whose mentions of bears all sit in the first quarter of each document (start), its middle (middle), its last quarter (end), or a third of each (mix). papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is credited with teaching reasoning models to write {wait} before reconsidering a step, yet large RL accuracy gains do not require the word. This view can confuse what RL discovers with what a model inherits from its training data. We trace the word through open models' training histories, reading it with label-free indices of frequency, position, form and usage and an injected-error test, all computed from sampled outputs. We find that zero-RL almost never coins the marker: on bases that lack the word, RL raises MATH-500 accuracy substantially while {wait} stays near absent. It arrives with training data: mid-training in OLMo-3, and fine-tuning on reasoning traces installs it in most models whose base lacks it. Where the base already uses it, both released RL-Zero recipes (OLMo-3, MiMo) multiply it, whereas KL-free GRPO from the same base does not; OLMo-3's recipe wears down its form and makes it a more sensitive but more liberal alarm; RL after supervised fine-tuning barely changes it, and our GRPO recipe erases a marker seeded by fine-tuning. Finally, we show that marker frequency alone does not indicate RL-induced reasoning and caution against LLM-as-a-judge revision metrics, as automated judges can reverse human-labelled trends.
authors: Zhizhuo Kou, Sizai Hou, Long Chen, Jian Yang, Junyu Luo, Jingshu Peng, Wenkai Zhang, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Models typically inherit `{wait}` from mid-training or supervised reasoning traces; RL rarely creates it when absent.
On bases lacking the marker, RL can substantially improve MATH-500 accuracy while `{wait}` remains nearly absent.
When already present, released RL-Zero recipes increase its use, but KL-free GRPO may not; supervised fine-tuning can also seed or erase it.
RL changes the marker’s form and error-detection behavior, making it potentially more sensitive but less conservative.
Marker frequency is not a reliable measure of RL-induced reasoning, and LLM judges may disagree with human-labeled revision trends.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a model on its own trajectories with dense token-level supervision from a privileged copy conditioned on a reference solution. Existing methods typically use a single teacher distribution conditioned on the complete reference. We identify a limitation of this formulation: a reference is only one realization of the reasoning process. Although it provides evidence about the answer, it also encodes an ordering, phrasing, and solution path. Full-reference conditioning can therefore produce correct targets that depend excessively on information unavailable to the student at inference. We show that replacing one valid reference with another, while holding the problem and student state fixed, can substantially alter the teacher distribution, a phenomenon we call reference-induced target instability. To address this instability, we introduce Monte Carlo Privileged Distillation (MCPD), which models privileged context as a distribution over partial reference views and distills the marginal teacher distribution. MCPD evaluates the teacher under multiple views and averages the resulting next-token distributions. We show that this probability-space average is the exact target induced by minimizing the expected teacher-to-student KL divergence over privileged views. Across mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, we show that MCPD produces more reference-consistent supervision and consistently improves over full-reference OPSD.
authors: Khouloud Saadi, Di Wang
bullets: Full-reference teacher conditioning can make token-level targets depend on arbitrary solution phrasing, ordering, and path.
The resulting variation across valid references is termed reference-induced target instability.
MCPD treats privileged context as a distribution over partial reference views and averages the teacher’s next-token distributions.
This probability-space average exactly minimizes expected teacher-to-student KL divergence across views.
Across mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, MCPD yields more reference-consistent supervision and improves over full-reference OPSD.

For each problem, we use two valid reference solutions, generate one unprivileged student rollout, and evaluate both methods at matched prefix positions along the same trajectory. MCPD averages K = 4 partial views of each reference; positive values indicate lower reference sensitivity than OPSD. papers.abstract: Humanoid robots must coordinate locomotion and manipulation in everyday environments, yet progress is difficult to assess across differing policies, controllers, and task settings. LocoManiLab provides an integrated testbed spanning data collection and generation, policy training, evaluation, and physical deployment. Its task suite covers 234 atomic and compositional tasks across five household scene categories, supported by 51.5 hours of simulated teleoperation. The evaluation covers twelve policies with a shared controller across task and scene splits and perturbation levels, two policies across five controllers, and studies of demonstration scale and data-source mixtures. Success rates fall on unseen tasks and scenes and generally decline as visual perturbations increase, with differences in generalization and robustness across policies. For data generation, a humanoid motion generation model is fine-tuned for loco-manipulation to study the alignment of its outputs with task execution requirements and its integration into the data generation pipeline. Three simulated loco-manipulation tasks closely match real-world setups, enabling evaluation of three policies in both domains. Similar policy rankings support the reliability of simulation-based evaluation.
authors: Dewei Wang, Jinrui Han, Jiyuan Shi, Chenyun Zhang, Xianbo Lu, Jiabao Wu, Jiqin Feng, Jipeng Kong, Ping Luo, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li
bullets: Covers 234 atomic and compositional tasks across five household scene categories, supported by 51.5 hours of simulated teleoperation.
Evaluates policy and controller choices under task/scene splits, visual perturbations, demonstration scales, and mixed data sources.
Finds reduced success on unseen tasks and scenes, with further degradation under stronger visual perturbations and varying robustness across policies.
Includes loco-manipulation motion generation fine-tuning and examines how generated motions support task execution and data generation.
Three simulated tasks mirror real-world setups; consistent policy rankings across domains support simulation-based evaluation.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning has become a common way to customize text-to-image models, leading to community collections of over 100K lightweight adapters. Adapters sharing a base model can be merged with continuous coefficients. This turns a large collection into a high-dimensional continuous design space, which recent work explores interactively using preferential Bayesian optimization (PBO). However, existing approaches are limited to a few dozen preselected adapters and require expensive image generation in every interaction round. We introduce HimmBO, a two-stage method that scales preference-driven adapter merging to much larger collections while reducing image-generation cost. Its screening stage recovers the active adapter set through level-set estimation over pre-generated images, requiring no image generation. The refinement stage then optimizes merge coefficients in the recovered low-dimensional subspace. Both stages use a style-aware kernel, allowing preference information to transfer between visually similar adapters. In simulated-user image-matching experiments, HimmBO achieves higher final similarity than all comparisons while reaching a given similarity with under one tenth of the image generations required by prior work. Its performance remains stable as the collection grows to 1080 adapters, while competing methods degrade substantially.
authors: Jinyuan Mao, Zhihao Shen, Chenxi Liu

papers.abstract: Mix-policy optimization incorporates off-policy expert data into the reinforcement learning (RL) loop to transcend the capability boundary of on-policy RL. However, existing methods either provide static full-trace guidance that suppresses self-exploration, or adopt expert prefix guidance without correctness guarantees, leading to suboptimal performance or even training collapse. In this paper, we propose MOER, a mix-policy optimization framework that harmonizes expert guidance with self-exploration. MOER injects a decaying expert chain-of-thought prefix into the prompt and lets the model complete the remaining reasoning, with the prefix length progressively annealed to encourage self-exploration. A selective rollback mechanism replaces failed completions with the original full expert trace, guaranteeing the correctness of every off-policy trajectory. Furthermore, a harmonized mix-policy objective optimizes on-policy tokens with a GRPO loss while supervising both expert prefix and completion tokens with a trust-region SFT loss, substantially stabilizing training. Extensive experiments show that MOER achieves the highest average scores in mathematical and general domain reasoning tasks, outperforming all basic and mix-policy baselines, and generalizes consistently across diverse tasks, model scales, and base model categories. Codes are available at https://github.com/CityU-MLO/MOER.
authors: Xuyang Zhong, Jiuding Yang, Yiwen Guo, Chen Liu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between static expert guidance that limits exploration and prefix guidance that can produce incorrect off-policy trajectories.
Injects a decaying expert chain-of-thought prefix and progressively anneals its length to promote self-exploration.
Uses selective rollback to restore failed completions to the original expert trace, preserving trajectory correctness.
Combines GRPO for on-policy tokens with trust-region SFT for expert-prefix and completion tokens to stabilize training.
Reports the highest average scores across mathematical and general reasoning tasks, with consistent generalization across tasks, model scales, and base-model categories.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, placing greater demands on reliable AI-generated video detection. Existing artifact-based detectors typically identify generation artifacts as evidence for source prediction, yet they may either fail to recognize subtle artifacts or reach the correct source decision without faithfully identifying the evidence underlying it. In this work, we systematically investigate how to design and train effective artifact detectors and formulate artifact detection as a structured process comprising three complementary capabilities: Inspection Planning, which determines what should be examined; Evidence Verification, which verifies whether the inspected content exhibits genuine generation artifacts; and Evidence Aggregation, which integrates the verified evidence into the final source decision. Building on this formulation, we introduce Verus-Insight, trained with human-anchored full-process supervision and progressive capability training to strengthen both fine-grained artifact detection and video-level detection. We further introduce Verus-Bench, a benchmark with fine-grained human annotations of perceptible artifacts for evaluating artifact detection. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that Verus-Insight achieves strong performance in both fine-grained artifact analysis and AI-generated video detection, with substantial gains in recovering human-perceived artifacts. Further analyses reveal that the three capabilities are complementary yet distinct, and that Verus-Insight more reliably converts relevant inspection targets into supported artifact evidence without increasing spurious artifact claims.
authors: Zhuoran Zhang, Yang Shi, Qixun Wang, Tengfei Liu, Yuqi Tang, Xuanyu Zhu, Yizhuo Jia, Jingyun Hua, Shixuan Liu, Xianghua Ying, Haotian Wang, Yuanxing Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Wenjing Yang

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generation enables low-latency streaming, yet prevailing training pipelines separate causal adaptation from distribution matching. Recent representation-based text-to-video methods retain this separation by starting from ODE-initialized checkpoints, even when the target distribution is defined directly by reference videos. We introduce Direct Forcing, a single-stage framework that uses reference videos both as paired examples of how a history continues and as a target population for self-generated rollouts. Causal Continuation Alignment learns paired spatiotemporal correspondence under reference histories, while Rollout Distribution Matching uses maximum mean discrepancy to align the representation distributions of self-generated and reference videos. Together, these complementary signals allow a pretrained video model to learn causal continuation and the target video distribution in a single training stage. Dynamic Gradient Balancing adapts the relative gradient contributions of continuation alignment and distribution matching during training. Starting from bidirectional Wan2.1-1.3B, Direct Forcing learns a four-step autoregressive generator in 250 updates without a separate initialization stage or online diffusion-score supervision, achieving 84.63 VBench Total and 86.01 Quality. Ablation studies further demonstrate the benefits of dynamic gradient balancing and reveal distinct representation preferences: deeper features benefit continuation alignment, whereas intermediate features yield better performance for rollout distribution matching.

papers.abstract: An AI system can produce more economically valuable work while delivering less value for the energy it consumes. We therefore ask: How much economic value does an AI system create per unit of energy consumed? We formalize economic value in two ways: (1) net dollar value, the output's dollar value minus AI-system execution cost, and (2) time saving, the expert's completion time minus the AI system's completion time. Dividing each by measured end-to-end energy yields Net Value per Joule (NVJ) and Time Saving per Joule (TSJ), reported in USD/MJ and hours/MJ. We study 220 public GDPval tasks across 44 occupations, serving five open-weight models locally and evaluating four accelerator types. First, the occupation groups where AI systems succeed most often, deliver the greatest dollar value, or save the most time do not necessarily provide the greatest economic return per joule. For example, among the tested tasks, engineering work delivers about 10% more net dollar value per task than software development. Yet software development delivers about 27% more net value per joule. Second, GLM 5.2 delivers the highest average net dollar value, at $72.27 per task using 0.430 MJ, equivalent in energy to about four hours of active laptop use. By contrast, Gemma 4 31B delivers 56% of that net dollar value using just 23% of the energy, achieving approximately 2.5 times the NVJ and 2.8 times the TSJ. Third, across four single-accelerator deployments, Qwen3.6-27B's NVJ varies by a factor of 4.32 and TSJ by 9.27, with B200 leading both. Additionally, one and eight H100s deliver similar net dollar value, but eight reduce completion time by 22% at 3.24 times the energy. Our framework makes output value and expert time saving under an energy budget explicit objectives for improving models, accelerators, and software, while offering a new basis for assessing AI's potential economic effect on occupational work.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based audio-visual generation methods typically perform joint denoising of audio and video latents throughout the entire sampling trajectory, repeatedly executing modality-specific denoising branches and cross-modal attention at every timestep. However, we observe that such uniform joint computation is not always necessary. The key is a modality-asymmetric recoverability: audio-side drift introduced by mid-stage caching can be substantially reduced by only a few terminal joint denoising steps, whereas video-side degradation caused by caching leads to persistent loss of motion and temporal details. This asymmetry suggests that inference acceleration should selectively cache recoverable audio-side computation while preserving full video refinement. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Convergence-Adaptive Audio-Visual Cache (CAVC)}, a training-free modality-asymmetric caching framework. CAVC adopts a sandwich-structured computation allocation: after detecting that audio denoiser outputs enter a cache-tolerant regime, it caches and reuses the audio denoiser output to bypass audio denoising and cross-modal attention in the middle stage, while the video branch continues independent spatio-temporal refinement; a few joint steps are then restored at the end to reduce accumulated cross-modal drift and improve synchronization. Experiments across multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that CAVC achieves 1.10--1.35x wall-clock acceleration, improves several visual dynamics and temporal statistics, and maintains competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Yibo Zhao, Senlin cheng, Bolei Xu, Xiaobo Li, Can Ye, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses unnecessary joint audio-video denoising and cross-modal attention at every sampling step.
Uses a training-free, convergence-adaptive cache with sandwich-structured computation allocation.
Caches audio denoiser outputs in a cache-tolerant middle regime while video undergoes full spatio-temporal refinement.
Restores a few terminal joint denoising steps to reduce cross-modal drift and improve synchronization.

Across public benchmarks, achieves 1.10–1.35× wall-clock acceleration while maintaining competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment and improving several visual dynamics and temporal statistics.

(Trigger τ): An online monitor tracks audio prediction changes; once stabilized, the audio cache activates. (1B) Cached Continuation: Cached audio predictions are reused. Bypassing the expensive audio branch and AV attention frees the video branch for independent spatio-temporal refinement without being over-constrained by static audio. (2) Final Joint Refinement: Full joint computation is terminally restored for a few steps to reduce accumulated cross-modal drift and refine audio-visual synchronization before decoding.

papers.abstract: Reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) distillation has shown empirical promise for training language models, but its statistical guarantees and limits remain poorly understood. In particular, the effects of two design choices remain unclear: Does access to the teacher's full action distribution provide an advantage over observing only the probability it assigns to the sampled action? Must training trajectories come from the student (online distillation), or can teacher-generated trajectories (offline distillation) suffice? Our work takes a first step toward understanding the theory underlying these questions. We study the sample complexity of online reverse-KL distillation under two feedback models: the teacher reveals either its full action distribution or only the probability of the student-generated action. We establish minimax bounds for the former and show that substantially more data may be required for the latter. In contrast, offline reverse-KL distillation can attain the same minimax rate whether the teacher reveals its full distribution or only its probability of the teacher-generated action. The key distinction is that teacher-generated actions themselves reveal the teacher's preferences, while queries at student-selected actions can leave those preferences unobserved. This highlights an additional statistical challenge for online distillation compared to offline distillation. These statistical guarantees do not follow simply from optimizing standard distillation objectives: our lower bounds show that common online objectives can fail when candidates are evaluated only on past student-generated trajectories. We develop trajectory-loss and importance-ratio truncation techniques together with policy-space learning to achieve optimal online distillation guarantees.
authors: Haolin Liu, Chen-Yu Wei, Julian Zimmert
bullets: Studies online reverse-KL distillation with either the teacher’s full action distribution or only the probability of the student-selected action.
Proves minimax bounds showing limited feedback can substantially increase online sample complexity.
Shows offline distillation achieves the same minimax rate under full-distribution feedback or teacher-action probability feedback.
Attributes the online–offline gap to teacher-generated actions revealing preferences that student-selected queries may miss.
Develops trajectory-loss, importance-ratio truncation, and policy-space learning techniques for optimal online guarantees; lower bounds expose failures of common objectives.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of reverse-KL distillation for language model training.
papers.title: Reverse-KL Policy Distillation: Statistical Guarantees and Limits
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes when reverse-KL policy distillation is statistically efficient, showing that online distillation may need substantially more data with limited teacher feedback, while offline distillation can avoid this gap.

papers.abstract: Ambiguity is a central feature of natural communication: a sentence, image, or sound may remain underspecified until evidence from the other channels is considered. Yet current multimodal benchmarks mostly test perception, recognition, or reasoning over already determinate inputs, leaving unclear whether omni-modal large language models can resolve ambiguity distributed across text, vision, and audio. We introduce TRIAD, a benchmark for omni-modal ambiguity resolution. Each item is a text--image--audio triplet paired with a question and a set of answer options, and is constructed so that the full triplet determines a unique answer while removing any one modality makes the set of consistent options non-unique. TRIAD contains $327$ hand-written queries in $86$ scene groups and covers $18$ ambiguity categories across the three modalities. Evaluating $14$ omni-modal systems reveals that strong item-level performance does not translate into robust scene-level disambiguation: the best model still trails humans by over $20$ points in group accuracy. Removing answer options widens the gap further, driving model group accuracy to the single digits while humans remain robust. Leave-one-out and transcript/description counterfactuals further show that current systems often underuse audio cues when text and image are present. TRIAD reframes omni-modal evaluation around disambiguation rather than recognition, and provides a taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocol for measuring this capability.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Yidi Wang, Yile Li, Siqi Zeng, Yingjie He, Richeng Xuan, Zhichao hu
bullets: Introduces 327 hand-written text–image–audio queries across 86 scene groups and 18 ambiguity categories.
Each item has a unique answer only when all three modalities are available; removing one leaves multiple plausible answers.
Evaluations of 14 omni-modal systems show strong item-level results but substantially weaker scene-level disambiguation than humans.
Models rely insufficiently on audio, especially when text and images are present; removing answer options worsens performance sharply.
Provides an ambiguity taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocols for evaluating cross-modal disambiguation.

papers.abstract: Reliable traversability estimation is essential for autonomous navigation on unstructured terrain. State-of-the-art approaches typically evaluate traversability from deterministic terrain elevation, thereby overlooking spatial correlations in the terrain and failing to account for how elevation uncertainty propagates through nonlinear traversability mappings. We propose ProTrav, a probabilistic terrain representation that uses function-space sampling to generate spatially correlated terrain realizations and propagate elevation uncertainty to traversability cost. First, a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process (SVGP) reconstructs a probabilistic elevation field from observations. Then, posterior function-space sampling generates spatially correlated terrain realizations, preserving spatial dependencies between neighboring locations while propagating elevation uncertainty through geometric features into traversability cost. Consequently, a distribution of traversability cost at arbitrary location is established, where the mean and standard deviation quantify the expected traversability cost and associated uncertainty, respectively. A risk term is defined by moment-based Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) and incorporated into a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller for risk-aware navigation. Simulation experiments demonstrate navigation success rates exceeding 90\% on different terrains, compared with below 40\% for a baseline, while reducing attitude variations. Furthermore, the proposed approach is validated on a robot traversing real-world off-road terrain.
authors: Chuanlin Zuo, Milo\v{s} Pr\'{a}gr, Arun Kumar Singh, Mohammad Loni, Reza Ghabcheloo
bullets: Addresses the limitations of deterministic elevation-based traversability estimation, which ignores spatial correlations and uncertainty propagation.
Uses a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process to reconstruct a probabilistic elevation field.
Samples spatially correlated terrain realizations and propagates uncertainty through geometric features into a distribution of traversability costs.
Defines a moment-based Upper Confidence Bound risk term and integrates it into an MPPI controller.
In simulation, achieves over 90% navigation success versus below 40% for a baseline, reduces attitude variations, and is validated on real off-road terrain.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed probabilistic terrain traversability representation and navigation framework. These realizations are aggregated to obtain moment-based Gaussian approximation, from which a risk term is constructed by UCB and injected into the MPPI rollout cost. The resulting velocity command is sent to the robot for execution.

papers.abstract: Long chain-of-thought reasoning improves vision-language models (VLMs), but it also exposes a temporal grounding failure: as generation unfolds, models may drift from image evidence while reinforcement learning still provides only a final-answer reward. We study this gap through visual revisit, a temporally localized reactivation of image evidence during reasoning. Across three VLM backbones, revisit peaks are predictive of correctness and causally linked to performance: masking them degrades accuracy more than masking non-peaks, while injecting revisit-like peaks into failed rollouts partially restores correct answers. Control analyses show that this signal is not explained by raw attention strength, uncertainty, logit margin, or hidden-state norm. We propose RECAP, a GRPO-compatible training method that turns detached revisit traces into a credit-assignment signal. RECAP uses revisit-conditioned advantage estimation, dynamic discounting, and gated value prediction to propagate final rewards through visually important reasoning steps, without extra rewards, additional rollouts, or inference-time changes. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, and LLaVA-OV-7B, RECAP consistently improves over GRPO and VPPO, yielding $+6.1$--$+6.5$ HallusionBench gains over the SFT base while preserving reasoning and text-only performance. Results on larger LoRA-tuned models, Chinese zero-shot benchmarks, visual perturbations, and human evaluation further demonstrate robust improvements in image-grounded reasoning.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Tailong Luo, Chenxin Li, Yingjie He, Zhenyu Yu, Fengyu Zhou, Jiachen Qian, Lei Wei, Shuang Chen, Jiachen Li, Eric Hanchen Jiang, Rongchao Zhang, Zhengtao Yao, Hoi Leong Lee, Guansu Wang, Kaiyue Zhou
bullets: Long chain-of-thought can cause VLMs to drift from visual evidence because training often rewards only the final answer.
Visual revisit peaks predict correctness and are causally important: masking them hurts accuracy, while adding them can recover some failed answers.
RECAP uses revisit-conditioned advantages, dynamic discounting, and gated value prediction within GRPO, without extra rewards, rollouts, or inference-time changes.
Across three VLM backbones, RECAP improves over GRPO and VPPO, including +6.1–+6.5 HallusionBench points over the SFT base.
Additional evaluations support robustness across larger LoRA-tuned models, Chinese zero-shot benchmarks, visual perturbations, and human judgments.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The RECAP framework. A detached revisit signal r̃t is extracted from cross-modal attention and injected into three parts of the surrogate estimator: the trace-augmented input, dynamic discount, and revisit-gated value predictor. The rollout policy, clipped ratio, and KL anchor remain unchanged.

Figure 3: Causal and mechanistic evidence. Top revisit positions are more decision-relevant than random positions, and revisit peaks align with annotated decision steps. The revisit signal further concentrates in a small set of heads, and zeroing those heads reproduces most of the accuracy drop from masking cross-modal attention.

Figure 1: Visual revisits are causal and localized. Correct rollouts show recurring CMA peaks, while incorrect rollouts lose visual grounding after the initial window. Masking revisit peaks hurts accuracy more than masking random non-peaks, and peak injection partially recovers failed rollouts. A small set of heads explains most of the causal effect.

Figure 6: RECAP training consolidates revisit responsibility onto fewer heads. The top-10 head share of the total revisit signal rises from 34% (SFT base) to 54% after RECAP training, while GRPO on identical data produces only a +4 pt shift (±3 bootstrap CI). Concentration is therefore specific to revisit-aware optimization rather than to RL post-training in general. Similar pattern on the other two backbones (section G.3).

Figure 5: RAP correlates with HallusionBench accuracy on checkpoints from every method, not just RECAP. Pearson ρ ≥ 0.38 on all four methods with 95% bootstrap CIs strictly above zero (≥ 48 checkpoints per method pooled over three backbones), establishing RAP as a method-agnostic diagnostic. The correlation is highest on RECAP (as expected, since RECAP explicitly optimizes revisit-aware return propagation), but substantial non-RECAP correlations confirm RAP is not a restatement of the training objective.

Figure 7: RECAP is consistently more robust to image-side perturbations on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Across four perturbation families, RECAP has smaller relative accuracy drops than VPPO and maintains a clear advantage over GRPO under stronger perturbations.
Figure 4: RAP rises early under RECAP training. RECAP reaches a higher RAP plateau than VPPO, GRPO, and the SFT reference, and the plateau appears before final accuracy convergence.

Table 19: Where each method places its per-token visual signal, broken down by the five structural slots in the GRPO update. Only RECAP uses revisit at all three of post-hoc estimator context, discount, and value; every baseline touches exactly one slot (typically the advantage) and leaves the others at their GRPO defaults. This is the structural statement behind the expressiveness gap of Proposition 1: because dynamic discount acts multiplicatively across future tokens, no single-slot advantage reweighting (VPPO, λ-GRPO) can realize its effect, regardless of how wt is chosen. RECAP still forms the surrogate advantage AVR t in Eq. (11); “no local reweight” means that it does not multiply an otherwise fixed advantage by a same-step visual weight.

papers.abstract: Real-image editing commonly relies on inversion and iterative sampling, while efficient one-step editors often stabilize a large update by estimating and averaging editing fields at multiple noise levels. We ask a stricter question: is a single temporal field evaluation sufficient for reliable inversion-free editing? Our answer rests on a previously underused duality in a variance-preserving (VP) one-step model: one source-target query at a shared noisy state simultaneously determines a local angular semantic tangent and a clean endpoint displacement. We integrate the tangent over the analytically known remaining VP angle to obtain a nominal one-step transport, and use the endpoint displacement to correct its long-horizon extrapolation through a constrained projection. This transport-first, correction-second construction yields Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (ECT), a closed-form, training-free editor requiring only one noise level, two text conditions packed into one denoiser batch, and one latent update. ECT requires no image inversion, trajectory integration, second temporal observation, or iterative optimization, and can be directly applied to pretrained epsilon-prediction VP one-step generators. Across the reported benchmark settings, ECT delivers stable gains in editing quality within an extremely short editing time.

Reported benchmarks show stable editing-quality gains with extremely short editing time.

papers.abstract: Visual perception should be iterative and task-directed, with representations refined in response to the question and the need for further processing. While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly support extended reasoning, their visual tokens are still typically acquired in a single, task-agnostic encoder pass. This creates an evidence-acquisition bottleneck: models may reason longer without refining the visual evidence needed to answer the question. We propose LoopLook, a lightweight encoder-side recurrent perception framework that equips pretrained VLMs with adaptive visual depth. LoopLook recurrently revisits a middle-to-late window of the vision encoder, injecting question representations at each loop to guide visual refinement. A learned stopping mechanism adaptively determines the recurrent depth, while a token-wise Mixture-of-Looks (MoL) combines representations from different loops, allowing each visual token to selectively integrate information acquired across recurrent steps. Across four backbones and eight benchmarks, LoopLook consistently improves performance over the baseline, yielding gains of up to 8.6% on MMStar and 8.1% on HallusionBench. Our analysis shows that LoopLook progressively refines visual attention and adaptively allocates depth according to task difficulty. It also better preserves task-relevant visual information under reduced input resolution, while increasing time to first token (TTFT) by only 5.1-6.5%. By bringing recurrence from reasoning back into perception, LoopLook transforms visual perception from a one-shot glimpse into an adaptive process of recurrent refinement.
authors: Wencheng Ye, Anning Hu, Hongye Fang, Tianyi Wang, Junchi Yan
bullets: Addresses the evidence-acquisition bottleneck caused by one-pass, task-agnostic visual encoding.

Improves results across four backbones and eight benchmarks, with gains of up to 8.6% on MMStar and 8.1% on HallusionBench.
Allocates more depth to difficult tasks, preserves relevant information at lower resolution, and increases TTFT by 5.1–6.5%.

papers.abstract: Predicting relative trained performance from architectural specifications can guide design when training costs limit experimentation. Neural Spectral Capacity (NSC) provides such a heuristic, but scores projections independently and assigns identical scores to compatible reorderings of the same layer configurations. We introduce Residual-Aware Neural Spectral Capacity (ResNSC) for Transformers, using a specification-derived statistical reference for accumulated residual updates to determine the input and residual-state statistics in each projection's capacity calculation, while retaining additive evaluation without data or instantiated weights. When residual widths vary, earlier choices affect later scores, so we augment NSC's allocator (NSC-DP) with residual history beyond its layer-and-budget state. ResNSC-DP jointly allocates residual and feed-forward widths under a resource budget, with certified bounds on the best numerically evaluated ResNSC score within a specified finite candidate set. At the 121M and 374M pretraining scales, selected architectures achieve lower mean perplexity than uniform, variable-width, and tapered allocations on FineWeb-Edu, WikiText-2, and LAMBADA at comparable parameter budgets. In inherited-weight LLaMA-7B pruning using the LoNAS supernet, ResNSC-DP improves eight-task average accuracy over NSC by 3.28--5.46 percentage points across eight matched parameter budgets. Paired reversals preserve the projection shapes and NSC scores yet worsen performance in both settings, exposing performance differences hidden by position-independent scoring. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/Optima-CityU/neural-spectral-capacity.

Paired reversals reveal performance differences hidden by conventional NSC scores; results are evaluated at specific model scales, budgets, and task settings.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation in field-deployed settings requires more than executing a capable controller. As the execution conditions change, the system must decide, online and on the robot side, which control source should hold authority. Human teleoperation adapts readily to contact-rich and semantically ambiguous situations but depends on a stable communication link. Local autonomy is executed without continuous human intervention, but may fail under semantic ambiguity, long-horizon drift, and unforeseen contingencies. These two control sources exhibit complementary reliability profiles. We formulate this complementarity as a control authority routing problem and present Task-Evidence Authority Routing for Robotic Manipulation (TEAR), an edge-deployable framework that allocates authority between human teleoperation and local autonomy. TEAR arbitrates on the robot side using network-state evidence, which governs the usability of teleoperation, and task-semantic evidence, which reflects whether autonomous execution remains consistent with the current task. A lightweight temporal arbitrator observes both forms of evidence together with robot state and current authority to time authority transfers. Across simulated and real-world trials under dynamic network conditions, TEAR achieves task success rates close to pure teleoperation while limiting teleoperation to 19.8-27.4% of control steps and improves success by 30-40% over autonomy-only execution in our settings. These results demonstrate the potential of complementary authority routing to sustain successful manipulation with substantially reduced dependence on continuous human control.
authors: Shicheng Zhang, Hui Liu, Haoliang Li
bullets: Addresses the complementary weaknesses of teleoperation and autonomy in changing, field-deployed conditions.
Uses robot-side network-state and task-semantic evidence, plus robot state and current authority, to time control transfers.
Evaluated in simulated and real-world trials with dynamic network conditions.
Reports success rates near pure teleoperation while using teleoperation for 19.8–27.4% of control steps.
Improves success by 30–40% over autonomy-only execution in the reported settings.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of TEAR. (1) Problem setting. Remote teleoperation and local autonomy exhibit different failure conditions. Network degradation affects the timeliness and continuity of human commands, while task inconsistency, stagnation, or semantic anomalies can affect autonomous execution. (2) Our solution. TEAR introduces a robot-side authority router that jointly considers network and task evidence and assigns control to either human teleoperation or the local VLA policy. The selected source provides the action executed by the robot. (3) Methodology. Task specifications and demonstrations guide offline text-pair selection for a frozen VLM, which extracts progress, engagement, anomaly, and stagnation cues from image observations. These task cues are combined with network conditions, robot state, and current authority to construct a temporal history for handoff-event prediction. A causal temporal router predicts upcoming handoffs, and a stateful gate with hysteresis and cooldown converts the event scores into discrete authority transfers.

papers.abstract: Humanoid motion-tracking policies can reproduce diverse behaviors, yet connecting independently acquired motions into a continuous sequence remains challenging. Interpolation connects boundary poses without considering whether their relative position, heading, and timing provide suitable conditions for a transition. A generative motion prior can produce richer motion, but poorly arranged boundaries may cause it to generate excessive locomotion, turning, or another unintended action. We present Spatio-Temporal Alignment with a Motion Prior (STAMP), a framework for connecting independently acquired humanoid motions through a Robot-to-Human-to-Robot process. STAMP uses human motion space to draw on rich motion priors and reuse transition knowledge across robot embodiments. Its key component is a learned alignment model that determines the boundary conditions for motion inbetweening. Given the two motions retargeted to a human rig, the alignment model ranks candidate positions, headings, and transition durations for the following motion. A human motion prior generates the transition under the selected alignment. The completed sequence is retargeted to the robot and used as a reference to train a motion-tracking policy. We evaluate the tracking success of the generated transitions on Unitree~G1 and~ROBOTIS K1. Physical robot demonstrations further show that STAMP connects independently acquired motions into long-horizon sequences. Project page: https://childtoy.github.io/STAMP-project

bullets: Addresses failed transitions caused by incompatible relative position, heading, and timing between motions.

Uses a human motion prior to generate the transition, then retargets the result back to the robot for policy training.
Evaluated on Unitree G1 and ROBOTIS K1, with physical demonstrations of long-horizon motion sequences.
Scope: transition quality depends on suitable alignment and the capabilities of the human motion prior.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy's return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Tailong Luo, Lei Wei, Guangyuan Dong, Sihan Liu, Yingjie He, Siheng Wang, Shuaibo Li, Rongchao Zhang, Zhen Tian, Richeng Xuan, Zhichao Hu
bullets: Pixel prediction quality can misalign with policy utility: lower next-frame MSE may yield worse policy gradients.
DRILL uses bilevel optimization to update the world model based on returns after an inner GRPO update from imagined rollouts.
DRILL-VWI is a rollout-free surrogate that weights errors by policy visitation, GRPO advantage, and model confidence.
DRILL-IMG differentiates through the inner update with truncated Hessian-vector products; DRILL-VWI approximates its local one-step gradient under stated assumptions.
Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG improves mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World.

papers.abstract: Loco-manipulation extends the workspace of conventional manipulation by combining mobility with physical interaction, while aerial loco-manipulation further expands this capability into three-dimensional space, enabling robots to reach environments inaccessible to ground-based systems. Moving to an aerial platform, however, gives rise to a demanding control problem, since the vehicle must track trajectories accurately in three dimensions while the motion of the arm and its interaction with the environment continuously shift the center of mass, alter the inertia, and impose force and moment disturbances on the body. Conventional controllers address these effects through explicit models and estimation, whereas learning-based controllers infer dynamics from experience, yet control rewards provide no direct target for the response information retained from history, and fixed task sampling can leave persistent tracking difficulties insufficiently explored. We present ALMA, an aerial loco-manipulation framework for adaptive flight control under external arm commands. ALMA employs a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions, using action-conditioned prediction of future measurement representations to train its context to retain response information relevant to flight control. To expand the experience available for this adaptation, an evolutionary process uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze observed control difficulties and propose new structures of arm motion for subsequent training. In simulation, ALMA reduces position root-mean-square error (RMSE) by up to 24.7% relative to the strongest baseline, while the same policy transfers zero-shot to the aerial manipulator and reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion relative to the real-world baseline.
authors: Jingyu Ru, Xiangyuan Xie, Lixuan Jin, Jian An, Xingming Zhang, Binghao Li, Siyu Wang, Xiang Zhou, Lei Yuan, Hongli Xu, Yang Yu
bullets: Aerial loco-manipulation is difficult because arm motion shifts the vehicle’s center of mass, changes inertia, and introduces force and moment disturbances.
ALMA uses a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions.
Action-conditioned prediction of future measurement representations trains the policy context to retain flight-relevant response information.
An evolutionary process guided by an LLM analyzes control difficulties and proposes new arm-motion structures for training.
In simulation, position RMSE falls by up to 24.7%; on a real aerial manipulator, zero-shot transfer reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion.

papers.abstract: Training large language models for complex reasoning tasks relies on two complementary signals: sparse, outcome-grounded reinforcement learning (RL) for correctness, and dense, token-level distillation for guidance. However, complementarity in supervision does not guarantee compatibility in optimization; imitation-focused distillation can conflict with the outcome-driven RL objective, and existing hybrids lack a principled resolution. We propose \textbf{GIFT} (\textbf{G}radient-\textbf{I}nformed \textbf{F}il\textbf{T}ering for Distillation-Augmented Reasoning RL), a novel method that directly addresses the allocation problem of which teacher updates to apply. GIFT performs a token-level geometric analysis, decomposing the distillation gradient into a component \textbf{parallel} to the RL gradient, which measures first-order conflict and provides a \textbf{safety} filter, and a component \textbf{orthogonal} to it, which quantifies novel directional guidance and provides a measure of \textbf{value}. This decomposition yields a principled scoring rule to rank token-level guidance. We combine this with a progressive \textbf{coverage annealing} schedule that shrinks the budget of tokens receiving distillation, ensuring that the most conflicting updates are discarded first while the most complementary ones are retained at full strength. This facilitates a smooth transition from dense, geometrically-filtered guidance to a pure, outcome-grounded objective at convergence. Extensive experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks show that GIFT consistently outperforms strong baselines across multiple model scales, achieving relative gains of up to 9.5\% on difficult mathematical reasoning tasks. Code: https://github.com/lilifree/GIFT
authors: Shijie Li, Yilin Gao, Tieyuan Chen, Yun Luo, Weiyao Lin, Hang Yu
bullets: Addresses conflicts between dense imitation-based distillation and sparse, outcome-driven RL objectives.
Decomposes each distillation gradient into RL-parallel components for safety and orthogonal components for novel guidance value.
Ranks token-level updates using this geometric analysis and applies progressive coverage annealing to reduce distillation coverage over training.
Evaluations on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks report consistent gains over strong baselines, with up to 9.5% relative improvement on difficult math tasks.
The method transitions toward a pure outcome-grounded objective at convergence.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly embedded in software systems. Testing them raises two problems. Mutating either input can change the expected answer, so an output change is not by itself a failure. Some failures appear only when both inputs are mutated; attributing them to the combination requires testing each mutation alone. We present VLTest, a black-box VLM testing approach. It generates image variants by editing VQGAN latent codes and text variants with a rewrite-expand-prune pipeline, filters variants likely to change the expected answer, and tests each variant alone before testing combinations, so every joint failure has four matched cells. A VLM judge confirms a failure only after checking that the input keeps the expected answer. On three tasks with eight VLMs, including two commercial API models, the oracle confirms 81.7% of the candidates, with 88.8% to 94.6% precision against human labels, and four-cell confirmation rejects 22.5% of joint candidates. Under the same budget, VLTest's generators find 1.8 to 2.5 times as many confirmed failures as SINVAD and TextFooler, and its joint tests find 91 to 197 attributed joint failures per 1,000 joint calls, 1.3 times as many as the same pairing applied to the baselines' variants.
authors: Bin Duan, Jintao Lin, Guowei Yang
bullets: Generates image variants via VQGAN latent-code editing and text variants through rewrite, expansion, and pruning.
Filters variants likely to preserve the expected answer, then tests image-only, text-only, and combined mutations in four matched cells.
Uses a VLM judge to confirm failures while checking answer preservation; it confirms 81.7% of candidates with 88.8–94.6% precision against human labels.
Across three tasks and eight VLMs, VLTest finds 1.8–2.5× more confirmed failures than SINVAD and TextFooler under the same budget.
Four-cell confirmation rejects 22.5% of joint candidates and enables attribution of failures specifically to image-text interactions.

papers.abstract: LLM agents can evolve by learning from accumulated experience. Existing approaches extract reusable external knowledge, such as skills and memories, from experience to guide subsequent task solving, with some further internalizing this knowledge through model training. However, different ways of analyzing and transforming the same experience can yield knowledge with substantially different utility, even when the resulting guidance appears reasonable. Inspired by consistency regularization, we identify consistent utility gains across different ways of analyzing the same experience, rather than relying on any single way of analyzing it. We introduce SPLICE, a framework for consistency-regularized knowledge-model co-evolution. It constructs evolution views by perturbing how the same experience is analyzed, producing different knowledge candidates. Knowledge updates are then guided by common gain, which accounts for utility gains and their consistency across views. During model evolution, self-distillation internalizes the evolved knowledge alongside reinforcement learning, using knowledge associated with consistent utility degradation as a contrastive reference. The two processes interleave, with model updates driving further knowledge evolution. Experiments across diverse domains show that SPLICE outperforms knowledge evolution and model training baselines by up to 7.1 and 4.6 points in average accuracy, while its evolved knowledge reduces output tokens per correct solution by up to 44% and transfers across model sizes and families.
authors: Sirui Chen, Zhining Liu, Chao Zhang, Jingrui He, Zheng Li
bullets: Addresses the unreliability of deriving useful knowledge from a single interpretation of experience.
Perturbs experience analysis to create multiple evolution views and candidate knowledge updates.
Uses common gain to favor utility improvements that are consistent across views.
Interleaves self-distillation and reinforcement learning to internalize evolved knowledge, using consistently harmful knowledge as a contrastive reference.

Across diverse domains, improves average accuracy by up to 7.1 and 4.6 points over knowledge-evolution and model-training baselines, respectively; also reduces tokens per correct solution by up to 44% and transfers across model sizes and families.

papers.abstract: World models have recently emerged as a promising direction toward developing generalist agents capable of understanding, predicting, and interacting with diverse environments. However, despite growing interest, the concept of a world model remains loosely defined, encompassing approaches ranging from predictive dynamics models and learned simulators to models that jointly generate future observations and actions. This introductory paper aims to clarify the concept of world models and provide a unified perspective on their role in developing generalist agents. Starting from the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) framework, we connect world modeling to classical control, dynamical systems, signal processing, and reinforcement learning. We introduce different approaches to world modeling, emphasizing the knowledge they capture, their learning objectives, and how they support decision-making. We further explore the relationship between world modeling and policy learning, highlighting how these capabilities can be unified through conditional prediction without requiring separate models. Rather than offering an exhaustive survey of existing methods, this paper focuses on fundamental concepts, modeling principles, and connections, with the goal of providing an accessible and unified introduction to world models for generalist agents.
authors: Zhihui Zhu
bullets: Frames world modeling within the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) setting.
Connects world models to control, dynamical systems, signal processing, and reinforcement learning.
Organizes approaches by the knowledge they capture, their learning objectives, and how they support decision-making.
Explains how world modeling and policy learning can be unified through conditional prediction rather than separate models.
Focuses on foundational concepts and connections, not an exhaustive survey of existing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1: An integrated view ofworldmodeling and policy learning. Using the physical world as an illustrative setting, passive observations (e.g., images and videos) and action-labeled trajectories (e.g., robotic interactions) provide complementary learning signals for acquiringworld knowledge and learning action policies. World modeling and policy learning are closely connected and may share representations, learning objectives, or model architectures. The acquired world knowledge can support inference-time planning, simulated experience for policy improvement through reinforcement learning, or direct action through a learned policy. Together, these complementary approaches support the development of generalist agents capable of effective decision-making across diverse environments, tasks, and embodiments.

Figure 3: Policies, world models, and learned latent representations. (a) The underlying state st follows the true environment dynamics and generates observations. A latent encoder maps the interaction history to a learned representation zt = ϕ(ht), whose evolution is predicted by a latent dynamics model. Alternatively, the encoder may use only the current observation, zt = ϕ(ot), or observation history, zt = ϕ(o≤t). Neither direct access to st nor a one-to-one correspondence between st and zt is assumed. (b) The model families discussed in Section 3 differ in their prediction targets and conditioning information. Action-unconditioned dynamics models do not condition on the current action at. For passive data without action labels, observation prediction takes the form pθ(ot+1 | o≤t), and latent models use observation-only encodings. For inverse dynamics prediction, latent representations should not directly encode the target action at and may instead be constructed from current observation or observation histories. Throughout, pθ denotes a generic learned predictive model: the different conditional distributions may be modeled separately with distinct parameters or jointly within a unified model with shared parameters. Task conditioning may also be included when informative.

Figure 2: The POMDP interaction loop for generalist agents across diverse environments and tasks. Given its interaction history and task, the agent selects an action. The state evolves according to p(st+1 | st, at, e), and the environment generates an observation through p(ot+1 | st+1, e). The agent incorporates the new observation into its history before acting again. The environment e and task remain fixed within an episode but may vary across episodes, requiring the agent to adapt to different environments and objectives.

papers.abstract: Flexible endoscopes exploit structural compliance to traverse narrow lumens, pipes, and cavities, where navigation involves distributed environmental contact. This compliance makes tip motion depend on the evolving support configuration. We present external bird's-eye-view contact-aided navigation (EBV-CAN), a vision-language policy that combines one initial global static bird's-eye image with evolving endoscopic observations and motor state. Three supervised semantic queries locate the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target on the cached global image; their residual representations predict bending and insertion commands. We introduce the Vision-Language Contact-Aided (VLCA) dataset, linking 517 demonstrations and 75k action samples to 958k spatial entries and 93k remaining-route records. On 50 held-out episodes, tip-coordinate and waypoint localization reach 97.5% and 94.8%. Swapping the target instruction under identical observations changes target attention and motor output across 17 dual-target episodes. Across 1,920 physical trials of eight policies trained under a shared protocol, EBV-CAN achieves 183/240 successes (76.25%) under automatic blue-area scoring. Gated recurrent unit behavior cloning (GRU-BC) achieves the lowest matched-task offline mean absolute error (MAE), 0.056, and 1/240 physical successes, establishing distinct rankings for action imitation and task completion. Successful multi-guide executions and representative failures connect spatial progress, steering transitions, and visibility to physical navigation.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Shuchang Liu, Jinsong Lin, Yidong Zhang, Xizi Wang, Ho Yin Chim, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses navigation in compliant, contact-rich environments where support changes tip motion.

Achieves 97.5% tip localization, 94.8% waypoint localization, and 76.25% success across 1,920 physical trials.
Offline action imitation and physical task completion produce different rankings: GRU-BC has lower MAE but only 1/240 physical successes.

papers.abstract: Mixing requires not only applying processing but also assessing the resulting mix. Audio-language models can provide conversa- tional mixing advice, but existing evaluations do not separately test whether they can judge specific mixing issues. Since professional supervision for such judgments is scarce, we construct a curriculum of 11 vocal-mix issues at multiple severity levels and use it to train MixJudge, a language-queryable audio critic. MixJudge shows its ability to retrieve mixing issues, distinguish opposite issues, and order the severity of an issue. Moreover, its judgments transfer to menu selection: given a set of processing candidates, MixJudge often favors versions acoustically closer to a held-out professional version, demonstrating how explicit mixing judgment can support comparison and downstream mixing decisions.
authors: Kuan-Hsun Ho, Yuan-Chiao Cheng, Yen-Tung Yeh, Yi-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the lack of separate evaluation and professional supervision for specific vocal-mixing judgments.
Uses a curriculum covering 11 vocal-mix issues across multiple severity levels.
Can retrieve requested issues, distinguish opposing issues, and order issue severity.
Its judgments transfer to processing-menu selection, often favoring candidates acoustically closer to a held-out professional mix.
Scope: focuses on vocal-mix issues and comparative downstream selection; the abstract does not quantify performance.
