papers.abstract: Before acting on an object, a robot needs to anticipate how its hand motion will change the physical world and what the resulting scene will look like. Existing approaches typically entangle action-conditioned dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis within a video generation model, or represent dynamics as point trajectories without explicit object structure. We introduce DeXplicit, a dexterous manipulation world model that instead predicts how the world evolves explicitly in metric 3D before rendering its visual consequences. Given an initial scene and a future hand trajectory, a lightweight 3D dynamics network predicts object-centric motion and deformation, providing structured and geometrically grounded future world states. These predictions then serve as a strong scaffold for video generation: appearance is transported through the predicted 3D motion and projected into future views, allowing the renderer to focus on completing uncertain and newly visible content rather than implicitly learning world dynamics from pixels. This explicit-3D-first decomposition also enables efficient causal generation, requiring only two denoising steps per block while conditioning on generated history. Across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, DeXplicit reduces moved-point error by 27-40% relative to PointWorld and improves object fidelity IoU+ by 47% on HOT3D under a shared renderer. Our design with two-step causal generation achieves a 57x speedup from our 14B bi-directional configuration in video synthesis.
authors: Adam Lee, Mutian Xu, Yukang Cao, Shulin Tian, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis in existing video-based world models.
Uses a lightweight 3D dynamics network to predict object-centric motion and deformation from an initial scene and future hand trajectory.
Transports appearance through predicted 3D motion, letting video generation focus on uncertain or newly visible content.
Reports 27–40% lower moved-point error than PointWorld across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, plus 47% higher object-fidelity IoU+ on HOT3D under a shared renderer.
Two-step causal generation provides a reported 57× speedup relative to the authors’ 14B bidirectional configuration.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models reduce computation through sparse activation but still incur substantial storage costs. Mixed-precision post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces these costs by quantizing different model components at different bit widths, but existing methods often struggle to preserve generation quality under tight bit budgets. We identify two key challenges: (1) nonlinear quantization errors at extremely low precision are underestimated when cross-layer propagation is ignored; (2) direct router fine-tuning may cause routing drift, and calibration gains may not generalize to downstream tasks. To address these issues, we propose ProQuant, a weight-only PTQ framework for MoE models. Prune-or-Prioritize Mixed-Precision Allocation (PoP) jointly optimizes expert pruning and bit-width assignment. It allows higher-precision experts to substitute for severely degraded ones while improving bit-budget utilization. Routing-Consistent RMSNorm Finetune (RoCo) adapts expert input representations through mathematically equivalent transformations. It compensates for quantization errors to reduce routing drift. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ProQuant outperforms existing methods across diverse generative tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ThrowBug/ProQuant.git.
authors: Jiaqi Chen, Xianglong Yan, Chengzhu Bao, Xie Chen, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets storage overhead and quality loss in mixed-precision PTQ for sparsely activated MoE models.
PoP jointly optimizes expert pruning and bit-width allocation, letting higher-precision experts replace severely degraded ones.
RoCo finetunes RMSNorm-equivalent transformations to compensate for quantization errors while preserving routing behavior.
Experiments across diverse generative tasks show ProQuant outperforms existing methods.
The approach is scoped to weight-only post-training quantization and relies on calibration-aware adaptation.

papers.abstract: Lunar rovers will primarily rely on cameras for localization until navigation satellite services are deployed, and will continue to need them afterwards for relative navigation, hazard detection, and surface operations. Visual odometry (VO) and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) mostly estimate motion by matching features between frames. However, feature matchers are developed on urban, indoor and driving scenes, planetary studies compare them on orbital registration or within complete SLAM systems, and real lunar imagery with reference poses is scarce, so matching between rover frames on low-texture, harshly lit terrain, and its effect on VO, has not been compared. We benchmark eleven classical and learned detector-matcher combinations on nine synthetic, lunar-testbed, and terrestrial-analogue datasets, and a feature tracker, scoring pairwise pose accuracy against baseline and the trajectory error of the resulting VO. Under a common rotation-only metric, the SuperPoint pairings outperform SIFT with ratio-tested FLANN matching on both lunar testbeds and one analogue site, with smaller or unresolved differences on synthetic data. When rotation and translation direction are scored jointly, this SIFT pairing exceeds both SuperPoint pairings on four synthetic datasets, so synthetic results alone do not establish relative performance on real rover imagery. In stereo VO, the SuperPoint pairings are not consistently more accurate than SIFT, but only they keep tracking on all eight sequential datasets. Pairings with classical detectors depend on lighting while SuperPoint changes little: a low spotlight makes them more accurate than diffuse light on the same testbed views, consistent with more contrast and detected keypoints. SuperPoint with LightGlue is the fastest learned combination (16 ms per frame), and DINOv2 retrieval proposals still need geometric verification.
authors: Guillem Casadesus Vila, Grace Gao
bullets: Benchmarks 11 classical and learned detector–matcher combinations across nine synthetic, lunar-testbed, and terrestrial-analogue datasets.
SuperPoint pairings outperform SIFT under rotation-only scoring on lunar testbeds and one analogue site, while synthetic results are mixed when translation direction is included.
In stereo VO, SuperPoint is not consistently more accurate but is the only approach to maintain tracking across all eight sequential datasets.

SuperPoint with LightGlue is the fastest learned combination at 16 ms per frame; DINOv2 retrieval proposals still require geometric verification.

papers.abstract: This paper presents AgentDP, which aims to deploy pre-trained AI models on heterogeneous embedded devices by fully automating model optimization and adaptation (O&A) with Large Language Model (LLM) agents. AgentDP not only significantly reduces human effort via automation but also enhances model inference efficacy by integrating LLMs with device-specific domain knowledge. To deliver a robust automation framework, AgentDP develops novel solutions to address three key technical challenges: 1) To help users elicit clear requirements, we propose a user requirement standardization module; 2) To mitigate the execution environment mismatch between AI models and heterogeneous embedded devices, we design an operator-aware model partition paradigm that enables different parts of the model to be efficiently executed on distinct inference engines. 3) To avoid re-searching optimization hyperparameters for new tasks, we propose a configuration reuse module that heuristically retrieves previous hyperparameter configurations for efficient reuse. Extensive experiments demonstrate that by fully automating the entire O&A process, AgentDP reduces entire model adaptation time by up to 80% compared with manual O&A while achieving higher task accuracy (more than 13% on average) than the baselines. Additionally, a comprehensive user study also exhibits the robust generalizability of AgentDP in adapting to different user requirements for heterogeneous embedded devices.
authors: Leming Shen, Qiang Yang, Xinyu Huang, Zijing Ma, Yuanqing Zheng
bullets: Targets the high human effort and environment mismatch involved in deploying models across diverse embedded hardware.
Standardizes user requirements to make deployment goals clearer for automated optimization and adaptation.
Uses operator-aware model partitioning to execute model components across different inference engines.
Reuses previously effective hyperparameter configurations to avoid repeated optimization searches.
Experiments report up to 80% lower adaptation time and over 13% higher average task accuracy than baselines, with a user study indicating broad adaptability.

papers.abstract: LLM memory is widely used in long-term conversation understanding. Agentic memory systems often use mutation, structural organization, learned retrieval strategies, or other complex operations. Is this complexity always necessary? We study Raw-RAG, a naive RAG baseline using dense retrieval and reranking over raw history to supply evidence to a reader LLM. Across LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MEME, and MemoryAgentBench, Raw-RAG ranks first among the compared memory systems in six of seven benchmark-model settings, outperforming the strongest compared agentic memory system by 0.13-5.53 points. We investigate why raw-history retrieval remains competitive. Evidence analysis shows that its higher coverage of necessary evidence can offset lower utilization. Useful evidence includes both answer values and the relations and dependency paths needed to derive them. Even complete access to transformed memory stores leaves an accuracy gap relative to raw evidence, highlighting the importance of preserving raw information. These findings challenge the necessity of complex agentic memory for the evaluated conversation tasks and establish naive RAG as an essential baseline.
authors: Zhengye Bao, Shengtao Zhang, Haokai Zhang, Shiqi Lou, Muning Wen, Minnan Luo
bullets: Evaluates Raw-RAG, which uses dense retrieval and reranking over unmodified conversation history for an LLM reader.
Raw-RAG ranks first in six of seven benchmark-model settings across LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MEME, and MemoryAgentBench.
It outperforms the strongest compared agentic memory system by 0.13–5.53 points.
Higher coverage of necessary evidence—including answer values, relations, and dependency paths—can offset weaker evidence utilization.
The findings support preserving raw information and treating naive RAG as an essential baseline for evaluated conversation tasks.

papers.abstract: Complex camera motion is central to visual storytelling, yet translating cinematographic intent into controllable, executable camera trajectories remains challenging. We introduce FilmFlow, an agentic framework that converts natural-language instructions or reference videos into explicit camera trajectories for dynamic 3D environments. To generate these trajectories, a Director agent constructs executable camera plans by composing high-level motions from concurrent atomic operations that jointly control translation, rotation, and framing. The Director is supported by three specialized agents: an Interpreter that extracts scene-grounded cinematographic intent, a Scout that selects initial viewpoints, and a Critic that evaluates rendered results and provides visual feedback for iterative plan refinement. We also introduce CinemaBench, comprising 150 Blender scenes from self-created and licensed sources, with five camera instructions per scene for 750 text-directed tasks and 60 reference videos associated with a subset of scenes. CinemaBench supports evaluation of both text-directed camera generation and video reference-directed camera generation. Across a diverse set of evaluated baselines, FilmFlow achieves the strongest benchmark performance and the highest user preference, demonstrating effective spatial reasoning, temporal coordination, and visual composition for executable 3D cinematography.
authors: Yiming Zhang, Jiarui Guo, Haojia Wei, Yifei Liu, Yifan Yang, Hongjie Zhang, Xue Yang, Zhihang Zhong
bullets: Addresses the challenge of translating cinematographic intent into controllable camera motion in dynamic 3D scenes.
A Director agent composes high-level camera plans from concurrent atomic operations controlling translation, rotation, and framing.
Interpreter, Scout, and Critic agents extract intent, choose viewpoints, and iteratively refine plans using rendered visual feedback.
Introduces CinemaBench with 150 Blender scenes, 750 text-directed tasks, and 60 reference videos for evaluating 3D camera generation.
Reports the strongest performance across evaluated baselines and the highest user preference, indicating effective spatial reasoning, temporal coordination, and composition.

papers.abstract: Shadows are observable consequences of latent physical causes, arising from the interaction between illumination, object geometry, and scene structure. A model that understands shadows should be able not only to read a shadow's direction, but also to infer where a shadow should fall when it is absent, and to judge whether a shadow is physically consistent with the scene. We introduce ShadowBench, built from real photographs, which poses these three questions to vision-language models (VLMs). From each scene, we build a correct-shadow, a shadow-removed, and a human-annotated wrong-direction state. Evaluating 19 open VLMs (2B to 78B) and frontier proprietary models, we find that VLMs read a visible shadow's direction well above chance and improve with scale, yet infer the absent direction only weakly and fall to chance at judging physical consistency even under a bias-free two-alternative test that removes the yes-bias of single-image naturalness questions. Only Gemini-3.1-pro exceeds chance on validity, and even then only modestly and far below humans. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) does not help. The missing ingredient is not reasoning but knowledge that image generation models (IGMs) already hold. Routing a VLM through an IGM lifts its inference well above its direct attempt and helps it flag the wrong-direction shadows it otherwise accepts. Cast-shadow direction is a single facet of illumination understanding, but the sharp gap it reveals between VLMs and IGMs suggests image-generation or reconstruction objectives as a route toward illumination-aware VLMs.
authors: Ryugo Morita, Shunsuke Kitada, Stanislav Frolov, Brian Bernhard Moser, Ko Watanabe, Riku Takahashi, Jinjia Zhou, Andreas Dengel
bullets: ShadowBench evaluates VLMs on visible-shadow direction, absent-shadow inference, and physical-consistency judgments using real photographs with correct, removed, and human-annotated wrong-direction shadows.
Across 19 open and frontier proprietary VLMs, visible-direction reading improves with scale, but absent-direction inference is weak and validity judgments are near chance.
Only Gemini-3.1-pro exceeds chance on validity, modestly and far below human performance; Chain-of-Thought does not help.
Routing VLMs through image-generation models improves missing-shadow inference and helps identify wrong-direction shadows.
The findings suggest image-generation or reconstruction objectives may provide useful illumination knowledge for VLMs.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ShadowBench. From each real photograph, we recover the object and its cast shadow as an alpha-matted layer and recompose matched states on a shared background: the shadow-correct Isdw, the shadow-removed Iobj, and the physically-wrong composite Iflip, produced by a horizontal flip to change the shadow’s direction. The target object is highlighted in red. These states drive three tasks of increasing demand on the shadow–illumination relation: Direction Reading from a visible shadow at increasing angular resolution (Task 1); Direction Inference, recovering the direction from Iobj once the shadow is removed (Task 2); and Physical Validity, judging whether a shown shadow is consistent with the scene, in single-image and a bias-free two-alternative form on Isdw vs. Iflip (Task 3).

Figure 3. Shadow-detection psychometric curve. The object’s own cast shadow is recomposed at opacities from 0 (no shadow) to 1 (full), and at each level we ask whether the object casts a visible shadow. For the three models shown (InternVL3-8B, Qwen2.5VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B), the detection rate rises smoothly and monotonically with opacity, showing that shadow presence is perceived as a graded quantity that scales with physical strength. Some models instead answer “yes” at every opacity, a response bias rather than a perceptual deficit.

Figure 4. Naturalising the shadow-only rotation with an image editor. (a) the negative a bare rotation produces: the soft shadow matte is rotated about the annotated origin and recomposited, the object pixels left untouched. An image-space rotation cannot yield a silhouette the pictured object could actually cast, and it disturbs the fine compositing statistics along the shadow’s edge – cues a model can exploit without consulting the scene’s lighting at all. We therefore rebuild every negative: (b) the object and its rotated shadow are lifted onto a white canvas, the scene removed so the editor has no lighting context to re-infer the direction from; (c) FLUX.1-Kontext-dev redraws the shadow’s shape under an instruction to keep its direction, length and size, and the result is clamped to the seed’s rotated support so the direction cannot drift; (d) the redrawn shadow is recomposited into the captured background plate, with the object pixels taken unchanged from the positive so that the shadow is the only difference within a pair. Detectability falls from 64.0% on (a) to 56.3% on (d), while humans answer the same pairs at 94.4% (Table 12).
Figure 5. Failure cases. Top: direction inference on Iobj (Task 2). Bottom: single-image validity on Iflip (Task 3). The target object is highlighted in red, as in the evaluation prompts.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and improves VLM physical/spatial reasoning about cast shadows, fitting spatial intelligence in multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Where Did the Light Come From? Diagnosing Cast-Shadow Reasoning in VLMs and Borrowing the Missing Shadow Prior from Image Generation Models
papers.tldr: VLMs can read visible shadow directions but struggle to infer missing shadows or detect physically inconsistent ones, while routing through image-generation models substantially improves these abilities.

papers.abstract: Flow matching is now the dominant approach for vision-language action (VLA) robot policies, thanks to its expressiveness and simple training objective. However, inference for standard flow matching requires iteratively solving an ODE, limiting the control frequency at deployment. While several works have proposed novel methods to allow for single-shot action generation, we ask whether such additional objectives are actually necessary. We find that across six flow matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale: multi-step integration confers little to no consistent advantage at inference. We empirically find that this holds as long as models are sufficiently trained and have enough capacity. Practically, the implication is that for large VLAs, the single-step policy comes essentially for free from the multi-step model, enabling low-latency deployment without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives.
authors: Shivakanth Sujit, Luca Nunziante, Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa, Kai Arulkumaran
bullets: Flow-matching VLA policies typically require iterative ODE integration, which limits deployment control frequency.
Across six flow-matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale.
Multi-step integration provides little or no consistent inference advantage in the studied setting.
The finding depends on models having sufficient training and capacity.
Large VLAs can use single-step inference directly, without distillation, retraining, or auxiliary objectives.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in multi-task robotic manipulation by leveraging visual and language understanding for action generation. However, existing lightweight VLA models employ a single dense action expert to handle all tasks, which limits their multi-task capability under constrained computational budgets. To address this issue, we propose SmolVLA-MoE, a novel framework that introduces sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) into the FFN layers of the action expert in VLA models. SmolVLA-MoE replaces dense FFN layers with multiple parallel expert FFNs and a token-level router, enabling each token to adaptively select the most suitable expert for action generation. We further introduce a shared expert with a tunable weight parameter to balance the inheritance of pre-trained capabilities and task-specific expert specialization. Through sparse activation, SmolVLA-MoE activates only a single expert FFN during inference, with a total activated parameter count of approximately 500M including the frozen VLM backbone, while benefiting from approximately 800M total stored parameters. We evaluate our method on four task suites of the LIBERO benchmark. SmolVLA-MoE achieves an average success rate of 84.25%, outperforming SmolVLA (82.75%) and OpenVLA-7B (76.5%), while maintaining comparable inference efficiency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/dudu435/smolvla-moe.
authors: Shiyang Zhang, Miao Yang, Zhengda Li, Yang Shao, Ruifang Zhai, Hui Peng, Peng Song
bullets: Addresses the limited multi-task capacity of lightweight VLAs that rely on one dense action expert.
Replaces action-expert FFNs with parallel experts and a token-level router, activating only one expert per token at inference.
Adds a tunable shared expert to balance pretrained capability retention with task-specific specialization.
On four LIBERO task suites, achieves an 84.25% average success rate versus 82.75% for SmolVLA and 76.5% for OpenVLA-7B.
Maintains comparable inference efficiency with approximately 500M activated parameters and 800M stored parameters.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the SmolVLA-MoE architecture. The frozen VLM backbone processes visual observations and language instructions to produce contextual representations. The action expert replaces dense FFN layers with MoE-FFN layers, each containing a shared expert Es (always activated, weighted by α), N routed expert FFNs, a token-level router with top-K selection, and a scaling adapter. Through sparse activation, only K experts are selected per token during both training and inference.

Fig. 4: Per-suite success rate comparison across all methods on the LIBERO benchmark. SmolVLA-MoE (highlighted with black borders) achieves competitive or superior performance across all four suites with ∼500M total activated parameters (∼100M in the action expert).
Fig. 3: Visualization of complete rollouts in the LIBERO simulation environment. Each row shows key frames of the execution trajectory for a multi-step manipulation task from start to completion.

Fig. 2: Detailed structure of the MoE-FFN layer. The input token is processed by both the shared expert and the top-K routed experts selected by the router. The scaling adapter provides additional per-token adaptive scaling. The final output is a weighted combination of the shared expert output (scaled by α) and the routed expert output (scaled by 1− α).

Fig. 5: Heatmap visualization of the Top-K × shared expert weight (α) ablation study across all four LIBERO suites. Best values in each suite are shown in bold. Top-1 routing with α = 0.3 achieves the best overall performance.

papers.title: SmolVLA-MoE: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts for Efficient Multi-Task Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: SmolVLA-MoE improves efficient multi-task robotic manipulation by using sparse, token-routed experts in the VLA action module.

papers.abstract: Video provides a natural source of supervision: what happens next serves as a learning signal for visual world modeling. Yet masked video pretraining focuses on recovering missing content from surrounding context rather than predicting the future from the past. Autoregressive methods instead predict forward one token at a time, but have yet to match joint-embedding methods in representation quality. This gap motivates us to revisit the granularity and space of future prediction. In this work, we introduce VANE, a self-supervised visual pretraining framework built on next-frame prediction in embedding space. A causal encoder summarizes past observations for a state predictor that infers the representation of the entire next frame, making temporal evolution the primary learning signal. This prediction is carried out in a fixed embedding space provided by a frozen semantic tokenizer, emphasizing scene content and structure. To retain fine-grained spatial detail alongside semantic content, a lightweight auxiliary generative decoder reconstructs future-frame patches conditioned on the predicted representations. To unify visual modeling across images and videos, we construct a local-to-global crop sequence for still images, allowing the same encoder to predict newly revealed regions from earlier crops under the same objective. Experiments show that VANE improves with model and data scaling, achieving SOTA on most anticipation, recognition, and dense perception benchmarks among unified encoders. Especially on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation, it surpasses V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 points in mean-class recall@5. These results demonstrate that next-frame prediction in embedding space is effective and scalable for visual world modeling.
authors: Yifeng Yao, Jinghan Li, Zhihao Zhang, Yajiao Xiong, Yang Jin, Kun Xu, Huishuai Zhang, Dongyan Zhao
bullets: Motivation: Existing masked and autoregressive video methods do not fully capture future dynamics or match joint-embedding representation quality.
Method: A causal encoder summarizes past observations, while a state predictor infers the next frame in a fixed space from a frozen semantic tokenizer.
Detail: An auxiliary lightweight decoder reconstructs future-frame patches to preserve spatial detail alongside semantic content.
Unification: Still images are converted into local-to-global crop sequences so the same prediction objective applies to images and videos.

Results: VANE improves with model and data scaling, reaches state-of-the-art on most evaluated unified-encoder benchmarks, and exceeds V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 mean-class recall@5 points on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | Overview of VANE. VANE predicts the embedding of the next frame from the frames observed so far. Top: the causal encoder maps the observed frames 𝑥1, . . . , 𝑥𝑡 to context states ℎ1, . . . , ℎ𝑡, which are concatenated with prediction tokens 𝑝𝑡+1; the state predictor uses the context states only as keys and values and outputs the predicted state 𝑠𝑡+1. Middle: a projector maps 𝑠𝑡+1 to the embedding space of the frozen semantic tokenizer, where it is supervised by the embedding of the next frame 𝑥𝑡+1 with an 𝐿1 loss; the generative decoder, conditioned on 𝑠𝑡+1, predicts the flow velocity 𝑣𝑡+1 from the noisy next frame 𝑥𝑡+1. Bottom: images are presented as local-to-global crops and videos as frame sequences, so both share the same objective.

Figure 1 | From masked completion to next-frame prediction in embedding space. (a) V-JEPA masks part of a clip, encodes the visible patches with bidirectional attention, and predicts the embeddings of the masked regions, supervised by an EMA encoder of the full video. (b) VANE encodes previous frames with frame-causal attention and predicts the embedding of the entire next frame from them, with targets from a frozen semantic tokenizer. An auxiliary generative decoder, used only during pretraining, regularizes the predicted embedding to retain fine-grained spatial detail.

Figure 6 | Attention masks. Left: frame-causal attention in the causal encoder, bidirectional within each frame and unidirectional across frames. Right: context-isolated causal attention in the state predictor. Prediction tokens for frame 𝑡 + 1 read the context states of frames up to 𝑡, which supply only keys and values, and attend to each other only within the same target frame.

papers.selection_reason: Next-frame prediction in embedding space for scalable visual world modeling and video representation learning.
papers.title: Learning from Next-Frame Prediction: Towards Unified and Scalable Visual Representation Learning
papers.tldr: VANE learns scalable visual representations by predicting entire future-frame embeddings, combining semantic next-frame prediction with fine-grained spatial reconstruction across images and videos.

papers.abstract: Agents tasked with intercepting a moving target must learn how to reach it, ideally as efficiently as possible. As observers of animal pursuit behavior have noticed, different strategies are possible: on one extreme, the agent reactively moves toward the target's current location; on the other, the agent predicts the target's future location and moves directly there. Motivated by the desire to understand how such strategies might be learned, we introduce a continuous-time linear-quadratic model of open-loop target pursuit whose optimal control strategies interpolate between these possibilities. Usefully, a small number of interpretable parameters control which type of strategy is optimal, and it is possible to derive closed-form solutions for optimal strategies, policy learning dynamics, and value learning dynamics. Exploiting our model's linear structure, we find that the time scales of learning precisely correspond to the eigenvalues of certain matrices, and that relevant eigenvalue spectra generically have a gap. We show that this gap indicates that agents tend to learn how to reach their target before optimizing their movement. Our results provide a detailed mathematical characterization of pursuit behavior and its learning dynamics, which can both serve as a benchmark for empirical work, and as a foundation for more elaborate theoretical treatments of pursuit.
authors: John J. Vastola, Kanaka Rajan
bullets: Models continuous-time, open-loop pursuit with interpretable parameters controlling reactive versus predictive behavior.
Derives closed-form optimal strategies, policy-learning dynamics, and value-learning dynamics.
Shows learning time scales are determined by matrix eigenvalues, whose generic spectral gap separates learning stages.
Finds agents tend to first learn how to reach the target, then optimize how efficiently they move.
Provides a mathematical benchmark for empirical pursuit studies and a foundation for more complex theories.

From left to right: trajectory vs time (dashed line: target trajectory); control vs time; endpoint error vs total error over learning; sorted eigenvalues of M ; top three eigenvectors of M . In the first two columns, four different colors are shown: pink (initial), light red (10% of learning time), dark red (25% of learning time), and black (final).

Figure 4: Value function learning dynamics. Different value parameters (j, H and R) converge at different rates. For simplicity, Σ = σ2I , F = 2, and η = 1 here. Left: components of j̃ := QT j converge at a rate ησ2. Center: the off-diagonal entries of H̃ := QTHQ converge at a rate ησ4/2. Right: R and the diagonal entries of H̃ converge at more complicated rates, one of which equals ησ4/2 (black), one of which is above it (red), and one of which is below it (blue). Because of these scaling relationships, which parameters converge earliest depends on the size of σ2.

Figure 1: Basics of target pursuit. a) Efficient strategies for pursuing a moving target (orange) fall between two extremes: moving toward its predicted final location (black path), and chasing it (blue path). b) During each episode of our target pursuit task, a state vector z ∈ RF is drawn from N (0,Σ) and determines how the target moves. The agent’s task is to maneuver so that their location coincides with the target’s at the end of the episode. c) Strategies with high ‘effort cost’ take an overly circuitous path. d) Strategies with high ‘proximity cost’ do not remain near the target.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical model of learned pursuit and interception strategies for moving targets, directly relevant to embodied navigation and goal-conditioned navigation.
papers.title: Solvable models of learning to pursue a moving target
papers.tldr: A solvable linear-quadratic model shows how agents learn to pursue moving targets, transitioning between reactive and predictive strategies while typically learning target interception before movement efficiency.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video generation have substantially improved visual fidelity, yet existing models still struggle to understand the physical evolution implicit in user prompts, making it difficult to generate videos with continuous physical state evolution. Here, we propose PhyEvolve, a multi-agent framework that enhances natural-language prompts through structured state-evolution planning. PhyEvolve consists of three agents: a Director, a Physical Evolver, and a Composer. Given a user prompt and an optional first frame, the Director grounds the scene and disentangles physical events from observation changes. The Physical Evolver uses scene evidence to identify physical mechanisms then constructs causally linked state transitions that unfold throughout the video, whether visible or not. The Composer utilizes these transitions to enhance the original prompts. Without retraining or model modification, PhyEvolve works directly with existing generators through prompt replacement. Extensive experiments on four major benchmarks show that PhyEvolve achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the cutting-edge prior agentic baseline by 7.9 percentage points on average. These results demonstrate that explicit causal state-evolution planning improves physical consistency and state continuity in generated videos through natural-language prompt enhancement.
authors: Yang-Hao Zhou, Lixing Tan, Zhiqi Li, Guang Yang, Xiao Yang
bullets: Addresses poor modeling of continuous physical evolution in text-to-video generation.
Uses three agents: Director, Physical Evolver, and Composer.
Plans causally linked physical state transitions, including changes that may not be directly visible.
Works with existing video generators through prompt replacement and optional first-frame input.
Evaluated on four benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results and a 7.9-point average gain over a prior agentic baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PhyEvolve. The Director separates actions from observations, the Physical Evolver models causal state evolution under occlusion, and the Composer refines prompts for physically consistent video generation.

Figure 5: Role-level prompt template for the Director. Scene grounding establishes the initial conditions, while action–observation disentanglement separates physical drivers from visibility changes. A separate reviewer guides bounded local revisions of the structured plan.

Figure 6: Role-level prompt template for the Physical Evolver. Physical Mechanisms Analysis establishes evidence, prerequisites, and responses; causal state rollout propagates them into continuous physical evolution. Both steps share one generation call, followed by a joint review of their outputs and local revisions when needed.

Figure 7: Role-level prompt template for the Composer. Prompt construction integrates the source requirements and upstream physical records. Physical-fidelity refinement uses evidence-grounded sentence-level feedback to correct omissions and contradictions while locking unrelated text.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on state-evolution prompts. We compare Minimax-H3, NEWTON, Co-Director, and PhyEvolve (ours) on four cases from StEvo-Bench (Top) and other in-sight physical benchmark (Bottom). Frames are uniformly sampled along time from left to right; dark marks the light-off interval. green boxes mark physically consistent state changes, and red boxes locate failures.

Seven frames are sampled uniformly over time; green and red boxes mark correct and failed state evolution. papers.title: PhyEvolve: Multi-Agent State-Evolution Planning for Physics-Aware Video Generation
papers.tldr: PhyEvolve improves physics-aware video generation by using multi-agent causal state-evolution planning to enhance prompts without modifying or retraining the video generator.

papers.abstract: This paper studies the local geometry of semantic meaning in large language models. Current representation analyses ask whether meanings are close in embedding space, or whether linear probes separate semantic classes, but they do not characterize the within-concept local geometry: what is invariant across realizations of a single semantic factor, what varies, and what changes when meaning is refined. This paper characterizes that geometry through two controlled probes evaluated on four architecturally diverse decoder-only LLMs (Gemma 4, Llama 3.2, Qwen 2.5, Pythia). A cross-lingual probe uses language as a perturbation to separate exact meaning matches, same-factor realizations, nearby concepts, and out-of-domain contrasts. A refinement probe separates specificity-bearing semantic narrowing from high-probability attributive elaboration and adversarial controls; both probes are validated by blind human judgments. Four findings recur across all models: under mean pooling, once dominant variance directions are removed, sentence pairs order by semantic relatedness (same factor, then same domain, then different domain) without overlap over a band of layers; semantic factors organize around an invariant core surrounded by structured realization-specific variation; refinement produces directed displacement into tighter neighborhoods, including against controls built on the same base noun; and sentence-level and token-local readouts expose complementary geometry (volume contraction at the sentence level, sharper anisotropic endpoints at token-local readout). We interpret these results as evidence that LLM semantics are organized as local anisotropic neighborhoods in which meaning contracts under refinement.
authors: Andr\'es Daniel Godoy Ortiz
bullets: Existing analyses largely measure global semantic proximity or separability, leaving within-concept geometry undercharacterized.
Two controlled probes test cross-lingual meaning variation and specificity-driven semantic refinement, with blind human validation.
After dominant directions are removed, representations consistently order by semantic relatedness across a band of layers.
Refinement moves representations into tighter neighborhoods; sentence-level and token-local views reveal complementary contraction and anisotropy.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes local semantic geometry in LLM representations; relevant to LLM interpretability and representation analysis.
papers.title: Meaning Contracts: Local Semantic Geometry in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: Across four decoder-only LLMs, semantic meanings form local anisotropic neighborhoods with structured variation around invariant cores and contract under semantic refinement.

papers.abstract: Text embedding and text generation are two of the most useful capabilities of modern large language models, yet they are typically provided by separate specialized models (an embedder and a generator) trained with incompatible objectives and deployed side by side in retrieval-augmented generation and agent systems. Recent unified embedding-generation models such as GritLM share parameters between the two capabilities, but they either switch attention regimes between modes or optimize embedding and language modeling as parallel objectives that never supervise each other. We argue that these designs are only partially unified: the two capabilities coexist on the same weights, but do not shape each other. We propose ULME, a post-training framework that unifies embedding and language modeling on a causal decoder-only LLM through predictive coupling. ULME inserts a chain of learnable slots between the query and the answer, reads a semantic embedding and a reasoning embedding from two designated slots, and trains three objectives on a shared causal backbone: a contrastive loss anchoring the semantic slot to document representations, a language-modeling loss supervising answer generation, and a stop-gradient predictive loss that aligns the reasoning slot with a pooled summary of the answer, so that generation actively shapes what the embedding encodes. Across two model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3) and eight scales spanning 0.5B-8B parameters, a single ULME checkpoint improves MTEB by 3.3-4.1 points over the strongest open-source baseline, tightens BRIGHT and AdvBench-IR simultaneously, and remains on par with a generation-only fine-tune on standard accuracy benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval), demonstrating that genuine unification yields mutually reinforcing rather than merely coexisting capabilities.
authors: Yang Liu, Zhiqiang Yuan, Shu-Dong Huang, Jiancheng Lv, Liwei Yang, Qiwei Yan, Kailin Lv, Jinchao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited interaction between embedding and language-modeling objectives in existing unified models.
Uses learnable slots in a causal decoder-only LLM to produce semantic and reasoning embeddings.
Combines contrastive embedding, answer-generation, and stop-gradient predictive alignment losses.
Evaluated across Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 models from 0.5B to 8B parameters.
Reports improved MTEB and BRIGHT/AdvBench-IR performance while matching generation-only fine-tuning on standard benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of ULME. A single causal decoder is trained with three objectives on a shared chain of learnable slot tokens (flame icons: trainable slots; grey blocks: hidden states). Left (Lsem): symmetric InfoNCE pulls the query and document slot embeddings Eq, Ed together. Middle (Lgen): next-token prediction over the answer span A, with the slot chain on the causal path from Q to A. papers.abstract: Training-free few-step samplers are often described as nearly quality-lossless under conventional FID/CLIP-style evaluation. It remains unclear whether that conclusion transfers to more realistic and complex generation-quality benchmarks. We first systematize the quality metrics used to evaluate training-free sampling acceleration for diffusion and flow-matching models. We find that representative training-free step-shortening methods often remain nearly lossless under FID/CLIP-class metrics, yet can suffer substantial quality degradation when evaluated with semantic-composition, dense-instruction, and long-text-rendering benchmarks such as GenEval, DPG-Bench, and LongTextBench. Parallel sampling is a notable exception: by retaining the full-step discretization and removing only the solver's temporal dependency, it can preserve near-lossless quality while accelerating sampling. Building on this observation, we propose \textit{ParaLin++}, a step-parity parallel sampler that preserves the full-step discretization while accelerating the solver iterations. Experiments across Stable Diffusion-v2, LSUN Church, FLUX.1-dev, and Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 show that ParaLin++ preserves the full-step Euler quality profile at $2.6\times$--$4.8\times$, $1.68\times$ on FLUX, and $1.21\times$ on Ming. Project page: https://paralinplus.github.io/.
authors: Jianrong Lu, Zhiyu Zhu, Hui Liu, Junhui Hou
bullets: Conventional FID/CLIP metrics can miss substantial degradation from training-free few-step samplers on complex generation tasks.
Semantic-composition, dense-instruction, and long-text-rendering benchmarks provide a more demanding evaluation of sampling quality.
Parallel sampling avoids quality loss by retaining full-step discretization and removing only the solver’s temporal dependency.
ParaLin++ is a step-parity parallel sampler that accelerates solver iterations without shortening the discretization schedule.
It achieves reported speedups of 2.6×–4.8× on Stable Diffusion-v2 and LSUN Church, 1.68× on FLUX.1-dev, and 1.21× on Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 while preserving full-step Euler quality.

papers.abstract: An LLM agent can retrieve a memory correctly yet use it incorrectly after its validity state changes. We study governance-state corruption: faults that alter which retained records enter model-visible context while stored content and tasks remain fixed. Across six providers, 731 benchmark-grounded bases yield 2,080 matched fault pairs. In offline control-plane checks, corruption changes the operative projection in 96.25% of pairs, while oracle-backed enforcement restores it in 100%. For downstream evaluation, a deterministically selected, non-probability LongMemEval/Memora panel resolves 298 of 300 matched triplets (238 distinct bases). Clean-minus-corrupted contrasts are 40.54 percentage points in LongMemEval binary correctness (95% base-cluster interval [30.32, 50.71]) and 30.60 points in rescaled Memora FAMA ([23.31, 37.69]); both sources also show recovery. OAKS Novel native option parity holds for all 6,714 resolved outputs. Full-cohort frozen-scorer corruption/recovery effects (-27.55/+27.51 points) remain descriptive proxies, not validated native semantic population effects. These bounded findings motivate evaluating memory control-state integrity alongside retrieval accuracy.
authors: Bowen Liu, Youting Wang, Bonan Shen, Dingyan Shang
bullets: Studies faults that change which stored records enter model-visible context without changing memory content or tasks.
Across six providers and 2,080 matched fault pairs, corruption altered the operative projection in 96.25% of cases; enforcement restored it in 100%.
Downstream clean-versus-corrupted gaps were 40.54 points on LongMemEval binary correctness and 30.60 points on rescaled Memora FAMA, with recovery observed.
OAKS Novel native option parity held for all 6,714 resolved outputs.
Full-cohort frozen-scorer effects are descriptive proxies, not validated native semantic population effects.

The enforced path is an oracle-backed mediation condition used to measure recoverability, not an autonomous deployment-time repair algorithm.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robotic surgery has drawn increased attention in recent years due to its potential to relieve surgeons of time-consuming, mentally straining, and tedious tasks, particularly during prolonged operations. One suitable task for automation is suturing, which involves tracking the thread as it deforms during needle retrieval, de-tangling, knot tightening, and other tasks. Unlike rigid-object manipulation, deformable thread manipulation has no fixed pose to track and effectively infinite degrees of freedom, making its configuration difficult to predict and requiring the thread's state to be re-estimated rather than assumed. At the same time, thread manipulations involve sequential motions that depend on past and current thread contact points, which must be accurately and continuously tracked. This paper presents an image-to-manipulation pipeline that concurrently generates live thread reconstruction while conducting safe and optimized sequential manipulations to achieve long-horizon tasks.
authors: Emma Huang, Omar Hernandez, Zih-Yun Chiu, Michael Yip
bullets: Targets autonomous suturing tasks such as needle retrieval, de-tangling, and knot tightening.
Addresses the thread’s deformability, infinite degrees of freedom, and changing configuration.
Continuously tracks current and past thread contact points during sequential manipulation.
Combines live visual thread reconstruction with safe, optimized manipulation planning.
The abstract does not report specific experimental results or limitations.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is usually tied to the pretrained backbone on which it is learned. We ask whether LoRAs trained independently for the same task on different pretrained backbones can be summed and applied unchanged to all contributing backbones. We call this construction LoRA superposition. Across seven ViT-B/16 CLIP backbones and eight image-classification tasks, the exact sum improves all 56 backbone-task pairs and achieves a mean accuracy gain of 30.21 percentage points over the unadapted backbone. The exact sum achieves a mean accuracy only 0.28 percentage points below that of individually trained solo LoRAs. In contrast, a leave-one-model-out (LOMO) sum produces a mean gain of only 0.06 percentage points over the unadapted backbones. Backbone-specific solo LoRAs are nearly orthogonal in parameter space, while pairwise cross-backbone responses are strongly concentrated on the diagonal. These results support a component-wise non-interference hypothesis, under which the frozen backbone acts as an implicit selector of its own component without explicit routing or cross-model alignment.
authors: Keigo Watanabe, Hiroshi Kera, Kazuhiko Kawamoto
bullets: Evaluates LoRA superposition across seven ViT-B/16 CLIP backbones and eight image-classification tasks.
The exact sum improves all 56 backbone–task pairs, with a mean gain of 30.21 percentage points over unadapted backbones.
Its accuracy is only 0.28 percentage points below that of backbone-specific solo LoRAs.
Leave-one-model-out sums provide almost no benefit, suggesting the contributing model-specific components are necessary.
Near-orthogonal LoRA parameters and diagonal cross-backbone responses support a component-wise non-interference explanation without routing or alignment.

papers.abstract: Domain generalization (DG) aims to improve the generalization of the model to any unseen domains. Targeting this goal, existing DG methods mainly focus on learning domain-invariant features or prompts from the given source domains. However, these methods rely on source-domain data, and collecting and annotating large-scale single- or multi-source datasets is often infeasible, limiting the practical applicability of DG. To tackle this challenge, we propose {\underline{Do}}main \underline{P}rompt Learning (DoP), a method built on a large vision-language model (e.g., CLIP) for zero-shot domain generalization, which recognizes unseen classes in unseen target domains without access to source-domain data. DoP essentially learns the target domain knowledge via prompt both in text and visual modalities to overcome the domain shift in text-visual modalities under the test-time adaptation formulation. Specifically, DoP first takes text domain learning (TDL) to simulate various distribution shifts by learning diverse style tokens implicitly in the text space with inter-style diversity loss and intra-style consistency loss. Subsequently, DoP employs visual domain learning (VDL) to further refine the target-domain-relevant style token generated by TDL by making use of the test visual data with self-supervised learning. Extensive experiments on popular DG benchmark datasets (e.g., PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, and DomainNet) and ImageNet show that our DoP consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art DG approaches. Codes are available at: https://github.com/shiming-chen/DoP.
authors: Shiming Chen, Shuhuang Chen, Salman Khan, Fahad Shahbaz Khan
bullets: Addresses the impracticality of source-data-dependent domain generalization when labeled source datasets are unavailable.
Learns target-domain knowledge through text and visual prompt adaptation under a test-time adaptation setting.
Text Domain Learning simulates diverse style shifts using style tokens with inter-style diversity and intra-style consistency objectives.
Visual Domain Learning refines target-relevant style tokens using unlabeled test images and self-supervised learning.
Experiments on PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, DomainNet, and ImageNet report consistent improvements over existing DG methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: A schematic overview of DoP. DoP mainly consists of a text domain learning (TDL) module, a visual domain learning (VDL) module, and a classifier. Specifically, TDL first simulates various distribution shifts by learning diverse domain prompts implicitly in the text space with inter-style diversity loss and intra-style consistency loss and implicitly generates the style token S∗ that is relevant to the test image in target domains. Subsequently, VDL explicitly refines S∗ using the test visual data with self-supervised learning. Finally, DoP adopts the refined domain prompt for class prediction following the standard CLIP.

papers.abstract: We propose AgentDreamer, an agent-guided optimization framework that aligns text instructions with simulated motion through explicit 3D motion planning. Given a text instruction and scene geometry, an off-the-shelf agent translates the instruction into a structured semantic motion prior, specifying what should move, in which direction, and in what temporal order. The agent represents this prior using parametric functions over a series of temporal chunks, yielding dense 3D trajectories. We then optimize the parameters of a differentiable MPM simulator such that its rollout best matches the prior while remaining constrained by the scene dynamics. This allows the agent to provide semantic guidance from language, while the simulator grounds it in physically feasible motion. We further introduce Motion-IG, an information-theoretic metric for text-motion alignment based on masked text recovery. By comparing the likelihood of recovering masked motion-related content with and without the simulated motion, Motion-IG measures the information contributed by the motion beyond that available from the remaining text and scene context. Experiments show that AgentDreamer improves text alignment over video-based guidance, producing simulations that more closely follow the requested physical behavior.
authors: Mijeong Kim, Suho Park, Junha Park, Bohyung Han
bullets: Converts language into structured semantic motion priors describing objects, directions, and temporal order.
Represents priors as parametric dense 3D trajectories across temporal chunks.
Optimizes a differentiable MPM simulator to match the priors while respecting scene dynamics.
Introduces Motion-IG, an information-theoretic metric for measuring text–motion alignment.
Improves text alignment over video-based guidance in experiments.

papers.abstract: Safety probes trained on a model's activations are a standard tool for monitoring language models in real time. Each time a new model is released or a new harm area needs to be monitored, the probe must be retrained, which requires new labels and a choice of probe architecture. Yet neither the model nor the labels tell us in advance how well the resulting probe will perform. Finding out requires training and comparing many probe configurations. In this paper, we ask whether probe performance can instead be predicted in advance from model size and the number of labels. Existing safety datasets are insufficient for this, as they are either limited in scale or already saturated. We therefore construct six new safety datasets of sufficient size and difficulty. On these datasets, we train two probe architectures on 20 base models from five model families, with 32 to $10^{6}$ labels for each model. We measure performance using probe error, defined as 1 - AUROC, where lower values are better. We find that probe error follows two simple scaling laws. First, the lowest probe error a model can reach falls as a power law in its size. Second, probe error decreases towards its floor as the number of examples increases; the slope increases as the target model size increases. Both laws hold across tasks, model families and probe architectures, and only their fitted constants differ. When fitted on the smallest models of a family, the laws predict the error of the next larger model to within 0.02 in 72% of cases. They also identify whether more labels or a larger model is the cheaper way to reach a target error in 73% of cases. Finally, they choose the probe architecture with an extra error of only 0.006 on average when they pick the worse one. These laws allow safety researchers to determine how to create the best probe for any given model and label budget.
authors: Yuchen Wu (University of Washington), Jerry Wei (Anthropic)
bullets: The study addresses the costly retraining and configuration search required when monitoring new models or harm areas.
It introduces six large, challenging safety datasets and evaluates two probe architectures across 20 models from five families with 32 to 10⁶ labels.
Probe error decreases as model size grows and approaches a model-dependent floor as labels increase; these patterns generalize across tasks, families, and architectures.
Fitted on the smallest models in each family, the laws predict larger-model error within 0.02 in 72% of cases and correctly identify the cheaper path—more labels or a larger model—in 73% of cases.
The laws also select between probe architectures with only 0.006 average extra error when choosing the worse option.

papers.selection_reason: Derives scaling laws for safety probes, providing a predictive tool for monitoring LLM behavior, which is relevant to LLM safety and control.
papers.title: Scaling Laws for Safety Probes
papers.tldr: Safety-probe performance can be predicted from target-model size and label count using two scaling laws, reducing the need to train many probe configurations.

papers.abstract: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.
authors: Qince Luan, Jianhui Xu, Yang Xu
bullets: Intervenes on up_proj and down_proj matrices by spiking or smoothing singular values while preserving singular vectors and their geometric mean.
Evaluates five open Llama and Qwen instruction models across capability subtasks, reasoning, truthfulness, hallucination, safety, and personality probes.
Interprets behavioral changes using a three-dimensional basis of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning.
Positive spiking more consistently suppresses language and deductive responses, while moderate smoothing can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance.
Sensitivity varies substantially across model families, benchmark modules, and the underlying spectral inequality of layers.

papers.abstract: Visual Language Action (VLA) models are designed to be generalist robot models that can be implemented across embodiments, tasks and environments. However, their ability to collaborate with other robots and humans remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a framework to automate the generation of multi-robot collaborative data for decentralized VLA training without requiring human teleoperation. Our framework first utilizes a decentralized collaborative planning approach to generate multi-robot collaborative robot plans in the form of an executable function. We then utilize the collaborative plan to produce collaborative demonstration data to finetune VLA models in a decentralized manner. We show that our approach produces demonstration data that when used to finetune VLA models on decentralized collaboration tasks matches the task performance of VLA models finetuned on human-teleoperated collaborative data.
authors: Yi Loo, Siddhant Shrivastava, Minh Long Pham, Malika Meghjani
bullets: Addresses the limited study of VLA-based collaboration among robots and humans.
Uses decentralized collaborative planning to generate executable multi-robot task plans.
Converts these plans into collaborative demonstrations for decentralized VLA fine-tuning.
The resulting models match the task performance of models trained on human-teleoperated collaborative data.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as controllers in structured decision pipelines, yet their decisions are still executed by autoregressive text decoding. Hierarchical RAG is one such setting: at each frontier of a document tree, an LLM commits to $b$ of $k$ sections under an input-dependent action grammar, executed as either failure-prone free-form JSON or reliable but strictly serial grammar-constrained generation. We show that this serialization is unnecessary for bounded-horizon control: the reachable future forms a shallow action-prefix tree, which we compile --- one root prefill plus one tree-causal probe evaluate every prefix-conditioned action distribution with serial decoding's tokens, positions, and causal ancestry. A prefix-state lemma makes compiled control policy-exact in exact arithmetic: the same policy with a two-forward critical path and zero output tokens. One further probe pass certifies the exact order-marginalized MAP set. Across four document-disjoint splits and two scales on the primary MetaX device, compiled control matches the serial policy on $84$--$89\%$ of questions --- every instrumented divergence a floating-point near-tie --- and cuts control latency by $35$--$47\%$ versus token-wise serial decoding and $6$--$7\%$ versus an idealized chunked engine; an H800 repetition preserves the ordering.
authors: Zehao Lin, Qianfeng Shen, Xixuan Hao, Shaobo Cui, Chunyu Li, Kai Chen, Bo Tang, Zhenjun Wang, Jin Yan, Zhiyu Li, Feiyu Xiong
bullets: Hierarchical RAG controllers normally decode action choices serially, despite operating over a shallow, bounded action-prefix tree.
The method uses one root prefill and one tree-causal probe to evaluate every prefix-conditioned action distribution without generating output tokens.
A prefix-state lemma establishes policy equivalence to serial grammar-constrained decoding in exact arithmetic, with a two-forward-pass critical path.
Across four document-disjoint splits and two scales, compiled control matches the serial policy on 84–89% of questions; reported divergences are floating-point near-ties.
Control latency decreases by 35–47% versus token-wise serial decoding and 6–7% versus an idealized chunked engine, with the ordering preserved on an H800.

(c) Fresh split D, 7B: mean control latency −36%, zero output tokens and protocol failures; fp32 replay (split A): mean graph deviation ≈0.05.

papers.tldr: A tree-causal compilation method executes bounded-horizon LLM control for hierarchical RAG in parallel while preserving the serial policy in exact arithmetic and substantially reducing latency.

papers.abstract: Open-world geographic artificial intelligence (GeoAI) agents can transform public geospatial data into accessible decision support for real-world challenges, but must balance autonomous reasoning with reliable spatial analysis and human oversight. We present a topology-guided GeoAI agentic framework for urban flood screening that takes a place name, drawn region, or uploaded boundary and returns ranked candidate basins with an interactive map and report. A deterministic controller retrieves public elevation, rainfall, soil, land-cover, exposure, and infrastructure layers, extracts terrain depressions with discrete Morse theory, and ranks basins with a relative flood-priority score. The language model acts only at recorded decision points: selecting a persistence threshold from a precomputed candidate table, drafting recommendations from computed evidence, and reviewing each recommendation against the same evidence. Three human-in-the-loop checkpoints let users revise the threshold, factor weights, or recommendation. In a College Park, Maryland case study, the selected threshold reduced 278 raw terrain minima to 70 basins, with 77% of these basins' lowest points also identified as sinks by a separately computed eight-direction (D8) flow-routing model. Across four further study areas, agreement ranged from 61% to 83%. By combining open data, explicit spatial reasoning, traceable evidence, and human oversight, the framework enables transparent first-pass flood screening while keeping consequential recommendations inspectable and user-controlled.
authors: Yutian Tao, Haoan Feng, Xin Xu, Leila De Floriani
bullets: Accepts place names, drawn regions, or uploaded boundaries and returns ranked candidate basins with maps and reports.
Uses public elevation, rainfall, soil, land-cover, exposure, and infrastructure data to identify terrain depressions and compute relative flood-priority scores.
Restricts the language model to traceable decision points: threshold selection, evidence-based recommendations, and recommendation review.
Provides three human checkpoints for revising the persistence threshold, factor weights, or recommendations.
In the case studies, basin identification agreed with D8 flow-routing sinks for 61%–83% of basins, including 77% in College Park, Maryland.

papers.abstract: Social world models predict how interactions develop after an action, helping agents negotiate, cooperate and mediate. In these situations, one action can lead to several plausible futures, hence predicting only one future can overlook consequential alternatives, while exploring them through repeated simulations increases inference cost. We propose DSWM, a Distributional Social World Model that predicts alternative responses, their probabilities and immediate and final outcome values in one output per candidate action. We train a 4B model on repeated simulations using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO. At inference time, the actor uses these possible consequences to choose an action. Across three seen and two unseen environments, with interaction backbones absent from training collection, DSWM achieves the best average performance on 13 of 15 metrics. Ablations show that retaining multiple futures and their predicted probabilities improves outcomes in all five environments.

papers.abstract: The claim that speculative-decoding acceptance rate decays as a chain-of-thought grows longer has become a de facto industry narrative, motivating draft-model co-design and position-aware training. Nearly all direct evidence comes from trained drafters whose offline training length is far shorter than inference, so a purely positional law has never been isolated. We present the first systematic, full-length measurement of acceptance rate as a function of generation position on MATH-500 (all 500 problems), under greedy and sampling decoding, with two independent drafts against DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: a same-family draft (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B) and a cross-family draft (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct), yielding about 1.78M verification rounds. Using within-problem paired tests, we find that after isolating a greedy-decoding repetition pathology, acceptance rate does not decay with position in any of the four configurations within the supported ranges (greedy 0-8K, sampling 0-12K); the second half of each trajectory is slightly but significantly higher than the first. A controlled temperature sweep shows that the apparent sampling-mode degradation of high-entropy reflection tokens is a visibility artifact of argmax agreement, not a drop in expected acceptance probability. Rejections concentrate with high precision on reflection trigger tokens such as "wait", "however" and "check", an entropy-selective failure that a lightweight three-arm LoRA trajectory-alignment intervention (uniform, reflection-marked, entropy-weighted) fails to improve in mean accepted length. We thus supply the positional baseline that independent draft-target pairs were missing, and localize the residual failure to decision-point entropy rather than position.
authors: Zhiming Meng
bullets: Evaluated all 500 MATH-500 problems with greedy and sampling decoding against DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.
Used independent same-family and cross-family 1.5B drafts across about 1.78M verification rounds.

A three-arm LoRA trajectory-alignment intervention did not improve mean accepted length.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow instructions and navigate to target locations. However, current VLN agents often suffer severe performance degradation in unseen environments due to distribution shifts. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm to bridge this gap, yet existing methods that rely on unsupervised entropy minimization can propagate errors through the trajectory, causing cascading failures in navigation. Recent methods mitigate this by incorporating human feedback, but they apply trajectory-level supervision uniformly across all steps without localizing the actions is truly informative, leading to inefficient feedback utilization and mismatched optimization granularity. To address these limitations, we propose FETA, a Feedback-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation method that improves both feedback efficiency and optimization reliability. To reduce unnecessary human interventions, we introduce a hierarchical sample selection strategy to localize informative samples. Specifically, we first filter trajectories whose normalized policy entropy exhibits large fluctuations. Within each selected trajectory, we further select the critical action via an entropy-gradient saliency criterion and query a single binary feedback on its correctness. A discrepancy-aware entropy optimization objective then updates the policy only at the queried step, with adaptive scaling that assigns larger relative weights to samples with greater prediction-feedback discrepancy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FETA achieves state-of-the-art performance with fewer human interventions, while remaining robust under noisy feedback and continual adaptation settings.
authors: Zixu Wang, Huaquan Zhang, Shoukai Xu, Jinwu Hu, Zhiquan Wen, Mingkui Tan
bullets: Unseen environments can cause severe VLN degradation, while entropy minimization may amplify navigation errors.
FETA hierarchically selects high-value feedback: unstable trajectories first, then critical actions using entropy-gradient saliency.
It queries one binary correctness signal per selected action and updates the policy only at that step.
Discrepancy-aware entropy optimization adaptively emphasizes actions where predictions and feedback disagree.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance with fewer interventions, including robustness to noisy feedback and continual adaptation.

papers.abstract: Medical knowledge evolves as clinical guidelines revise recommendations, yet whether large language models (LLMs) faithfully incorporate such changes remains unclear. We introduce ChronoEvo, comprising 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 forms of medical knowledge change, to distinguish recognition of revised guidance from incorporation into clinical recommendations. In the primary model, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions and 80.2% were clinically correct, but only 58.5% fully incorporated guidance, yielding a 32.3-percentage-point recognition-incorporation gap. This dissociation persisted across 14 models and was corroborated by two clinicians' adjudicated assessment of 300 responses, yielding a 40.3-percentage-point gap in the validation sample. Changes in recommendation strength and patient eligibility were associated with retention of outdated guidance. A revision-salience intervention reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness but did not significantly improve full incorporation. These findings identify faithful incorporation of evolving medical knowledge as a distinct challenge for clinical LLM reliability, even when updated guideline evidence is available.
authors: Min Zeng, Zaifu Zhan, Kai Yu, Rui Zhang
bullets: ChronoEvo evaluates 1,709 recommendation-level revisions spanning 12 types of medical knowledge change.
In the primary model, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions, but only 58.5% fully incorporated them; 80.2% were clinically correct.
A recognition–incorporation gap persisted across 14 models and was confirmed by clinician assessment.
Changes in recommendation strength and patient eligibility were linked to retaining outdated guidance.
Making revisions more salient reduced outdated content and improved correctness, but not full incorporation.

Model responses are evaluated along three dimensions—revision recognition, clinical correctness and full incorporation—and further examined using revision-gain, semantic-error, change-type, multivariable, cross-model and evaluator-robustness, and intervention analyses. papers.abstract: Faithfully understanding the internal process that occurs as models form their chain of thought is an important problem with the rise in model capabilities. However, this remains challenging due to the variance in sampled responses, making it difficult to isolate the effects of interventions and compare model reasoning systematically. We propose a method for localizing and analyzing how a given intervention affects the model's reasoning through behavioral counterfactuals: given a fixed response, how does introducing an intervention to the prompt change the next-token distributions? We train a module to edit the residual stream such that it minimizes the KL divergence between the output distributions for a fixed response under a source prompt and its counterfactual target prompt. We find that matching the output distributions recovers the counterfactual behavior more effectively than standard activation reconstruction objectives and validate that attribution of the trained module outputs is effective for identifying causally important locations for counterfactual recovery. The attribution maps and visualizations of the downstream effects of model edits provide an interface for generating hypotheses about the original model's computation, which can then be tested with activation patching. In a case study on Gemma-4-E4B-it and DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B, we investigate how a suggestion influences model reasoning even when it is not verbally acknowledged. Our analysis identifies representations at the question statement and filler tokens that mediate a substantial part of the suggestion's influence, with downstream effects such as changing the framing of the justification or even the final answer.
authors: Shawn Im, James Oldfield, Adel Bibi, Sharon Li
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of interpreting chain-of-thought changes caused by interventions amid response-sampling variability.
Trains a residual-stream editing module to minimize KL divergence between next-token distributions for a fixed response under source and counterfactual prompts.
Finds behavioral distribution matching recovers counterfactual behavior more effectively than standard activation reconstruction objectives.
Uses attribution maps and downstream-effect visualizations to identify candidate causally important locations, which can be tested with activation patching.
A case study finds that suggestions can influence reasoning through representations at question and filler tokens, altering justification framing and sometimes the final answer.

papers.abstract: Relighting and novel view synthesis of human portraits are essential in applications such as portrait photography, virtual reality (VR), and augmented reality (AR). Despite recent progress, 3D-aware portrait relighting remains challenging due to the demands for photorealistic rendering, real-time performance, and generalization to unseen subjects. Existing works either rely on supervision from limited and expensive light stage captured data or produce suboptimal results. Moreover, many works are based on generative NeRFs, which suffer from poor 3D consistency and low real-time performance. We resort to recent progress on generative 3D Gaussians and design a lighting model based on a unified neural radiance transfer representation, which responds linearly to incident light. Using only in-the-wild images, our method achieves state-of-the-art relighting results and a significantly faster rendering speed ($\times12$) compared to previous 3D-aware portrait relighting research. Project page: http://www.geometrylearning.com/GSHeadRelight/.
authors: Henglei Lv, Bailin Deng, Jianzhu Guo, Xiaoqiang Liu, Pengfei Wan, Di Zhang, Lin Gao
bullets: Targets 3D-aware portrait relighting and novel-view synthesis for VR, AR, and photography.
Uses generative 3D Gaussians instead of generative NeRFs to improve 3D consistency and real-time performance.
Introduces a unified neural radiance transfer lighting model with a linear response to incident light.
Requires only in-the-wild images, avoiding reliance on limited and expensive light-stage supervision.
Reports state-of-the-art relighting and 12× faster rendering than prior 3D-aware portrait-relighting methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. We incorporate a lighting model based on unified radiance transfer into a generative 3D Gaussian framework. The generator G takes in Gaussian noise and camera pose as condition and generates for each Gaussian an embedding x, which is then linearly transformed into the albedo 𝜌 and geometry attributes {g} including position, scale, rotation and opacity. A light-weight decoder conditioned on view direction transforms x into radiance transfer coefficients t, which are used to compute the unified light transport with the light condition. Color is obtained by multiplying the light transport component with the albedo. The image is then rendered by standard splatting and sent to the discriminator D, which takes both camera pose and light condition as input. Mapping modules are omitted for simplicity. Gaussian noise and camera pose are represented as icons, and light condition as a diffuse sphere.
