papers.abstract: Scaling large language models has substantially improved linguistic fluency, yet reliable autonomous agents require more than fluent generation. In multi-turn inference, current agentic systems often produce semantically plausible but structurally ungrounded reasoning, especially under incomplete observations. We propose Structure-Grounded Uncertainty Reduction (SGUR), a training-free framework that complements token-level generation with active uncertainty reduction over structured hypothesis spaces. SGUR represents incomplete observations as a query graph and aligns them with candidate hypothesis graphs through a prior-weighted partial graph matching mechanism, where database-derived empirical priors assign greater importance to decision-relevant relations rather than treating all graph edges uniformly. The resulting inference state is iteratively refined by an active information-gain strategy that selects the next most informative node to query, systematically pruning the candidate space. We instantiate SGUR on a challenging PrimeKG-derived sequential medical diagnosis benchmark, demonstrating that structural grounding can partially substitute for model scale: starting from only two observed symptoms, SGUR achieves 92.5% Hit@3, outperforming the strongest Graph-RAG baseline by 9.4 percentage points while using approximately 5x fewer tokens. Notably, SGUR enables smaller backbone models to match or exceed the performance of models up to 10x larger, suggesting that structural grounding provides a more robust and efficient paradigm for scaling agent performance than relying exclusively on increasing model size.
authors: Amirhossein Aghaei, Liangyan Li, Shiyi Yang, Shaohua Wang, Yan Wang
bullets: Targets structurally ungrounded reasoning in agentic systems operating with incomplete observations.
Uses a query graph, prior-weighted partial graph matching, and active information-gain queries to prune hypotheses.
Evaluated on a PrimeKG-derived sequential medical diagnosis benchmark from two observed symptoms.
Reports 92.5% Hit@3, 9.4 percentage points above the strongest Graph-RAG baseline, with about 5× fewer tokens.
Findings suggest structural grounding can let smaller models match or exceed models up to 10× larger.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the SGUR framework. The offline phase constructs a hierarchical expert graph database Gdb from expert data under a shared schema. The online phase performs closed-loop multiturn inference through four stages: (a) query graph construction, which grounds observations Ot into G (t) q with latent routing; (b) candidate pruning, which applies path filtering and specificity-aware structural priors to obtain G (t) cand; (c) prior-weighted partial FGW alignment, which ranks candidate graphs by structural consistency with the query; and (d) active acquisition, which selects informative unobserved nodes to obtain Ot+1. Across rounds, SGUR progressively contracts the candidate space under partial observation.

Figure 2: Accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier in the complex regime. The x-axis reports average total tokens over three interaction rounds, and the y-axis reports final Hit@3 after round 3. Higher is better on the y-axis and lower is better on the x-axis. SGUR achieves the highest retrieval accuracy with the lowest inference cost.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a structure-grounded framework using graph matching and active information gain for reasoning, which aligns with spatial intelligence and graph-based reasoning.
papers.title: Better Reasoning, Not Just Bigger Models: A Structure-Grounded Framework for Efficient and Reliable Inference

papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have recently emerged as important remote sensing platforms, and UAV navigation has shown great potential in remote sensing applications. However, existing methods do not explicitly incorporate kinodynamic modeling or safety distances into trajectory generation, resulting in high absolute yaw rates, frequent collisions, and low navigation success rates, which limit safety and motion stability. To address this challenge, we introduce KinoUAV, a kinodynamic benchmark comprising a dataset and KinoUAV-Agent. First, we develop a hierarchical kinodynamic trajectory generation pipeline that drives UAV through acceleration actions. It uses waypoint chains from global planning and generates trajectories segment by segment under velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints, reducing oscillations and improving trajectory stability. Furthermore, we introduce directional free-space distance (DFD) labels into the constructed dataset to describe the available clearance for safe motion decisions. The proposed KinoUAV-Agent predicts DFDs and uses them to generate safe actions, decoupling perception from action decision-making. This design enables autonomous obstacle avoidance and improves navigation safety. The benchmark incorporates the proposed Cruise-Seek task, in which the UAV first enters the target region and then searches for the target, reducing the difficulty of target search and improving navigation success. Experiments on KinoUAV show that KinoUAV-Agent outperforms existing methods, achieving the highest success rate while maintaining lower absolute yaw rates and collision rates. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of kinodynamic modeling for safe and stable UAV navigation.
authors: Chenyao Yang, Peijin Wang, Yingchao Feng, Wenhui Diao
bullets: Targets unstable and unsafe UAV navigation caused by missing kinodynamic constraints and safety-distance modeling.
Generates trajectories segment by segment from waypoint chains under velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints.
Adds directional free-space distance (DFD) labels, which the agent predicts to guide safe action selection and obstacle avoidance.
Introduces the Cruise-Seek task, where UAVs first enter a target region before searching for the target.
Experiments report the highest success rate among compared methods, with lower absolute yaw rates and collision rates.

papers.abstract: Motion planning is central to robotics, and it is increasingly used to correct the motions proposed by learned planners and policies. In both uses, constraints must hold at every instant of the motion, not only at sampled times. To our knowledge, no algorithm provably converges to a globally optimal motion once a smoothness cost is combined with such constraints. We cast planning and steering as a single continuous-time program: robots avoid one another and static or moving obstacles, and a learned proposal is steered by keeping the motion close to it. The program is elementary to state, yet nonconvex. We propose GlobMP (Global Motion Planning), a gradient projection method over piecewise-polynomial curves, on which each constraint is one polynomial per piece that must stay nonnegative over the whole motion; it alternates cost reduction with feasibility restoration. Under mild assumptions, we show that, from a fine grid start, its cost approaches the global optimum as the number of polynomial pieces grows, with every constraint met to any chosen tolerance, or exactly on stable instances. We demonstrate its superior performance over strong baselines in real and synthetic experiments, including teams of up to $200$ robots, multi-robot planning on the Robotarium testbed and an extended benchmark, maze navigation, and steering tactile-reactive policies on a bimanual humanoid.
authors: Mohsen Amiri, Sima Didari, Davoud Ataee Tarzanagh, Hankyu Moon, Yeongdae Kwon
bullets: Addresses motion planning and steering with continuous-time collision and obstacle constraints, rather than checking only sampled states.
Represents trajectories as piecewise-polynomial curves and uses gradient projection to alternate cost reduction with feasibility restoration.
Under mild assumptions, approaches the global optimum as the number of polynomial pieces increases, with constraints satisfied to any chosen tolerance or exactly on stable instances.
Demonstrates strong performance across synthetic and real settings, including teams of up to 200 robots, Robotarium planning, maze navigation, and humanoid tactile-reactive policy steering.

papers.abstract: Dynamic interactive object search in large-scale human environments presents substantial challenges for existing methods. Current scene representations like 3D Scene Graphs (3DSG) only provide coarse-grained spatial segmentation and cannot identify functional areas such as storage or leisure areas. Without functional area understanding, existing methods are constrained to exhaustive sequential exploration at large scales, resulting in inefficient search behaviors -- particularly in open-layout environments with numerous interactive objects such as drawers and cabinets. Moreover, these methods lack adaptability to environmental dynamics such as object relocations. To address these limitations, this paper proposes CMAR-search, a novel framework built upon Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning (CMAR). Our approach leverages commonsense about area functionalities and aggregates environmental memory to construct a Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG), which organizes the environment into functional areas with their associated containers. Through this structured representation, CMAR enables hierarchical action planning at both macro-area and micro-container levels, empowering the system to efficiently identify and inspect semantically relevant areas for effective object search. Notably, CMAR continuously integrates real-time perception, accumulated memory, and commonsense to dynamically relocalize objects in changing environments. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that CMAR-search significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both success rate and search efficiency for object search in dynamic interactive environments.
authors: Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Xinlei Zhang, Chen Chen, Qing Sun, Jianwei Niu
bullets: Addresses coarse 3D scene representations, exhaustive exploration, and difficulty handling relocated objects.
Builds a Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG) that organizes spaces by functional areas and associated containers.
Uses hierarchical planning to select relevant areas first, then inspect specific containers such as drawers and cabinets.
Continuously integrates perception, memory, and commonsense to relocalize objects as environments change.
Experiments in simulation and real-world settings show higher search success and efficiency than existing baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Fig. 1. Our CMAR-search framework empowers the agent to perform hierarchical action planning using the F3DSG, enabling rapid object relocation in dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Traversability estimation is critical for ground vehicle teleoperation, yet existing methods often neglect the human operator's preferences for speed and risk tolerance. To address this gap, we propose PATH-Net, a Preference-Aware Traversability estimation Hierarchical Network that adaptively generates preference-conditioned traversability cost maps and speed profiles for off-road teleoperation. Our framework integrates visual and geometric bird's-eye-view features with short-term historical vehicle states through a multi-head shared-backbone architecture. Our PATH-Net infers traversability cost maps while optimizing speed recommendations by using maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning and sparse speed supervision. Our method incorporates operator preference via an asymmetric feature aggregation mechanism, splitting inference into a cost branch that prioritizes high-risk traversability regions and a speed branch that outputs preference-adjusted recommended speeds. Experiments with 15 operators across 225 teleoperated trajectories show alignment with user-specific navigation strategies, achieving modified Hausdorff distance of 0.17 m (aggressive) and 0.15 m (conservative). In the questionnaire assessment, participants reported lower NASA-TLX workload scores with PATH-Net recommendations than without recommendations, decreasing from 34.7 to 22.2. These results support preference-conditioned trajectory and speed recommendation for off-road teleoperation.
authors: Xianghao Meng, Wenshuo Wang, Cheng Shao, Lewei Feng, Qingxiao Liu, Canyu Wang, Junqiang Xi
bullets: Addresses the limited consideration of human preferences in existing traversability estimation methods.
Combines visual and geometric bird’s-eye-view features with short-term vehicle-state history.
Uses maximum-entropy inverse reinforcement learning and sparse speed supervision to infer cost maps and speed recommendations.
Separates cost and speed branches, emphasizing high-risk regions while adapting speeds to operator preferences.
In studies with 15 operators and 225 trajectories, recommendations aligned with aggressive and conservative strategies and reduced reported NASA-TLX workload from 34.7 to 22.2.

papers.abstract: LLMs have shown strong in-context learning (ICL) capability, but extending it to Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains challenging. Prior multimodal ICL methods often rely on ICL-specific datasets for additional training or task vector extraction, which can improve performance on the same ICL benchmark used for adaptation. However, they do not generalize well to other benchmarks and often induce forgetting in previously well-solved tasks. For this reason, we identify 'visual grounding' as the key bottleneck in multimodal ICL; MLLMs often fail to attend to task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, instead over-relying on textual cues and producing hallucinated outputs. To address this, we propose ProCoRe to enhance visual grounding through contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data for improving multimodal ICL. ProCoRe generates captions for contrastive image pairs, decomposes them into propositions, and optimizes contrastive rewards that encourage alignment with corresponding images while discouraging mismatched ones. Despite never seeing ICL-formatted training examples, ProCoRe improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over the off-the-shelf Qwen-VL-3-8B model, outperforming ICL-data-dependent state of the arts across benchmarks. Finally, we introduce PICL, a personalized multimodal ICL captioning benchmark that tests whether MLLMs genuinely understand visual demonstrations rather than relying on pre-trained semantic priors.
authors: Minhyuk Seo, Minjae Lee, Chaeeun Lee, Wei Lin, Muhammad Jehanzeb Mirza, Tinne Tuytelaars, Jonghyun Choi
bullets: Problem: MLLMs often rely on textual cues instead of task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, causing hallucinations, poor cross-benchmark generalization, and forgetting.
Method: ProCoRe uses contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data, rewarding captions aligned with matching images and penalizing mismatches.
Results: It improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over Qwen-VL-3-8B.
Scope: The method is evaluated across benchmarks and compared with ICL-data-dependent approaches.
Contribution: The authors introduce PICL, a personalized captioning benchmark designed to test genuine understanding of visual demonstrations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of ProCoRe. (1) MLLM f predict captions t̂1, t̂2 for contrastive images. (2) Decompose them into propositions using ChatGPT: unique to I1 (i.e., P̂1), I2 (i.e., P̂2), or shared (i.e., P̂s). (3) Compute proposition-level contrastive reward: RI and RT encourage t̂1 to reflect discriminative visual details (i.e., fire hydrant vs. parking meter), while Rs preserves shared details.

Figure 2: ICL data-dependent methods show limited generalization. Blue-shaded bars denote ICL data-dependent baselines trained on TrueMICL ICL dataset, while red-shaded bars denote those based on ISEKAI. They often outperform the off-the-shelf model when evaluated on the same ICL dataset used for training (i.e., train: TrueMICL→ test: TrueMICL), but degrade significantly when their training and test ICL datasets differ (i.e., train: ISEKAI→ test: TrueMICL). In contrast, even without using any ICL data, ProCoRe outperforms them through strong visual grounding.
Figure 7: Comparison of hallucinations on MS COCO ICL captioning benchmark. ProCoRe consistently reduces hallucinations across varying numbers of demonstrations compared to baselines.

Figure 8: Accuracy heatmap over reward weights (λI , λT ) with λs = 4. If the text reward weight (λT ) outweighs the visual contrastive reward weight (λI ), the model over-focuses on textual demonstrations, weakening visual grounding and degrading performance. Conversely, if λI is too large compared to λT , the model underutilizes useful information from ground-truth captions, also leading to performance drops. Moderate ratios that emphasize visual rewards while retaining text signals (e.g., λI/λT = 2, red dotted box) consistently show strong performance across shots. We evaluate ICL performance on the MS COCO captioning benchmark, with InpaintCOCO used for contrastive RL training in ProCoRe.

Figure 5: Effect of ICL training on simple VQA tasks. ICL training-based methods, which perform additional instruction tuning on ICL datasets, degrade performance on previously well-solved simple VQA tasks (i.e., IconQA, TextVQA) due to forgetting. In contrast, ProCoRe improves these tasks by enhancing visual grounding, while also achieving strong multimodal ICL performance (Tab. 2).

Figure 6: Comparison of target attention score (TAS) on multimodal ICL captioning benchmarks. While hallucination-mitigation baselines sometimes enhance TAS compared to off-the-shelf model, our proposed ProCoRe significantly outperforms both off-the-shelf model and baselines.

Figure 11: Comparison across ICL-shot settings. Higher-shot settings require reasoning over increasingly complex relationships among demonstrations, rather than simply providing more context. For example, in the 3-shot case, the first demo lets the model infer that the dinosaur is “Henry”, while the second remains ambiguous since “Ava” and “Mason” perform the same action; only after the third demo (where the fox is identified as “Henry”) can the model resolve the ambiguity and infer that the pink character in the second demo is “Ava”. In contrast, lower-shot settings can be easier due to fewer required inferences (e.g., in 1-shot, the pink character can be directly identified as “Amella”).

Figure 4: Example of 2-shot PICL. (left) Query image alone cannot infer the personalized identity. (right) (1) Identifying the dinosaur as “Charlotte” in the first demo and (2) linking it to the dinosaur in the second enables (3) inferring that the pink beaver is “Emma” in the second, allowing correct prediction of the personalized identifier for the query. See Fig. 10 and Fig. 11 for more examples.

While PICL requires visual understanding all demonstrations to answer correctly (e.g., resolving “Mason” in the first demo is necessary to correctly identify “Isabella” for Pororo in the second, enabling the query prediction), MS COCO ICL task can often be solved using pre-trained priors without understanding demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy. However, existing methods often involve a trade-off: lightweight online mapping is efficient but captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and is more vulnerable to distractors. They also struggle to relocalize objects after scene changes. To address these challenges, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS), a unified system for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. Motivated by the observation that indoor scenes are organized around stable semantic anchors, OASIS represents the environment using a sparse set of anchor nodes, each maintaining a unified multimodal representation that integrates semantic descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation. Its compact anchor-centric memory supports on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval, reducing redundant storage while improving retrieval reliability. To handle scene dynamics, OASIS further reuses transient observations collected during navigation to relocalize moved objects. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, including standard retrieval benchmarks and navigation tasks under both static and dynamic settings, demonstrate that our system can perform complex open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation, while also enabling relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.
authors: Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Chen Chen, Xiaoze Wu, Qing Sun, Jianwei Niu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–semantic richness trade-off in online mapping and the difficulty of relocalizing objects after scene changes.
Represents scenes with sparse anchor nodes that combine semantic, visual, and geometric information for reasoning, verification, and navigation.
Uses on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval to reduce redundant storage while supporting complex queries.
Reuses transient navigation observations to relocalize objects that have moved.
Validated in simulation and real-world settings across retrieval benchmarks and static/dynamic navigation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: System architecture of OASIS. To build the episodic memory, it utilizes scaleaware scoring and spatial-visual cluster assignment to continuously update and retain high-quality representative frames. By assigning these selected frames to their corresponding stable anchor instances, the system constructs the unified multimodal OASIS Graph, structured as shown on the right. Leveraging this graph alongside multimodal foundation models (LLM/VLM), the agent effectively executes hierarchical retrieval and robust view-driven navigation in dynamic environments.

Figure 3: Visual relocalization via Transient Visual Buffer (TVB). If the retrieved target is absent from the current view, OASIS uses CLIP to match transient crops to the query and a VLM to verify candidate frames and confirm the target’s new location.

Figure 1: Comparison of retrieval paradigms for complex open-vocabulary queries. Unlike traditional dense mapping (left) which struggles with redundant context and visual distractors, our OASIS (right) constructs a lightweight anchor-centric memory. By leveraging an LLM to filter irrelevant regions and performing on-demand VLM verification, OASIS efficiently isolates the target based on fine-grained attributes and spatial relationships, significantly improving retrieval reliability.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in foundation-model agents have enabled increasingly capable embodied systems for long-horizon planning and interaction. However, embodied agents require fast, closed-loop decisions as they continuously perceive and act on a changing environment. Deploying strong cloud agents leaves the platform idle for seconds between consecutive actions, while lightweight local models respond quickly but are more vulnerable to errors. Existing hierarchical architectures typically assign models fixed roles, whereas conventional model routers make stateless per-request decisions. We present CARE, a critic-guided adaptive execution framework that dynamically determines when to escalate control from a local executor to a stronger cloud model. A lightweight critic model monitors execution reliability and triggers escalation when local execution becomes unreliable; once escalated, control persists until the agent recovers, avoiding step-wise switching. To support such control transfer, a shared handoff memory maintains execution context and task-level progress across executors, enabling the model to intervene without restarting from scratch. Across diverse embodied benchmarks, CARE improves task success by 6.3-18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline. CARE further approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8-82.6%.
authors: Wei Zhang, Lirong Xiang, Charles Fleming
bullets: Targets the latency of cloud-only agents and the error vulnerability of lightweight local agents in long-horizon embodied tasks.
Uses a lightweight critic to monitor local execution and trigger persistent escalation rather than making stateless per-step routing decisions.
Maintains shared handoff memory so cloud control preserves execution context and task progress without restarting.
Across diverse embodied benchmarks, improves task success by 6.3–18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline.
Approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8–82.6%.

papers.abstract: AI control protocols aim to get useful work from models that may be misaligned by monitoring their behaviour. One approach uses a second copy of the same model as the monitor. This avoids relying on a weaker reviewer the model could outsmart, but risks collusion: the model, now monitoring itself, may cover up its own misbehaviour. One remedy is to fine-tune the monitor on whatever examples of misbehaviour the control team has caught. We ask whether this training also removes collusion that the control team has not yet found. We fine-tune Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen2.5-72B to install five policy-monitor behaviour pairs, correct the monitor on 300 honest reviews of one caught collusion, and measure collusion on the other four in unseen prompt formats. Averaged over the three seeds of each family, correction reduces held-out collusion from 91% to 14-20% under three of the four methods we compare (individual seeds 10-32%), while a control fine-tuned on the same number of unrelated examples leaves 56-93%. Family-average accuracy on control items changes by at most five points and capability is preserved, apart from a drop in mathematical accuracy on one Llama seed. Under the tested training configuration, methods with similar caught-task accuracy differ in held-out transfer, from 58% to 83% average reduction, so the caught behaviour alone does not reveal how far a correction reaches. Catching one collusion lets the control team reduce, but not remove, collusion it has not caught, by retraining the monitor alone.
authors: Juan-Pablo Rivera, Ari Spiesberger, Juan J Vazquez, Arun Jose, Axel Ahlqvist, Adeline Kassler, Meru Gopalan, Sandy Tanwisuth, John Hughes

Across three of four methods, held-out collusion fell from 91% to 14–20%; unrelated-example controls remained at 56–93%.
Normal control-item accuracy changed by at most five points and capabilities were generally preserved, though one Llama seed lost mathematical accuracy.
Similar performance on the caught task produced different transfer rates, so caught-task accuracy alone does not predict generalization.

papers.abstract: Unlike conventional GUI agents, personalized GUI agents require user preferences to guide sequential execution over changing GUI states. This raises two challenges: determining HOW each preference should alter execution strategy and WHEN it should take effect along the interaction trajectory. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate overall task success, offering limited insight into these questions. We introduce PrefDiag-Bench with two components: (1) a categorization of preferences into five types, characterizing HOW they affect execution; and (2) a stage-wise diagnostic framework with 1,664 probes, tracing WHEN preferences should take effect and where failures occur. We evaluate eleven GUI agent systems, including end-to-end agents and agentic workflows, under two forms of user context: explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs. Although existing agents achieve relatively high completion rates on non-personalized tasks, performance is substantially lower on preference-personalized tasks. Even the best-performing model, Seed-2.0-Pro, achieves only 47.17% on Process preferences under explicit user profiles. Agents struggle particularly with Ranking and Process preferences. Further analysis reveals two key capability bottlenecks: selecting relevant evidence from user history and recognizing when preferences should take effect during execution. Controlled interventions that explicitly provide relevant evidence improve end-to-end task success by up to 7.06%. PrefDiag-Bench offers a more systematic evaluation of GUI agents' personalization capabilities beyond overall task success. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Zhixin-L/PrefDiag-Bench.
authors: Zhixin Lin, Dongliang Xu, Jungang Li, Shidong Pan, Jun Feng, Yanbin Sun, Jing Li, Liang Liu, Yue Yao
bullets: Categorizes preferences into five types based on how they alter execution.
Uses 1,664 stage-wise probes to identify when preferences should take effect and where failures occur.
Evaluates 11 GUI agent systems using explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs.
Agents struggle most with Ranking and Process preferences; the best reported Process score is 47.17% under explicit profiles.
Providing relevant evidence from user history improves end-to-end success by up to 7.06%.

The distributions reveal how failures identified by individual diagnostic stages relate to failures in complete task execution.

Figure 3: The heatmaps show P2 Evidence Selection, P3 Relevance Selection, and P4 Trigger Recognition. Rows represent evaluated systems and columns represent the five preference types. Darker colors indicate higher task-level accuracy.

PrefDiag-Bench complements end-to-end evaluation with stage-wise diagnostic probes across information processing, contextual reasoning, and action formulation to identify capability gaps in preference application.

papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly act as analysts whose decision can often be cast as hypothesis tests. Classical tests control the Type I error rate, the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis, for fixed procedures. However, AI analysts introduce internal randomness and can evolve continuously over time. As AI analysts evolve, the risk of approving versions with Type I error rates above the target can accumulate, and adaptive use of evaluation feedback can lead to overfitting. We introduce continual validation, which evaluates each proposed AI analyst version before deployment using simulated data under the null hypothesis, with scenarios that can be randomized and expanded over time. We prove that, regardless of how updates are chosen or how many are proposed, the lifetime probability of ever deploying a version whose Type I error rate exceeds the allowed level remains bounded. This guarantees that every subsequent decision controls the Type I error rate at the target level across these scenarios. At the same time, updates with sufficiently low Type I error rates pass validation with high probability, allowing the analyst to continuously improve its performance without sacrificing rigor. In two examples involving evolving AI analysts for bioequivalence studies and product A/B tests, Type I error rates reached 0.098 and 0.183 without continual validation, compared with at most 0.045 and 0.044 with it, while retaining 82% and 96% of the power from optimally selected valid updates.
authors: Xiaojing Sun, Yuhan Zeng, Xiao Wang
bullets: AI analysts can accumulate false-positive risk as they evolve and adapt to evaluation feedback.
The proposed method validates every candidate version on simulated null-hypothesis data before deployment.
The lifetime probability of ever deploying an invalid version remains bounded, regardless of update strategy or number of proposals.
In bioequivalence and A/B-testing examples, continual validation reduced Type I error rates to at most 0.045 and 0.044 while retaining 82% and 96% of selected valid-update power.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Continual validation and the two examples. (A) A human developer or the AI analyst itself proposes updates. The validator freezes the updated version and runs it alongside a reference analysis on datasets newly simulated under the null hypothesis. The update is deployed only when the upper confidence bound on its Type I error rate is at most the validation level α′ across all simulated scenarios. The bound for update 2 exceeds α′ in one scenario so it is rejected and v1 stays in use. The proposer receives this result as feedback. Over any number of updates the chance of ever deploying a version above α′ remains at most the lifetime risk δ. In every real study where the data follow a simulated null scenario a true H0 is rejected with probability at most α = α′ + δ(1− α′). The examples use α = 0.05 and δ = 0.005 which gives α′ = 0.0452. (B) The two examples and the experiment setup. In Example 1 the agent decides whether a test product and a reference product are bioequivalent under the standard average bioequivalence framework. The true ratio is the ratio of their geometric mean exposures for a measure such as the peak concentration. The null hypothesis states that this ratio lies outside the regulatory acceptance limits of 0.80 and 1.25. The data come from replicate crossover studies where subjects receive the formulations in successive periods and the reference product is given at least twice. The agent claims bioequivalence and rejects H0 when the computed confidence interval lies entirely within these limits. The agent can also defer a study to a human. In Example 2 users of a shopping application are randomized to the current version or to a new feature over 14 days. The true change represents the difference in the share of users who make a purchase. The agent uses the statistics engine of the GrowthBook platform and makes launch decisions according to the rule specified by each version. A false launch constitutes a Type I error. In the experiment Claude Sonnet 5.5 proposes one update per round. The update either changes a setting or introduces a new decision rule. Each method is run 20 times for 10 rounds. Example 1 also tests the open-weight models Qwen 3.8 and DeepSeek-R1 as developers under three of the methods.

Figure 2: Continual validation and four comparison methods evaluated across two evolving AI analysts. Each method was tested in 20 independent runs of 10 rounds from the same initial version. In each round, Claude Sonnet 5.5 acted as the developer and proposed one update based on feedback from earlier rounds. (A to D) Bioequivalence analyst. (E to H ) Product experiment analyst. (A and E) Updates proposed under continual validation in the first ten runs, with one row per run. Circles denote setting changes, squares denote new decision rules, and crosses denote malformed updates. Filled markers indicate deployed updates. Colors indicate the true Type I error rate of the proposed version, showing rates within α′ (grey), above α′ (pink), and above α (dark red). (B and F) Largest true Type I error rate of the deployed version over the full validation set after each round. Lines show the median over runs and bands extend to the worst run for no validation (vermilion), the static benchmark (orange), the improvement test (bluish green), Learn then Test (sky blue), and continual validation (blue). The dashed line marks the validation level α′ = 0.0452, the dotted line marks the target level α = 0.05, and the shaded region lies above α. In F, the axis ends at 0.2 and an arrow indicates the largest rate in the worst run of the improvement test. (C and G) Share of runs that ever deployed a version above α, showing Wilson 95 percent intervals and the raw count out of 20 runs. (D and H ) Mean true statistical power of the deployed version after each round. The dashed line represents an oracle that deploys only valid updates that strictly increase power.

Figure 3: Continual validation with random scenarios in the bioequivalence analyst. (A) Largest true Type I error rate of the deployed version at sample sizes of 30, 42, and 60, outside the original validation grid of 24, 36, and 48. Filled circles indicate deployed versions, while open circles indicate rejected updates. Orange circles highlight four rejected updates that would increase Type I error outside the original grid while leaving the analysis unchanged on the grid. The dashed and dotted lines mark the validation level α′ = 0.0452 and the target level α = 0.05, respectively. The shaded region indicates rates above α. (B) Mean true power of the deployed version across 20 runs with Claude Sonnet 5.5 proposing updates. The dashed line shows the oracle in Fig. 2, and the percentages indicate power relative to the oracle after ten rounds.

papers.abstract: LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web content. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self-evolution in its type system. First, nine role-specialised agents decide jointly: four analysts read news feeds, SEC filings, macroeconomic series and market data and emit typed reports, from which a Portfolio Manager sets target positions that a protected Risk Manager audits. Second, a seven-layer shared memory, assembled by code from the system's own record, gives each decision its position context, the market narrative, calibration and the agent's past decisions. Third, the system improves itself by review: code grades every trade and forecast nightly and writes the grades into memory, and each quarter a reflector proposes prompt learnings that a deterministic gate applies reversibly and replay of recorded inputs verifies. All three operate around an invariant core of order arithmetic, risk rules and discipline-agent prompts that no self-edit can reach. In a five-month live deployment (102 trading days, 1,632 LLM calls), the system contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; in replay of its recorded inputs, a single model given the same raw data traded more and lost 1.35 points against the market over five days where the joint design showed no significant loss, and no injected instruction was followed; and a 2015-2026 backtest shows the core alone lowering the maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry policies. The reflector traced the dominant failure to its root cause, and the gate applied a learning that the agent adopted on trigger evenings and on no control evening. papers.abstract: Human motion retargeting bridges the embodiment gap between humans and humanoid robots by converting human demonstrations into reference trajectories for whole-body control and loco-manipulation. For object-interaction tasks, successful execution depends on accurately preserving body--object relations at critical stages. However, uniform per-frame iteration budgets do not account for these localized accuracy requirements, limiting the computational efficiency of retargeting. To address this limitation, we present Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), which uses keyframes and key body parts to allocate optimization effort. Specifically, a vision-language model selects relevant motion signals and body parts, and keyframes are identified from changes in the selected signals. Based on these selections, STR assigns additional solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to the selected parts. To further improve contact fidelity, we introduce Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA) to refine object-surface contact positions using an approximate object-wrench model while retaining the selected surface directions. Building on the resulting references, we develop Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL), which combines adaptive key-stage sampling with a contact reward based on target proximity and object contact forces for downstream control. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 and real-world experiments on a Unitree R1 demonstrate that STR improves geometric contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, while the resulting references improve downstream task completion across diverse object-interaction motions.
authors: Xiongbo Shi, Shihang Du, Zongyou Yu, Ao Zhou, Xudong Zhang, Ziyu Lin, Haodong Zhang, Junqiao Zhao, Guang Chen
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of uniform per-frame optimization, especially when accurate body–object relations matter only at critical stages.

Assigns extra solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to selected body parts.
Adds Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring to refine object-surface contacts, and STRL uses adaptive key-stage sampling with contact-aware rewards.
Simulation and real-world experiments show improved contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, with better downstream task completion across diverse interactions.

papers.abstract: Predicting surrounding vehicles' lane-change intentions enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate potential hazards and respond proactively rather than relying solely on reactive maneuvers. This study investigates the benefits of integrating lane-change prediction, based on knowledge graph embeddings and Bayesian inference, into autonomous vehicle decision-making. Three driving strategies are evaluated in risky merging scenarios simulated in CARLA: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal action, and prediction-based lateral action. The proposed prediction model anticipates the surrounding vehicle's lane change approximately 3-4 seconds before its occurrence, allowing the ego vehicle to adjust its behavior accordingly. In the representative simulation records, reactive driving results in a collision accompanied by aggressive deceleration. In contrast, prediction-based longitudinal action initiates early braking to establish a safe gap, while prediction-based lateral action performs a lane change when a safe adjacent lane is available. Both predictive strategies avoid collisions in the evaluated records. Compared with reactive driving, peak deceleration before impact is reduced by 31.5% with longitudinal action and 91.0% with lateral action. Additionally, an ISO 2631-1-based horizontal vibration estimate is used to provide a ride comfort assessment. Overall, the results highlight the potential of lane-change prediction to support safer and smoother driving through proactive decision-making, with additional insights into ride comfort provided by vibration-based estimates.
authors: Mohamed Manzour, Aditya Kumar, Rub\'en Izquierdo, Miguel \'Angel Sotelo
bullets: The study addresses the limits of reactive driving when surrounding vehicles make hazardous lane changes.

papers.abstract: Forecasting future human motion requires jointly reasoning about an agent's global trajectory and 3D body pose, which are tightly coupled, particularly in team sports where multiple interacting players introduce complex social dynamics. We exploit a socio-temporal encoder that fuses trajectory and pose at the input level and models them jointly through shared factorized attention. The model is further enhanced by a per-joint loss reweighting scheme that emphasizes dynamic joints and prevents degenerate solutions, and a frequency-domain trajectory smoothing term that improves trajectory prediction while indirectly benefiting pose forecasting. To ensure fair comparison with prior joint forecasting methods, we identify and correct evaluation biases arising from overlapping sequence construction, adopting instead a non-overlapping protocol and a deterministic, oracle-free strategy for multi-future prediction. Our approach improves over prior joint forecasting methods on both WorldPose and 3DPW, with the largest gains on pose accuracy, demonstrating that the proposed joint formulation generalizes beyond the densely interactive scenarios that motivate it.
authors: Marc Peral, Guillem Capellera, Luis Ferraz, Antonio Rubio, Stella Gra{\ss}hof, Dan Witzner Hansen, Antonio Agudo
bullets: Targets tightly coupled global motion and 3D body-pose forecasting in socially interacting sports agents.
Uses socio-temporal encoding with input-level trajectory–pose fusion and shared factorized attention.
Adds dynamic-joint loss reweighting and frequency-domain trajectory smoothing.
Corrects evaluation bias from overlapping sequences using non-overlapping data and deterministic, oracle-free multi-future prediction.
Outperforms prior joint forecasting methods on WorldPose and 3DPW, with the largest gains in pose accuracy.

papers.abstract: Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) can generate diverse and visually appealing human motion; yet, the resulting trajectories frequently violate physical constraints, limiting their downstream use in simulation and control. We present PhysibleMDM, a framework that promotes physical feasibility of MDM output by optimizing at inference time the diffusion noise without retraining the generative model. We introduce a set of surrogate feasibility constraints that can be evaluated without full trajectory simulation. These constraints combine kinematic checks (e.g., ground penetration, slip, and self-collision) with dynamic feasibility tests computed via an inverse-dynamics inner loop formulated as a cone program. We solve the resulting black-box noise optimization problem using the Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (Sep-CMA-ES), thereby avoiding reliance on computationally expensive and discontinuous gradients. An autoregressive scheme then chains optimized segments to synthesize long motion sequences. Across 100 motion styles on an SMPL humanoid, PhysibleMDM reduces mean ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and ground slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%, respectively, relative to unoptimized diffusion output. Across 11 sequences for a custom bipedal robot, it achieves median reductions of 89.5% in per-sequence mean acceleration-reconstruction error and 79.5% in the mean inverse-dynamics residual.
authors: Maximilian St\"olzle, David M\"uller, Agon Serifi, Ruben Grandia, Espen Knoop, Moritz B\"acher
bullets: Addresses physically implausible motion trajectories that limit diffusion models’ use in simulation and control.
Combines surrogate kinematic constraints with dynamic feasibility checks from an inverse-dynamics cone program.
Uses gradient-free Sep-CMA-ES to optimize diffusion noise and an autoregressive scheme to generate long sequences.
On an SMPL humanoid across 100 motion styles, it reduces ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%.
On 11 custom-biped sequences, it reduces acceleration-reconstruction error by 89.5% and inverse-dynamics residual by 79.5% in the median.

papers.abstract: World models help agents assess the consequences of their actions before acting. Many real systems, however, involve multiple actors who make their own decisions, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and are only partially observed through event logs. We formalize these systems as event worlds and ask whether large language models can predict future observations from the log and the agent's proposed actions. We build complementary benchmarks from human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trades. Our hierarchical framework compares prediction with and without other actors' actions, then tests multi-step rollouts, predictions for actions never taken, and usefulness to agents. Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors' recorded actions are given. With only the agent's action, models struggle when other actors strongly affect the outcome, and larger models and longer histories help little. This gap also limits multi-step prediction and agent decisions, with models overestimating plan success. Yet imagined experience and initialization from world models can still improve policy learning. Anticipating other actors' actions remains a central challenge for event world modeling.
authors: Juntong Ni, Zewen Liu, Bohan Wang, Lige Zhang, Wei Jin
bullets: The study extends world modeling from single-actor settings to partially observed event worlds with autonomous actors and ongoing dynamics.
It evaluates LLMs on human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trading logs.
A hierarchical framework tests prediction with or without other actors’ actions, multi-step rollouts, counterfactual actions, and agent usefulness.
Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors’ recorded actions are available, while larger models and longer histories help little when they are hidden.

Hidden-actor uncertainty harms multi-step prediction and decision quality, with models tending to overestimate plan success; imagined experience and world-model initialization can still aid policy learning.

papers.abstract: Personal intelligence systems are taking on increasingly complex everyday tasks, yet repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations, and unwanted outreach can turn capable assistance into interaction burden. Reducing this burden requires agents to remember how users want to be assisted. However, existing memory benchmarks focus on factual recall and personalized answers and rarely test how agents learn and act on interaction preferences. We introduce MemPABench, an interactive environment for on-policy evaluation of memory in personal agents. MemPABench poses long-horizon tasks requiring agents to decide when to clarify, confirm, or act autonomously. Four grounded simulated users hold 14 preferences across work and personal contexts. Their feedback spans 99 sessions over four months, with five event-driven changes per user testing memory updates. We evaluate preference selection, delivered behavior, and sensitivity to context and preference change. Evaluating four memory systems across four LLM backbones, we find that current memory brings limited gains in preference selection. Retrieval-based systems (i.e. Mem0, MemOS, simple RAG) do not outperform No Memory, while File-based memory improves accuracy but applies preferences beyond relevant contexts. Our analysis shows that current memory struggles to retrieve interaction preferences and adapt to preference changes. Even with the correct preference available, overriding the agent's default interaction habits remains challenging. The environment and dataset are available at https://mempabench.com.
authors: Jialin Li, Zhenhao Chen, Hanjun Luo, Hanan Salam
bullets: Benchmarks decisions about when to clarify, confirm, or act autonomously—not just factual recall.
Uses four simulated users with 14 work and personal preferences across 99 sessions and five preference changes per user.
Evaluates preference selection, behavioral execution, contextual sensitivity, and adaptation to changes across four memory systems and four LLM backbones.
Retrieval-based memory systems do not outperform No Memory, while file-based memory improves accuracy but often applies preferences outside their relevant contexts.
Agents struggle to retrieve interaction preferences, adapt to changes, and override default interaction habits even when the correct preference is available.

papers.abstract: Weight-only quantization keeps LLM activations in floating point and stores weights as low-bit integers, turning the dominant workload into floating-point-integer (FP-INT) general matrix multiplication. Recent quantizers reach a 2-3-bit average with mixed precision, but hardware has not kept pace: GPUs dequantize weights to FP16 before the tensor-core multiply-accumulate, and bit-parallel FP-INT accelerators run at a single weight precision, so fewer bits save memory but not computation. In this paper, we present FIGFLEX, an algorithm-hardware co-designed mixed-precision accelerator whose bit-parallel datapath scales throughput as precision falls. FIGFLEX contributes (1) a shift-add, radix-4 reformulation of FP-INT multiplication that fuses the multiply-accumulate into a unified, precision-flexible partial-product reduction and roughly halves the partial products, together with a novel INT3 optimization that reclaims the idle datapath radix-4 leaves at that precision; and (2) a mixed-precision quantizer that assigns each channel group its bit-width according to the error GPTQ cannot compensate, with a per-input-channel column scaling whose power-of-two normalization keeps the scaled activations out of the FP16 subnormal range, so that the quantized model maps directly onto FIGFLEX's datapath with the same accuracy as on a GPU. On LLaMA-2-7B, FIGFLEX attains 5.85 and 8.77 WikiText-2 perplexity at 3- and 2-bit average precision, lower than GPTQ, AWQ, SliM-LLM, AMQ, and QuIP# (without fine-tuning), while delivering 1.56x and 1.42x higher whole-chip throughput per area on the linear GEMMs of a 3-bit mixed-precision model than AxCore and FIGLUT, respectively.
authors: Faraz Tahmasebi, Haocheng Xu, Andrew Trauger, Yomal Perera, Zhenyu Tang, Nael Chowdhury, Sitao Huang
bullets: Targets weight-only quantized LLMs, whose main computation is floating-point–integer GEMM.
Uses a shift-add, radix-4 FP-INT formulation that unifies accumulation, reduces partial products, and optimizes INT3 execution.
Introduces channel-group bit allocation based on quantization error and power-of-two column scaling for direct hardware mapping.
On LLaMA-2-7B, reports 5.85 and 8.77 WikiText-2 perplexity at 3- and 2-bit average precision without fine-tuning.
Achieves 1.56× and 1.42× higher whole-chip throughput per area than AxCore and FIGLUT, respectively, on 3-bit mixed-precision GEMMs.

papers.abstract: Should an embodied agent's experience be baked into its policy weights, or kept external and retrieved at inference? A memory-augmented teacher (a VLM that retrieves lessons, with their episode images, from its own past attempts) produces trajectories on a vision-conditioned reach task; from the same trajectories we distil LoRA student policies and evaluate them under matched protocols, including one that re-attaches the teacher's frozen retrieval buffer to a fixed set of student weights. We pre-registered the hypotheses, arms, tests, and analysis rules before training and before any p-value. Distilling the memory-augmented behaviour into weights beat an action-only control by +1 pp (n.s.); the registered test proves underpowered for its own minimum effect, so we withdraw - rather than refute - the memory-in-weights claim. Attaching retrieval to a fixed set of student weights added +34 pp (z=5.15), reaching the pooled memory-augmented teacher reference (49.3%); the pre-registered protocol contrast agrees (+23 pp, z=3.36); under a pre-registered auto-reset sensitivity count the two are +36 and +29 pp. An exploratory behavioural probe with pre-registered per-arm predictions is consistent with behavioural distillation transferring the marginal correction but not the conditional, situation-specific correction that retrieval supplies. The recipe that follows is to externalise the memory: in follow-up controls registered before they ran, the same frozen buffer lifts the base model with no adapter to 48% (sensitivity 48%) and the other three adapters from 19-26% to 53-55% (sensitivity 17-21% to 50-55%), and the adapter adds nothing detectable once the buffer is attached. On a second, harder task, the retrieval advantage points the same direction but falls short of significance (+6 pp, 95% CI [-4.5, +16.4]); exploratory diagnostics tie the attenuation to memory coverage.
authors: Cheng-Yin Tu
bullets: A pre-registered study compares memory-augmented retrieval, weight-distilled policies, and fixed student policies with the teacher’s retrieval buffer attached.

Distilling memory-augmented behavior into weights improved performance by only 1 percentage point over an action-only control; the test was underpowered, so the claim was withdrawn rather than refuted.
Attaching the frozen retrieval buffer to student weights produced a large gain (+34 percentage points), matching the memory-augmented teacher’s 49.3% reference performance.
Follow-up controls found the buffer substantially improved the base model and other adapters, while adapters added no detectable benefit once retrieval was attached.
On a harder second task, the retrieval advantage was smaller and not significant, with exploratory evidence linking the reduction to limited memory coverage.

papers.tldr: For this embodied reach task, keeping experience in an external retrieval buffer is more effective than distilling it into policy weights alone.

papers.abstract: Kernelized attention provides a useful perspective for understanding self-attention as a similarity-based aggregation mechanism, but existing approaches often rely on fixed or stationary kernels, limiting their ability to adapt the similarity structure to complex token interactions. In this paper, we propose flow-based spectral kernel attention (FSKA), a framework for learning expressive nonstationary attention kernels. FSKA formulates kernelized attention through spectral density learning and parameterizes the resulting bivariate spectral density with normalizing flows. This design enables flexible and regularizable kernel learning while remaining compatible with scalable linear-attention computation. We further show that expressive kernel learning enables a simplified attention design with removed query--key projections and fixed orthogonal value projections, resulting in a more parameter-efficient architecture. Controlled experiments on classification, ablation, and scalability profiling show that FSKA achieves competitive or improved performance over existing attention mechanisms, while reducing projection-related trainable parameters by approximately $40\%$--$47\%$ compared with most baselines and maintaining favorable linear-attention memory scaling. Code Available: https://github.com/ziyang18/FSKA.
authors: Zi Yang, Ying Li, Alejandro Lancho, Dar\'{i}o C. Larese, Pablo M. Olmos, Michael Minyi Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited adaptability of fixed or stationary kernels in kernelized self-attention.
Learns a bivariate spectral density using normalizing flows for expressive, regularizable kernel modeling.
Removes query–key projections and fixes orthogonal value projections to simplify the attention architecture.
Reports competitive or improved results in classification, ablation, and scalability experiments.
Reduces projection-related trainable parameters by approximately 40%–47% versus most baselines while retaining favorable linear-attention memory scaling.

papers.abstract: Learning useful representations from continually changing value targets remains a challenge in deep reinforcement learning. We study the temporal horizon of this supervision: smaller discounts make these targets less sensitive to distant bootstrap changes, but using them for behavior changes the control objective. We introduce Short-to-Long (S2L), which supplies a long-horizon behavior learner with features trained by smaller-discount source networks. Detached connections prevent the behavior value loss from updating the sources, allowing each source to follow its own value objective while the behavior discount remains unchanged. Across Atari, online continuous control, and offline continuous control, the approach yields aggregate performance gains, improving the paired terminal median on 40 of 57 Atari games. Matched Atari ablations support the roles of feature transfer, smaller source discounts, and gradient isolation. Fixed-trajectory measurements further show reduced drift in source value targets with mixed discounts.
authors: Tong Che, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone
bullets: Addresses representation instability from continually changing long-horizon value targets in deep reinforcement learning.
Uses smaller-discount source networks to learn more stable features, while the behavior learner retains its original long-horizon discount.
Detached connections isolate source networks from the behavior value loss, letting each network optimize its own value objective.
Across Atari, online continuous control, and offline continuous control, S2L improves aggregate performance; it improves paired terminal median on 40 of 57 Atari games.
Ablations support feature transfer, smaller source discounts, and gradient isolation; fixed-trajectory measurements show reduced source-target drift with mixed discounts.

papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one. Deciding when to stop is a metareasoning problem: the model must weigh what further reasoning could achieve against its cost, given what it can already answer. Direct utility training learns a stopping representation at a chosen token price; supporting new prices can require additional controller training. We introduce BELT (BELief-based Termination), which separates outcome prediction from stopping control. It learns beliefs about current and future answers from a frozen LLM's hidden states, then fits a linear stopping policy on the frozen features. The prediction targets are independent of token price, so one probe supports different accuracy-cost trade-offs through CPU policy refitting or threshold adjustment. Averaged over five out-of-distribution (OOD) math benchmarks, BELT reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without loss of accuracy. The same math-trained BELT transfers to coding and agentic tasks without training on code or agentic data. In all three domains, its accuracy-cost trade-offs are competitive with or better than those of end-to-end controllers. On OLMo3, its probe has 21.2x fewer parameters than one checkpoint of the strongest baseline, OS-Pruner, and needs 55x fewer training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner's five price-specific checkpoints.
authors: Jingwei Ni, Dmitry Abulkhanov, Vladislav Smirnov, Markus Leippold, Elliott Ash, Timothy Baldwin, Artem Shelmanov, Mrinmaya Sachan
bullets: Addresses unnecessary or harmful continued reasoning after an answer is already correct.
Predicts current and future answer beliefs, then fits a lightweight linear stopping policy.
Supports new accuracy–cost trade-offs by refitting or adjusting the policy without retraining the representation.
Reduces generated tokens by 41% on Qwen3-1.7B and 51% on OLMo-3-7B-Think without accuracy loss across five OOD math benchmarks.
Transfers from math to coding and agentic tasks; uses substantially fewer parameters and training GPU-hours than OS-Pruner on OLMo3.

papers.abstract: Multi-task generalization is an important yet underexplored problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). Many real-world applications require multi-agent systems to generalize across complex, temporally extended tasks with diverse inter-agent coordination requirements. We introduce a specification language that combines temporal-logic task specifications with operators for expressing such requirements. We propose SpecMAGIC, a hierarchical framework that leverages the automaton structure of task specifications for subtask decomposition. A centralized high-level planner identifies and allocates compatible subtask sequences across agents, while decentralized low-level policies execute individual subtasks. This enables zero-shot generalization to new tasks by composing reusable subtask policies according to new specifications, without retraining. We establish soundness and probabilistic completeness of the high-level planner. Experiments on multi-agent navigation tasks show that SpecMAGIC substantially outperforms existing approaches on unseen task specifications and maintains strong performance as the number of agents increases.
authors: Zijian Guo, \.Ilker I\c{s}{\i}k, H. M. Sabbir Ahmad, Wenchao Li
bullets: Targets multi-task generalization in MARL with complex coordination requirements.
Introduces a specification language combining temporal logic with multi-agent requirement operators.
Uses a hierarchical design: centralized planning allocates subtask sequences, while decentralized policies execute them.
Provides soundness and probabilistic completeness guarantees for the high-level planner.
Experiments on multi-agent navigation show strong performance on unseen specifications and as team size grows.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct access to physical interactions at the contact interface, making it a critical modality for robust and dexterous manipulation. Over the past several decades, tactile-based manipulation research has evolved from mechanics-driven approaches, which explicitly interpret tactile signals through contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning, to data-driven approaches that learn tactile representations and manipulation policies directly from data. This paper reviews the development of tactile-based manipulation from these two complementary perspectives. We first introduce the fundamentals of tactile sensing, and then review, from a mechanics-driven perspective, how those signals form manipulation-relevant state representations and subsequently influence the robot action. We then examine the recent advances in data-driven tactile manipulation, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future opportunities toward scalable, generalizable, and robust tactile-enabled robotic systems.
authors: Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Wenzhen Yuan
bullets: Tactile sensing exposes physical contact information important for robust and dexterous manipulation.
Mechanics-driven methods interpret tactile signals using contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning to form state representations and guide actions.
Data-driven methods learn tactile representations and manipulation policies from data, including imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models.
The paper surveys tactile sensing fundamentals and developments across both perspectives.
It identifies open challenges and future opportunities for broader, more robust tactile-enabled robotics.
papers.selection_reason: Review of tactile-based manipulation covering mechanics-driven and data-driven approaches, including imitation learning, RL, VLA models, and predictive models.
papers.title: Tactile-Based Robotic Manipulation: From Mechanics-Driven to Data-Driven Perspectives
papers.tldr: This review traces tactile robotic manipulation from mechanics-based reasoning to data-driven learning and outlines challenges for scalable, generalizable, and robust systems.

papers.abstract: Recently, electroencephalography (EEG)-based brain--computer interfaces (BCIs) have gained traction as portable neural measurement systems. However, the practical deployment of these instruments is often hindered by nonstationarity and cross-subject distribution shifts, which lead to significant intersubject inconsistency. Existing adaptation methods remain impractical for real-time measurement scenarios, as they typically require offline access to source or aggregated target data. To address these challenges, this article proposes memory-augmented online test-time adaptation (OTTA) with perturbation consistency and confidence calibration (MOPC), a source-free framework designed to enhance the reliability of BCI instrumentation. MOPC enables the measurement system to update its decoding parameters on the fly during the inference stage, facilitating single-pass adaptation without accessing sensitive source data. We introduce random-mask perturbations to enforce prediction consistency against inherent EEG signal noise and acquisition artifacts. Furthermore, a confidence-calibrated reweighting loss is designed to integrate feature-space similarity, effectively mitigating unreliable pseudolabels and class imbalance during continuous signal acquisition. To ensure system stability and prevent the catastrophic forgetting of established neural patterns, a lightweight memory module is incorporated to regularize parameter updates within a tight latency budget. Evaluated on the BCI IV IIb and OpenBMI datasets, MOPC achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods by 2.22~\% and 3.67~\%, respectively, while keeping the per-trial adaptation latency to approximately 40--60 ms. This study provides a robust, recalibration-free solution for real-time EEG decoding, marking a significant advancement in the precision and usability of practical BCI measurement instruments.
authors: Kunkun Zhang, Kehao Wu, Zhitao Chen, Haigen Hu, Qianwei Zhou
bullets: Addresses nonstationarity and intersubject distribution shifts that hinder practical EEG-based BCIs.
Uses random-mask perturbations to promote prediction consistency under EEG noise and artifacts.
Applies confidence-calibrated, feature-similarity-based reweighting to reduce unreliable pseudolabel effects and class imbalance.
Adds a lightweight memory module to stabilize updates and limit catastrophic forgetting within a tight latency budget.
On BCI IV IIb and OpenBMI, it reports improvements of 2.22% and 3.67%, respectively, with approximately 40–60 ms per-trial adaptation latency.

papers.abstract: Adding control to video generation often requires training, which demands additional computational resources, data, or architectural changes. We propose a training-free approach that utilizes pretrained video diffusion models to control object layout and motion using coarse layouts. Our method operates in two passes: first, it steers spatiotemporal placement through prompt-guided cross-attention to produce a coarse visual guide; second, this guide conditions the same model to generate a high-quality, layoutconsistent video. The approach enables coordinated motion with strong temporal consistency, supporting diverse trajectories and object interactions without additional training. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms prior work in overlap and trajectory accuracy, as well as visual quality across static, dynamic, and multi-object scene settings.
authors: Asaf Joseph, Moshe Mandel, Ohad Fried
bullets: Addresses the computational and architectural costs of training-based video-generation control.
Uses prompt-guided cross-attention to create a coarse spatiotemporal visual guide.
Conditions the same pretrained model on this guide to generate layout-consistent videos.
Supports diverse trajectories, coordinated motion, and multi-object interactions without additional training.
Experiments report improved overlap, trajectory accuracy, and visual quality across static and dynamic scenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our training-free layout-guided video synthesis pipeline. Given a text prompt and spatiotemporal layout constraints, we first perform Layout Generation, where the latents of a frozen text-to-video diffusion model are optimized using a cross-attention-based layout loss. This latent refinement process aligns token-specific attention with the target layout and produces a coarse spatiotemporal guiding video in latent space. Next, after the guide is optionally spatially and/or temporally upsampled, we render the final video: the guiding video is injected at an early timestep into the video diffusion pipeline. This second stage refines appearance and details while preserving the imposed layout and motion, yielding the final high-quality video.

Fig. 4. Outputs of Text-to-Video (T2V) and our method (Ours) across different backbone models (LTX-2, WAN 2.2), together with the corresponding attention maps extracted from an intermediate timestep. Attempting to control layout via textual prompt (underlined) fails, whereas controlling the attention map results in a video that corresponds to the desired layouts (orange/blue bounding boxes).

Fig. 7. Comparison of our refined video (Ours) against competing methods. Left: dynamic object layout. While T2V produces high-quality visuals, it does not follow the layout. Trailblazer (TB) and FreeTraj (FT) introduce bicycle artifacts, and Peekaboo (Peek.) shows weaker alignment. Right: multiple-object layout; empty frames indicate unsupported methods. Remaining methods fail to maintain spatial and temporal consistency: the explosion occurs prematurely, and the person does not follow the left-to-right trajectory specified by the blue box.

Fig. 8. Additional applications of our method. Left: video editing, where the input video is transformed according to the text prompt. Right: stylization, where only selected semantic elements retain color while the rest of the scene remains monochrome.

Fig. 6. Comparison between the video guide generated using an ensemble of Text-to-Image methods (left) and the refined video produced by a pre-trained video model (right). The guide fails to capture the interaction between the boy and the scarf: the hands remain static instead of grasping and moving the scarf, resulting in motion that lacks coordination between the objects.

In contrast, the right column (high learning rate) achieves stronger layout adherence, but at the cost of reduced visual quality.
