papers.abstract: We address the problem of real-time multi-agent path planning under prescribed initial and final configurations, formulated as a high-dimensional optimal control problem subject to inter-agent collision avoidance and obstacle constraints. Classical solvers based on the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation or Pontryagin's maximum principle (PMP) become computationally intractable as the number of agents grows, due to the curse of dimensionality and the non-convexity introduced by interaction constraints. We propose OCFormer, a transformer-based neural network that parameterizes the inverse of a coordinate transformation mapping a simple, analytically tractable latent space, in which agents evolve independently under a decoupled Hamiltonian, to the physical space of the coupled, interacting system. The model is trained by minimizing a physics-informed loss comprising the Hamiltonian ODE residual from the PMP and a boundary matching term, without requiring pre-computed trajectory data. The self-attention mechanism endows OCFormer with permutation equivariance over agents, a structural symmetry that prior symplectic network approaches do not natively enforce. When trained on a distribution of boundary conditions, the amortized OCFormer produces near-optimal trajectories for unseen initial and final configurations in a single forward pass ($\sim$220ms), enabling real-time inference without retraining. We further introduce a lightweight transfer learning framework that adapts a pretrained OCFormer to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds via L-BFGS fine-tuning. Numerical experiments on two- and three-dimensional multi-agent navigation with up to 128 agents demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of the proposed approach.
authors: Qian Zhang, Shanqing Liu, Jerome Darbon, George Karniadakis
bullets: Targets the computational difficulty of high-dimensional optimal control with agent interactions, collision avoidance, and obstacles.
Learns an inverse coordinate transformation from a decoupled latent system to the coupled physical system.
Trains without precomputed trajectories using PMP Hamiltonian ODE residuals and boundary-matching losses.
Self-attention provides permutation equivariance across agents, while amortized inference handles unseen boundary conditions in a single forward pass (~220 ms).
A lightweight L-BFGS transfer-learning procedure adapts pretrained models to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds; experiments scale to 128 agents in 2D and 3D navigation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Flowchart of the OCFormer framework. For a pair of prescribed initial and terminal configurations, boundary data are first encoded into latent variables (y, q), which serve as the input to the transformer-based inverse coordinate map ϕ−1. The network predicts the physical position and momentum trajectories (x,p) over the time grid without solving an ODE at inference time. During training, the predicted trajectories are differentiated with respect to time and evaluated in the Hamiltonian system so that the model satisfies the physics-informed residual loss associated with Pontryagin’s maximum principle, while a boundary matching term enforces the initial and final constraints. The total loss is minimized over the network parameters, yielding a model that directly maps varying boundary conditions to feasible multi-agent trajectories in real time.

Figure 3. Architecture of OCFormer. y, q are first reshaped into RN×d. Ey, Eq : Rd → RD are tokenwise embedding layers, which are applied on the last axis of reshaped input. zi, ri ∈ RN×D. Partial transformer blocks Tup and Tlow are depicted by the dashed rounded rectangle. ID is identity mapping in RD. Ti (i = 1, · · · , n) are the transformer blocks. Dx,Dp : RD → Rd are tokenwise deembedding MLPs, whose output are flattened back into RNd. INd is the identity mapping in RNd, serving as residual connection.

Figure 2. Coordinate-transformation view of the proposed trajectory representation. The forward map ϕ sends the physical trajectory pair (x,p) to a simpler latent trajectory pair (y, q) associated with a decoupled Hamiltonian system, while the inverse map ϕ−1 reconstructs the interacting multi-agent trajectories in physical space.

Figure 5. Predicted multi-agent trajectories for the random-perturbation experiment with n = 32 drones at times t = 0, 1 3 , 2 3 , 1 from left to right. Starting from the perturbed initial condition, the transferred model generates collision-free paths that progressively reorganize the swarm toward the prescribed terminal arrangement. The intermediate snapshots show that the learned corrections adapt the reference solution while preserving the overall interaction structure encoded by the original OCFormer.

Figure 6. Predicted trajectories for the 3D room experiment with n = 100 drones at times t = 0, 1 3 , 2 3 , 1 from left to right. The snapshots illustrate how the learned model coordinates a large collection of agents in a confined threedimensional domain, moving them from their initial configuration to the terminal one while maintaining collision-free motion throughout the room. The intermediate frames highlight the scalability of OCFormer to high-dimensional multi-agent path-planning problems.

Figure 7. Predicted trajectories for the 3D ball-obstacle experiment at times t = 0, 1 3 , 2 3 , 1 from left to right. The figure shows the agents moving from their initial to terminal positions while simultaneously avoiding pairwise collisions and steering around the spherical obstacle. The intermediate configurations make clear that the learned dynamics capture both inter-agent avoidance and obstacle-avoidance behavior in a genuinely three-dimensional setting.
Figure 4. Predicted trajectories at t = 0, T/3, 2T/3, T for M = 128 drones, the largest and most demanding configuration in Table 1. Drones shown as colored circles with paths as gray curves.

Table 1. Quantitative results for the 2D room symmetry setup, and direct comparison against SympOCNet (JAX implementation) on the identical circle benchmarks, using the same boundary data, parameters (r, T , room size, ϵ, l, λ), and training budget (100k–500k Adam + L-BFGS on an NVIDIA RTX A6000). JLB = ∑ i ∥∆xi∥2/(2T ) is the analytic lower bound (unconstrained optimum). Cost is evaluated via trapezoidal integration of 1 2 ∥v∥2; Gap is relative to JLB. SympOCNet was not evaluated at M = 64. For every configuration, OCFormer’s fine-grid constraint minimum mini̸=j,t ∥xi−xj∥−2r is positive, in the narrow range [1.2, 1.5] × 10−4, confirming collision-free trajectories throughout.

Table 2. Zero-shot amortized inference results. Trained on 100 rotated boundary pairs, tested on 20 held-out rotations. Inference time is the wallclock time for a single forward pass (JIT-compiled, averaged over 100 runs).

papers.title: A Transformer-based Approach for Real-time Multi-agent Path Planning with Varying Initial/Final Conditions
papers.tldr: OCFormer uses a physics-informed transformer to generate near-optimal, collision-free multi-agent paths in real time for varying start and goal configurations.

papers.abstract: LLM correctors of ASR output are judged by aggregate WER, which hides what they fix and what they break. We decompose every WER change exactly into repaired tokens, damaged tokens and insertions, and use this to ask what the source audio adds to a corrector. We compare correction with and without the audio, for the model's own draft and for the output of an independent recogniser, on three corpora. With Gemini 2.5 Flash, text-only correction of its own draft breaks 13-32% of already-correct transcripts; with the audio, 1-3%. Damage falls in both settings. Repair falls against the own draft and rises against the recogniser. On medical dictation, kept insertions cancel the gain in net WER. The open-weight Voxtral, which rarely edits, does not show this pattern. Prompts differ between the two arms, so the contrasts bound the effect of the audio and do not isolate it.
authors: Vasiliy Kudryavtsev, Kirill Borodin, Nikita Vasiliev, Mikhail Gorodnichev, Grach Mkrtchian
bullets: Aggregate WER is decomposed into repaired tokens, damaged tokens, and insertions to expose correction trade-offs.

papers.selection_reason: Audio-grounded LLM correction of ASR output is a multimodal LLM application, and the repair-damage decomposition is a transferable evaluation method for multimodal language models.
papers.title: Text-Only LLM Correctors Break Correct Transcripts: A Repair-Damage Analysis of Audio Grounding in ASR Error Correction
papers.tldr: Audio grounding substantially reduces the tendency of Gemini 2.5 Flash to damage already-correct ASR transcripts, but its net benefit depends on the recognizer, domain, and retained insertions.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are flexible in language interaction, but using them as long-horizon planners is costly and prone to hallucinated or invalid actions. This paper targets a different role for LLMs: constrained bridges between language and symbolic planning. We propose MemPlan, a memory-conditioned PDDL planning framework for partially observable interactive text environments. MemPlan keeps the PDDL domain fixed and reconstructs the PDDL problem at each step from parsed observations, candidate hypotheses, and interaction memory. Positive graph memory assigns relevance-based action costs to candidate hypotheses for missing objects, locations, or conditions, guiding the planner toward more plausible checks. Negative memory records execution-refuted assumptions and compiles them into exclusion constraints, preventing repeated attempts at candidates already contradicted by feedback. A unified schema-conditioned language--symbol interface, trained offline with supervised fine-tuning, connects text environments to the planning loop through observation-to-fact parsing and symbolic-action-to-command grounding. Experiments on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille show that MemPlan improves task completion and step efficiency over language-only and PDDL-aware baselines, while substantially reducing online token cost compared with LLM-planning baselines such as ReAct. The same fine-tuned interface is also reused across TextWorld task types without task-specific fine-tuning. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/tewiSong/MemPlan.
authors: Tengwei Song, Robert Hoehndorf
bullets: Addresses costly, hallucination-prone long-horizon planning by constraining LLMs to translate between language and symbolic planning.
Reconstructs the PDDL problem after each observation using parsed facts, hypotheses, and interaction memory.

Evaluated on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille, improving task completion and step efficiency while reducing online token cost versus LLM-planning baselines.
The same offline fine-tuned interface transfers across TextWorld task types without task-specific fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Large language models often apply complex reasoning indiscriminately, leading to overthinking on simple tasks and underthinking on harder ones. We present Route-and-Generate (Rouge), a hierarchical training framework that enables LLMs to adaptively decide when and how much reasoning is required for each input. Our approach decouples reasoning effort allocation from answer generation by introducing a routing policy that allocates a fixed sampling budget across multiple reasoning formats, while the base model is optimized with GRPO using per-sample rewards. To promote efficient reasoning, we employ a rank-based reward that favors shorter correct solutions, and update the routing policy via a closed-form KL-regularized policy improvement step distilled into a neural router. This design encourages concise answers on easy problems while reserving longer reasoning for harder ones, achieving improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across multiple reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Tien-Phat Nguyen, Truong Nguyen, Thanh-Thien Le, Hoang Phan, Thien Huu Nguyen, Linh Ngo Van, Trung Le
bullets: Targets indiscriminate reasoning, which can waste effort on easy tasks and underserve difficult ones.
Separates reasoning-effort allocation from answer generation through a hierarchical routing framework.
Allocates a fixed sampling budget across reasoning formats and trains the base model with per-sample GRPO rewards.
Uses rank-based rewards favoring shorter correct solutions and a KL-regularized policy improvement step distilled into a neural router.
Reports improved accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across multiple reasoning benchmarks; specific results are not provided in the abstract.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hierarchical training framework for LLMs to adaptively allocate reasoning effort using a KL-regularized router, addressing architectural efficiency in reasoning.
papers.title: Route-and-Generate: KL-Regularized Router Improvement for Reasoning Routing in LLMs
papers.tldr: Rouge trains LLMs to route each problem to an appropriate reasoning format and effort, improving the accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

papers.abstract: Training Arabic large language models faces challenges from noisy web data, dialectal variation, and the high cost of continual pretraining (CPT). We introduce AQL-Lite (AQL: Arabic Quality Language), a time- and resource-efficient framework for adapting a multilingual LLM to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). AQL-Lite couples a quality-first curation pipeline (structural cleaning, heuristic and model-based filtering, MSA selection, and deduplication) with a partial-parameter CPT recipe that trains RS-LoRA adapters across the network together with the last eight transformer blocks and the embedding matrix, under layer-wise learning rates. At a matched 1B-token budget, CPT on AQL-curated data raises a four-benchmark Arabic mean by 3.51 points over CPT on raw web text, which yields no gain over the base model. In a controlled 5B-token comparison, AQL-Lite recovers 94% of the gain of full-parameter CPT (mean 73.19 vs. 73.58) in 52% of the wall-clock time and outperforms adapter-only baselines on every benchmark, and a component ablation shows that adapters, unfrozen blocks, and embedding training each contribute. Scaled to 40B MSA tokens and instruction-tuned on one million examples, the resulting 12B model scores 75.3 on the seven-benchmark Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard v2 (OALL v2) suite. These results suggest that partial-parameter CPT on a carefully curated corpus is a practical route to efficient MSA adaptation.
authors: Houssam Eddine Boukhalfa, Mourad Bouache, Mourad Dahmane
bullets: Addresses noisy web data, dialectal variation, and the cost of continual pretraining for Arabic LLMs.

papers.abstract: We introduce Foundation4D, a unified feed-forward model for geometry estimation, 3D detection, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction from multi-camera driving video. A shared backbone uses factorized spatiotemporal attention to efficiently combine observations across cameras and time. Our video inference pipeline uses pose graph optimization to refine camera trajectories and assembles object tracks across input windows. We also develop a data annotation pipeline and release PAI-Foundation4D, a benchmark with dense depth and semantic occupancy labels for 1,253 driving clips. With benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Foundation4D achieves the lowest depth AbsRel on Waymo and nuScenes, the highest detection mAP on nuScenes, and the highest occupancy mIoU on OpenOccupancy among the compared methods. Our task-combination study shows benefits for both detection and geometry: co-training detection with geometry and occupancy improves top-class mAP by 1.2 points over detection-only training, while co-training geometry with detection reduces camera-to-rig translation error by $13.4\%$ relative to geometry-only training. We further use the predicted geometry and trajectories as priors for lidarless NuRec, supporting reconstruction of driving scenes for simulation.

papers.selection_reason: Unified 3D perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles, combining geometry, detection, occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction; strong 3D vision and embodied-perception relevance.

papers.abstract: In recent years, Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have gained massive attention as an energy-efficient neural computing paradigm due to their event-driven and sparse computing capability. However, maintaining accuracy under low-precision constraints, necessary for practical deployment, has been largely unexplored for SNN models. In addition, existing Hessian-based approaches for quantization, such as HAWQ-V2, incur significant memory and computational overhead due to temporal unrolling across multiple SNN timesteps. We propose a spike-aware gradient-based mixed-precision quantization framework for SNNs that adaptively assigns bit-widths using first-order gradient information, avoiding costly second-order Hessian computations. We evaluate our method across various SNN-based architectures, including VGG, ResNet, and Vision Transformer models obtained from both ANN-to-SNN conversion and direct training frameworks, on CIFAR10/100, ImageNet, and DVS-CIFAR-10 datasets. Notably, on ResNet-34 evaluated on ImageNet, our method achieves 73.30% accuracy at 4.78$\times$ compression, which is comparable to that provided by HAWQ-V2, while reducing memory consumption by 2.31$\times$ and bit-allocation runtime by 100$\times$. We also present an energy analysis for mixed-precision SNNs showing that the proposed quantization strategy enables energy-efficient deployment without compromising performance.
authors: Rajshekhar Rakshit, Devgokul B. V, Rakshitha Kalkura, Gopalakrishnan Srinivasan
bullets: Targets accuracy degradation under the low-precision constraints needed for practical SNN deployment.
Uses first-order, spike-aware gradient information to adaptively assign layer bit-widths without costly Hessian computations.

On ImageNet ResNet-34, achieves 73.30% accuracy at 4.78× compression, comparable to HAWQ-V2, with 2.31× lower memory use and 100× faster bit allocation.
Includes an energy analysis indicating efficient mixed-precision SNN deployment without compromising performance.

papers.abstract: Generating an articulated object from a single image requires recovering both its appearance and the mechanism governing its parts. A compact encoding of joint attributes does not by itself ensure that reconstruction preserves the resulting motion. We present MoRE, Motion-Regularized Encoding for articulated 3D generation. MoRE represents coordinate-aligned joint lines with axis classification and two axis-orthogonal Pl\"ucker moment coefficients, removing the arbitrary choice of an origin along the axis. During representation learning, decoded joint hypotheses are used to move corresponding three-dimensional anchors, and their motions are compared with those of annotated joints. A differentiable expectation over joint types and axis directions couples attribute reconstruction to the motion it induces. An image-conditioned flow learns the resulting functional latents, while a multi-state-adapted Gaussian model supplies appearance. At inference, recovered part assignments and joints articulate a single set of rest-pose Gaussians without regenerating the object for each state. Experiments on PartNet-Mobility and ACD show stronger part-box agreement, articulated-state geometry and visual similarity than the compared baselines, while joint prediction reduces axis, origin and range errors relative to ArtiLatent. Controlled ablations support the joint-line encoding and show that motion supervision reduces anchor-motion error. Code and pretrained checkpoints will be released in the future.
authors: Guantian Zheng, Shan Jin
bullets: Represents joints using axis classification and axis-orthogonal Plücker moment coefficients, avoiding arbitrary axis-origin choices.
Uses decoded joint hypotheses to move 3D anchors and matches those motions to annotated joints through differentiable motion supervision.
Combines image-conditioned functional latents with a multi-state Gaussian appearance model.
Articulates one set of rest-pose Gaussians across states instead of regenerating the object for each pose.

On PartNet-Mobility and ACD, improves part-box, articulated-state geometry, visual similarity, and joint-prediction errors over compared baselines; ablations support the encoding and motion supervision.

papers.abstract: Designing and tuning reward functions remains one of the main challenges in building effective reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines for humanoid locomotion. While shaping rewards can accelerate learning, naively formulated terms often conflict with the desired behavior, overfit to a specific robot, or become unstable under small weight changes. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) offers an alternative solution: shaping the reward via differences of a potential function to guide exploration without changing the optimal policy. In this paper, we study Multi-PBRS for humanoid locomotion and propose a unified reward configuration. We then evaluate the same reward structure and weights across nine humanoid robots, requiring only robot-specific metadata (joint/link mappings and default poses) rather than per-robot reward redesign. Our experiments show that, compared to standard shaping, MPBRS provides more consistent scaling behavior and reduced tuning sensitivity across robots, making it easier to tune without altering the optimal policy.
authors: Van Chung Nguyen, Hung Manh La
bullets: Addresses conflicting, robot-specific, and unstable reward shaping in humanoid RL.

papers.abstract: Dynamic representations based on 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) have shown strong capabilities in reconstruction and rendering, yet current methods remain limited in supporting complex natural-language referring in dynamic scenes. Existing 4D Gaussian methods are primarily designed for rendering-oriented dynamic modeling, while current semantic extensions often rely on scene-specific semantic optimization or are evaluated on relatively simple query settings. In this paper, we study Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a task for grounding temporally varying, multi-target or reasoning-intensive, and zero-target or distractor expressions in dynamic 4D scenes. To support this task, we introduce R4D-Bench-QA, a benchmark with structured query annotations. We further present ReferGaussian, a unified framework built upon 4DGS that converts low-level dynamic Gaussians into persistent, language-addressable entities for training-free referring inference. ReferGaussian organizes mask-supported Gaussian entities in an EntityBank, uses Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to decompose complex queries into trackable object phrases and structured referring constraints, and performs constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization. Experiments on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol demonstrate improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding without scene-specific semantic training. Project resources are available at https://chenbangpu.github.io/R4DGS/.
authors: Bangpu Chen, Yaxuan Li, Shirui Peng, Xiangtian Si, Liuxin Chu, Xitong Cao, Hongbo Jin, Jiayu Ding

Introduces R4D-Bench-QA with structured query annotations for evaluating referring segmentation.
ReferGaussian converts dynamic Gaussians into persistent language-addressable entities stored in an EntityBank.
MLLMs decompose queries into object phrases and referring constraints, enabling constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization.
Shows improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.
authors: Huiwon Jang, Suhyeok Jang, Hyeonmo Kang, Seungku Kim, Jinwoo Shin, Sihyun Yu
bullets: WAMs use future video representations to guide action prediction without costly iterative video denoising.
FRED self-distills representations predicted from noise using representations from ground-truth future observations as targets.

Across real-world manipulation tasks, FRED outperforms competing WAMs, especially on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks.
For skills shown only in human videos, FRED reaches 50.0% task success versus 19.4% for the best competing WAM.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and real-world deployments. Its standard training recipe, however, is expensive across all existing paradigms: imitation learning requires fleet-scale driving logs whose behavior distribution only thinly covers the safety-critical tail; closed-loop reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator, while offering diverse behaviors, is bottlenecked by sample-efficiency, per-step cost of rendering, and a forward pass through a large vision backbone. Self-play in vectorized simulators changes the economics: at millions of rollout steps per second, one can obtain a state distribution with natural diversity in collisions, near-misses, and recoveries that no driving log contains, and a highly reactive policy emerges from a basic driving-quality reward. Our approach exploits this asymmetry. We pretrain a single policy by self-play, distill its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher that also plans, and train lightweight adapters on a frozen pretrained vision backbone to reproduce the latent space of either teacher through the action KL divergence, a batch-relational low-rank structural loss, and, for the planner, a trajectory-matching loss. Every target traces back to the self-play policy, so alignment never supervises against a logged trajectory: a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames suffices, with no need for the curated expert demonstrations that imitation pretraining is built on. From this one self-play teacher we obtain two end-to-end students: a closed-loop policy that outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method on the photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark HUGSim, and a planner that reaches 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard, above every published method including DriveZero-Scale (57.1), and 95.5 PDMS on navtest, without human demonstrations.
authors: Zikang Xiong, Weixin Li, Zhouchonghao Wu, Akshay Rangesh, Saarth Bonde, Grantland Hall, Chen Tang, Yihan Hu, Wei Zhan
bullets: Addresses the cost, limited safety-tail coverage, and inefficiency of imitation learning and photorealistic closed-loop reinforcement learning.
Pretrains a policy through self-play in fast vectorized simulators, then distills it into a flow-matching trajectory teacher and end-to-end students.
Trains adapters on a frozen vision backbone using action KL, relational low-rank structural, and trajectory-matching losses from paired image–scene-state data.
Produces both a closed-loop policy and a planner without human or curated expert demonstrations.
Reports 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard and 95.5 PDMS on navtest; the policy also outperforms published imitation-based methods on HUGSim.

figures.caption: Fig. 1.Conventional training pipeline vs. our reinforcement-learning pretraining pipeline. Conventional recipes imitate fleet logs and fine-tune on curated demonstrations, logged trajectories, or rendered simulation. They therefore need human data or rendering at every stage. Phase 1 (top right) trains a self-play policy 𝜋𝜃 with proximal policy optimization (PPO) in a multi-agent vectorized simulator. Phase 2 (middle right) freezes the policy as the self-play teacher and distills its rollouts into a trajectory teacher that also outputs a planned trajectory; both teachers read vector state. Phase 3 (bottom right) aligns an image-conditioned student to either frozen teacher: the self-play teacher yields the closed-loop student, and the trajectory teacher yields the planning student. The student keeps the teacher’s ego encoder unchanged and is not aligned on it; only the teacher’s scene features (road and partner, plus traffic for the trajectory teacher) enter the structural loss. An action loss matches the teacher’s action distribution, while a structural loss matches its pairwise relationships among scenes; for the planning student, an L2 loss also matches the plan the trajectory teacher selects among 16 samples. Alignment uses paired (image, scene-state) frames; it needs neither demonstrations nor online rendering during training. Blue modules are trainable; outlined modules are frozen. In the blue DINOv3 + Adapter block, only the adapter trains; the backbone stays frozen. The trajectory head and the L2 loss apply to the planning student only.

papers.abstract: We introduce EgoHand, a monocular 3D hand reconstruction model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on egocentric video. Central to our approach is the curation of a high-quality training corpus of 14 million images, combining synthetic data, in-the-wild video, and multi-camera motion capture to balance scene diversity and supervision quality. The model adopts SOMA-Hand as its parametric representation and processes 2D hand crops with a transformer encoder, incorporating camera cues and an auxiliary 2D branch to improve geometric consistency and image alignment. Zero-shot evaluations on HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O demonstrate strong out-of-domain generalization, with lower joint-position, root-translation, and acceleration errors than competing baselines at an inference latency of approximately 9.69 ms. A blinded user preference study further shows that participants favor EgoHand's reconstructed hand poses over those from Apple EgoDex and Ropedia Xperience-10M. We release the EgoHand model and source code under the OpenMDW license, allowing free commercial use of the model.
authors: Chao-Yeh Chen, Tiffany Chen, Lin Duan, Tianyi Hu, Yu-Hsiang Huang, Umar Iqbal, Jiefeng Li, Edy Lim, Yanchen Liu, Yihan Pang, Hang Qiu, Jun Saito, Shao Su, Qingsi Wang, Xiufeng Xie
bullets: Addresses accurate 3D hand reconstruction from challenging egocentric video.
Trains on a 14-million-image corpus combining synthetic, in-the-wild, and multi-camera motion-capture data.
Uses SOMA-Hand with a transformer encoder, camera cues, and an auxiliary 2D branch for geometric and image consistency.
Performs strongly on zero-shot HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O evaluations, with approximately 9.69 ms inference latency.
Model and source code are released under the OpenMDW license with free commercial use.

figures.caption: Figure 2: EgoHandmodel architecture. A DINOv3 encoder supports two branches. The 3D hand reconstruction branch uses a CLIFF-conditioned hand query to cross-attend to image features augmented with ray positional encoding, predicting SOMA-Hand pose, shape, and wrist translation. The 2D joint prediction branch uses separate learned joint queries to cross-attend to image features. Its predicted 2D joints, together with the SOMA-Hand 3D joints and camera intrinsics, refine lateral wrist translation while preserving the predicted depth, yielding hand geometry in camera coordinates.

Figure 3: Inference pipeline from egocentric video to world-coordinate hand motion, comprising hand detection, crop preparation, batched EgoHand inference, and transformation of predictions to world coordinates. Fisheye regions are resampled into virtual pinhole views; pinhole images use standard crops. Predictions are assembled in frame order, their hand parameters are smoothed in an adaptive window. A synchronized external camera trajectory supplies the camera-to-world rotations and translations that place the hands in a shared world frame. Benchmark annotations may supply hand boxes in place of detections. The EgoHand network is detailed in Section 3. Illustrations are schematic.
Figure 1: EgoHand hand reconstruction results. Our approach achieves robust reconstructions under challenging poses across diverse environments.

papers.title: EgoHand: Monocular 3D Hand Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
papers.tldr: EgoHand reconstructs 3D hands from monocular egocentric video using diverse training data and camera-aware transformer modeling, achieving strong zero-shot generalization and fast inference.

papers.abstract: Coding agents spend substantial computation generating actions and processing long interaction histories. Poor action choices can steer agents into low-value states, wasting computation and increasing API costs. Sampling and verifying alternative actions can improve the agent's decisions, but applying this procedure at every step adds substantial overhead. We introduce SWE-Verifier, a lightweight generative model that selectively triggers candidate sampling and verification. It scores the coding agent's proposed action to determine when additional candidate sampling is needed, then ranks the resulting actions before execution. We train SWE-Verifier from Qwen3.5-4B using preference data that groups contrasting actions with their resulting environment observations and rubric-guided teacher scores. Using the mini-swe-agent harness, SWE-Verifier improves resolution from 75.47% to 77.20% on MiniMax-M2.7 at 1.09 times cost and generalizes to DeepSeek-V4-Flash without training on its actions, improving resolution from 72.60% to 74.27% at 1.13 times cost. Across both models, SWE-Verifier verifies fewer than 4% of steps and achieves comparable or higher resolution than the trajectory and all-step baselines at substantially lower cost. These results demonstrate that selective candidate sampling and lightweight verification provide complementary gains in coding-agent performance and inference efficiency. Our model, code, and data are available at https://github.com/zkjzou/SWE-Verifier.

papers.abstract: Visual mathematical reasoning can fail before reasoning begins: when a vision-language model (VLM) misreads a diagram, subsequent reasoning proceeds from false premises. This perceptual bottleneck is especially pronounced in smaller models, while accurate textual descriptions can substantially narrow the gap to larger models. Because obtaining such descriptions at inference requires additional annotation or model calls, we propose minimal-edit corrective on-policy distillation. Using reference figure descriptions and verified reference solutions as training-only information, a teacher scores incorrect student rollouts under a minimal-edit objective, and only teacher-disfavored tokens contribute to the corrective loss. Correct rollouts receive task-reward reinforcement learning. This preserves on-policy supervision while avoiding full-response imitation. Across model scales, the method requires no descriptions at test time and meets or exceeds the corresponding base model supplied with a reference figure description at inference. It also improves perception-oriented performance, particularly low-level geometric perception, and transfers to external mathematics and perception benchmarks. Because the minimal-edit teacher evaluates corrections rather than generating its own solution, the method remains effective with a frozen same-size teacher, although its gains are smaller than with a larger teacher on most metrics.

papers.abstract: To enable Industry 5.0, where autonomous systems are widely adopted and integrated with people to promote sustainable development in industries, it is imperative to adapt complex deep learning models to operate efficiently on resource-constrained hardware for edge inference. However, adapting these models remains challenging due to the hardware heterogeneity of edge computing in industrial settings, performance degradation caused by model compression, and the lack of clear guidance on which compression techniques are practical and effective for applications such as predictive maintenance. To address these challenges, this paper presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of four state-of-the-art model compression techniques applied to a high-performance convolutional neural network for predictive maintenance using a real-world dataset of rotating machinery, equipment typically used in industry. The compressed models were evaluated across a heterogeneous set of nine computing platforms, ranging from highly constrained edge computing devices to general purpose and high-performance processors, reflecting the diversity and fragmentation typical of industrial edge environments. By jointly prioritizing classification performance, inference speed, and compression ratio, we found that compression using knowledge distillation emerged as the most effective approach. The model had more than 90% speedup across all devices while maintaining a 91.22% balanced F-score, with a very small drop in predictive performance relative to the uncompressed model, along with a 98.9% size reduction. Through successful deployment across multiple edge platforms and a systematic comparison of compression strategies, we demonstrated a clear path to achieving Industry 5.0 targets, drastically cutting computational costs and, consequently, energy consumption without sacrificing predictive performance.

papers.abstract: Global warming and climate change are major catalysts for plant diseases, significantly affecting food production worldwide. Addressing this issue requires continuous monitoring and early detection of plant diseases. While recent advancements in deep learning offer potential solutions, most models demand high processing power and struggle to perform efficiently on low-end electronic hardware. Furthermore, many existing works focus on specific crop diseases, limiting their broader applicability. This paper presents a lightweight Group Equivariance Attention Network (GANet) designed for the prediction and monitoring of 38 types of plant diseases. GANet introduces a novel Group Attention block and Group-Wise Feature Fusion block, making it both sparse and efficient. With only 0.001M parameters, the model achieves an impressive 99.99% accuracy on the PlantVillage dataset. Additionally, GANet is optimized for deployment on edge devices such as the Raspberry Pi 4b and Jetson Nano, where it reaches 5 FPS and 11 FPS, respectively, demonstrating its potential for real-time plant disease monitoring on low-power devices.

papers.abstract: LLMs can act as scientific agents using tools to consult specialists and run experiments. Yet specialist information must enter their context, generally as text, images, audio or video: a bottleneck between models with rich, high-dimensional representations. We advocate direct representation exchange: a mindmeld conveying many properties, including information an LLM would not think to request. It should be extensible to new specialists, flexible across questions and tasks, and compositional across independently connected specialists without joint training. The Latent Interconnect Protocol (LIP) learns connectors mapping specialist representations into LLM internal states. Training only connectors keeps this practical as LLMs grow and evolve. We connect three protein and three small molecule specialists to Gemma 3 (4B and 12B parameters) and Kimi K2.6 (1T total, 32B active), freezing all pretrained models. Independently trained connectors provide useful information without changing the LLM or existing connectors, supporting familiar and new question types about unseen objects. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to cross-domain tasks without joint training. Task performance and compositionality generally improve with LLM capability, with especially strong gains in zero-shot task transfer. Limitations remain: current LLMs were not trained for specialist representations as native inputs; access does not ensure reliable interpretation, integration or use in reasoning. We call on specialist developers to provide consistent representation interfaces and, especially, on LLM developers to train models to receive, combine and reason with these inputs. These efforts could expand scientific agents' information while preserving conventional tools' flexibility. Data, pretrained connectors, and code for training, evaluation and interactive inference: https://github.com/PolymathicAI/AI-Mindmeld
authors: Siavash Golkar, Jake Kovalic, Shirley Ho

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model capacity efficiently by activating a small subset of parameters per token. However, in long-context inference, memory remains a major bottleneck because the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length. Existing KV cache compression methods reduce this cost for dense transformers, but overlook a problem specific to MoE: KV eviction can change which experts are selected during answer generation, degrading the generation quality. We propose MoEZip, a routing-aware KV cache compression for sparse MoE language models. To estimate the sensitivity of expert routing to perturbation, we propose a novel metric based on the Fisher information matrix of routing distributions. MoEZip combines this metric with attention weights for routing-aware scoring of contexts. Finally, we compose a complementary scoring system that combines eviction methods for dense and sparse-MoE architectures. Experiments show that MoEZip achieves robust performance under aggressive cache compression on various benchmarks. At a KV retention ratio of 10\%, MoEZip improves over the SoTA baseline by +24 and +20 points on average on LongBench and RULER, corresponding to 2.3$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ higher scores, respectively.
authors: Minsang Kim, Seungjun Baek
bullets: Addresses KV-cache memory growth in long-context MoE inference, where eviction can alter expert selection and harm quality.
Scores context tokens using both attention weights and a Fisher-information-based measure of routing sensitivity.
Combines routing-aware eviction with complementary dense-model KV compression methods.
At 10% KV retention, improves over the prior state of the art by 24 points on LongBench and 20 points on RULER on average.
Demonstrates robust performance under aggressive compression across multiple benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Average performance over 12 tasks across different KV cache ratios. a)–(d) present ablations on the main components of MoEZip, including Fisher-based fragility modeling, adaptive budget allocation, head-wise aggregation, and the choice of base scorer. The full method consistently performs best, especially in the high-compression regime.

Figure 2: Overview of MoEZip. MoEZip estimates routing fragility from instruction-token router states, transfers it to context positions via instruction-to-context attention, and reserves the top-scoring positions as routing-aware anchors. The base scorer fills the remaining budget, and thus the final cache size and decoding procedure remain unchanged.

Figure 3: Performance on 12 LongBench tasks across different KV cache ratios. MoEZip consistently preserves higher task performance than existing KV compression baselines, especially under aggressive compression.

Figure 6: Generalization to sigmoidrouted MoE models. On GLM-4.7-Flash, MoEZip consistently achieves the best average performance across 12 LongBench tasks, with the largest gains under aggressive KV compression.
Figure 4: Performance heatmaps over context length and document depth across different KV cache ratios. We compare MoEZip, KVZip, SnapKV, and PyramidKV under KV cache keep ratios from 0.1 to 0.9.
Figure 5: Average performance on 13 RULER tasks across different KV cache ratios.
Figure 1: Router instability is associated with answer-quality degradation. As KV compression becomes more aggressive, expert selection changes more often, and performance drops accordingly.

Figure 9: Softmax-router worst-case bound versus Fisher trace. The worst-case Fisher-bound score performs comparably to Fisher trace on several tasks, but does not consistently improve performance and can be less robust under aggressive compression. We therefore use Fisher trace as the default routing-fragility proxy.

Figure 10: Sigmoid-router worst-case score versus Fisher trace. For sigmoid-style routing, the Fisher matrix is diagonal and the worst-case curvature is given exactly by maxe ge(1 − ge). We compare this exact worst-case score with the Fisher trace on six LongBench tasks. The two scores show similar trends overall, but the worst-case score does not consistently outperform Fisher trace and can degrade more sharply in the high-compression regime.

Figure 8: Empirical expert-flip rate across Fisher-trace quantiles. We bin (sample, decode step, layer) observations by Fisher trace from the full-KV router softmax and measure the mean top-1 expert-flip rate under compressed KV. Across both HotpotQA and Qasper, higher Fisher-trace bins consistently show higher flip rates, and the separation becomes larger as compression becomes more aggressive.

Figure 14: Task quality and router flip rate across compression ratios. We compare task performance and expert flip rate of answer-tokens under increasing KV compression. Across all six tasks, MoEZip consistently maintains lower flip rates than KVZip. The shaded region marks the compression range where KVZip begins to exhibit a sharp quality drop, while MoEZip remains notably more stable.

Figure 12: Sensitivity analysis of ρmax on representative LongBench tasks. We vary the maximum anchor ratio ρmax ∈ {0.1, 0.25, 0.3} while fixing ρmin = 0.05. Across QMSum, Qasper, MultiFieldQA, and 2WikiMQA, the overall performance is relatively stable over a broad range of ρmax values. The default setting ρmax = 0.25 consistently provides strong or near-best performance, while overly small values can slightly weaken robustness in the high-compression regime by limiting the number of route-aware anchors.

Figure 16: Layer-wise router flip rate of SnapKV across compression ratios, averaged over Qasper and HotpotQA. Similar to KVZip, router instability grows under aggressive compression and is concentrated in the middle-to-late MoE layers.

Figure 15: Layer-wise router flip rate of KVZip across compression ratios, averaged over Qasper and HotpotQA. Router instability increases steadily with compression and becomes most pronounced in the middle-to-late MoE layers.

Figure 18: Input-wise router flip rates of SnapKV on sampled SQuAD v2 contexts. Each dot denotes one input associated with the same context, and the red bar indicates the within-context range. Router instability still varies noticeably across inputs sharing the same context, indicating that it depends not only on the context but also on the input.

Figure 17: Input-wise router flip rates of KVZip on sampled SQuAD v2 contexts. Each dot denotes one input associated with the same context, and the red bar indicates the withincontext range. Even under an identical context, router flip rates vary substantially across inputs, showing that routing instability is strongly inputdependent.

Figure 13: Sensitivity analysis of ρmin on representative LongBench tasks. We vary the minimum anchor ratio ρmin ∈ {0.0, 0.05, 0.1} while fixing ρmax = 0.25. The results remain highly stable across all four tasks, indicating that MoEZip is not overly sensitive to the exact choice of ρmin. The default setting ρmin = 0.05 achieves consistently strong performance, while different values lead only to minor variations across KV cache ratios.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces routing-aware KV cache compression for MoE LLMs, directly targeting memory-efficiency in inference.
papers.title: MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.tldr: MoEZip compresses KV caches in sparse MoE LLMs while preserving expert-routing decisions, enabling strong long-context performance with only 10% KV retention.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into embodied robotic planning, yet standard benchmarks primarily evaluate end-to-end task completion in nominal environments, obscuring failure origins across the execution stack. We present Alpha, a systematic fault-injection and robustness-evaluation framework for LLM-driven manipulation in simulation. Alpha injects calibrated faults across perception (sensor lag), actuation (grip slip), kinematics (unreachable targets), and planning (planner-output corruption), alongside concurrent conditions. To separate physical vulnerabilities from planner sensitivities, we introduce a matched methodology pairing an LLM agent (Llama-3 via Ollama) against a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner across a balanced 150-episode matrix under identical seeds, geometries, and safety criteria. Across the matrix, the Oracle achieves 64.0% (48/75) success while the LLM achieves 44.0% (33/75) (paired McNemar p = 3.01 x 10^-4). Crucially, excluding planner-output corruption, performance across all physical and kinematic conditions is identical: 55.0% (33/60) for both planners with zero discordant pairs (McNemar p = 1.00). This demonstrates that physical actuator slip, kinematic reach boundaries, and perceptual staleness affect deterministic controllers and LLM planners equivalently. The performance gap is driven entirely by planner-output corruption (100% Oracle vs. 0% LLM), isolating the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface rather than a cognitive reasoning deficit. We also audit 169 historical pilot attempts for transparency.
authors: Jona Joy
bullets: Evaluates robustness under sensor lag, grip slip, unreachable targets, planner-output corruption, and concurrent faults.
Matches an LLM agent with a deterministic Scripted Oracle across 150 simulated episodes using identical conditions.
The Oracle succeeds in 64.0% of episodes versus 44.0% for the LLM.
Excluding planner-output corruption, both planners achieve 55.0% success with no discordant outcomes.
The performance gap is isolated to the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface, not physical robustness or reasoning deficits.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. System architecture of the Alpha evaluation harness. Controlled faults (F1–F4) are injected by ChaosRoboticsWrapper at four operational boundaries without altering the Brain’s prompt definitions or the Body’s inverse-kinematics control routines. The PyBullet Safety Monitor synchronously inspects multi-link contact dynamics at 240 Hz.

Fig. 2. Task success rate across fault conditions for the Scripted Oracle baseline (N = 75) versus the LLM agent (N = 75) across the 150- episode matrix. On all physical and kinematic conditions (Control, F1, F2, F3, and Concurrent), both planners achieve identical performance with zero discordant pairs. The overall divergence is localized entirely to F4 planneroutput corruption.

Fig. 4. F2 grip slip results: Calibrated slip probability curve versus realized empirical slip rates and task success rates. Both planners exhibit identical monotonic degradation across intensities with zero discordant pairs.

Fig. 7. Complete accounting of 169 historical pilot attempts. All 99 rejected OpenAI attempts failed due to external API infrastructure aborts prior to simulation. The accepted local Ollama cohort (N = 70) executed with a 0% crash rate.

Fig. 3. F1 sensor lag analysis: (a) Requested lag versus realized lag, showing saturation at the 0.500 s available history buffer depth. (b) Spatial staleness divergence (2.50 cm) compared against the physical gripper opening envelope (8.0 cm), explaining 100% task completion.

Fig. 5. Continuous placement error under F3 unreachable IK. Final distance to place-zone center increases monotonically for the Scripted Oracle, while the LLM displays a non-monotonic response due to kinematic deflection at higher reach limits.

Fig. 6. Execution path divergence under F4 planner-output corruption. The LLM text stream passes through JSON serialization where corruption triggers Pydantic schema rejection (0% success). The Scripted Oracle bypasses serialization, executing directly via in-memory objects (100% success).

papers.title: Alpha: Systematic Fault Injection and Robustness Evaluation for LLM-Driven Embodied Manipulation

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning adapts language models to specialized tasks but can disrupt previously acquired behavior. Existing approaches constrain parameters, gradients, or replay objectives, yet the connection between the protected object, the intervening trajectory, and retained outputs remains unclear. We develop a functional-path account that decomposes old-loss changes along realized updates into the controlled direction, gradient staleness, probe mismatch, and finite-step effects. The account yields a conditional refresh budget and identifies the restoring direction supplied by informative replay. Matched QLoRA interventions separate constraint granularity from placement before or after Adam: placement strongly affects retention across the studied code-label audits, whereas the granularity interaction depends on the endpoint. Checkpointed generation separates endpoint recovery from higher sampled-path accuracy, and matched replay schedules reveal loss exposure concealed by final scores. A sequential-task comparison extends this distinction to backward transfer: subspace regularization and projection improve average retention while trading off different old tasks; supervised replay protects both more consistently in this setting. Additional response interfaces distinguish content gains from exact-response retention. These findings connect update-level protection to task-wise behavior and motivate mitigation through explicit functional anchors, trajectory evaluation, and joint old/new auditing.
authors: Qingsen Ma, Dianyun Wang, Jiahong Liu, Irwin King
bullets: Existing parameter, gradient, and replay constraints do not fully explain how protected objects translate into retained outputs.

The framework decomposes old-loss changes into controlled direction, gradient staleness, probe mismatch, and finite-step effects, yielding a conditional refresh budget and a replay-based restoring direction.
In matched QLoRA studies, optimizer placement strongly affects retention, while constraint granularity interacts with the endpoint.
Checkpointed generation and matched replay reveal differences between endpoint recovery, sampled-path accuracy, and loss exposure.
Across sequential tasks, subspace methods improve average retention with task-specific trade-offs, whereas supervised replay protects tasks more consistently.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses continual supervised fine-tuning and forgetting, fitting continual/online learning under adaptation and memory.
papers.title: Why Constrained Updates Still Forget: A Functional-Path Analysis of Continual SFT
papers.tldr: A functional-path analysis shows that preventing forgetting depends not only on what updates constrain, but also on where constraints are applied and how the entire training trajectory affects behavior.

papers.abstract: Canada's increasing wildfire activity requires frequent national hazard mapping to guide proactive mitigation, including fuel management, land-use planning, infrastructure protection, and evacuation routing. However, process-based wildfire simulation frameworks (e.g., BurnP3 and BurnP3+) rely on computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulations to model burn probability, fire intensity, and rate of spread. These workflows can take days to weeks to process a single regional modelling unit. To overcome these computational bottlenecks, we present three contributions developed through collaboration between AI researchers and wildfire modelling experts: (a) a standardized framework for training, fine-tuning, and evaluating AI surrogate models against process-based wildfire simulators; (b) a multi-task deep learning surrogate trained on national-scale data to emulate burn probability, mean fire intensity, and mean rate of spread at a fraction of the computational cost (seconds); and (c) domain-specific metrics and counterfactual evaluation protocols to probe out-of-distribution generalization. Integrating geospatial data (fuel, terrain, ignition likelihood) and regional weather, our model approximates BurnP3+ simulation outputs, achieving strong performance across agreement, rank-correlation, error, and spatial-overlap metrics. It preserves downstream hazard classifications and produces physically plausible responses to expert-informed counterfactual interventions. On a representative region, the surrogate achieves 806-fold end-to-end CPU acceleration and uses 13% of BurnP3+'s host memory, facilitating rapid scenario analysis.
authors: Hager Radi Abdelwahed, Toluwaleke Olutayo, Chirag Goel, Jana Osea, Aldo Zaimi, Tom Swystun, Sandy Erni, Francisco Emiliano Lopez Saavedra, Yan Boulanger, Ga\'etan Marceau Caron
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of Monte Carlo process-based wildfire simulations for national hazard mapping.
Introduces a framework for training, fine-tuning, and evaluating AI surrogates against wildfire simulators.
Uses geospatial and regional weather inputs to predict burn probability, mean fire intensity, and mean rate of spread.
Achieves strong agreement and spatial performance, with 806-fold end-to-end CPU acceleration and 13% of BurnP3+ host memory on a representative region.
Evaluates out-of-distribution behavior using domain-specific metrics and expert-informed counterfactual interventions.

papers.selection_reason: Develops an AI surrogate modeling framework to emulate the dynamics of wildfire spread, acting as a learned predictor of environment dynamics with significant acceleration.
papers.title: Accelerating Wildfire Hazard Mapping Across Canada with an AI Surrogate Modelling Framework
papers.tldr: A multi-task AI surrogate reproduces key BurnP3+ wildfire hazard outputs across Canada in seconds, enabling substantially faster scenario analysis while preserving hazard classifications and physical plausibility.

papers.abstract: Model fusion aims to integrate the capabilities of multi-expert models into a single model. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage of reasoning with long chains of thought and tool use, while strong average performance can mask substantial losses in individual expert capabilities. We introduce FusionEval, a benchmark that provides controlled expert pools, integrates fusion methods with and without additional training, and offers a unified evaluation suite. The pools contain domain experts independently trained from Qwen3 and Llama base models across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use. The suite evaluates capability retention and computational cost on eight public benchmarks under comparable data access rules, reporting normalized average and worst performance, runtime, and peak GPU memory usage. Extensive experiments show that training-free methods preserve reasoning performance but substantially degrade tool use at both model scales. In contrast, MOPD preserves tool use and achieves a more balanced capability profile, but requires additional data preparation, inference, and training. Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low computational cost remains a challenge. We hope FusionEval supports future research on efficient model fusion that jointly preserves expert capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/Baicaihaochi/FusionEval_Benchmark.
authors: Shuo Cai, Yanggan Gu, Yuhang Liu, Su Lu, Yuanyi Wang, Yang Yu, Zhen Li, Zhitian Hou, Guanghao Zhu, Ming Li, Hongxia Yang
bullets: Introduces controlled expert pools from Qwen3 and Llama across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use.
Evaluates training-free and training-based fusion methods on eight public benchmarks using capability retention and cost metrics.
Training-free methods preserve reasoning but substantially weaken tool use across model scales.
MOPD better preserves tool use and balances capabilities, but requires extra data preparation, inference, and training.
Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low cost remains unresolved.

papers.abstract: We study mountain-bike action quality assessment (AQA) with weak labels and candidate feedback. The training corpus comprises 95 field-recorded jump clips with binary labels denoting good or poor technique. These are coarse categorical labels, not continuous expert quality scores; phase-boundary and aspect-level annotations are unavailable. Our pipeline summarizes four heuristic phases using frozen V-JEPA 2 video features and two-dimensional pose and motion measurements. A small transformer predicts a binary-label score. A separate reference layer compares phase-specific measurements with those of clips labelled as good technique to propose phase, body-parameter, and direction cues. We detail the measurements, network, and evaluation so that the limits of each output are explicit. In five-fold clip-level cross-validation, the full scorer obtained pooled out-of-fold AUROC 0.768 and average precision 0.812. These are exploratory figures because the reporting fold also selected the neural training epoch and riders were not separated between folds. Removing biomechanical scoring inputs raised AUROC to 0.809. A separate inner-selection run obtained AUROC 0.678, but used about 57 rather than 76 training clips per outer fold, so its difference from the test-selected run does not quantify selection bias. The unsupervised aspect head did not learn distinct factors. On a 17-clip external probe, an earlier checkpoint obtained binary accuracy 0.412 and Spearman association -0.135 with expert scores. Candidate cues had precision 0.118 and recall 1.0 against each of two coaches, with substantial disagreement about direction. These findings do not establish rider-independent scoring or reliable corrective feedback; they identify the empirical work needed to evaluate either use.
authors: Santhiya Rajan, Savio Cardoz
bullets: Uses 95 field-recorded jump clips with coarse good/poor technique labels, rather than continuous expert scores or phase/aspect annotations.
Summarizes four heuristic phases with frozen V-JEPA 2 features and 2D pose/motion measurements; a small transformer predicts binary quality.
A separate reference layer compares phase-specific measurements with good-technique clips to generate body-parameter and directional feedback cues.
Five-fold clip-level cross-validation yielded pooled AUROC 0.768 and average precision 0.812, but epoch selection used the reporting folds and riders were not separated.

The external probe showed weak performance and feedback agreement: binary accuracy 0.412, Spearman association −0.135, and cue precision 0.118 with recall 1.0; the aspect head found no distinct factors.

papers.selection_reason: Action quality assessment from video using temporal representations and pose/motion measurements; fits video understanding.
papers.title: V-JEPA 2 Meets AQA: Phase-Based Scoring and Reference-Based Feedback for Mountain Biking
papers.tldr: An exploratory mountain-bike AQA pipeline using frozen video features, pose/motion measurements, and reference-based cues shows moderate binary-label discrimination but does not yet support reliable rider-independent scoring or feedback.

papers.abstract: AI agents require interfaces to interact with external systems such as files, APIs, databases, and cloud services. Two competing paradigms have emerged: CLI (Command Line Interface), where agents execute shell commands directly, and MCP (Model Context Protocol), a structured JSON-RPC protocol providing governed, typed tool access. This paper presents a comparative analysis across 14 evaluation dimensions, supported by worked examples, security assessment against established compliance frameworks, and economic modeling. Our analysis indicates that CLI provides superior efficiency for single-user, local-only workflows, while MCP addresses requirements that CLI fundamentally cannot satisfy, including fine-grained access control, credential isolation, structured audit, and multi-tenant governance. We further examine how progressive disclosure techniques eliminate MCP's historical weakness (context window overhead), yielding token efficiency comparable to CLI while preserving its architectural benefits. A hybrid architecture is recommended for production systems. This analysis draws upon academic, government, and industry sources including NSA formal guidance (CSI U/OO/6030316-26), OWASP security standards, and economic modeling from BCG and Gartner.
authors: Arun Malik, Nitish Talasu, Bradley Klemick, Vineet Tushar Trivedi, Prachi Shah, Sanay Devi, Junjie Zhang, Kunal Sonawane
bullets: Compares CLI and MCP across 14 dimensions, including usability, security, governance, and economics.
CLI suits single-user, local-only tasks with direct shell access.
MCP provides typed, governed tool access with fine-grained permissions, credential isolation, structured auditing, and multi-tenant support.
Progressive disclosure can reduce MCP’s context-window overhead to near-CLI token efficiency.
The analysis recommends combining CLI and MCP in production architectures.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Security and compliance scorecard: requirements satisfied (of 8) and frameworks met (of 6) by each paradigm.
Fig. 6. Risk/scale matrix: CLI suits small, low-risk local use; MCP suits large, high-sensitivity multi-tenant use; a hybrid covers the middle.
Fig. 1. Multi-dimensional comparison of CLI and MCP across ten evaluation dimensions (normalized 0–10; higher is better).
Fig. 4. Total cost of ownership vs. organization size. CLI is cheaper for small teams; MCP breaks even near five users and dominates at scale.
Fig. 5. MCP adoption timeline: major vendors adopted the protocol within roughly twelve months of its late-2024 open-source release.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the token efficiency and architectural trade-offs between CLI and MCP (Model Context Protocol) for tool integration, focusing on context window overhead and governance.
papers.title: MCP vs CLI for AI Agents: A Comparative Analysis of Tool Integration Strategies for Autonomous Systems
papers.tldr: CLI is efficient for simple local workflows, while MCP offers stronger governance and security for production AI agents; a hybrid approach is recommended.

papers.abstract: Every interaction between AI agents begins with a handshake: the initiating agent must locate its counterpart, learn what it can do, and establish a session before the first useful message can be sent. Surveys of agent communication protocols name handshake overhead as an efficiency criterion, yet none report measurements. This paper presents the first empirical, phase-decomposed benchmark of the handshake in three major agent protocols: MCP (in both its 2025 initialize and 2026 discover eras), A2A, and ACP. Using each protocol's official SDK, we instrument every request for round trips, per-phase latency, wire bytes, and token cost across cold-start, warm-repeat, capability-mismatch, and degraded-metadata scenarios (N=50 per cell, on loopback and under an emulated 50 ms RTT). Round-trip count dominates handshake cost. A legacy MCP handshake takes three round trips and 230 ms at 50 ms RTT; A2A needs one round trip and 61.0 ms. Round trips are not the whole bill: when an LLM reads the counterpart's metadata, handshake cost scales with the counterpart's capability inventory at 24-107 tokens per capability, so a 200-capability counterpart spends 11% of a 200k-token context window before the agent reads its own task. MCP's own 2026 revision cuts its handshake from three round trips to two and, with era pinning, to zero on warm reconnects, protocol evolution that corroborates the cost we measure. We release the full harness, raw data, and analysis at https://github.com/pvarshh/handshake-benchmark.
authors: Pranav Varshney
bullets: The study benchmarks handshake phases in MCP, A2A, and ACP across cold, warm, mismatch, and degraded-metadata scenarios.
Round-trip count is the primary cost driver: legacy MCP uses three round trips and takes 230 ms at 50 ms RTT, while A2A uses one and takes 61.0 ms.
LLM-readable metadata adds 24–107 tokens per advertised capability; a 200-capability counterpart can consume 11% of a 200k-token context window.
MCP’s 2026 revision reduces the handshake from three to two round trips, and era pinning enables zero-round-trip warm reconnects.
The authors release the benchmark harness, raw data, and analysis.

papers.selection_reason: Empirically measures handshake overhead (latency, bytes, token cost) in agent communication protocols, directly addressing efficiency and token usage in AI systems.
papers.title: The Cost of Saying Hello: An Empirical Study of Handshake Overhead in AI Agent Communication Protocols
papers.tldr: Handshake overhead in AI agent protocols is dominated by round trips and can become substantial when agents inspect large capability inventories.

papers.abstract: Forming an accurate theory-of-mind (ToM) is key to successful multi-agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories-of-mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test-time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings (Overcooked-AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi-agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train-time, including a proprietary model (GPT-5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task-specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.
authors: Nithin Sivakumaran
Ali Payani
Hyunji Lee
Mohit Bansal
Elias Stengel-Eskin
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of representing multiple possible partner states in LLM text space.
Trains a fixed budget of latent reasoning tokens to abstract and match partners’ actual thoughts.
At test time, each agent generates these tokens to condition its reasoning and actions.
Improves performance across collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive environments over the base model and several baselines.

papers.abstract: Real-time whole-body humanoid teleoperation remains challenging due to the computational latency introduced by optimization-based retargeting pipelines and future-frame conditioning. Existing motion tracking policies typically require dense reference targets including full joint positions, body-part transformations, and even future frames, which tightly couples the controller to expensive upstream modules. In this work, we present HuMiT, a whole-body teleoperation system built on a unified tracking policy that requires only a compact reference target, consisting of root height, root velocity, and the SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints at the current frame, yet achieves competitive tracking fidelity compared to methods relying on more diverse reference states including complete joint positions, dense body-part transformations, and even future frames. Experiments show that our policy achieves a communication-to-inference latency of $\sim$20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video-based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) across different motion types. We validate the system on a Unitree G1 humanoid, showcasing split-second reactive responses such as catching a tossed ball, as well as coordinated loco-manipulation capabilities. Project page: https://xiaohu-art.github.io/Track/.

papers.abstract: Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models. It somehow works, but it breaks the providers' terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on long-term. We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher's answer as input, and generate the reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student's own model family. Training is two-stage, supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family's own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher's answer, the generator writes one in the family's style. An independent judge rates how likely traces are to be genuine on a scale from 0 to 1: ours average 0.68, real traces 0.66, and traces selected by the critic from four candidates 0.82. These are authenticity scores, not correctness rates. We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5's own thinking content. With the same 5,000 questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint. We suspect that reasoning written in the student's family style is easier for it to learn from.
authors: Yan Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of accessible reasoning traces from closed frontier models without relying on prohibited encrypted-trace recovery.
Uses a two-stage supervised and adversarial setup: a generator reconstructs family-style traces, while a critic evaluates their authenticity.
Generated traces received average authenticity scores comparable to real traces; critic-selected traces scored higher.
Across five benchmarks, results were similar on general tasks, while coding performance improved by 3.7 points on HumanEval+ and 7.1 on MBPP+ under matched data and teacher answers.
The authors hypothesize that reasoning in the student model’s own style is easier to learn from; reported scores measure authenticity, not correctness.

papers.abstract: Cinematic multi-shot video generation requires both narrative planning and iterative refinement. Existing methods either lack narrative reasoning or rely on feed-forward workflows without policy updates. In this paper, we propose CineEvolve, an agentic self-evolution framework for cinematic multi-shot video generation that unifies a Director and a Critic within a single vision-language policy. Emulating real-world filmmaking that couples iterative direction with critical feedback, we train CineEvolve via alternating reinforcement learning, where the Director surfaces flaws to sharpen the Critic, and the updated Critic guides the Director's targeted revisions. To stabilize co-evolution, we introduce Evolutionary GRPO (E-GRPO), leveraging historical anchoring and revision safeguarding to mitigate advantage inflation. Additionally, we contribute CineTraj, a 40K cinematic trajectory dataset spanning creation, critique, and revision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CineEvolve outperforms existing approaches. Our code will be available at https://github.com/JingZhe-8/CineEvolve.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained multimodal intelligence requires models to both understand a designated region and localize it from language. Existing methods learn these directions with separate objectives and task-specific annotations. We present Generalized CycleGRPO, the first unified reinforcement learning framework coupling region understanding and localization across spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal domains. Given a region, a multimodal large language model generates candidate descriptions and then localizes each description to reconstruct the input region. Reconstruction overlap provides a verifiable reward for captioning, while individual localization rewards improve the inverse mapping. A common region-space formulation extends this cycle from image masks and boxes to video intervals and timestamped spatial evidence, without reference captions or an external language-model judge during reinforcement learning. In videos, the cycle encourages descriptions that distinguish a target event from similar recurrences. We introduce DOVE (Distinctive Occurrence-level Video-caption Evaluation), a human-verified contrastive benchmark for this temporal distinctiveness. CycleGRPO improves SAMTok's overall gIoU from 57.5% to 68.2% on GroundingSuite and average gIoU from 71.2% to 78.7% on GRES. For temporal tasks, it achieves 51.9% tIoU on Charades and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE, compared with 45.6% and 14.8% for the Qwen3-VL initialization. These results establish region-text cycle consistency as a general self-evaluation principle for multimodal understanding and localization. Models, code, and DOVE are available at https://devinxzhang.github.io/Generalized-CycleGRPO-Page/.
